Kubernetes deep dives

How Kubernetes schedules, isolates and runs workloads: from kube-scheduler and gang scheduling to cgroups, ENIs and EBS. Each idea is shown as a real scenario first, then the diagram that explains it.

By Morteza Kiadi

I drew these diagrams while working through how Kubernetes and Amazon EKS really behave in production. Every section here starts with a scenario, a concrete problem or question, followed by the part of my diagram that explains it and a short note on what to take away.

The Designs section turns those ideas into complete platform designs, one use case at a time: requirements, threat model, architecture, configuration and the trade-offs behind each choice.

Click any diagram to open it full screen, then scroll or pinch to zoom and drag to move around.

How to read the colours: actions the system takes, concepts and Kubernetes objects, and tools and projects. In config snippets, the highlighted lines are the ones that matter for that point.

Deep dive 01 · 4 sections

How kube-scheduler picks a node

  1. Phase 1: filtering
  2. Phase 2: scoring plugins
  3. Score × weight
  4. When a preferred affinity loses

Every pod goes through the same decision. The scheduler first chooses a node in two phases: it filters out the nodes that can't run the pod, then scores the ones that can. Then it binds the pod to the winner, which is a separate final step that just records the choice. This deep dive follows that decision step by step.

Phase 1: filtering

Scenario. A developer deploys a new service, but the pod never starts. It sits in Pending, and kubectl describe pod shows 0/12 nodes are available. The developer is confused: the monitoring dashboard shows every node at around 35% CPU, so there seems to be plenty of room. Why won't Kubernetes place the pod, and how do you find out which rule is blocking it?

What the picture shows. The scheduler chooses a node in two phases, filtering then scoring, and then binds the pod to the chosen node. This picture is the first phase: find every node that is physically and logically able to host the pod. Each node runs through a series of checks (filter plugins, formerly called predicates), and failing even one check removes it.

1Kubernetes scheduler ("EKS Scheduler" box)
the "brain" that decides where every new pod lives.
2Phase 1: Filtering (the "predicate" phase)
the goal is simple, keep only the nodes that can run the pod.
3Insufficient resources (the fit check)
this is the answer to the scenario. The scheduler counts what pods request, not what they actually use, while the dashboard shows real usage. So a node can be 35% busy and still be fully booked on paper. How the check works: the scheduler takes the node's allocatable CPU and memory (its capacity minus what's reserved for the kubelet, the operating system and the eviction buffer), subtracts the requests of the pods already there, and checks that what's left is at least the new pod's request. This is a yes/no feasibility check, not bin-packing. "Not bin-packing" means this step only checks whether the pod fits on a node; it doesn't decide which of the fitting nodes is best.
  • Worked example, one node: 4 CPU cores of capacity, about 3.9 allocatable. Three pods already run there: pod A requests 1.5 cores and uses 0.3, pod B requests 1.5 and uses 0.5, pod C requests 0.8 and uses 0.6.
  • Reserved vs. used: together they request 3.8 cores but use only 1.4, about 35% of the node. The dashboard shows the 35%.
  • The new pod: it requests 0.5 cores. The scheduler computes 3.9 − 3.8 = 0.1 cores left. That's less than 0.5, so the node fails the filter, even though about 2.5 cores are sitting idle.
  • At a glance: the same numbers side by side.
    CPU coresScheduler's view (requests)Dashboard's view (real usage)
    Pod A1.50.3
    Pod B1.50.5
    Pod C0.80.6
    Total on the node3.8 of 3.9 allocatable1.4 (about 35%)
    Room left0.1about 2.5
    New pod needs 0.5✗ doesn't fit: node filtered out✓ would easily fit
  • All 12 nodes look like this: the result is 0/12 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient cpu, which is exactly the scenario.
  • Why it works this way: a request is a promise. If pod A suddenly needs its full 1.5 cores, it must be able to get them, so the scheduler can't hand that reserved space to another pod just because it's idle right now.
  • The usual fix: right-size the requests to match real usage (tools like Goldilocks or the Vertical Pod Autoscaler help) instead of adding nodes.
  • Which part of the scheduler runs the fit check: a plugin called NodeResourcesFit, one of the scheduler's internal modules (filtering and scoring are made of many of them). It's built into kube-scheduler and on by default, so there's nothing to install or enable.
  • What you write vs. what's built in: your pod only supplies the requests; you never name the plugin. The plugin's own settings live in the scheduler's configuration. The YAML just below this list shows both: first your pod, then the scheduler's configuration with its default values.
  • You normally don't write that configuration: the KubeSchedulerConfiguration in the second half of the YAML is only there to make the hidden defaults visible; they already apply without it. You'd write one only to change them, and on managed control planes like EKS you can't change the default scheduler at all.
  • Passing is a plain yes: a nearly full node with just enough room and an almost empty node pass equally. Choosing between them happens later, in scoring, where the default (LeastAllocated) spreads pods and bin-packing (MostAllocated) must be turned on deliberately (see Phase 2: scoring plugins).
apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: apispec:  containers:  - name: api    image: my-company/api:1.4    resources:      requests:          # the scheduler adds up requests, not real usage        cpu: "500m"        memory: "1Gi"---# kube-scheduler's own config file, passed with --config. NOT applied with kubectl.# Without it, the scheduler uses these same built-in defaults.apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler  pluginConfig:  - name: NodeResourcesFit     # filter: does the pod fit? + score: which node is best?    args:      scoringStrategy:        type: LeastAllocated   # the default (spread); MostAllocated = bin-pack        resources:        - name: cpu          weight: 1        - name: memory          weight: 1

Note: when would you actually write a KubeSchedulerConfiguration?

Only when you want to change the scheduler's built-in settings. Two things to know first:

  • It isn't a Kubernetes object. It has apiVersion and kind, but you don't kubectl apply it (the API would reject it). It's a config file the kube-scheduler program reads at startup, passed with --config.
  • Where you can use it depends on who runs the scheduler:
    • Self-managed clusters (for example kubeadm): point the scheduler's static pod at your own file, for example to switch to MostAllocated bin-packing or change plugin weights.
    • Managed clusters (EKS, GKE, AKS): the provider runs the default scheduler, so you can't change its file. (EKS exposes one scoring setting, spread or pack by resource use, covered under LeastAllocated below.) For anything else, run a second scheduler as a normal Deployment with its own KubeSchedulerConfiguration from a ConfigMap, and point specific pods at it with schedulerName. Volcano and KAI work the same way, as replacement schedulers. A complete, ready-to-apply example is in Appendix A: Running a second scheduler. For the full list of built-in plugins, and what changes once a second scheduler shares the cluster, see Built-in plugins, and what a second scheduler changes in the Kubernetes Multi-Scheduler deep dive.
4Node selector mismatch
if the pod has a nodeSelector (for example disktype: ssd), any node without that exact label is dropped.
apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: apispec:  nodeSelector:    disktype: ssd        # only nodes labelled disktype=ssd pass the filter  containers:  - name: api    image: my-company/api:1.4
5Taints and tolerations (the "keep out" sign)
a taint lets a node repel pods; only pods with a matching toleration may stay in the list. The taint is set on the node and the toleration on the pod; the YAML below shows both.
# 1. The taint lives on the NODE. You add it with a command:#      kubectl taint nodes gpu-node-1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule#    (or in the node group / Karpenter NodePool config). The node then looks like this:apiVersion: v1kind: Nodemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1spec:  taints:  - key: dedicated    value: gpu    effect: NoSchedule        # pods without a matching toleration are filtered out---# 2. The toleration lives on the POD that is allowed inapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: trainerspec:  tolerations:  - key: dedicated    operator: Equal    value: gpu    effect: NoSchedule  containers:  - name: trainer    image: my-company/trainer:2.0
6Affinity and anti-affinity violations
A required node affinity ("must run in us-east-1a") or pod anti-affinity ("never on a node that already runs a copy of me") removes nodes that break the rule.
apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: api-1  labels:    app: apispec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:        nodeSelectorTerms:        - matchExpressions:          - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone            operator: In            values: ["us-east-1a"]    podAntiAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:      - labelSelector:          matchLabels:            app: api        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname   # never two api pods on one node  containers:  - name: api    image: my-company/api:1.4

Note: can one pod use taints, tolerations, affinity and anti-affinity together? Does the order matter?

Yes, one pod can use all of them at once, and no, the order doesn't matter.

  • They're separate fields: tolerations, nodeSelector, affinity.nodeAffinity, affinity.podAffinity, affinity.podAntiAffinity and topologySpreadConstraints are all named fields of the pod spec, so you can write them in any order.
  • Every hard rule must pass: the scheduler runs its filters in its own fixed order, and a node survives only if it passes all of them. That's a logical AND, which gives the same answer in any order.

  • Inside node affinity: several nodeSelectorTerms are combined with OR (matching any one term is enough); several matchExpressions inside one term are combined with AND (the node must match all of them).

    apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: report-builderspec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:        nodeSelectorTerms:          # term 1 OR term 2        - matchExpressions:         # term 1: zone a AND an SSD          - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone            operator: In            values: ["us-east-1a"]          - key: disktype            operator: In            values: ["ssd"]        - matchExpressions:         # term 2: OR any m6i node          - key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type            operator: In            values: ["m6i.2xlarge", "m6i.4xlarge"]  containers:  - name: builder    image: my-company/report-builder:3.1

  • Preferred (soft) rules are wishes with points: each node earns the weight of every preferred rule it matches, and the node with the most points is favoured. The order you list the rules in doesn't make one more important. In the example below, a node in zone a earns 90 points, an SSD node earns 10, a node with both earns 100 and a node with neither earns 0, and swapping the two rules in the YAML gives exactly the same result. (Those points then become NodeAffinity's score, which is added to the other plugins' scores.)

    apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: report-builderspec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:      - weight: 10                  # listed first, but counts little        preference:          matchExpressions:          - key: disktype            operator: In            values: ["ssd"]      - weight: 90                  # listed second, but counts most        preference:          matchExpressions:          - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone            operator: In            values: ["us-east-1a"]  containers:  - name: builder    image: my-company/report-builder:3.1

    What if these were required instead? The story changes. Required rules are pass/fail filters, not scores: there's no weight or preference, a node either passes or is removed, and if no node passes the pod stays Pending instead of running somewhere less ideal.

    One term or two: AND vs. OR. A required rule lists its conditions under nodeSelectorTerms, and how you group them decides the logic. Conditions inside the same term must all match (AND); separate terms are alternatives, and matching any one is enough (OR). So you have to decide whether you mean "SSD and zone a" or "SSD or zone a":

    # Both conditions in ONE term → AND: an SSD node that is also in us-east-1aapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: report-builderspec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:   # no weights allowed        nodeSelectorTerms:        - matchExpressions:          # one term, two conditions = AND          - key: disktype            operator: In            values: ["ssd"]          - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone            operator: In            values: ["us-east-1a"]  containers:  - name: builder    image: my-company/report-builder:3.1---# Each condition in its OWN term → OR: an SSD node anywhere, or any node in us-east-1aapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: report-builderspec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:        nodeSelectorTerms:        - matchExpressions:          # term 1          - key: disktype            operator: In            values: ["ssd"]        - matchExpressions:          # term 2 (OR)          - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone            operator: In            values: ["us-east-1a"]  containers:  - name: builder    image: my-company/report-builder:3.1

    How the three versions treat each kind of node:

    NodePreferred (10 / 90)Required, ANDRequired, OR
    SSD, in zone abest choice✓ allowed✓ allowed
    Zone a, no SSDstrong choice (90)✗ removed✓ allowed
    SSD, other zoneweak choice (10)✗ removed✓ allowed
    Neitherallowed, lowest score✗ removed✗ removed
    No matching node at allpod runs anywaypod stays Pendingpod stays Pending

    Order still doesn't matter in any of them, and IgnoredDuringExecution still means a running pod isn't moved if labels change later. A common pattern is to mix them: a required rule for what's non-negotiable (say, the zone where the data lives) plus a preferred rule for nice-to-haves (say, SSD with weight 50).

  • Why you usually want them together: a toleration only allows a pod onto a tainted node; it doesn't send it there, so the pod could still land on any untainted node. Dedicated nodes therefore use three pieces: a taint on the nodes (keeps other pods off), a toleration on the pod (lets it in), and node affinity or nodeSelector on the pod (sends it there). Pod anti-affinity is often added to spread replicas across those nodes.

    # Toleration only: ALLOWED onto GPU nodes, but nothing sends it there.# The scheduler may still pick any ordinary node.apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: trainer-loosespec:  tolerations:                       # lets it in  - key: dedicated    value: gpu    effect: NoSchedule  containers:  - name: trainer    image: my-company/trainer:2.0---# Toleration + nodeSelector: allowed in AND sent there.apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: trainer-pinnedspec:  tolerations:                       # lets it in  - key: dedicated    value: gpu    effect: NoSchedule  nodeSelector:                      # sends it there    node-type: gpu  containers:  - name: trainer    image: my-company/trainer:2.0

    The full version, with node affinity and pod anti-affinity to spread replicas, is the "dedicated GPU nodes" example right below this note.

The long affinity names, decoded. Each name has two halves: when scheduling and while running.

  • requiredDuringScheduling…: a hard rule, checked in the filter phase. No matching node means the pod stays Pending.
  • preferredDuringScheduling…: a soft rule, checked in the scoring phase with a weight from 1 to 100. The pod still runs if nothing matches.
  • …IgnoredDuringExecution: the rule is checked only when the pod is placed. If a node's labels, or the other pods around it, change later, the running pod is not moved.
  • requiredDuringSchedulingRequiredDuringExecution: described in the Kubernetes docs as a possible future variant that would evict running pods when the rule stops matching. It has never been implemented, so affinity rules are never re-checked once a pod is running.

  • Both versions (required… and preferred…) exist for all three kinds of affinity: ("both" in the table means you can write either version)

    KindWhat it controlsVersionsNeeds topologyKey?
    nodeAffinitywhich nodes to run on, by node labelbothno
    podAffinityrun near certain other podsbothyes
    podAntiAffinityrun away from certain other podsbothyes

    What topologyKey does. "Run near" or "run away from" another pod raises a question: how close is near? On the same node? In the same zone? topologyKey answers it. You give it the name of a node label, and the scheduler treats two nodes as the same place when they have the same value for that label.

    Example: a pod with anti-affinity "stay away from app: api pods" is being placed, and an api pod already runs on node A.

    Nodehostname labelzone labeltopologyKey: hostnametopologyKey: zone
    A (already runs an api pod)node-aus-east-1atogethertogether
    Bnode-bus-east-1aapart: allowedtogether: avoided
    Cnode-cus-east-1bapart: allowedapart: allowed

    With topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname: every node has its own value, so only node A counts as "the same place". Node B is fine, even though it's in the same zone.

    With topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone: nodes A and B both say us-east-1a, so they count as the same place. The pod avoids both and goes to node C in another zone.

    So the same anti-affinity rule spreads pods across nodes or across zones, depending only on which label you name.

  • If you need "move the pod when things change", use a different tool. Affinity can't do it, but two other features can:

    • Taints with effect: NoExecute: taints are a separate feature, set on the node. Their effect decides how strict they are: NoSchedule (hard rule for new pods), PreferNoSchedule (soft, scoring only) and NoExecute, which also evicts pods that are already running there without a matching toleration (tolerationSeconds lets a pod stay for a set time first). So the taint's NoExecute effect behaves like the "during execution" half that affinity never got.

      # The NODE carries the taints (here one of each effect, to compare them)apiVersion: v1kind: Nodemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1spec:  taints:  - key: dedicated    value: gpu    effect: NoSchedule           # new pods without a toleration: not scheduled here  - key: spot    value: "true"    effect: PreferNoSchedule     # new pods: avoided if possible (scoring only)  - key: maintenance    value: "true"    effect: NoExecute            # running pods without a toleration: evicted NOW---# The POD tolerates all three; for NoExecute it may stay 10 minutes, then is evictedapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: inferencespec:  tolerations:  - key: dedicated    operator: Equal    value: gpu    effect: NoSchedule  - key: spot    operator: Exists    effect: PreferNoSchedule  - key: maintenance    operator: Exists    effect: NoExecute    tolerationSeconds: 600       # stay up to 10 min after the taint appears, then leave  containers:  - name: server    image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest

      Add the NoExecute taint to a running node with kubectl taint nodes gpu-node-1 maintenance=true:NoExecute: pods without that toleration are evicted at once, and this pod is evicted after 600 seconds. Without tolerationSeconds, a pod with the toleration would stay forever.

      The running pod has…When the NoExecute taint is added
      no matching tolerationevicted right away
      a matching toleration with tolerationSeconds: 600stays 600 seconds, then evicted (unless the taint is removed first)
      a matching toleration without tolerationSecondsnever evicted by this taint

      Note: doesn't that defeat NoExecute? Yes, if the pod's author wants it to. A toleration is an opt-out that whoever writes the pod controls: a toleration for maintenance with no tolerationSeconds means this taint never evicts that pod. Worse, a toleration with no key and operator: Exists matches every taint:

      tolerations:- operator: Exists      # no key, no effect: tolerates ALL taints, forever

      This is by design: taints and tolerations are a placement tool, not a security tool, and some pods legitimately must stay put (node agents run as DaemonSets, such as the CNI, log shippers and the GPU device plugin, get indefinite tolerations from Kubernetes itself). If you need to enforce it, put the control where the pod's author can't change it:

      1. An admission policy that rejects such pods. The built-in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (stable since Kubernetes 1.30), or Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper. This one rejects any pod outside kube-system that tolerates the maintenance taint, or every taint, without a time limit:

      apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicymetadata:  name: noexecute-needs-time-limitspec:  failurePolicy: Fail  matchConstraints:    resourceRules:    - apiGroups: [""]      apiVersions: ["v1"]      operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]      resources: ["pods"]  validations:  - expression: >-      !has(object.spec.tolerations) ||      object.spec.tolerations.all(t,        has(t.tolerationSeconds) ||        !((!has(t.effect) || t.effect == 'NoExecute') &&          (!has(t.key) || t.key == '' || t.key == 'maintenance')))    message: "Tolerations for the maintenance NoExecute taint (or for all taints) must set tolerationSeconds."---apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBindingmetadata:  name: noexecute-needs-time-limitspec:  policyName: noexecute-needs-time-limit  validationActions: ["Deny"]  matchResources:    namespaceSelector:      matchExpressions:      - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name        operator: NotIn        values: ["kube-system"]        # node agents there legitimately tolerate forever

      2. Use kubectl drain for maintenance, not just the taint. Drain cordons the node and evicts its pods through the eviction API whatever their tolerations (except DaemonSet pods), while still respecting PodDisruptionBudgets. In practice the taint signals that a node is going away, and drain actually empties it.

      3. RBAC and review: limit who can create pods in sensitive namespaces, and check tolerations in CI before manifests reach the cluster.

    • The descheduler: a separate add-on (a Kubernetes SIG project, installed with Helm) that runs every few minutes, usually as a CronJob. It looks for running pods that are now in the "wrong" place and evicts them, so their controller creates replacements and the normal scheduler places those again, this time following the rules. It never chooses nodes itself. Its RemovePodsViolatingNodeAffinity plugin catches pods whose node no longer has the labels their required node affinity asks for, and RemovePodsViolatingInterPodAntiAffinity catches pods that now sit next to pods they should avoid. Evictions respect PodDisruptionBudgets.

      # Helm values: helm install descheduler descheduler/descheduler -n kube-system -f values.yamlkind: CronJobschedule: "*/10 * * * *"                 # check every 10 minutesdeschedulerPolicy:  profiles:  - name: fix-affinity    pluginConfig:    - name: DefaultEvictor      args:        nodeFit: true                    # only evict if another node could take the pod    - name: RemovePodsViolatingNodeAffinity      args:        nodeAffinityType:        - requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution    - name: RemovePodsViolatingInterPodAntiAffinity    plugins:      deschedule:        enabled:        - RemovePodsViolatingNodeAffinity        - RemovePodsViolatingInterPodAntiAffinity

  • The full "dedicated GPU nodes" example is in the YAML right below this note.

# 1. The GPU nodes: a label (to be found) and a taint (to keep others out)#    Usually set in the node group or Karpenter NodePool, not by hand.apiVersion: v1kind: Nodemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1  labels:    node-type: gpuspec:  taints:  - key: dedicated    value: gpu    effect: NoSchedule---# 2. The GPU workload: toleration + node affinity + pod anti-affinityapiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: inferencespec:  replicas: 3  selector:    matchLabels: {app: inference}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: inference}    spec:      tolerations:                     # allowed onto the tainted GPU nodes      - key: dedicated        operator: Equal        value: gpu        effect: NoSchedule      - key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable        operator: Exists        effect: NoExecute        tolerationSeconds: 60          # stay 60 s on an unreachable node, then get evicted      affinity:        nodeAffinity:                  # sent to the GPU nodes (hard rule)          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:            nodeSelectorTerms:            - matchExpressions:              - key: node-type                operator: In                values: ["gpu"]        podAntiAffinity:               # spread replicas across nodes (soft rule)          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:          - weight: 100            podAffinityTerm:              labelSelector:                matchLabels: {app: inference}              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname      containers:      - name: server        image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest        resources:          limits:            nvidia.com/gpu: 1

Why does this example have two tolerations? tolerations is a list, and each entry tolerates one kind of taint. A pod can tolerate as many as it needs; here the two entries do different jobs.

  • Entry 1, our own GPU taint (dedicated=gpu, NoSchedule): it matches the taint we put on the GPU nodes, so it decides where the pod may go. operator: Equal means the key and the value must both match.
  • Entry 2, a built-in taint (node.kubernetes.io/unreachable, NoExecute): nobody adds this one by hand. Kubernetes adds it automatically when a node stops talking to the control plane (a crash, a lost network). A NoExecute taint doesn't only block new pods; it evicts pods already running there. operator: Exists matches any taint with that key, whatever its value.
  • What tolerationSeconds: 60 changes: Kubernetes already gives every pod this toleration automatically, with a default of 300 seconds. Writing it yourself only changes the timing: the pod stays on an unreachable node for 60 seconds, then is evicted and recreated on a healthy node. For a GPU inference service, 5 minutes on a dead node is a long outage. The trade-off is that a short network blip could move the pod unnecessarily.
  • In short: entry 1 controls where the pod may go; entry 2 controls how quickly it leaves when its node fails.
7Topology spread constraints (keep replicas balanced)
A topologySpreadConstraints rule spreads a group of pods evenly across places, such as zones or nodes. It isn't a box in the picture, but with whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule it's another filter: a node is removed if placing the pod there would make the busiest place exceed the emptiest by more than maxSkew.
  • What counts as a "place": the topologyKey, the same field used in pod affinity. topology.kubernetes.io/zone means zones, kubernetes.io/hostname means nodes.
  • Hard or soft: DoNotSchedule filters nodes out; ScheduleAnyway only lowers their score.
  • How it differs from pod anti-affinity: anti-affinity says "not where a pod like me already runs", so a hard rule allows only one per place: 6 replicas in 3 zones means 3 stay Pending. A spread constraint allows several per place as long as they stay balanced, so all 6 run, 2 per zone.
  • When to use which: anti-affinity for "never two on one node" (say, one database replica per node); spread constraints for "balance across zones" (most web services). Even without either, the scheduler applies a soft default spread across nodes and zones.
# 6 replicas spread evenly across 3 zones: 2 per zone.apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: webspec:  replicas: 6  selector:    matchLabels: {app: web}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: web}    spec:      topologySpreadConstraints:      - maxSkew: 1                                # zones may differ by at most 1 pod        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone  # a "place" is a zone        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule          # hard rule; ScheduleAnyway = soft        labelSelector:          matchLabels: {app: web}                 # which pods to count      containers:      - name: web        image: nginx:1.27

Note: using pod anti-affinity and topology spread together

A common case is a service that must survive both a node failure and a zone outage, say 6 replicas of an API. Each rule covers one level:

  • Pod anti-affinity (required, per node): never two replicas on the same node, so losing one node takes down at most one replica.
  • Topology spread (per zone): replicas stay balanced across zones, so losing a zone takes down about a third of them, not half.
apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: apispec:  replicas: 6  selector:    matchLabels: {app: api}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: api}    spec:      affinity:        podAntiAffinity:          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:          - labelSelector:              matchLabels: {app: api}            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname      # at most one per NODE      topologySpreadConstraints:      - maxSkew: 1        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone     # balanced across ZONES        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule        labelSelector:          matchLabels: {app: api}      containers:      - name: api        image: my-company/api:4.2

How they work together: both are filters, and a node must pass every filter, so the scheduler keeps only nodes that have no api replica yet and sit in a zone that won't get too far ahead of the others. With 3 zones of 3 nodes each, the result is 2 replicas per zone, each on its own node.

Where they can collide: say zone c has only one node. Anti-affinity lets zone c hold just one replica. The spread rule then caps the other zones at 2 each (at most 1 more than zone c), so only 5 replicas can run and the 6th stays Pending, even though zones a and b have empty nodes. The fixes are to add a node to zone c, set whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway so the zone spread becomes a preference, or make the anti-affinity preferred.

Could topology spread do both jobs? Yes: list two constraints, one with topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname and one with the zone key, each maxSkew: 1. The difference is that a per-node spread allows a second replica on a node once every node has one, while required anti-affinity never does.

# Topology spread doing both jobs: one constraint per node, one per zone.apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: apispec:  replicas: 6  selector:    matchLabels: {app: api}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: api}    spec:      topologySpreadConstraints:                       # no podAntiAffinity needed      - maxSkew: 1        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname            # balanced across NODES        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule        labelSelector:          matchLabels: {app: api}      - maxSkew: 1        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone       # balanced across ZONES        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule        labelSelector:          matchLabels: {app: api}      containers:      - name: api        image: my-company/api:4.2

With 9 nodes this gives the same result as before: one replica per node, 2 per zone. Scale to 12 replicas and the two versions differ: here replicas 10 to 12 can double up on nodes (as long as nodes and zones stay within 1 of each other), while the anti-affinity version leaves them Pending because every node already has one.

8Port conflicts
if the pod asks for a hostPort (say port 80 on the EC2 instance) and another pod on that node already uses it, the node is out. Two tenants can't share one mailbox.
apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: edge-proxyspec:  containers:  - name: proxy    image: nginx:1.27    ports:    - containerPort: 8080      hostPort: 80       # only one pod per node can claim host port 80
Going deeper2 points

  • For GPUs, these same filters do the steering: node labels pick the GPU model, a taint keeps other pods off GPU nodes, and the GPU count is checked just like CPU and memory. How GPUs get advertised to the scheduler, how to steer pods to the right one, and Dynamic Resource Allocation are covered in the next deep dive, Kubernetes and GPU.

  • Filtering also runs one pod at a time: a distributed job's workers are judged separately, which is the root of the gang problem. Setting parallelism doesn't fix this; it only creates the pods together. "All 8 or none" needs something that knows the pods belong together:

    • a queue in front of the scheduler, such as Kueue, which admits the whole job only when there's room for all of it (Volcano vs. Kueue);
    • a batch scheduler such as Volcano, KAI or YuniKorn, running as a second scheduler (what a second scheduler changes and the landscape, both in Kubernetes Multi-Scheduler);
    • the coscheduling plugin (a PodGroup with minMember) or, from Kubernetes 1.35, the native Workload API (beta in 1.37, off by default), both covered in gang scheduling.
# 8 workers that must all run together, but nothing here says so.# parallelism only lets the Job controller create 8 pods at once; it does NOT# make them a gang. The default scheduler filters and places each pod on its# own: with 6 free GPUs, 6 start (and sit idle) while 2 stay Pending.apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: distributed-trainspec:  parallelism: 8  completions: 8  completionMode: Indexed  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: worker        image: my-company/trainer:2.0        resources:          limits:            nvidia.com/gpu: 1

Phase 2: scoring plugins

Scenario. Three nodes pass filtering, yet a team notices the scheduler keeps putting their pods on the same node, even though another node is nearly empty. One day it places a critical API pod on a node that is already 90% full and the API slows down. Why did the scheduler prefer that node?

What the picture shows. Once filtering has narrowed the list, the scoring phase (also called the ranking phase) picks the best of the capable nodes. Every remaining node runs through several priority functions, gets a score from each, and the highest total wins.

1LeastAllocated (the "spreader")
the default strategy of the NodeResourcesFit plugin. It compares requested CPU and memory to capacity and gives emptier nodes higher scores, which spreads pods out and helps availability. On EKS you can switch it to MostAllocated (packing) for the whole cluster, and set the weights of CPU, memory and GPUs, with a cluster setting, without running a second scheduler (AWS docs).
2BalancedResourceAllocation (the "balancer")
keeps CPU and memory use even on a node. A node with lots of CPU but almost no free RAM scores lower for a memory-heavy pod, so nodes don't become lopsided.

Note: how BalancedResourceAllocation works, and how to tune it

  • Nothing to install or enable: it's one of the scheduler's built-in scoring plugins and is on by default, so every cluster already uses it.
  • What it looks at: for each node, the share of CPU and the share of memory that would be reserved if the pod landed there. It uses the pods' requests, not real usage, like the fit check.
  • How it scores: the closer those two shares are to each other, the higher the score. A memory-heavy pod (memory: 8Gi, cpu: 250m) on a node that's already 90% booked on memory and 20% on CPU makes that node even more lopsided, so the node scores low; a node at 50% and 45% scores high.
  • What your pods control: only their requests. Accurate requests are what make this plugin useful.
  • What a configuration can change: its weight compared with the other scoring plugins, and which resources it balances (CPU and memory by default; you can add GPUs, for example). Both live in the scheduler's configuration, not in pod YAML:
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler  plugins:    score:      enabled:      - name: BalancedResourceAllocation        weight: 2                     # counts double vs. other scoring plugins (default 1)  pluginConfig:  - name: BalancedResourceAllocation    args:      resources:                      # which resources to keep in balance      - name: cpu        weight: 1      - name: memory        weight: 1      - name: nvidia.com/gpu          # e.g. also balance GPUs against CPU and memory        weight: 1
  • On EKS: you can't edit the default scheduler's configuration, so changing these needs a second scheduler that pods opt into with schedulerName.
3ImageLocality (the "speedster")
scores nodes higher when the pod's images (say a 2 GB Java image) are already on local disk, so the pod skips the pull and starts faster. Bigger cached images count more. The points are also scaled by how many nodes already have the image (spread scaling, explained in the note below).

Note: how ImageLocality scores, and why it uses spread scaling

  • What it's for: if a node already has a pod's container image, the pod starts faster there because nothing has to be downloaded. So ImageLocality gives points to nodes that already hold the image, and bigger images earn more points because skipping their download saves more time.
  • The catch it guards against: say a new image exists on only 1 of 100 nodes. If that node got full points, every new pod using that image would pile onto that one node. The cluster ends up unbalanced, and the scheduler never spreads the image to other nodes.
  • The fix, spread scaling: the image's points are multiplied by the share of nodes that already have it:
points ≈ image size × (nodes that have the image ÷ all nodes)
The image is on… Scaling factor Points for a node that has it
1 of 100 nodes 0.01 almost nothing
50 of 100 nodes 0.5 half
100 of 100 nodes 1.0 full

So an image cached on only a few nodes gives very little advantage, and the pod is placed mostly on other grounds. An image already present almost everywhere counts fully.

4Node / inter-pod affinity (the "socialite")
handles your preferred (soft) rules, such as "I'd like to run near my database". Nodes in the same rack or zone as the database score higher. It's the main score you steer from the pod spec (along with soft topology spread and PreferNoSchedule taints); the others are computed by Kubernetes.
# Three soft preferences a pod (or a node) can express. None of them can# block scheduling; they only add or remove scoring points.apiVersion: v1kind: Nodemetadata:  name: node-old-1spec:  taints:  - key: hardware    value: old    effect: PreferNoSchedule         # 3. "avoid me if you can" (TaintToleration score)---apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: reports-apispec:  replicas: 3  selector:    matchLabels: {app: reports-api}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: reports-api}    spec:      affinity:        podAffinity:          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:   # 1. soft: scored, never filtered          - weight: 80                                      # how much this wish counts (1-100)            podAffinityTerm:              labelSelector:                matchLabels: {app: postgres}                # "near my database"              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone      # "near" = same zone      topologySpreadConstraints:      - maxSkew: 1        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname        whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway                   # 2. soft spread: scored, not filtered        labelSelector:          matchLabels: {app: reports-api}      containers:      - name: api        image: my-company/reports-api:1.4
5The default-weights trap
most of these plugins have the same small weight (1 or 2). In a large cluster that can lead to poor choices, and this is the scenario: the full node won because it already had the image cached, and the CPU contention showed up later.
Going deeper6 points
  • For GPU training I switch NodeResourcesFit to MostAllocated (bin-packing) and give nvidia.com/gpu a higher weight than CPU and memory.
# A separate profile for GPU training, so ordinary pods keep the default spread.# On EKS this runs in your own kube-scheduler (see the second-scheduler appendix).apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler        # unchanged: LeastAllocated (spread)- schedulerName: gpu-binpack              # GPU training pods opt in to this one  pluginConfig:  - name: NodeResourcesFit    args:      scoringStrategy:        type: MostAllocated               # pack: prefer the FULLEST node that still fits        resources:        - name: nvidia.com/gpu          weight: 5                       # GPUs dominate the "how full" score        - name: cpu          weight: 1        - name: memory          weight: 1---apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: finetunespec:  template:    spec:      schedulerName: gpu-binpack          # use the packing profile      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: trainer        image: my-company/trainer:2.0        resources:          limits:            nvidia.com/gpu: 2
  • Packing leaves whole nodes empty, so the autoscaler can remove them. For example, 4 GPU nodes with 8 GPUs each, and 8 training pods that each need 1 GPU:
Strategy Where the 8 pods land Result
Spread (LeastAllocated, the default) 2 pods on each of the 4 nodes All 4 nodes busy, each only 25% used
Pack (MostAllocated) All 8 pods on node 1 Node 1 full; nodes 2, 3 and 4 completely empty
  • Why only packing saves money: the cluster autoscaler (or Karpenter) removes a node only when nothing important runs on it. Spreading leaves no empty node, so nothing can go; packing leaves three empty nodes that can be shut down.
  • That matters when a GPU node costs tens of dollars an hour: a p4d.24xlarge (8 A100s) costs roughly $20–40 an hour on demand, depending on region and pricing. Removing three idle ones saves around $60–120 an hour, over $1,000 a day. For cheap CPU nodes the difference is small; for GPU nodes it's large.
  • The catch is a bigger blast radius per node: "blast radius" is how much breaks when one thing fails. With all 8 pods on node 1, losing that node kills all 8 at once; spread out, a node failure took down only 2. For a training job that's often acceptable, since it restarts from its last checkpoint anyway. For a critical service, such as a web API with 8 replicas, losing them all at once is an outage.
  • So it's a separate profile, not a change to the default:
    • training Jobs opt in with schedulerName: gpu-binpack and get packed, which is cheap;
    • critical services keep the default scheduler and stay spread out, which is resilient.

Score × weight

Scenario. In a design review, a new engineer asks how the scheduler turns "points" into a decision. "If one plugin likes node A and another likes node B, who wins?" You want to explain it on a whiteboard in two minutes.

What the picture shows. A worked example: one pod, two nodes, and three of the scoring plugins. The real scheduler runs all seven, but three are enough to see how it works.

1The pod and the two nodes
web-api requests 2 CPU, uses a 1.2 GB image and has a preferred rule for zone us-east-1a. Node A is in zone a, fairly empty, without the image; node B is in zone b, busier, with the image cached. Both pass filtering, so scoring decides.
# The pod from the picture: what each plugin reads from itapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: web-apispec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:   # read by NodeAffinity      - weight: 80                                      # ranks this preference INSIDE NodeAffinity        preference:          matchExpressions:          - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone            operator: In            values: ["us-east-1a"]  containers:  - name: api    image: my-company/web-api:2.3        # 1.2 GB; read by ImageLocality    resources:      requests:        cpu: "2"                         # read by NodeResourcesFit        memory: 2Gi
2The score (0 to 100), one per plugin per node
each plugin asks its own question and grades every node from 0 to 100. It's a measure of quality: how good this node is by that plugin's standard. (Older material calls it a "priority"; that's the name from before Kubernetes 1.19.)
3NodeResourcesFit (LeastAllocated)
counts the node's requests including this pod's. Node A would have 4 of 10 cores requested, so it's 60% free and scores 60; node B would have 8 of 10, so 20% free and 20. In a real cluster it does this for CPU and memory and averages them; the example uses CPU only.
4ImageLocality
node B already has the 1.2 GB image, so it scores high (90); node A has nothing cached, so 0. Spread scaling would lower B's score if only a few nodes had the image.
5NodeAffinity
works in two steps. First it adds up the weights of the pod's preferred rules that each node matches: node A matches the zone-a rule (weight: 80), so its raw score is 80; node B matches nothing, so 0. Then it scales the raw scores so the best node gets 100: node A's 80 becomes 100, node B stays 0. That's why the 80 from the YAML shows up as 100 in the picture.
6The weight (the multiplier)
a measure of importance, set per plugin in the scheduler's configuration, not in the pod. The defaults here are NodeResourcesFit 1, ImageLocality 1, NodeAffinity 2.
# Where the plugin weights live: the scheduler's configuration, not the pod.# These are the defaults; you don't need to write them. Changing them on EKS# needs your own scheduler (see the second-scheduler appendix).apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler  plugins:    score:      enabled:      - name: NodeResourcesFit        weight: 1      - name: ImageLocality        weight: 1                        # the picture's "what if": set 3 and node B wins      - name: NodeAffinity        weight: 2

Note: who decides the plugin weights?

  • The Kubernetes project sets the defaults: the scheduler's maintainers (the Kubernetes SIG Scheduling group) chose them, and they're built into kube-scheduler's code. Every cluster uses them unless someone overrides them:
Plugin Default weight
TaintToleration 3
NodeAffinity 2
InterPodAffinity 2
PodTopologySpread 2
NodeResourcesFit 1
BalancedResourceAllocation 1
ImageLocality 1
  • The pattern behind the numbers: things someone asked for explicitly (a PreferNoSchedule taint, a preferred affinity, a soft spread) count more than housekeeping the scheduler works out by itself ("prefer emptier nodes", "keep CPU and memory balanced", "the image is already here").
  • The cluster operator can override them: whoever runs the scheduler, usually a platform team, can change any weight in its KubeSchedulerConfiguration, as in the YAML above.
  • On EKS, AWS runs the default scheduler and exposes only one scoring setting: whether NodeResourcesFit spreads or packs, and the weights of CPU, memory and GPUs inside it (AWS docs). The plugin weights above always apply. Different plugin weights need your own scheduler (a second scheduler, or a profile in it), chosen with schedulerName.
  • Pod authors can't change plugin weights at all: the only weights a pod controls are the ones inside its own preferred rules, like the weight: 80, and those only rank its preferences inside one plugin's score.
7Points and the final score
points = score × weight for each plugin, and the final score is their sum. Node A gets 60 + 0 + 200 = 260, node B 20 + 90 + 0 = 110, so node A wins even though node B had the image.
8Who wins when plugins disagree
that's the scenario's question. Here ImageLocality prefers B while the other two prefer A, and the weights settle it. Raise ImageLocality's weight to 3 and B wins, 290 against 260 (the box at the bottom of the picture).
9Two different weights, don't mix them up
the weight: 80 in the pod's preferred rule only matters inside NodeAffinity's own score, to rank the pod's preferences against each other. With a single rule, any weight from 1 to 100 ends up as 100 after scaling; it matters once there are several rules. For example, with rules weighted 80 and 20, a node matching both gets a raw 100 and one matching only the second gets 20, so they scale to 100 and 20. The plugin weight (×2 in the picture) is different: it multiplies NodeAffinity's whole score against the other plugins.
10A pod with no rules is still scored
if a Deployment says nothing about placement, the built-in plugins still grade every node with their default weights. NodeResourcesFit, BalancedResourceAllocation, ImageLocality and the default topology spread decide; NodeAffinity and InterPodAffinity give every node 0, so they don't change anything. A plain pod still gets a reasoned placement, driven by spreading, balance and image caching.
# No nodeSelector, no affinity, no tolerations: placement is still scoredapiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: plain-appspec:  replicas: 3  selector:    matchLabels: {app: plain-app}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: plain-app}    spec:      containers:      - name: app        image: my-company/plain-app:1.0   # ImageLocality: is it cached on the node?        resources:          requests:                        # NodeResourcesFit + BalancedResourceAllocation            cpu: 500m            memory: 512Mi# Also scoring: the default topology spread (keeps the 3 replicas apart)# and TaintToleration (nodes with a PreferNoSchedule taint lose points).# NodeAffinity and InterPodAffinity give every node 0: there are no rules.
11A preferred rule must have a weight
it has to be between 1 and 100. Leave it out and the API server rejects the object, so kubectl apply fails before the scheduler ever sees the pod.
# Rejected: a preferred rule without a weightapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: webspec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:      - preference:                        # no "weight:" line          matchExpressions:          - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone            operator: In            values: ["us-east-1a"]  containers:  - name: web    image: nginx:1.27# kubectl apply -f web.yaml# The Pod "web" is invalid:#   spec.affinity.nodeAffinity.preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution[0].weight:#   Invalid value: 0: must be in the range 1-100## Fix: add "- weight: 50" (any value from 1 to 100) above "preference:".

When a preferred affinity loses

Scenario. A team adds a preferred pod affinity so their API runs on the same node as its Redis cache, and a soft rule to spread API replicas across zones. Most API pods end up next to the cache, but a new replica lands on another node: emptier, in a zone with no API pods yet, and with the API image already cached from an earlier pod. The team asks why their affinity rule "lost".

# The cache, and the API that would like to run next to itapiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: cachespec:  replicas: 1  selector:    matchLabels: {app: cache}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: cache}                   # the label the API's affinity looks for    spec:      containers:      - name: redis        image: redis:7        resources:          requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 20Gi} # memory-heavy: makes its node lopsided---apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: apispec:  replicas: 3  selector:    matchLabels: {app: api}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: api}    spec:      affinity:        podAffinity:          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:   # wish 1: next to the cache          - weight: 100            podAffinityTerm:              labelSelector:                matchLabels: {app: cache}              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname      topologySpreadConstraints:                            # wish 2: spread across zones      - maxSkew: 1        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone        whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway                   # soft: scored, not filtered        labelSelector:          matchLabels: {app: api}      containers:      - name: api        image: my-company/api:1.4            # 1.8 GB        resources:          requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi}# See where they landed: kubectl get pods -l 'app in (api, cache)' -o wide

What the picture shows. Two candidate nodes for one new api replica, the plugins that grade them differently, and two ways to make the affinity win. Every number is calculated in the note under "The result".

1The setup
both nodes have 8 CPU and 32 GiB. Node 2 (zone b) runs the Redis cache, which requests a lot of memory; node 1 (zone a) is lightly used and still has the api image from an earlier api pod. Zone b already has two api replicas, on another node; zone a has none.

The two nodes, side by side

What each node has, and the points it earns. Only your affinity favors node 2; your spread rule and three built-in plugins favor node 1.

2Affinity on its own would win
InterPodAffinity gives node 2 a grade of 100 (the only node with a cache pod) and node 1 a grade of 0. At its default weight of 2, that's 200 points for node 2.
3Three built-in plugins prefer node 1
NodeResourcesFit (75 vs 34.4), BalancedResourceAllocation (100 vs 84.4) and ImageLocality (89.8 vs 0), each at weight 1.
4…but together they can't beat the affinity
without the spread rule, node 1 would total 75 + 100 + 89.8 = 264.8 and node 2 34.4 + 84.4 + 200 = 318.8, so the affinity would win. A weight-1 plugin can favor one node by at most 100 points, and in practice these three fall well short of 200 combined.
5Your spread rule tips it
it prefers the zone with fewer api pods. Zone a has 0 and zone b has 2, so node 1 gets 100 × 2 = 200 and node 2 gets 0.
6The result
node 1 gets 75 + 100 + 89.8 + 200 = 464.8, node 2 gets 34.4 + 84.4 + 0 + 0 + 200 = 318.8, and node 1 wins. Your two soft rules disagreed, and the spread rule plus the built-in plugins outvoted the affinity. A preferred affinity is one vote among several, not a guarantee.

Note: how the numbers are calculated

Both nodes have 8 CPU and 32 GiB allocatable. The new api pod requests 1 CPU and 2 GiB, and every plugin counts it as if it were already placed. The cluster has 4 nodes; the 1.8 GB api image is cached on 2 of them (node 1, and node 4, which runs the two zone-b replicas).

Already requested CPU share (incl. new pod) Memory share (incl. new pod)
Node 1 1 CPU, 6 GiB (a few small pods) 2 of 8 → 25% 8 of 32 → 25%
Node 2 3 CPU, 24 GiB (cache: 1 CPU, 20 GiB; others: 2 CPU, 4 GiB) 4 of 8 → 50% 26 of 32 → 81.25% 
1. NodeResourcesFit (LeastAllocated): average share left free   score = average over CPU and memory of (1 − share) × 100   Node 1: ((1 − 0.25) + (1 − 0.25)) ÷ 2 × 100     = 75   Node 2: ((1 − 0.50) + (1 − 0.8125)) ÷ 2 × 100   = 34.375 ≈ 34.4 2. BalancedResourceAllocation: how close the CPU and memory shares are   score = (1 − standard deviation of the shares) × 100         = 100 − |CPU share − memory share| × 50     (with two resources)   Node 1: 100 − |25% − 25%| × 50                  = 100   Node 2: 100 − |50% − 81.25%| × 50               = 84.375 ≈ 84.4 3. ImageLocality: image size, scaled by how many nodes have it   sum   = image size × (nodes with the image ÷ all nodes)   score = (sum − 23 MB) ÷ (1000 MB − 23 MB) × 100, kept within 0–100   Node 1: 1800 MB × 2 ÷ 4 = 900 MB → (900 − 23) ÷ 977 × 100 = 89.8   Node 2: image not on the node                   = 0 4. PodTopologySpread (your soft per-zone rule): fewer api pods in the zone is better   raw = api pods already in the node's zone; then scaled, fewest = 100, most = 0   Node 1: zone a has 0 → 100                      Node 2: zone b has 2 → 0 5. InterPodAffinity (your preferred rule, weight 100 in the pod)   raw = 100 for each cache pod on the node; then scaled, best = 100   Node 1: no cache pod → 0                        Node 2: one cache pod → 100
  • Left out on purpose: TaintToleration and NodeAffinity give both nodes the same score (no taints, no node rules), so they add the same to each total and can't change the winner.
  • Decimals: the scheduler works in whole numbers and rounds each score down (34.375 becomes 34), which changes the totals slightly but not the winner.
  • Why the spread rule is written out: a pod that has its own topologySpreadConstraints uses only those; the scheduler's built-in default spread applies only to pods that have none.
7Choice A, the hard rule (filtering)
change preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution to requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution. The rule moves from scoring to filtering: node 1 has no cache pod, so it's removed before scoring and node 2 is the only candidate. The trade-off: if node 2 is full, the pod waits in Pending.
apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: apispec:  replicas: 3  selector:    matchLabels: {app: api}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: api}    spec:      affinity:        podAffinity:          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:   # now a filter, not a score          - labelSelector:              matchLabels: {app: cache}            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname      containers:      - name: api        image: my-company/api:1.4
8Choice B, scheduler configuration (advanced)
keep the rule preferred, but give the InterPodAffinity plugin a higher weight in a KubeSchedulerConfiguration profile. Node 2 has 118.8 points from the other plugins, so it needs more than 464.8 − 118.8 = 346 points from affinity: weight 3 gives 418.8 (still loses), weight 4 gives 518.8 (wins). On EKS you can't change the default scheduler, so this runs as a second scheduler that pods choose with schedulerName. The full second-scheduler example in Appendix A goes further and uses weight 100, so affinity beats everything else.
# config file passed to a kube-scheduler you run yourself (--config)apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: affinity-first-scheduler  plugins:    score:      enabled:      - name: InterPodAffinity        weight: 4                       # was 2: node 2 gets 118.8 + 400 = 518.8 > 464.8 (3 gives 418.8)

How GPUs become schedulable

  1. The NVIDIA device plugin
  2. How GPUs are advertised
  3. Steering pods to the right GPU
  4. Dynamic Resource Allocation
  5. Different GPUs in one server, and MIG

The NVIDIA device plugin

Scenario. A team adds GPU nodes to their Kubernetes cluster and deploys a pod that requests nvidia.com/gpu: 1. The pod stays Pending with "Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu", even though the nodes clearly have GPUs installed. Kubernetes can't see them yet.

What the picture shows. How the NVIDIA device plugin turns physical GPUs into a count the scheduler can use, in numbered steps.

1AWS cloud and the GPU instance
an EC2 GPU instance (here a p4d.24xlarge with 8 A100s) gives the worker node its physical GPUs. The NVIDIA driver must already be on the node; the EKS-optimized accelerated AMIs include it.
2Control plane
the API server stores each node's status, including its GPU count; kube-scheduler checks that count the same way it checks CPU and memory.
3Step 1, the plugin registers
the device plugin runs on every GPU node as a DaemonSet. It finds the node's GPUs and registers with the kubelet over a local socket.
4Step 2, the kubelet reports the count
the kubelet adds nvidia.com/gpu: 8 to the node's capacity and allocatable. From then on GPUs are a countable resource. This is the missing piece in the scenario: without the plugin the node never reports any nvidia.com/gpu, so every node fails the fit check.
5Step 3, a pod asks for a GPU
the user or CI deploys a pod with nvidia.com/gpu: 1 under resources.limits.
apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: inferencespec:  containers:  - name: inference    image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/gpu: 1    # schedulable only after the device plugin registers GPUs
6Step 4, the scheduler subtracts and binds
a node fits if enough of its GPUs are still unreserved. The scheduler picks one and binds the pod to it.
7Step 5, the kubelet asks for a device
on that node, the kubelet asks the plugin to allocate one GPU. This happens on the node, not in the control plane.
8Step 6, the container gets the GPU
the plugin returns the device files and NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, and the container starts with exactly that GPU. The scheduler never knew which GPU it would be, only that one was free.
Going deeper9 points

Installing it. Each GPU node first needs the NVIDIA driver and container toolkit; the EKS-optimized accelerated AMIs already include them. Then install the plugin with Helm:

helm repo add nvdp https://nvidia.github.io/k8s-device-pluginhelm repo updatehelm upgrade -i nvdp nvdp/nvidia-device-plugin \  --namespace nvidia-device-plugin --create-namespace

On EKS Auto Mode the plugin is already built in. The NVIDIA GPU Operator is the all-in-one alternative: it installs the driver, toolkit, device plugin, NFD and GPU Feature Discovery together.

Check (device plugin): kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GPUS:.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu

# What the NODE shows (written by the kubelet; see it with kubectl get node -o yaml)apiVersion: v1kind: Nodemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1status:  capacity:    nvidia.com/gpu: "8"              # reported by the device plugin  allocatable:    nvidia.com/gpu: "8"              # what the scheduler counts against---# What the POD writes: just a numberapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: trainspec:  containers:  - name: trainer    image: my-company/trainer:2.0    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/gpu: 1            # "any one free GPU on the node"
  • The device plugin does four jobs:
    • it discovers the devices;
    • it advertises them as nvidia.com/gpu for scheduling;
    • it allocates them exclusively to containers;
    • it monitors their health, and an unhealthy GPU is taken out of the node's allocatable count.
  • Two labeling tools usually run next to it: on a typical GPU node there are three separate NVIDIA-related pods. All three are DaemonSets (one pod per GPU node), and the NVIDIA GPU Operator usually installs them together:
Tool What it does What it produces Do you need it?
Device plugin Counts the GPUs, and gives one to a container when a pod asks A count in the node's capacity (nvidia.com/gpu: 8), plus the actual GPU device inside the container Always. It's the only one that hands out GPUs; without it pods can't get one at all.
Node Feature Discovery Scans the hardware Generic labels such as feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present=true ("an NVIDIA card is here") Only as a helper: GPU Feature Discovery needs it to write its labels, and the GPU Operator uses it to find which nodes need the GPU driver and plugin.
GPU Feature Discovery Reads the GPU details Labels such as nvidia.com/gpu.product=…A100… and nvidia.com/gpu.memory=81920 Only when your GPUs differ and pods must pick a model or size, and nothing else describes the GPU already. Often unnecessary on EKS (see below).
  • They describe the GPUs; only the device plugin hands them out: Node Feature Discovery and GPU Feature Discovery only write information onto the Node object as labels, like a sign on the door saying "this room has A100s with 80 GB". The device plugin is the only one that gives a GPU to a container: when a pod asks for nvidia.com/gpu: 1, the kubelet asks the device plugin for a GPU, and the plugin hands one over.
  • Why it matters: a pod that only uses the labels (nodeSelector: nvidia.com/gpu.product: …A100…) lands on an A100 node but gets no GPU. It still needs nvidia.com/gpu: 1 so the device plugin hands one over. Labels choose the node; the device plugin gives the GPU. More on the labels in How GPUs are advertised.
  • Why not just the device plugin? Its count treats every GPU the same: a 16 GB T4 and an 80 GB H100 are both "1". So with the device plugin alone, a pod can ask for "one GPU" but not "an A100" or "at least 40 GB". That's the gap the labels fill.
  • What you actually need:
    • one GPU type everywhere: the device plugin alone; every GPU is the same, so "one GPU" is all a pod needs to say;
    • several GPU types: the device plugin plus a way to label the model, either GPU Feature Discovery (which brings Node Feature Discovery) or labels you already have;
    • with the GPU Operator: you get all three by default, whether you need them or not.
  • On EKS you may not need GPU Feature Discovery: every node already has node.kubernetes.io/instance-type, and on AWS the instance type tells you the GPU (a p4de.24xlarge has 8 × A100 80 GB, a g5 has A10Gs). With Karpenter you also get karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-name and instance-gpu-memory. A nodeSelector or affinity on those picks the GPU model without GFD. GFD earns its place on on-prem or mixed hardware, where nothing else describes the GPU.
  • A minimal vLLM Deployment on such a node still needs a GPU limit, a toleration for the GPU taint, and a PVC as a model cache, so restarts don't re-download the weights. The Recreate strategy matters too: the cache is a single-node volume, so a rolling update would start the new pod while the old one still holds it, and the new pod would wait.
# 1. The model cache: survives pod restarts, so weights aren't re-downloadedapiVersion: v1kind: PersistentVolumeClaimmetadata:  name: model-cachespec:  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]           # one node at a time (an EBS volume on EKS)  storageClassName: gp3  resources:    requests:      storage: 100Gi---# 2. The inference serverapiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: vllmspec:  replicas: 1  strategy:    type: Recreate                         # RWO volume: the old pod must let go first  selector:    matchLabels: {app: vllm}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: vllm}    spec:      tolerations:      - key: nvidia.com/gpu                # allowed onto the tainted GPU nodes        operator: Exists        effect: NoSchedule      containers:      - name: server        image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest      # pin a version in production        args: ["--model", "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct", "--port", "8000"]        env:        - name: HF_HOME                    # Hugging Face downloads go to the cache volume          value: /models        ports:        - containerPort: 8000        resources:          limits:            nvidia.com/gpu: 1              # the device plugin hands over one GPU          requests:            cpu: "4"            memory: 24Gi        volumeMounts:        - name: model-cache          mountPath: /models        - name: shm                        # vLLM uses shared memory between processes          mountPath: /dev/shm        readinessProbe:                    # no traffic until the model is loaded          httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}          initialDelaySeconds: 60          periodSeconds: 10      volumes:      - name: model-cache        persistentVolumeClaim:          claimName: model-cache      - name: shm        emptyDir:          medium: Memory          sizeLimit: 8Gi
  • Plugins expose counts, not topology: the scheduler doesn't know which GPUs share an NVLink or a PCIe switch. That gap is why topology labels, Dynamic Resource Allocation and topology-aware schedulers (topology bin-packing) exist.

How GPUs are advertised

Scenario. A platform team must make sure a new inference service lands only on GPUs with at least 40 GB of memory. Reading the docs, they find five things that all seem to "advertise GPUs" to Kubernetes: the device plugin, Node Feature Discovery, GPU Feature Discovery, Karpenter's labels and DRA. Which one does what, which ones do they actually need, and which one decides the GPU a pod gets?

What the picture shows. The three kinds of advertising side by side, and what each one lets the scheduler do.

1Labels (left column)
Node Feature Discovery, GPU Feature Discovery and the cloud/Karpenter labels write facts about the GPUs on the Node object. Pods match them with a nodeSelector or node affinity. They only help choose a node; nothing is reserved.
2Count (middle column)
the device plugin publishes nvidia.com/gpu: 8 in the node's capacity. Pods ask for a number, and the scheduler reserves against that count like CPU or memory.
3DRA (right column)
a DRA driver publishes every device as its own entry in a ResourceSlice, with its attributes. Pods bring a ResourceClaim that describes the device they need, and the scheduler matches it against individual devices.
4Bottom row, who picks the exact GPU
with labels, nobody; with a count, the device plugin picks one when the container starts; with DRA, the scheduler picks it and records it in the claim.
5The classic setup uses two of them together
labels to choose the node, plus the count to reserve a GPU on it. DRA replaces both with one mechanism.
Going deeper2 points
  • How a node tells Kubernetes about its GPUs is the main thing that sets DRA apart. There are two kinds of advertising, and before DRA they came from different tools:
    • Labels are information about the node ("this node has A100s with 80 GB"). They only help you choose a node, with a nodeSelector or node affinity.
    • A count is something the scheduler reserves ("this node has 8 GPUs, 3 are free"). The device plugin publishes it, and a pod asks for it with nvidia.com/gpu: 1. The scheduler only picks the node; the device plugin then hands over any free GPU on it.
    • DRA replaces both with one entry per device (a ResourceSlice) that carries that device's own attributes. The scheduler matches a claim against individual GPUs and records exactly which one the pod gets.
Mechanism Kind What it publishes How a pod uses it
Device plugin (NVIDIA; also AMD amd.com/gpu, AWS Neuron aws.amazon.com/neuron) Count A count in the node's capacity, e.g. nvidia.com/gpu: 8 resources.limits
Node Feature Discovery Label Generic hardware labels, e.g. feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present (10de = NVIDIA) nodeSelector / node affinity
GPU Feature Discovery (NVIDIA, installed with the GPU Operator; needs NFD running) Label Node labels with GPU details: model, memory, count nodeSelector / node affinity
Cloud and Karpenter labels Label Labels from the instance type: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type, karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-name, instance-gpu-memory, instance-gpu-count Node affinity, or NodePool requirements
DRA driver DRA (per device) One ResourceSlice entry per device, with its attributes A ResourceClaim with CEL selectors
  • A few things follow from that table. GPU Feature Discovery's nvidia.com/gpu.count label is still only a label: the scheduler reserves against the device plugin's nvidia.com/gpu count, never against it. GPU Feature Discovery builds on Node Feature Discovery, adding GPU details to its generic "there's an NVIDIA card" label. Karpenter's labels are known before a node exists, so they can make Karpenter launch the right instance; GPU Feature Discovery can only label a node once it's running. DRA doesn't need any of these labels, though they can still be used alongside it (for example to keep a node pool for one GPU model). And NVIDIA's DCGM exporter, often seen next to these, only reports GPU usage and health for monitoring; the scheduler never reads it.

How each mechanism works, step by step. The same cluster in each picture: a control plane on the left, a GPU node on the right, numbered arrows explained underneath. Picture 1, the device plugin, is the previous section.

Installing it. NFD has its own Helm chart:

helm install nfd oci://registry.k8s.io/nfd/charts/node-feature-discovery \  --namespace node-feature-discovery --create-namespace

Skip this if you use the GPU Operator, or the device plugin chart with gfd.enabled=true: both install NFD for you.

Check (NFD): kubectl get node gpu-node-1 --show-labels | tr ',' '\n' | grep feature.node

# What the NODE shows (labels written by the NFD master)apiVersion: v1kind: Nodemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1  labels:    # The GPU Operator configures NFD to label by vendor only:    feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present: "true"    # NFD's own default labels by class + vendor (0302 = 3D controller):    # feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-0302_10de.present: "true"---# What the POD writes: "any node with an NVIDIA card"apiVersion: apps/v1kind: DaemonSet                      # a typical user: per-GPU-node agentsmetadata:  name: gpu-monitorspec:  selector:    matchLabels: {app: gpu-monitor}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: gpu-monitor}    spec:      nodeSelector:        feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present: "true"      containers:      - name: exporter        image: my-company/gpu-monitor:1.0

Installing it. GPU Feature Discovery now ships in the same repository and Helm chart as the device plugin, so you turn it on there. The chart also installs NFD for you unless you say you already have it:

helm upgrade -i nvdp nvdp/nvidia-device-plugin \  --namespace nvidia-device-plugin --create-namespace \  --set gfd.enabled=true# NFD already installed separately? add: --set nfd.enabled=false

With the GPU Operator, GPU Feature Discovery is on by default.

Check (GFD): kubectl get node gpu-node-1 --show-labels | tr ',' '\n' | grep nvidia.com/gpu

# What the NODE shows (labels written by GPU Feature Discovery via NFD)apiVersion: v1kind: Nodemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1  labels:    nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB    nvidia.com/gpu.memory: "81920"   # per-GPU memory, in MiB    nvidia.com/gpu.family: ampere    nvidia.com/gpu.count: "8"        # only a label: nothing counts against it---# What the POD writes: pick a node by label, then still ask for a GPUapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: inferencespec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:        nodeSelectorTerms:        - matchExpressions:          - key: nvidia.com/gpu.memory            operator: Gt            values: ["40000"]  containers:  - name: server    image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/gpu: 1            # the device plugin still allocates the GPU

Installing it. node.kubernetes.io/instance-type needs nothing: the kubelet sets it on every node. The karpenter.k8s.aws/... labels come from Karpenter, which you install with Helm once its IAM role and interruption queue exist (Karpenter's getting-started guide creates them):

helm upgrade --install karpenter oci://public.ecr.aws/karpenter/karpenter \  --version "${KARPENTER_VERSION}" --namespace kube-system \  --set settings.clusterName="${CLUSTER_NAME}" \  --set settings.interruptionQueue="${CLUSTER_NAME}" \  --wait

Then apply an EC2NodeClass and a NodePool like the one below. On EKS Auto Mode, Karpenter is built in and run by AWS, and the same labels use the eks.amazonaws.com/ prefix instead (for example eks.amazonaws.com/instance-gpu-name).

Check (Karpenter): kubectl get nodes -L karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-name,karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-memory

# A Karpenter NodePool that may launch big-GPU instancesapiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1kind: NodePoolmetadata:  name: gpuspec:  template:    spec:      nodeClassRef:        group: karpenter.k8s.aws        kind: EC2NodeClass        name: default      requirements:      - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-name        operator: In        values: ["a100", "h100"]      - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-memory   # per GPU, in MiB        operator: Gt        values: ["40000"]      taints:      - key: nvidia.com/gpu        effect: NoSchedule---# What the POD writes: affinity on the same labels Karpenter will setapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: inferencespec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:        nodeSelectorTerms:        - matchExpressions:          - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-gpu-memory            operator: Gt            values: ["40000"]  tolerations:  - key: nvidia.com/gpu    operator: Exists    effect: NoSchedule  containers:  - name: server    image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/gpu: 1

Installing it. DRA itself is built into Kubernetes 1.34 and later; you install a DRA driver for your hardware. For NVIDIA GPUs:

helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidiahelm repo updatehelm install nvidia-dra-driver-gpu nvidia/nvidia-dra-driver-gpu \  --create-namespace --namespace nvidia-dra-driver-gpu \  --set resources.computeDomains.enabled=false \  --set gpuResourcesEnabledOverride=true

Don't run the classic device plugin on the same nodes. Version requirements, the chart's new name and EKS caveats are in "How do you install DRA?" in the Dynamic Resource Allocation section.

Check (DRA): kubectl get deviceclass and kubectl get resourceslices

# What the DRIVER publishes (one ResourceSlice per node, one entry per GPU)apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceSlicemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1-gpu.nvidia.com-x8k2p   # generated namespec:  driver: gpu.nvidia.com  nodeName: gpu-node-1  pool:    name: gpu-node-1    generation: 1    resourceSliceCount: 1  devices:  - name: gpu-0    attributes:      productName: {string: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB}      architecture: {string: Ampere}    capacity:      memory: {value: 80Gi}  - name: gpu-1    # ... one entry for each of the 8 GPUs---# What the POD writes: a claim that describes the device (full example below)apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: gpu-40gb-plusspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com          selectors:          - cel:              expression: device.capacity["gpu.nvidia.com"].memory.compareTo(quantity("40Gi")) >= 0

Steering pods to the right GPU

Scenario. Three teams share a cluster with T4, A10G, A100 and H100 nodes. The batch team wants exactly A100s, the inference team wants "at least 40 GB, Hopper if possible", and the web team's ordinary pods keep landing on expensive GPU nodes.

What the picture shows. Four GPU nodes with their labels and taint, and how three different pods are filtered and scored against them.

1The four GPU nodes
GPU Feature Discovery labels each one with its model, memory and family: a g4dn (T4, about 15 GB, Turing), a g5 (A10G, about 23 GB, Ampere), a p4de (A100, 80 GB, Ampere) and a p5 (H100, 80 GB, Hopper).
2The taint on every GPU node
nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule keeps away any pod without a matching toleration. This is the fix for the web team.
3Pod A, pin a model (Option 1)
