a nodeSelector with nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB. nvidia.com/gpu.product is the label's key ("which GPU model?") and NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB is the value it must equal. A nodeSelector is an exact match, so only the p4de passes: the g4dn, g5 and p5 have the same key with other values (Tesla-T4, NVIDIA-A10G, NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3), and the CPU node has no such label. Even a p4d wouldn't match, since its A100s are the 40 GB model (NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB).
4Pod B, a range plus a preference (Option 2)
a required rule nvidia.com/gpu.memory greater than 40000 removes the g4dn and the g5; a preferred rule for the hopper family adds points to the p5, so the p5 wins when it has room and the p4de is the fallback.
5Pod C, a web pod
it has no toleration, so every GPU node is filtered out and it runs on a regular CPU node.
6The GPU request
pods A and B still ask for nvidia.com/gpu: 1. The labels only choose the node; the count reserves a GPU on it.
Going deeper3 points
  • nvidia.com/gpu: 1 is purely resource-based, so every GPU counts the same: a 16 GB T4 and an 80 GB A100 are both "1".
apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: inferencespec:  containers:  - name: server    image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/gpu: 1      # "any one GPU": a 16 GB T4 and an 80 GB A100 both count as 1
  • A nodeSelector on GPU labels pins an exact model, node affinity can say "at least 40 GB, prefer Hopper", and a taint on GPU nodes keeps everything else off them.
# The GPU NODE: labels (added automatically by NVIDIA GPU Feature Discovery,# part of the GPU Operator) and a taint (set in the node group / NodePool).# Shown trimmed: a real node has many more labels.apiVersion: v1kind: Nodemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1  labels:    nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB   # the exact model    nvidia.com/gpu.memory: "81920"                  # per-GPU memory, in MiB    nvidia.com/gpu.family: ampere                   # GPU generation    nvidia.com/gpu.count: "8"spec:  taints:  - key: nvidia.com/gpu    value: present    effect: NoSchedule                              # keeps non-GPU pods off---# Option 1: pin an exact GPU model with nodeSelectorapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: inference-a100spec:  nodeSelector:    nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB  tolerations:                       # GPU nodes are usually tainted  - key: nvidia.com/gpu    operator: Exists    effect: NoSchedule  containers:  - name: server    image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/gpu: 1---# Option 2: "at least 40 GB, prefer Hopper" with node affinityapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: inference-big-gpuspec:  affinity:    nodeAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:        nodeSelectorTerms:        - matchExpressions:          - key: nvidia.com/gpu.memory            operator: Gt            values: ["40000"]        # more than ~40 GB      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:      - weight: 50        preference:          matchExpressions:          - key: nvidia.com/gpu.family            operator: In            values: ["hopper"]  tolerations:  - key: nvidia.com/gpu    operator: Exists    effect: NoSchedule  containers:  - name: server    image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/gpu: 1
  • In Option 2, node affinity only picks a node with big GPUs; nvidia.com/gpu: 1 is what actually reserves a GPU there. Leave it out and the scheduler counts no GPU for the pod, so the container gets none, or, on nodes that trust the image's NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all setting, quietly uses GPUs other pods have reserved.

Dynamic Resource Allocation

Scenario. The inference team wants "any NVIDIA GPU with at least 40 GB" without depending on node labels, and the training team needs each worker's GPU on the same PCIe root as its network card. Neither can be said with nvidia.com/gpu: 1.

The words you will meet. DRA adds a few Kubernetes objects. If you know storage, the idea will feel familiar: a pod doesn't name a disk, it makes a claim for one of some class, and Kubernetes finds a match. DRA does the same for devices. Kubernetes' own DRA documentation makes that comparison with storage classes and PersistentVolumeClaims. The other two storage matches in the table are our own comparison.

Word What it is Who creates it Storage comparison
ResourceSlice The list of devices on one node, each with its facts: product name, architecture, memory. The DRA driver, per node PersistentVolume (our comparison)
DeviceClass A named category of devices, such as gpu.nvidia.com. A request says which class it wants. The device driver's side (NVIDIA ships its classes in the driver's Helm chart); a cluster admin can add more A StorageClass
CEL (Common Expression Language) A one-line rule that is true or false for each device, such as "memory is at least 40Gi". It narrows the devices down. A class has one, and your claim may add one. Why it is needed: a count or a node label can only say "one GPU" or "this node has A100s", while a rule can test each device's own facts. The driver or an admin, inside a class. You, optionally, inside a claim n/a
ResourceClaimTemplate A recipe for a request: which class, an optional CEL rule, how many devices (an exact count, one by default; the only other mode is "all matching devices"). A request has no "shared" or "immediate" setting. You volumeClaimTemplates in a StatefulSet (our comparison)
ResourceClaim One actual request, made from the recipe. The scheduler records which device it picked in the claim. Kubernetes, one per pod A PersistentVolumeClaim

The storage side as YAML, for comparison:

# STORAGE: a class, and a StatefulSet that makes one claim per podapiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1kind: StorageClass                   # "a named kind of disk"metadata:  name: gp3provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com---apiVersion: apps/v1kind: StatefulSetmetadata:  name: dbspec:  replicas: 3  # (selector, serviceName and the pod template are left out here)  volumeClaimTemplates:              # a recipe: every pod gets its own claim  - metadata:      name: data    spec:      storageClassName: gp3          # which class to ask for      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]      resources:        requests:          storage: 100Gi             # how much
1A device and its facts: the ResourceSlice

The driver on each node publishes a ResourceSlice: one entry per device, with its attributes (descriptive facts such as productName, architecture and type) and its capacity (amounts such as memory). Every DRA decision is made from these facts, and the names depend on the driver. kubectl get resourceslices -o yaml shows the real ones on your cluster. A device reports a little less than its advertised size (a T4 sold as 16 GB shows about 15 GB, NVIDIA forum), so read the real value there before you choose a threshold. Here is the ResourceSlice of one illustrative node, gpu-node-1, a lab server with four different GPUs (trimmed, illustrative values):

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceSlicemetadata:  name: gpu-node-1-gpu.nvidia.com-x8k2pspec:  driver: gpu.nvidia.com  nodeName: gpu-node-1  pool: {name: gpu-node-1, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 1}  devices:                           # four GPUs, one entry each  - name: gpu-0    attributes: {type: {string: gpu}, productName: {string: Tesla T4}, architecture: {string: Turing}}    capacity: {memory: {value: 15Gi}}  - name: gpu-1    attributes: {type: {string: gpu}, productName: {string: NVIDIA A10G}, architecture: {string: Ampere}}    capacity: {memory: {value: 23Gi}}  - name: gpu-2    attributes: {type: {string: gpu}, productName: {string: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB}, architecture: {string: Ampere}}    capacity: {memory: {value: 80Gi}}  - name: gpu-3    attributes: {type: {string: gpu}, productName: {string: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3}, architecture: {string: Hopper}}    capacity: {memory: {value: 80Gi}}
2CEL: which devices exactly

CEL stands for Common Expression Language, a small language for writing true-or-false rules. DRA needs it because a count or a node label can only say "one GPU" or "this node has A100s". A rule can say "memory at least 40Gi" about each device, and the scheduler tests it against the facts in the ResourceSlices. It runs the rule on every device and keeps only those where it comes out true. device.attributes[...] reads an entry's attributes and device.capacity[...] reads its capacity, so the rules use the names from Step 1. Three rules, from simple to combined:

  • device.capacity["gpu.nvidia.com"].memory.compareTo(quantity("40Gi")) >= 0 reads "memory is at least 40Gi". quantity("40Gi") turns the text into an amount Kubernetes can compare, and compareTo(...) >= 0 means "greater than or equal".
  • device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].architecture == "Hopper" reads "the architecture is Hopper". Attributes are descriptive facts such as the product name or architecture; capacity holds amounts such as memory.
  • Join two rules with && ("both must be true"), for example Hopper and at least 40Gi.

The picture applies the three rules to the four GPUs of gpu-node-1 from Step 1:

3DeviceClass: a named category of devices

gpu.nvidia.com means "an NVIDIA GPU". A class is itself a CEL rule that a device must pass before a request can use it: NVIDIA's says "the device is published by the driver gpu.nvidia.com and its type is gpu", which is how the class keeps only GPUs. The class comes with NVIDIA's DRA driver chart (source), so installing the driver creates it, while the ResourceSlices are published by the running driver. You usually don't write a class, you pick one, and kubectl get deviceclass lists what your cluster has. Here is NVIDIA's class (trimmed):

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: DeviceClassmetadata:  name: gpu.nvidia.comspec:  selectors:  - cel:                             # the class's own rule, shipped by the driver's chart      expression: "device.driver == 'gpu.nvidia.com' && device.attributes['gpu.nvidia.com'].type == 'gpu'"

All four devices in the ResourceSlice of Step 1 pass this rule, because each is published by that driver with type gpu.

4Your request: the ResourceClaimTemplate

A template is a recipe for a request: which class, an optional CEL rule of your own, and how many devices (one by default). A device must pass two filters before it can be given to your pod: the class's rule from Step 3 (FILTER 1) and the template's own rule (FILTER 2). The API requires both, so the numbers are only labels for reading. This template asks for an NVIDIA GPU with at least 40Gi of memory:

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplate          # a recipe: class + optional CEL rulemetadata:  name: gpu-40gb-plusspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com      # FILTER 1 comes in here: the class's rule from Step 3 is inherited by this request          selectors:          - cel:                               # FILTER 2: your claim's own rule (optional). A device must pass both              expression: device.capacity["gpu.nvidia.com"].memory.compareTo(quantity("40Gi")) >= 0

On gpu-node-1 from Step 1, FILTER 1 keeps all four GPUs and FILTER 2 keeps the A100 (gpu-2) and the H100 (gpu-3). What each line means:

  • name: gpu-40gb-plus: the name the pod uses to point at this request.
  • requests: - name: gpu: "I need one device, and I'll call it gpu."
  • exactly:: allocate exactly one device that matches. DRA can also list alternatives ("this, or else that"); here there's only one option.
  • deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com: only look at NVIDIA GPUs. This is where FILTER 1 comes in.
  • The cel selector: FILTER 2, the rule from Step 2 that reads "this device's memory compared with 40Gi is 0 or more", that is, at least 40 GiB.

You do not have to write any CEL. A template (or claim) that names only the class gets every device the class allows. Its own rule is optional and can only narrow further: the API requires a device to satisfy the class's selectors and the request's selectors, and an administrator can even create an empty class if users may ask for anything. This template has FILTER 1 only:

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: any-nvidia-gpuspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com      # every device the class allows is a candidate: all four GPUs of gpu-node-1

The three rules from Step 2 as templates. Each template holds one rule as FILTER 2, with the GPUs of gpu-node-1 that it keeps:

# Rule 1: memory is at least 40Gi  -> keeps gpu-2, gpu-3apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: rule-1-memoryspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com          selectors:          - cel:              expression: device.capacity["gpu.nvidia.com"].memory.compareTo(quantity("40Gi")) >= 0---# Rule 2: architecture is Hopper  -> keeps gpu-3apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: rule-2-hopperspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com          selectors:          - cel:              expression: device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].architecture == "Hopper"---# Rule 3: both, joined with &&  -> keeps gpu-3apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: rule-3-bothspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com          selectors:          - cel:              expression: |-                device.capacity["gpu.nvidia.com"].memory.compareTo(quantity("40Gi")) >= 0 &&                device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].architecture == "Hopper"
5Why the class checks the device type

The class's rule from Step 3 has a second part: the type must be gpu. This part exists because of MIG. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) cuts one physical GPU into small, isolated slices. The last section of this deep dive explains it in full (Different GPUs in one server, and MIG). The GPU Operator's MIG manager creates the slices. The NVIDIA DRA driver then finds them and lists each slice as its own device, next to the whole GPUs (NVIDIA's DRA driver install notes). So one driver lists two kinds of device: whole GPUs and slices.

The picture compares two devices on the same node: a whole GPU on the left and a small slice of a GPU on the right. They look almost identical, with the same product name and the same architecture. Only the type differs, "gpu" on the left and "mig" on the right. In the top row, your claim asks only for "Hopper". Both devices are Hopper, so both qualify, and the orange box warns that your pod could be handed the small slice by mistake. In the bottom row, the class's rule is added, and it says the type must be "gpu". The slice's type is "mig", so the class removes it, and that is the grey box. Only the whole GPU is left, which is what you wanted.

The same idea on a whole node. Here is a whole node with four devices: a T4, an A100, an H100, and a slice of a second H100. We call the node gpu-node-2, and it is made up for this example. A real node can mix whole GPUs with GPUs that are split into slices. Your claim asks for a Hopper GPU, from the class for whole GPUs. The picture checks each device against both filters:

The same node as YAML. The comments say which filter each device passes:

# What the driver publishes (trimmed, illustrative values)apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceSlicemetadata:  name: gpu-node-2-gpu.nvidia.com-x8k2pspec:  driver: gpu.nvidia.com  nodeName: gpu-node-2  pool: {name: gpu-node-2, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 1}  devices:  - name: gpu-0                      # passes FILTER 1, fails FILTER 2 (Turing, not Hopper)    attributes: {type: {string: gpu}, productName: {string: Tesla T4}, architecture: {string: Turing}}  - name: gpu-1                      # passes FILTER 1, fails FILTER 2 (Ampere, not Hopper)    attributes: {type: {string: gpu}, productName: {string: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB}, architecture: {string: Ampere}}  - name: gpu-2                      # passes both filters: the only candidate    attributes: {type: {string: gpu}, productName: {string: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3}, architecture: {string: Hopper}}  - name: mig-0                      # would pass FILTER 2, but fails FILTER 1: its type is mig    attributes: {type: {string: mig}, profile: {string: 1g.10gb}, productName: {string: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3}, architecture: {string: Hopper}}---# FILTER 1: the class, from the driver's chartapiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: DeviceClassmetadata:  name: gpu.nvidia.comspec:  selectors:  - cel:      expression: "device.driver == 'gpu.nvidia.com' && device.attributes['gpu.nvidia.com'].type == 'gpu'"---# FILTER 2: your claim's own rule, on top of the classapiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: one-hopper-gpuspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com            # brings in FILTER 1          selectors:          - cel:              expression: device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].architecture == "Hopper"

Only gpu-2 is left. Take the claim's rule away and gpu-2 is still allowed, but so are gpu-0 and gpu-1, since the class only asks for whole NVIDIA GPUs. Take the class away and mig-0 would pass the Hopper rule, which is what the class's type check prevents.

Your own category. Anyone can define another category by writing another rule. Kubernetes' own documentation gives the example of a cost-optimized class and a high-performance class (DRA docs). This class is ours, not something NVIDIA ships. It admits only Hopper GPUs, so the template that uses it needs no CEL of its own:

# Example (ours): an admin defines a category of their own, Hopper GPUs onlyapiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: DeviceClassmetadata:  name: hopper-gpuspec:  selectors:  - cel:      expression: "device.driver == 'gpu.nvidia.com' && device.attributes['gpu.nvidia.com'].type == 'gpu' && device.attributes['gpu.nvidia.com'].architecture == 'Hopper'"---# A claim for that category needs no CEL of its ownapiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: one-hopperspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: hopper-gpu
6The pod that uses the template

The pod names the template from Step 4, and its container asks for the claim that Kubernetes makes from it:

apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: inference-draspec:  resourceClaims:  - name: gpu    resourceClaimTemplateName: gpu-40gb-plus     # "make me a claim from this template"  containers:  - name: server    image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest    resources:      claims:      - name: gpu                                # this container gets what the claim allocates
  • spec.resourceClaims: create a claim for this pod from the gpu-40gb-plus template. Each pod gets its own ResourceClaim (named something like inference-dra-gpu-x7k2p), which is deleted with the pod. That's why it's a template: ten replicas get ten separate claims instead of fighting over one GPU.
  • containers[].resources.claims: - name: gpu: give the server container access to that device. In a pod with several containers, you choose which ones see the GPU.
  • No GPU count under resources.limits: the container lists claims instead. The claim is the request, so there is nothing to count. Notice there is no nvidia.com/gpu: 1 anywhere in these manifests: that line belongs to the older device-plugin way used in the GPU labels example (Option 1 and Option 2), not to DRA.
7The claim Kubernetes makes for the pod

When the pod is created, Kubernetes copies the template's spec into a new ResourceClaim for that pod. Once the scheduler has picked a device, the claim looks like this (the status is written by the scheduler):

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaim                  # one real requestmetadata:  name: inference-dra-gpu-x7k2p      # generated namespec:                                # copied unchanged from the template gpu-40gb-plus  devices:    requests:    - name: gpu      exactly:        deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com            # brings in FILTER 1, the class's rule        selectors:        - cel:                                     # FILTER 2 came along in the copy            expression: device.capacity["gpu.nvidia.com"].memory.compareTo(quantity("40Gi")) >= 0status:  allocation:    devices:      results:      - request: gpu        driver: gpu.nvidia.com        pool: gpu-node-1        device: gpu-2                # a device that passed both filters (the A100): the scheduler's pick  reservedFor:                       # who uses the claim: the pod inference-dra  - resource: pods    name: inference-dra    uid: 7c1f6b2e-0a4d-4f4e-9b0a-2f6d5e8a1c33   # illustrative

What happens when you apply the pod and the template:

  1. The claim is created: Kubernetes makes the pod's ResourceClaim from the template.
  2. The scheduler filters and allocates: its DynamicResources plugin checks the devices each node publishes (as ResourceSlices, written by the driver) and filters out nodes with no free NVIDIA GPU of 40 GiB or more. Then it picks a node and records the exact GPU it chose in the claim.
  3. The kubelet prepares the device: on that node, the kubelet asks the driver's kubelet plugin to set up that GPU and expose it to the server container. The plugin answers with the GPU's CDI names, and the container runtime uses them to add the GPU to the container (see the CDI point under Going deeper).
  4. The server starts: vLLM starts and sees exactly one GPU that's big enough.
8Template or claim?

A claim you write by hand is one request that several pods can share, and it outlives any pod. A template gives every pod its own claim, made when the pod starts and removed with it. Ten replicas then get ten separate GPUs instead of sharing one.

The same two cases as YAML. Left: one claim you write, and three pods that name it. Right: one template, and three pods that name it. The only line that differs in the pods is the one that names the claim or the template.

# A. A ResourceClaim you write by hand: all three pods share itapiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaim                  # one request, written by youmetadata:  name: shared-gpuspec:  devices:    requests:    - name: gpu      exactly:        deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com---apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: notebooks-sharedspec:  replicas: 3  selector:    matchLabels: {app: notebooks-shared}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: notebooks-shared}    spec:      resourceClaims:      - name: gpu        resourceClaimName: shared-gpu          # all 3 pods name the same claim      containers:      - name: jupyter        image: jupyter/base-notebook:latest        resources:          claims:          - name: gpu
# B. A ResourceClaimTemplate: every pod gets its own claim# (the template gpu-40gb-plus is the one from Step 4)apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: notebooks-own-gpuspec:  replicas: 3  selector:    matchLabels: {app: notebooks-own-gpu}  template:    metadata:      labels: {app: notebooks-own-gpu}    spec:      resourceClaims:      - name: gpu        resourceClaimTemplateName: gpu-40gb-plus   # Kubernetes makes one claim per pod      containers:      - name: jupyter        image: jupyter/base-notebook:latest        resources:          claims:          - name: gpu

Check (claims): kubectl get resourceclaims. With A you see one claim, shared-gpu, and it stays after the pods are deleted. With B you see three claims with generated names, one per pod, and each disappears with its pod. In A, the claim's allocation records where its device is available (a node selector in the claim's status, API reference), so the three pods run where that device is.

Is sharing a claim like sharing a CPU? Roughly, yes. Pods that share a claim get access to the same GPU, a bit like programs sharing a CPU. But the claim only gives access. How the pods actually share the GPU is a setting of the driver. With NVIDIA's time-slicing, the pods' workloads interleave on the GPU, and NVIDIA's docs say there is no memory or fault isolation between them (NVIDIA's time-slicing docs). In NVIDIA's DRA driver, time-slicing is still in alpha (AWS's EKS guide). With MIG, each pod gets its own isolated slice with its own memory instead. These are separate pods, not threads of one program.

9Putting it together

The driver publishes the devices (ResourceSlices) and the categories (DeviceClasses). You write a template that names a class and, if you want, adds a CEL rule. The pod points at the template, Kubernetes turns it into a claim, and the scheduler matches the claim against the ResourceSlices. Dynamic Resource Allocation (stable since Kubernetes 1.34) lets a pod describe the device it needs, and the driver picks a match at scheduling time.

Going deeper, by topic.

1How the chosen GPU gets into the container (CDI)
DRA does two jobs: the scheduler chooses the GPU, and then that exact GPU has to reach the container. The second job uses CDI (Container Device Interface), an open standard for container runtimes, not a Kubernetes feature. A CDI entry is a named device, and it lists what the runtime must change when it creates the container: device files, mounts, hooks and environment variables (CDI tutorial). The driver's kubelet plugin prepares the allocated GPU and answers the kubelet with its CDI names (DRA kubelet API), and the container runtime (containerd or CRI-O) applies the matching entries from the CDI files on the node, so the container starts with that GPU's device files and driver libraries in place. This is a requirement for DRA: NVIDIA lists a container runtime that supports CDI, and is set to use it for DRA-allocated devices, as a prerequisite of its DRA driver (NVIDIA docs).
2How do you install DRA?
You don't install DRA itself. The API (ResourceClaim, ResourceClaimTemplate, DeviceClass) is built into Kubernetes 1.34 and later. What you install is a DRA driver for your hardware: it advertises the devices on each node and allocates the one a claim asks for. For NVIDIA GPUs that's the NVIDIA DRA driver, installed with Helm:
helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidiahelm repo updatehelm install nvidia-dra-driver-gpu nvidia/nvidia-dra-driver-gpu \  --create-namespace --namespace nvidia-dra-driver-gpu \  --set resources.computeDomains.enabled=false \  --set gpuResourcesEnabledOverride=true    # turn on GPU allocation # check that the driver pods are runningkubectl get pods -n nvidia-dra-driver-gpu # the driver's chart creates the DeviceClass gpu.nvidia.com (Step 3)kubectl get deviceclass gpu.nvidia.com
3Before you rely on it

check these points.

  • Kubernetes version: NVIDIA asks for 1.34.2 or later.
  • Container runtime: it must support CDI and be set to use it for DRA-allocated devices (see the CDI point).
  • Chart name: from v0.4.0 the driver moved to kubernetes-sigs and the chart is called dra-driver-nvidia-gpu; use the name that matches your version.
  • Don't run two allocators: if the NVIDIA GPU Operator is installed, use v25.10.0 or later with its device plugin turned off, and label the GPU nodes (for example nvidia.com/dra-kubelet-plugin=true) so the driver runs only there.
  • Old-style requests aren't DRA: a pod that asks for nvidia.com/gpu: 1 under resources.limits still goes through the device plugin path, even with a DRA driver installed.
  • Kueue quotas: if you use Kueue, a quota on nvidia.com/gpu does not count devices that pods claim through DRA unless you map them. See counting DRA devices in Kueue quotas.
  • On EKS: Bottlerocket nodes work with the NVIDIA DRA driver once you turn off the NVIDIA device plugin built into the Bottlerocket NVIDIA images (this needs Bottlerocket 1.63.0 or later, per AWS). Karpenter 1.15 or later needs settings.enableDRA: true (alpha; Karpenter docs). EKS Auto Mode includes the NVIDIA and EFA DRA drivers on Kubernetes 1.36 and later, as AWS announced in November 2026; you create the DeviceClass objects yourself. Some AWS pages written earlier, including the 1.37 release notes, still say Auto Mode doesn't support the NVIDIA DRA driver, so check the current AWS docs.
4How DRA differs from the device plugin

the table compares the two. In short, CDI does not change how DRA finds a GPU. It changes how the found GPU reaches the container: through a standard file the runtime reads, instead of a setting that NVIDIA's runtime has to interpret.

Device plugin DRA
What the scheduler knows A count of free GPUs per node Each GPU's own facts (ResourceSlice) and which one a claim got
Who picks the exact GPU The plugin, when the kubelet asks at container start. The scheduler never knows which one. The scheduler, and it records the pick in the claim
How the container gets the GPU The plugin's reply lists device files and a setting that names the GPU. NVIDIA's container runtime reads that setting. This is the plugin's default in its README for version 0.17.1. The plugin can use CDI instead, and the GPU Operator has done so by default since 25.10. Always CDI: the driver returns CDI names and the runtime applies them
What the runtime must support Nothing special by default. CDI is optional. CDI, required
5When GPUs on a node differ
a node label describes the node as one thing, so a node with one 80 GB and one 24 GB GPU can't be described honestly. DRA checks every GPU separately, so asking for two big GPUs only matches if both are big:
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: two-big-gpusspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpus        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com          count: 2                          # two devices...          selectors:          - cel:                            # ...and each one must pass this check              expression: device.capacity["gpu.nvidia.com"].memory.compareTo(quantity("40Gi")) >= 0
6The network card has its own driver, slices and class

The GPU and the EFA card come from two different drivers, so each has its own objects. The NVIDIA driver publishes the ResourceSlices for the GPUs, and the dranet driver publishes the ResourceSlices for the EFA cards. You never apply a ResourceSlice yourself, because the drivers publish them on each node. The slices expose attributes such as pciBusID, rdmaDevice and resource.kubernetes.io/pcieRoot. On EKS, the AWS-supported aws-dranet Helm chart installs the dranet driver, a DaemonSet that publishes only EFA devices, and the DeviceClass for them. The dranet docs list EKS 1.34 or newer with EFA-enabled worker nodes as the prerequisite (dranet docs on EKS).

The EFA class is efa.networking.k8s.aws. Its rule keeps a device only if it comes from the dranet driver (dra.net) and its PCI device name is "Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA)". A claim names this class to ask for an EFA card, the same way it names gpu.nvidia.com to ask for a GPU. This is the class as the dranet docs show it:

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: DeviceClassmetadata:  name: efa.networking.k8s.awsspec:  selectors:  - cel:      expression: |        device.driver == "dra.net" &&        device.attributes["dra.net"].pciDevice == 'Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA)'
7When several devices must fit together

a GPU and the network card it sends data through should sit on the same PCIe root, so traffic doesn't cross the CPU. A PCIe root (formally the PCIe Root Complex) is the part of the machine that connects the CPU and memory to PCIe devices such as GPUs and network cards, and devices under the same root share one PCIe switch hierarchy (Kubernetes docs, root complex).

Two drivers publish the devices in this example. The NVIDIA GPU DRA driver publishes the GPUs. The dranet driver publishes the network card, which on EKS is an EFA device (its slices and class are in the point "The network card has its own driver, slices and class"). Both publish the standard attribute resource.kubernetes.io/pcieRoot for their devices (dranet docs on EKS), and matchAttribute requires the two devices to share it. The same constraint with requests: ["gpus"] and count: 2 keeps two GPUs on the same PCIe root.

This claim asks for a GPU plus an EFA device that share a PCIe root:

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: gpu-plus-efaspec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        exactly:          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com      - name: efa        exactly:          deviceClassName: efa.networking.k8s.aws   # from the dranet driver      constraints:      - requests: ["gpu", "efa"]                   # these two devices...        matchAttribute: resource.kubernetes.io/pcieRoot   # ...must share a PCIe root
8RDMA, GDR and EFA in plain words

Normally, data sent from one server to another passes through the operating system's network stack, and the CPU handles it. On AWS, NCCL (the library that moves data between GPUs) normally uses that stack and the ENA network driver (AWS docs). RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) skips this: the network card reads and writes the memory of the other server directly, without the other server's operating system or CPU in the middle (NVIDIA guide).

GDR (GPU Direct RDMA) takes the same idea to the GPU. The network card reads and writes GPU memory directly, so the data does not pass through CPU memory (NVIDIA docs). NVIDIA says the main limit is that the GPU and the card must share the same upstream PCIe root (NVIDIA overview). That is why the PCIe root matters for network cards.

EFA (Elastic Fabric Adapter) is AWS's network card for this. Applications talk to it through libfabric, which skips the operating system's network stack, and NCCL reaches libfabric through the aws-ofi-nccl plugin (AWS docs, aws-ofi-nccl). The picture shows the traditional path, the EFA path, the software steps inside the pod, and what Kubernetes adds.

On Kubernetes, the pod must be given an EFA card. EKS offers two ways: the EFA device plugin, which hands out a count of cards, and the EFA DRA driver. Each card goes to one pod only. EFA also needs 2 MiB hugepages, so the pod requests them next to the card (EKS docs). The Kubernetes Networking deep dive shows a full pod that does this. GDR then needs the GPU and the card under one PCIe root, which is what the claim in the point "When several devices must fit together" asks for.

9What the same root is worth

Someone ran the same network speed test twice on AWS machines. The first time, the GPU and the network card sat on the same PCIe root. The second time, they sat on different roots.

On the same root, data went straight between the card and the GPU, at about 11.35 GB/s. On different roots, the data had to detour through the CPU, and the speed dropped to about 6.04 GB/s, roughly half.

The test comes from the dranet project's EKS example. It used p4d.24xlarge machines, which have 8 GPUs and 4 EFA cards spread over 4 PCIe roots. Two machines took part, each with one GPU.

The test was the NCCL all-reduce test, which measures how fast GPUs exchange data. In both runs the machines had the same GPU and the same number of EFA cards.

The detour also switches off GDR (GPU Direct RDMA), the direct path between the network card and the GPU's memory. This is one test on one machine type, so don't read it as a general rule (dranet docs on EKS). The table has the exact roots and speeds:

Run GPU root EFA root Direct path (GDR) Speed the test reported
Same root pci0000:10 pci0000:10 Yes about 11.35 GB/s
Different roots pci0000:10 pci0000:a0 No about 6.04 GB/s
10When pods share a GPU
create one ResourceClaim by name (not a template) and point several pods at it, so they all get the same GPU. How they share it is a driver setting; here NVIDIA's time-slicing (it may need to be turned on in the driver). Time-slicing means the pods take turns on the GPU. There is no memory or compute isolation between them (AWS docs); MIG is what isolates. A claim made from a template is a separate claim for every pod, so template replicas share a GPU only when the driver's consumable shares are on. That is an alpha feature in NVIDIA's driver, and the Kubernetes side is on by default from 1.36 (NVIDIA docs). Without it, each replica gets a whole GPU. Here is one claim and one of the pods that share it:
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaim                # one claim, not a templatemetadata:  name: shared-gpuspec:  devices:    requests:    - name: gpu      exactly:        deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com    config:    - requests: ["gpu"]      opaque:                      # passed to the driver as-is        driver: gpu.nvidia.com        parameters:          apiVersion: resource.nvidia.com/v1beta1          kind: GpuConfig          sharing:            strategy: TimeSlicing---apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: notebook-a                 # notebook-b is the same, with its own namespec:  resourceClaims:  - name: gpu    resourceClaimName: shared-gpu  # by name, so every pod gets the same GPU  containers:  - name: jupyter    image: jupyter/base-notebook:latest    resources:      claims:      - name: gpu
11When you want a fallback

Say a job runs best on one Hopper GPU (such as an H100) but also works on two Ampere GPUs (such as A100s). A plain request can name only one of these. If it asks for Hopper and none is free, the pod waits in Pending, even while two Ampere GPUs sit idle. The API had no way to say which devices are acceptable and in what order of preference (KEP-4816).

The fix is to give a ranked list of acceptable options instead of one request. The list is called firstAvailable, and Kubernetes calls the feature the prioritized list (Kubernetes v1.36 post). The scheduler tries the first option. If it can't be satisfied, it tries the next, and it uses the first option it can satisfy. It works like ordering at a restaurant: "the fish, or else the chicken" (our comparison).

The catch is that the pod may get one GPU or two, so the application has to cope with either, for example by reading how many GPUs it was given at startup. Here is one Hopper GPU, or else two Ampere GPUs:

apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: h100-or-two-a100spec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: gpu        firstAvailable:                 # try these in order        - name: one-hopper          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com          selectors:          - cel:              expression: device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].architecture == "Hopper"        - name: two-ampere              # only if no Hopper GPU is free          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com          count: 2          selectors:          - cel:              expression: device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].architecture == "Ampere"

Different GPUs in one server, and MIG

Scenario. A research lab runs on-prem servers that mix GPU models, and wants to split one 80 GB H100 so several notebooks can share it. Node labels, the device plugin's count and DRA each see these servers differently, and only some of them can tell the GPUs apart.

First, what MIG is. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) is a feature built into NVIDIA GPUs from the Ampere generation on, such as the A100 and H100 (NVIDIA GPU Operator docs). It cuts one physical GPU into isolated slices, up to seven on an A100 or H100, each with its own memory and its own share of the compute units. Kubernetes can then hand each slice to a different pod.

A slice is named by its size, for example 3g.40gb: the number before the g is how many of the GPU's seven compute slices it gets, and the number before gb is its memory in GB.

Now the same lab server, seen through each advertising method:

What the picture shows. Two servers, and what each advertising method reports for them.

1The mixed server
one A100 (80 GB) and one T4 (16 GB) in the same machine. Cloud GPU instances always have identical GPUs, but on-prem and lab servers can mix models.
2Labels on the mixed server
a node label holds one value, so nvidia.com/gpu.product and nvidia.com/gpu.memory can't describe both GPUs honestly.
3Count on the mixed server
nvidia.com/gpu: 2. A pod asking for one GPU can get either the A100 or the T4.
4DRA on the mixed server
each GPU is its own entry, so a claim for "at least 40Gi" can only get the A100.
5The MIG server
one 80 GB H100 cut into four slices, named as in the slice-name picture: one 3g.40gb, one 2g.20gb and two 1g.10gb. No slice is a whole GPU, and each one is advertised on its own.
6MIG is not another way to advertise GPUs.
It changes what the GPU is, and the mechanisms you already know then report slices instead of whole GPUs:
  • Count (device plugin): each slice is counted and handed to one container, like a GPU. The single strategy calls every slice nvidia.com/gpu and needs them all the same size; the mixed strategy gives each size its own count, such as nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 2. Either way the layout is set in advance.
  • Labels (GPU Feature Discovery): with mixed, the node gets labels per slice size, so pods can still choose a node by what it holds. With single, the product label gains the slice profile instead.
  • DRA: each slice is its own device under the mig.nvidia.com class, with a profile attribute and its own memory, so a claim can ask for a profile or a minimum size. The class's device-type check, explained in Step 5 of the Dynamic Resource Allocation section, is what keeps these slices out of whole-GPU claims.
  • Reserving works the same: labels choose the node, and the count or the claim reserves one slice on it. The difference is that the unit is a slice.
Going deeper3 points
  • Do you need to install anything? Yes, on the Kubernetes side. The card has MIG built in, but Kubernetes sees no slices until something creates them and something else advertises them. These are separate jobs with separate pieces:
Job Who does it Needed?
Cut the GPU into slices (switch MIG on, create the layout) MIG Manager, part of the GPU Operator. NVIDIA's mig-parted tool does the same by hand on a host. Always. The device plugin and DRA only advertise slices that already exist (the alpha DynamicMIG feature is the exception).
Advertise the slices as a count (nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 2) Device plugin, with a MIG strategy The classic path.
Advertise each slice as a device (class mig.nvidia.com) DRA driver, with the device plugin turned off The DRA path, instead of the device plugin.
Label the slices (nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb.count, .memory) GPU Feature Discovery Optional. Only if pods must choose a node by slice size.
Mark the node as having an NVIDIA card Node Feature Discovery A helper only. GPU Feature Discovery builds on it.

Installing it (device plugin path). Nothing is installed on the card itself. You need a MIG-capable GPU (on AWS, MIG is available on the P-family instance types with A100 and H100 GPUs, per AWS's MIG on EKS guide) and the NVIDIA GPU Operator, which installs the driver, device plugin, NFD and GFD. Install it with a MIG strategy, which also deploys the MIG manager, then label a node with the layout you want:

helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidiahelm repo updatehelm install --wait --generate-name \  -n gpu-operator --create-namespace \  nvidia/gpu-operator \  --set mig.strategy=mixed # "balanced" on an 80 GB H100: one 3g.40gb, one 2g.20gb, two 1g.10gbkubectl label node gpu-node-1 nvidia.com/mig.config=all-balanced --overwrite

The strategy only decides how slices are advertised; it does not switch MIG on. The MIG manager does that when it sees the layout label: it stops the operator's GPU pods on that node, turns MIG mode on, cuts the slices and restarts them. Nothing else may be using the GPUs while it runs, so move pods that use them off first, and some cloud nodes need a reboot (see NVIDIA's GPU Operator MIG page). To change the layout later, label the node again, for example nvidia.com/mig.config=all-1g.10gb. Pin a chart version in production.

With DRA instead: install the Operator with its device plugin turned off and the DRA driver on, as in the Dynamic Resource Allocation section, and set the layout with the same node label. Then restart the DRA driver pod so it discovers the slices the MIG manager created.

Check (MIG): kubectl get node gpu-node-1 --show-labels | tr ',' '\n' | grep mig, and wait for nvidia.com/mig.config.state=success.

  • Newer versions of NVIDIA's DRA driver can also create MIG slices on demand for a claim and remove them when the claim is released (an alpha feature called DynamicMIG), instead of relying on a fixed layout.
  • Asking for a MIG slice, with the device plugin and with DRA:
# Device plugin, "mixed" MIG strategy: ask for a slice size by resource nameapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: notebook-smallspec:  containers:  - name: jupyter    image: jupyter/base-notebook:latest    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1---# DRA: ask for a MIG slice by profileapiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1kind: ResourceClaimTemplatemetadata:  name: small-mig-slicespec:  spec:    devices:      requests:      - name: mig        exactly:          deviceClassName: mig.nvidia.com          selectors:          - cel:              expression: device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].profile == "1g.10gb"---apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: notebook-small-draspec:  resourceClaims:  - name: mig    resourceClaimTemplateName: small-mig-slice  containers:  - name: jupyter    image: jupyter/base-notebook:latest    resources:      claims:      - name: mig
Deep dive 03 · 10 sections

When one scheduler isn't enough

  1. Built-in plugins, and what a second scheduler changes
  2. Configuring a scheduler: stages, plugins and profiles
  3. How a Pod finds its scheduler
  4. Gang scheduling
  5. Topology bin-packing
  6. Queueing and fair sharing
  7. Hardware-aware scheduling
  8. Volcano vs. Kueue
  9. The landscape
  10. What every scheduler relies on

The default scheduler places pods one at a time and knows nothing about jobs, teams or GPU topology. This deep dive covers the problems that pushed the ecosystem toward Kueue, Volcano, KAI and YuniKorn, and how to choose between them.

Built-in plugins, and what a second scheduler changes

Scenario. After learning in the scheduler deep dive that the fit check is done by "a plugin", the team wants the full list: which plugins run by default, what each one does, which ones filter and which ones score, and with what weight. Then the architect asks the follow-up: if we add a second scheduler, do these plugins still apply, and what can go wrong when two schedulers share one cluster?

What the picture shows. Every scheduling decision runs through the same stages, left to right, and each stage is made of plugins.

1Pending pod
its spec.schedulerName decides which of the three lanes handles it. Exactly one scheduler handles each pod.
2The stages (column headers)
  • Queue sort: decides which pending pod is considered next.
  • Filter: removes nodes that can't run the pod (Phase 1).
  • PostFilter: runs only when no node passed; this is where preemption happens.
  • Score: ranks the nodes that passed (Phase 2), each plugin's score multiplied by its weight.
  • Reserve / Permit: holds the chosen node's volumes and devices while the decision is finalized.
  • Bind: writes the chosen node into the pod (spec.nodeName).
3Blue lane, default-scheduler
the built-in kube-scheduler. On EKS it runs on the AWS-managed control plane, and every plugin shown is built in and on by default. The Score box lists the default weights (×1, ×2, ×3).
4Amber lane, a second kube-scheduler with your own profile
the same program and the same plugins, run as your own Deployment (the full example is in Appendix A). Only the highlighted Score box differs: InterPodAffinity weighted ×100, and NodeResourcesFit switched to MostAllocated (bin-packing).
5Teal lane, a replacement scheduler (Volcano, KAI, YuniKorn)
a different program that works in sessions, with its own actions (steps such as allocate or reclaim) and plugins: queues and PodGroups for gang scheduling, queue-based reclaim instead of plain preemption, GPU and network topology scoring, and binding a whole job together. It reuses kube-scheduler's filter checks (through its predicates plugin), so taints and affinity still mean the same thing, but the scoring plugins and weights above don't apply to its pods.
6Grey bar, shared by all three
the same nodes and the same API server. The schedulers don't coordinate with each other.

The built-in plugins (all on by default; "–" means the plugin doesn't take part in that stage):

Plugin What it does Filter Score weight
PrioritySort Orders the queue: higher-priority pods are scheduled first – –
SchedulingGates Holds back pods that still have schedulingGates set – –
NodeUnschedulable Skips cordoned nodes (spec.unschedulable) ✓ –
NodeName Honours a pod that already names its node ✓ –
NodeResourcesFit CPU, memory, GPU and other resources: does it fit? Then LeastAllocated scoring ✓ 1
BalancedResourceAllocation Prefers nodes where CPU and memory use stay balanced – 1
ImageLocality Prefers nodes that already have the pod's images – 1
NodeAffinity nodeSelector and required node affinity (filter); preferred node affinity (score) ✓ 2
InterPodAffinity Required pod affinity / anti-affinity (filter); preferred (score) ✓ 2
PodTopologySpread DoNotSchedule spread constraints (filter); ScheduleAnyway (score) ✓ 2
TaintToleration NoSchedule taints (filter); prefers fewer untolerated PreferNoSchedule taints (score) ✓ 3
NodePorts Rejects nodes where the pod's hostPort is taken ✓ –
VolumeRestrictions Volume conflicts, such as a ReadWriteOncePod volume already in use ✓ –
NodeVolumeLimits The node's limit on attached volumes (for example EBS) ✓ –
VolumeZone The volume's zone must match the node's zone ✓ –
VolumeBinding PVCs can be bound or provisioned on this node; reserves them ✓ –
DynamicResources DRA device claims (GPUs and other devices) can be satisfied; reserves them ✓ –
DefaultPreemption PostFilter: evicts lower-priority pods when nothing fits – –
DefaultBinder Bind: writes spec.nodeName – –

From pod spec to plugin: you never write a plugin's name in a pod. You write a field, and the plugin that reads it does the work. The diagram and the table above use plugin names; this is how they map to what you write:

You write in the pod spec The plugin that reads it
resources.requests NodeResourcesFit, BalancedResourceAllocation
nodeSelector, affinity.nodeAffinity NodeAffinity
affinity.podAffinity / podAntiAffinity InterPodAffinity
topologySpreadConstraints PodTopologySpread
tolerations TaintToleration
nodeName NodeName
ports[].hostPort NodePorts
priorityClassName PrioritySort, DefaultPreemption
volumes (PVCs) VolumeBinding, VolumeZone, VolumeRestrictions, NodeVolumeLimits
resourceClaims (DRA) DynamicResources
the image in containers[].image ImageLocality
schedulingGates SchedulingGates

What a second scheduler changes:

7One pod, one scheduler
a pod is handled only by the scheduler named in its schedulerName. The other schedulers' plugins never see it.
8Same program, different profile (amber lane)
you can change weights, switch the scoring strategy, or disable plugins (for example turn off ImageLocality). One kube-scheduler process can even serve several profiles, each under its own schedulerName.
9Different program (teal lane)
you get features the built-in plugins don't have, such as gang scheduling, queues and GPU topology. In return, its pods follow its rules, not the table above.
10No coordination
two schedulers can pick the same free space at the same moment, because each one only sees its own decisions in flight. The kubelet then rejects the pod that arrives second (OutOfcpu / OutOfmemory) and its controller creates a new one. The usual fix is to give each scheduler its own nodes, with taints and node labels, or to send all pods of one kind (for example all GPU pods) to a single scheduler.
11Preemption crosses the boundary
the default scheduler's DefaultPreemption can evict pods placed by your scheduler if they have lower priority, and the other way round. Use PriorityClasses consistently across both.
12Autoscalers
Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter decide whether to add nodes by simulating the default scheduler's rules. Check whether yours acts on pods with a custom schedulerName at all, and remember that custom filters it doesn't know about can lead to nodes being added that your scheduler then won't use.

Configuring a scheduler: stages, plugins and profiles

Scenario. The platform team wants pods packed onto fewer nodes so idle nodes can be removed, and a gang plugin for training jobs. They open a KubeSchedulerConfiguration and find profiles, plugins, pluginConfig, a dozen stage names and two different weight fields. Before changing anything, they need to know what each part controls.

What the picture shows. The stages every pod passes through inside kube-scheduler, the plugins the default scheduler puts at each one, and the three parts of the configuration file that control them.

1The stages (extension points)
kube-scheduler is a pipeline of fixed stages, numbered 1 to 10 in the picture. Each stage is filled with plugins, and filtering, scoring and binding are just the best-known stages.
2preEnqueue and queueSort (1, 2)
decide whether a pod may enter the queue at all (SchedulingGates holds it back until its gates are removed) and in what order waiting pods are taken (PrioritySort: higher priority first).
3preFilter and filter (3)
filtering. Each plugin removes nodes that break one rule: resources, ports, taints, affinity, topology spread, volumes, devices.
4postFilter (4)
runs only when no node passed. DefaultPreemption looks for lower-priority pods to evict to make room.
5preScore and score (5)
scoring. The only stage where plugins have a weight, which says how much each plugin counts in the total.
6One plugin, several stages
NodeResourcesFit filters ("does it fit?") and scores ("how full would the node be?"). NodeAffinity, TaintToleration, InterPodAffinity and PodTopologySpread do both too: their required or hard rules filter, their preferred or soft rules score.

Note: why NodeResourcesFit is at both filter and score

It answers two different questions about the same numbers: the node's allocatable CPU and memory minus the requests of the pods already there.

Stage Question Answer
Filter Does the pod fit on this node at all? Yes or no. If its requests exceed what's left, the node is removed ("Insufficient cpu").
Score Of the nodes where it fits, how good is each one? A number from 0 to 100, based on how full the node would be after placing the pod.

For example, a pod requests 1 CPU and three nodes each have 4 CPU allocatable:

Node Already requested Filter Score with LeastAllocated (default)
A 3.5 CPU ✗ only 0.5 left –
B 2 CPU ✓ lower (would be 75% full)
C 0.5 CPU ✓ higher (would be 37.5% full)
  • The filter removes A. Scoring then prefers C, because LeastAllocated favors emptier nodes and so spreads pods out.
  • Switch the strategy to MostAllocated and the same plugin prefers B instead: it fills nodes up (bin-packing) so empty nodes can be removed. That's why the fit check itself is "not bin-packing": the filter only says yes or no, and packing versus spreading is decided at the score stage.
  • Why one plugin and not two: both stages need the same calculation, so one plugin computes it once and uses it twice. NodeAffinity, TaintToleration, InterPodAffinity and PodTopologySpread work the same way: they filter on their hard rules and score on their soft ones.
7reserve and permit (6, 7)
reserve holds the chosen node's resources (volumes, devices) while binding is in progress. Permit can approve, deny or make a pod wait; nothing runs there by default, but gang plugins use it to hold each pod until its whole group has a place.
8The binding cycle (8 to 10)
preBind prepares what the pod needs (for example provisioning its volume), bind writes the chosen node into the pod, postBind cleans up. This part runs in the background, so the scheduler can start on the next pod.
9profiles[]
one entry per scheduler name. A pod picks one with schedulerName, and one kube-scheduler process can serve several.
10plugins
per stage, which plugins are enabled or disabled, and under score, each plugin's weight.
11pluginConfig
per plugin, its own settings (args), which change how it calculates rather than whether it runs.
Going deeper5 points
  • Reading a real configuration: in this example, plugins says BalancedResourceAllocation's score counts double, and pluginConfig says which resources it compares when it measures balance. BalancedResourceAllocation is already on by default, so listing it under enabled only changes its weight; it doesn't add a second copy.
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler     # profiles[]: one scheduler  plugins:                             # plugins: which run, per stage    score:      enabled:      - name: BalancedResourceAllocation        weight: 2                      # counts double vs. other scoring plugins (default 1)  pluginConfig:                        # pluginConfig: how a plugin calculates  - name: BalancedResourceAllocation    args:      resources:                       # which resources to keep in balance      - name: cpu        weight: 1      - name: memory        weight: 1      - name: nvidia.com/gpu           # e.g. also balance GPUs        weight: 1
The weight in… What it weighs
plugins.score.enabled[].weight This plugin against the other scoring plugins
pluginConfig[].args.resources[].weight One resource against the others, inside this plugin's own calculation

Note: two plugins tuned in one file

The fit check section shows NodeResourcesFit's settings, and the BalancedResourceAllocation section shows that plugin's. They're pieces of the same kind of file, each showing only the plugin it's about. A real file that tunes both has one profile (one scheduler) with one pluginConfig list holding two entries, one per plugin:

apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler   # the only profile  plugins:    score:      enabled:      - name: BalancedResourceAllocation        weight: 2                    # this plugin's vote counts double  pluginConfig:  - name: NodeResourcesFit           # entry 1: how the fit plugin scores    args:      scoringStrategy:        type: LeastAllocated         # spread (default); MostAllocated = bin-pack        resources:                   # what counts when judging how full a node is        - name: cpu          weight: 1        - name: memory          weight: 1  - name: BalancedResourceAllocation # entry 2: what the balancer compares    args:      resources:                     # what it tries to keep even with each other      - name: cpu        weight: 1      - name: memory        weight: 1      - name: nvidia.com/gpu        weight: 1
  • How to read it: profiles: is a list, and each - schedulerName: item is one scheduler. Under it sit that scheduler's plugins and pluginConfig. pluginConfig is a list too, and each - name: is one plugin's settings.
  • Both plugins have a resources list, but they mean different things: for NodeResourcesFit it's what counts when judging how full or empty a node is; for BalancedResourceAllocation it's what it tries to keep even.
  • A second scheduler would be a second - schedulerName: item under profiles, with its own plugins and pluginConfig.

  • There isn't an entry for every plugin:

    • you only list what you change; everything else keeps its default (on, with its default weight and settings);
    • only about half the plugins have settings at all, for example NodeResourcesFit (scoringStrategy), BalancedResourceAllocation (resources), InterPodAffinity, PodTopologySpread (default spread rules), NodeAffinity (an extra node filter for every pod), VolumeBinding and DefaultPreemption; others, like TaintToleration or ImageLocality, can only be switched on or off and weighted;
    • there's at most one pluginConfig entry per plugin in each profile, and each profile can have its own.

      Note: different scoring for different pods

      A pod can't pick plugins directly: every enabled scoring plugin runs for every pod, and the scores are added up. What a pod can pick is the profile, through schedulerName. So you create two profiles with different scoring, and each pod chooses one. For example, one profile without BalancedResourceAllocation and one without NodeResourcesFit's score:

      apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: fit-scorer                # profile 1  plugins:    score:      disabled:      - name: BalancedResourceAllocation   # turned off for this profile's pods- schedulerName: balance-scorer            # profile 2  plugins:    score:      disabled:      - name: NodeResourcesFit             # turned off at the SCORE stage only---# Each pod picks its profileapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: pod-aspec:  schedulerName: fit-scorer                # scored without BalancedResourceAllocation  containers:  - name: app    image: my-company/app:1.0---apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: pod-bspec:  schedulerName: balance-scorer            # scored without NodeResourcesFit  containers:  - name: app    image: my-company/app:1.0
      • disabled under score only affects scoring: NodeResourcesFit still does the fit check at the filter stage for balance-scorer pods. Turning it off there would let pods land on nodes they don't fit on.
      • The other scoring plugins still run (ImageLocality, NodeAffinity, TaintToleration and others); you only removed one plugin from the sum. To make one plugin dominate instead of removing another, give it a high weight in that profile.
      • A pod's own spec already decides some of it: NodeAffinity and InterPodAffinity only add points when the pod has preferred rules, so a pod without them gets nothing from those plugins anyway.
      • On EKS you can't add profiles to the default scheduler, so you'd run these two profiles in your own kube-scheduler, as in the second-scheduler appendix. One process can serve both names.

  • Turning off a filter is rarely a good idea: without TaintToleration, for example, pods would ignore every taint. Custom setups usually add plugins, such as a gang plugin at permit.

Note: one file, several schedulers, and other schedulers' formats

  • kube-scheduler reads a KubeSchedulerConfiguration: the default scheduler, and any second scheduler that is just another copy of kube-scheduler (like the one in the appendix), reads this file at startup through --config. It decides which plugins run, their weights and their settings. Without a file, the built-in defaults apply.
  • One file can define several schedulers: the file holds a list of profiles, each with its own schedulerName and plugin setup, all served by one kube-scheduler process. A pod chooses a profile with schedulerName, exactly as it would choose a separate scheduler:
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler        # normal behavior- schedulerName: bin-packing-scheduler    # same process, different scoring  pluginConfig:  - name: NodeResourcesFit    args:      scoringStrategy:        type: MostAllocated               # pack nodes full instead of spreading
  • So a "second scheduler" can be a second profile: no second program is needed, as long as you control the scheduler's configuration. On EKS you control only one of the default scheduler's scoring settings, not its profiles or plugin weights, which is why the appendix runs a separate copy.
  • Other schedulers have their own formats: the idea is the same, but the files differ.
    • Volcano: a ConfigMap (volcano-scheduler.conf) listing the scheduling actions to run (such as enqueue, allocate, backfill) and the plugins in priority tiers (gang, drf, proportion and others).
    • YuniKorn: a ConfigMap (yunikorn-configs) that mainly describes the queue hierarchy, with quotas and policies per queue.
    • KAI: settings through its Helm values and its own custom resources (queues, scheduling shards).
    • Kueue (a queue in front of a scheduler, not a scheduler): its own configuration file plus custom resources such as ClusterQueue and LocalQueue.
  • Do other schedulers use these stages? Only schedulers built on kube-scheduler's framework:
    • the same stages: the default scheduler, any second copy or profile of kube-scheduler, and schedulers built from the scheduler-plugins project (such as coscheduling, which hooks into permit);
    • Volcano and KAI (both descend from kube-batch) work in sessions: on each cycle they snapshot the cluster and run a list of actions in order (for example enqueue, allocate, preempt, reclaim, backfill; KAI adds consolidation), and their plugins plug decision functions into those actions, which is how they place a whole job at once;
    • YuniKorn runs allocation cycles over a hierarchy of queues, connected to Kubernetes through a "shim";
    • the Fargate scheduler is run by AWS and can't be inspected or configured;
    • Kueue isn't a scheduler: it decides when a job may start, and its pods are then placed by a normal scheduler.
  • What every scheduler shares anyway: most reuse kube-scheduler's node checks (resources, taints, affinity), so a taint or a nodeSelector means the same thing whoever places the pod, and every scheduler ends by binding the pod to a node through the API server, after which the kubelet takes over.

How a Pod finds its scheduler

Scenario. A team runs one EKS cluster where some pods run on EC2 nodes and others on Fargate. Nobody on the team ever sets schedulerName by hand, yet the staging pods always end up on Fargate and everything else on EC2. A new engineer asks how Kubernetes knows which scheduler should handle each pod.

What the picture shows. How a pod is routed to the right scheduler, using Fargate as the example.

1Workflow, step 1 (user submission and Fargate profile)
you create a Fargate profile in AWS that says "any pod in the staging namespace with the label type: serverless runs on Fargate". Then you submit an ordinary pod YAML to the API server.
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5kind: ClusterConfigmetadata:  name: prod  region: us-east-1fargateProfiles:- name: staging-serverless  selectors:  - namespace: staging    labels:      type: serverless
2Step 2 (EKS control plane, mutating webhook)
the EKS mutating webhook sees the pod, checks it against your profiles, and on a match injects schedulerName: fargate-scheduler into the pod spec, before scheduling starts. Pods that don't match keep the standard spec.
# the pod as stored after the webhook mutates itapiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: web  namespace: staging  labels:    type: serverlessspec:  schedulerName: fargate-scheduler   # injected by EKS, not written by you  containers:  - name: web    image: my-company/web:1.0
3Step 3 (scheduling phase, the result)
the modified pod is picked up by the AWS Fargate scheduler.
4How pods reach the right scheduler
the API server doesn't route pods; it only stores them. Every scheduler watches for unscheduled pods (no nodeName yet) and takes only the ones whose schedulerName matches its own name, like separate buckets. What each scheduler then does with a pod is set by its own configuration; see Configuring a scheduler.
  • Bucket A (default-scheduler): the standard kube-scheduler on the control plane places these on EC2 nodes.
  • Bucket B (fargate-scheduler): the Fargate scheduler takes only these, ignores bucket A, and starts a dedicated micro-VM for each pod.
Going deeper3 points
  • Ray (through KubeRay) is another two-scheduler setup.
  • Kubernetes places and restarts the Ray head and worker pods, and Ray's own scheduler places tasks and actors inside them.
  • That suits Python teams well, but capacity accounting and debugging now span two layers.

Gang scheduling

Scenario. A research team submits a distributed PyTorch job with 8 GPU workers. The cluster only has room for 6, so the default scheduler starts 6 workers and leaves 2 Pending. The 6 running workers sit idle for hours, burning expensive GPU time while they wait for teammates that may never arrive. How do you stop that from happening?

What the picture shows. Gang scheduling (all-or-nothing) and why the default scheduler can't do it.

1The problem
standard Kubernetes schedules pods one at a time. In distributed training, all 8 workers must start together to run collective operations such as all-reduce. If only 6 fit, those 6 start and wait, wasting GPU time.
2The custom solution
a gang scheduler won't start any of the job's pods until the cluster has room for all of them.
3Can the standard scheduler do it?
Not out of the box: it has no all-or-nothing start. A native one is beta in 1.37 but off by default (see the note after "Going deeper").
  • The workaround: you calculate cluster capacity yourself and make sure at least 8 GPU slots are free before you run kubectl apply.
  • The failure point: in a shared cluster, a coworker's 1-GPU pod submitted one second before yours can take a slot. Your job starts with 7 workers, hangs, and wastes money. Standard Kubernetes can't say "hold these 7 slots until the 8th is free."
4Best at this
Volcano and KAI are built specifically for this kind of atomic scheduling.
Going deeper3 points

The reason is the rendezvous barrier: distributed PyTorch workers wait until every rank has joined, so 7 of 8 workers will sit on their GPUs forever. The options sit at different layers:

  • the coscheduling plugin: a PodGroup with minMember and a timeout, inside kube-scheduler;
  • Kueue: decides at the job level whether a job may start;
  • KAI or Volcano: replace the scheduler.

Upstream Kubernetes now has a native Workload API with gang scheduling: alpha in 1.35, rewritten in 1.36 and beta in 1.37, still off by default (see the note below). Model-parallel inference has the same property: if one shard's pod is missing or dies, the whole replica is down, so it needs all-or-nothing scheduling and group restarts too.

Note: Kubernetes' own gang scheduling, and where EKS stands

A PodGroup is a Kubernetes object that holds a set of pods and carries one scheduling policy for them. The policy is either basic, which schedules the pods one by one as usual, or gang, which is all-or-nothing: if fewer than minCount pods can be placed, none are bound (gang scheduling docs). So a PodGroup is the group, and gang scheduling is one rule you can set on it. The same group can also carry a rule to stay in one rack and settings for how it can be preempted. A Workload is the template that a controller, such as the Job controller, copies into PodGroups.

Status (checked November 2026). The Workload and PodGroup APIs and gang scheduling began as alpha in 1.35 and were rewritten in 1.36. They are beta in 1.37, and off by default: the GenericWorkload feature gate must be enabled on the API server, the controller manager and the scheduler (1.37 release post). The topology rule for a group, groups of groups, and the Job controller's automatic creation of groups are still alpha in 1.37.

On EKS. EKS has offered Kubernetes 1.37 since October 2026. AWS's 1.37 release notes do not mention these features, and AWS's list of control plane settings you can change contains no feature gates. So there is no documented way to turn this on in EKS today. The designs in this blog use Kueue, or a second scheduler, for gangs instead. Check the AWS release notes for newer versions before relying on this.

Don't confuse it with the older PodGroup. The scheduler-plugins project, mentioned above as the coscheduling plugin, has its own object with the same name. Pods join it through a label, and it is built only for all-or-nothing starts. It is a separate project.

On a Job. The Job controller can create the group for you, but this is a separate alpha feature (since 1.36) with its own gate, WorkloadWithJob, on top of GenericWorkload (Workload API docs). You opt in with .spec.scheduling.schedulingPolicy.gang on the Job. If you leave out minCount, it defaults to the Job's parallelism, so every pod must fit. The disruptionMode setting decides whether preemption may take the Job's pods one at a time (single) or only as a whole (all). After creation the .spec.scheduling block cannot change, except minCount (1.37 release post).

Topology bin-packing

Scenario. A training job's two pods talk to each other constantly. The default scheduler puts them on two different GPU nodes because both nodes look "least allocated". Now every gradient exchange crosses the network instead of NVLink, and the training run takes several times longer than expected.

What the picture shows. Bin-packing for GPU topology: keeping chatty pods on the same fast interconnect.

1The problem
the default LeastAllocated scoring spreads pods across nodes. In ML that's bad for performance, because pod-to-pod traffic then goes over the much slower network.
2The goal
a scheduler that uses MostAllocated (bin-packing) to put the pods on the same physical GPU node.
3The benefit
pods can talk over NVLink, which has an order of magnitude or more bandwidth than the node's network, cutting training time sharply.
4Topology-aware bin-packing
goes further and looks at how the GPUs are wired. On an NVIDIA HGX system, it places pods that talk to each other on GPUs linked by NVLink (fast) rather than only PCIe (slow).
5Can the standard scheduler do it?
Partly.
  • The workaround: a required podAffinity with matchLabels: job: my-training-run and topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname, which forces pod 2 onto the node where pod 1 landed. 
    apiVersion: v1kind: Podmetadata:  name: trainer-2  labels:    job: my-training-runspec:  affinity:    podAffinity:      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:      - labelSelector:          matchLabels:            job: my-training-run        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname   # same node as the other trainers  containers:  - name: trainer    image: my-company/trainer:2.0    resources:      limits:        nvidia.com/gpu: 1
  • The failure point: it only works if pod 1 finds a home first, and writing these rules for 100 pods is a management nightmare. A custom scheduler does it automatically for the whole batch.
6Newer Kubernetes (alpha)
since 1.36 you can put a topology rule on a PodGroup, such as "all these pods in one rack", and the scheduler keeps the whole group inside one such domain. If no domain can hold the whole group, none of the pods start. It is still alpha in 1.37 and off by default (the TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling feature gate). A separate 1.37 alpha adds several levels, for example one zone for the whole job and one rack for each part. It builds on PodGroups, so the EKS caveat in the gang scheduling note applies here too.
7Best at this
the KAI Scheduler, NVIDIA's open-source scheduler with topology-aware placement for GPU fabrics.
Going deeper3 points

Placement depends on how the model is split:

  • Tensor parallelism splits every layer and exchanges results constantly. Keep it inside one node on NVLink/NVSwitch.
  • Pipeline parallelism splits by layers and only hands activations across once per stage, so it tolerates the slower links between nodes.
  • Hybrid: tensor parallelism inside nodes and pipeline parallelism between them is the common setup.

Even inside one server, not every GPU pair may share the same NVLink group. nvidia-smi topo -m shows it, and a job may rightly wait in the queue rather than start on badly connected GPUs.

Queueing and fair sharing

Scenario. In a shared research cluster, one user submits 100 training jobs on Monday morning and every GPU is taken. Other teams' jobs fail immediately with quota errors instead of waiting their turn, and over the weekend the GPUs reserved for one team sit idle while another team is desperate for capacity.

What the picture shows. Queueing and fair sharing, and where namespace quotas fall short.

1The problem
one greedy user can lock everyone else out of a shared cluster.
2Priority queues
queueing systems such as Kueue (a queue controller in front of the scheduler, not a scheduler itself) let you define resource flavors and workload priorities, so jobs wait in line instead of failing.
3Preemption
a high-priority inference pod serving a live model can evict a low-priority research training pod when GPUs run short. The default scheduler can already do this with PriorityClasses; what the custom tools add is preemption that understands quotas and whole jobs.
4Fair sharing
when the cluster is idle one team can use all of it, but as soon as another team submits work, the first team's over-quota pods are preempted to give the second team its fair share.
5Can the standard scheduler do it?
Only with static quotas.
  • The workaround: a ResourceQuota per namespace, for example 10 GPUs for the marketing team. 
    apiVersion: v1kind: ResourceQuotametadata:  name: gpu-quota  namespace: marketingspec:  hard:    requests.nvidia.com/gpu: "10"   # static: idle GPUs can't be lent to others
  • The failure point: these quotas are static. If marketing isn't using its 10 GPUs, no one else can borrow them. And a team that hits its limit gets an immediate error; the pod doesn't queue and start later when space opens up.
6Best at this
Apache YuniKorn and Run:ai (via KAI), and Kueue, covered below.
Going deeper6 points

In Kueue terms:

  • ClusterQueues hold each team's nominal quota and borrowing limit.
  • Teams submit to LocalQueues.
  • A cohort lends idle quota between teams and takes it back by preemption when its owner needs it.

WorkloadPriorityClasses decide admission order, and fair sharing favors teams that have used less recently. Hard namespace ResourceQuotas can't do any of this: idle GPUs in one namespace never help another team's queue.

Three defaults decide how this behaves:

  • Queue order: a ClusterQueue's queueing strategy is BestEffortFIFO unless you change it. A workload that cannot be admitted does not hold up newer ones that fit. With StrictFIFO, an older workload that cannot be admitted blocks everything behind it (Kueue docs).
  • Borrowing: by default, queues in a cohort borrow first come, first served. Fair sharing is switched on in Kueue's own configuration, and Design 17 shows how. A queue also gets its quota back by preemption only if reclaimWithinCohort is set. The default is Never, and the example below sets it (preemption docs).
  • Priority: a WorkloadPriorityClass sets the workload's place in Kueue's queue and in its preemption decisions. It does not change the pods' own priority. If a job names both a WorkloadPriorityClass and a PriorityClass, each applies to its own part (Kueue docs).

Note: counting DRA devices in Kueue quotas

A Kueue quota counts only what it is told to count. A pod that asks for GPUs the old way (nvidia.com/gpu: 2 in its limits) is counted under that name. A pod that asks through DRA writes no GPU count at all, so a quota on nvidia.com/gpu has nothing to count unless Kueue is set up to account for DRA devices. The Kueue DRA docs describe two ways to do that:

  • Claim templates: the pod points at a ResourceClaimTemplate. In its configuration you map each DeviceClass to a quota name (deviceClassMappings), and Kueue charges the template's count against it.
