  • Proxy runs first: most decisions (mixture weights, clip values, filtering thresholds) are made with small models and short runs, then confirmed at full scale. The platform makes "same recipe, smaller model" a one-line change.
  • Determinism where possible: fixed seeds, pinned images and recorded data order make ablations meaningful. Full determinism isn't achievable across GPU kernels, so run important comparisons with two seeds.
  • Cost per experiment is a first-class metric: GPU hours, rollout tokens and the share of rollouts that carried signal, shown next to the results.

Evaluation and final model behavior

Scenario. A new recipe wins on every benchmark and is promoted. Within a week, users notice it's twice as verbose, refuses more borderline requests and hedges on simple questions. None of the benchmarks measured that.

The design.

  • Capability suites: reasoning, code, tool use and domain tasks, with held-out verifiers different from the training rewards, run every N steps and on every candidate checkpoint.
  • Behavior suites: response length distribution, refusal rate on borderline prompts, over-refusal on safe prompts, instruction-following precision, tone and style classifiers, honesty and calibration checks.
  • Safety suites: harmful-request refusals, jailbreak resistance, and the red-team set, owned by the safety team and versioned.
  • Regression checks against the previous release: a candidate must not regress more than an agreed margin on any suite, not just improve on average.
  • Human review: a fixed weekly sample of outputs per candidate, blind-compared against the current release.
Going deeper2 points
  • Decontaminate eval sets against all training data, including SFT mixtures and RL prompts, and keep a private test set nobody trains on.
  • Promote through the registry with gates (see From training to serving): a recipe's output only reaches users after its eval results are attached and approved.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Scenario. The team wants better recipes, faster, starting this quarter.

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, reproducibility: recipe files in Git, the launcher, run IDs and tracking, standard eval suites on every checkpoint. Nothing new about the training itself, but every result becomes comparable.
  • Phase 2, RL platform: RayJob-based RL with separate rollout, reward and training components, sandboxed verifiers, health signals and alerts, frequent checkpoints.
  • Phase 3, efficiency: one-step off-policy and then asynchronous rollouts with staleness limits, dynamic sampling, partial rollouts, mismatch corrections.
  • Phase 4, distillation and pipelines: on-policy distillation, multi-stage pipelines (SFT → RL → distill) launched as one recipe.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Config-driven recipes over free-form notebooks: less flexibility for one-off exploration, in exchange for runs that can be reproduced, diffed and compared.
  • Asynchronous RL: much higher GPU utilization, at the cost of off-policy corrections and one more source of instability to monitor.
  • Several frameworks (TRL for SFT and small RL, verl for large RL): the right tool for each scale, at the cost of keeping their configs and metrics aligned.
  • Sandboxed rewards: slower than running tests in-process, but a reward function is exactly where a model will learn to exploit any weakness.

Open questions for the next review.

  • Agentic RL: multi-turn rollouts with tools and environments (browsers, terminals) make rollouts longer, stateful and harder to replay. Does the reward pool become an environment platform?
  • Algorithm choice at our scale: run a controlled comparison of GRPO variants and on-policy distillation on our own tasks, since published rankings change with model size.
  • Bitwise-consistent rollouts: inference engines are starting to offer kernels that match training exactly. When available, can we drop mismatch corrections?
  • Data flywheel: feeding production traffic (with consent and filtering) back into SFT and RL prompt sets.
Design 07 · 12 sections

Design 07: Scaling RL beyond the small-run regime

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. What changes when you scale each axis
  3. Predict before you spend: compute–performance curves
  4. The scaling ladder
  5. Where the time goes: the step-time breakdown
  6. Long trajectories and the long tail
  7. Larger models: two layouts and the weight sync between them
  8. Numerics and MoE: the mismatch that grows with scale
  9. Rewards and environments at scale
  10. Stability over thousands of steps
  11. Failures and recovery on multi-week runs
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we take a post-training recipe that works on a small run (an 8B model, 4K-token answers, a few hundred steps, 32 GPUs) and make it work with more tokens, longer trajectories, larger models, more steps and a much larger compute budget, and how do we find the bottlenecks that only appear once we leave the small-run regime? It builds directly on Design 06 (recipes, objectives, health signals), Design 02 (capacity and queues), Design 03 (training jobs and checkpoints), Design 04 (long-running state and recovery) and Design 05 (the fabric that moves weights).

The short version: scaling RL is two problems at once. The algorithm problem: a recipe that looks best at small scale may hit a lower ceiling at large scale, so we predict with fitted compute–performance curves before committing a big budget. The systems problem: at scale, the bottleneck moves from the trainer to rollout long tails, weight synchronization, numerical mismatch between engines, reward throughput, memory for long contexts, and failures over multi-week runs. The platform runs a scaling ladder (each rung roughly 4× bigger than the last), measures where time and stability go at every rung, and only climbs when the previous rung's curve and bottleneck profile are understood.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The recipe from Design 06 works: on an 8B model with 4K-token answers it improves math and code steadily for 500 steps on 32 GPUs. The team now wants a 235B mixture-of-experts model, answers up to 64K tokens, multi-turn tool use, 5,000+ steps and a budget of about 200,000 GPU hours. The first attempt at 8× scale ran at 11% GPU utilization, spent 40% of each step waiting for weight sync, and collapsed on day nine with no obvious cause.

What the platform must do.

  • Predict before spending: estimate where a recipe will plateau and how fast it gets there, from runs costing a few percent of the full budget.
  • Find the bottleneck at each scale: break every step's time into rollout, reward, training, weight sync and waiting, and show which one grew as scale grew.
  • Keep GPUs busy despite long tails: answers whose lengths vary 50× must not leave most GPUs idle.
  • Move weights fast: pushing a hundreds-of-billions-parameter policy to the rollout fleet every step without stalling.
  • Stay stable for thousands of steps: detect slow drifts (entropy, mismatch, length) and recover from instability without losing days.
  • Survive failures: a multi-week run on thousands of GPUs will see node failures; resume in minutes, not hours.

Out of scope: the choice of objective and reward itself (Design 06), and the GPU fleet (Design 02).

What changes when you scale each axis

Scenario. The team scales everything at once and can't tell which change caused which problem. They need a map of what each scaling axis breaks, so they can scale one axis at a time.

What the picture shows. The five scaling axes and the bottleneck each one tends to expose first.

1More tokens per step (bigger batches, larger groups)
rollout throughput and reward throughput become the limit; the trainer waits. Larger batches also change the optimization (fewer, larger updates).
2Longer trajectories (16K → 64K+ tokens, multi-turn)
the long tail dominates step time, the KV cache limits how many sequences fit on a rollout GPU, and training activations for long sequences need context parallelism. Multi-turn tool use adds environment latency inside the rollout.
3Larger models (dense 8B → MoE with hundreds of billions of parameters)
training needs tensor, pipeline, expert and context parallelism; rollout engines need their own, different layout; weight sync moves hundreds of gigabytes per step; MoE routing differs between engines.
4More steps (hundreds → thousands)
slow drifts (entropy collapse, length growth, mismatch accumulation) have time to matter, the prompt set gets used up, and hardware failures become certain.
5Larger compute budgets
the cost of a wrong recipe choice grows, so prediction from small runs becomes the most valuable tool, and run-level operations (checkpointing, preemption, quotas) start to matter as much as algorithms.
Going deeper2 points
  • Scale one axis per rung. A rung that changes model size and trajectory length and step count can't tell you which one caused a regression.
  • Some bottlenecks are invisible below a threshold. Weight sync is negligible for 8B over NVLink and dominant for a large MoE over the network; the long tail barely matters at 4K tokens and dominates at 64K. The ladder exists to find those thresholds.

Predict before you spend: compute–performance curves

Scenario. Two recipes are compared at 2,000 GPU hours. Recipe A is clearly ahead. At 30,000 hours, recipe B passes it and keeps rising while A flattens. Choosing from the small comparison would have wasted the budget on the recipe with the lower ceiling.

What the picture shows. Fitting a saturating (sigmoid) curve of held-out performance against compute, and what its parameters mean.

1Ceiling (A)
the performance the recipe approaches with unlimited compute. Choices that change the ceiling matter most at scale.
2Efficiency (B) and midpoint (C_mid)
how quickly the recipe gets to the ceiling, and how much compute it takes to get halfway. Choices that only change efficiency are worth less at large budgets, because every good recipe gets there eventually.
3Fit early, check late
fit on the first part of a run (excluding the noisy start) and check the extrapolation against later checkpoints; the gap between predicted and observed is the trust you can place in the curve.
4Held-out metric, not training reward
fit on a fixed validation set (for example, mean pass rate over 16 samples per problem), since training reward is measured on a moving, filtered subset.

The published study behind this approach fitted such curves across more than 400,000 GPU hours of experiments and found that some design choices mainly shift the ceiling while others (loss aggregation, normalization, curriculum, the off-policy algorithm) mainly change efficiency. Its extrapolation from the first half of a 100,000-GPU-hour run closely matched the second half.

The code. Fit and compare recipes from their eval history (Python, SciPy).

import numpy as npfrom scipy.optimize import curve_fit def sigmoid(C, A, B, C_mid, R0):    """Held-out pass rate as a function of compute C (GPU hours)."""    return R0 + (A - R0) / (1.0 + (C_mid / C) ** B) def fit_recipe(gpu_hours: np.ndarray, pass_rate: np.ndarray, skip_hours: float = 1500):    keep = gpu_hours > skip_hours                     # drop the noisy start    R0 = pass_rate[0]    f = lambda C, A, B, C_mid: sigmoid(C, A, B, C_mid, R0)    (A, B, C_mid), cov = curve_fit(f, gpu_hours[keep], pass_rate[keep],                                   p0=[0.6, 1.0, 5000], bounds=([R0, 0.1, 100], [1.0, 5.0, 1e6]))    return {"A": A, "B": B, "C_mid": C_mid, "A_std": float(np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]))} for name, hist in runs.items():                       # runs: recipe -> (hours, pass_rate) arrays    p = fit_recipe(*hist)    print(f"{name:<14} ceiling A={p['A']:.3f}±{p['A_std']:.3f}  B={p['B']:.2f}  C_mid={p['C_mid']:.0f} h")# Commit the big budget to the recipe with the highest ceiling whose fit is tight,# not the one that is ahead at the budget you happened to measure.
Going deeper2 points
  • Uncertainty matters. A ceiling estimated from a run that hasn't reached its midpoint is weak; the platform shows the confidence interval and refuses to "rank" recipes whose intervals overlap.
  • Curves per axis: fit separate curves for larger models and longer generation lengths; both can raise the ceiling while making early progress look slower.

The scaling ladder

Scenario. Leadership asks "when can we start the big run?" The honest answer is "after the rung below it is understood," and the platform needs to make that concrete.

What the picture shows. A sequence of runs, each roughly 4× the previous, with explicit exit criteria.

1Rung 1, recipe search (~1–2% of budget)
small model, short answers; many ablations; fit curves; pick candidates.
2Rung 2, length
same model, much longer answers; measures the long tail, KV cache pressure and length dynamics.
3Rung 3, model size
the target architecture (for example, the MoE) on fewer steps; exposes parallelism, weight sync and routing mismatch.
4Rung 4, duration
the target model and length for many steps; exposes drift, prompt exhaustion and failure handling.
5The production run
the full budget, with the curve from rung 4 as the forecast it's checked against.
6Exit criteria at every rung
the curve fit is stable, the step-time breakdown is understood (no unexplained waiting), the health signals are flat or explained, and a restart from checkpoint has been tested.

The YAML. A rung is just a recipe overlay: the base recipe plus the axis being scaled (applied by the launcher from Design 06).

# recipes/assistant-v13/ladder/rung3-model-size.yamlextends: recipes/assistant-v13/rl-base.yamlladder:  rung: 3  axis: model_size                       # exactly one axis changes per rung  previous: runs/assistant-v13-rung2-8b-64k  budget_gpu_hours: 12000  exit_criteria:    curve_fit_ceiling_ci: 0.03           # ±0.03 on the ceiling estimate    unexplained_wait_fraction_max: 0.10  # of step time    restart_from_checkpoint_tested: truemodel:  path: registry://base-235b-a22b-moe@v1  trainer_parallelism: { tp: 4, pp: 4, ep: 8, cp: 2 }   # training layout  rollout_parallelism: { tp: 4, ep: 8, dp: 16 }         # inference layout, differentrollout:  max_response_tokens: 65536             # unchanged from rung 2
Going deeper2 points
  • Budget the ladder explicitly: roughly 10–15% of the total compute for rungs 1–4 is a cheap insurance policy against spending the other 85% on the wrong recipe or a run that collapses.
  • Keep a "reference rung" (small, cheap, fixed) that re-runs nightly on the current code; it catches framework regressions before they reach a big run.

Where the time goes: the step-time breakdown

Scenario. At rung 3, a step takes 14 minutes. Nobody knows whether to buy more rollout GPUs, optimize the trainer or fix the network, because the 14 minutes have never been broken down.

What the picture shows. How one RL step's time splits as scale grows, and which part to attack.

1Rollout generation
at small scale, roughly half the step; with long trajectories, commonly most of it. The long tail (the slowest few percent of answers) often decides the whole step.
2Reward and environment time
small for exact-match math; large for sandboxed tests, judges and multi-turn tools.
3Reference and old-policy log-probabilities
an extra forward pass over every token; grows with tokens per step.
4Training (forward + backward + optimizer)
grows with model size and tokens, but usually isn't the largest share in RL.
5Weight sync
negligible for a small model on one node; tens of seconds to minutes for a large model across nodes, every step.
6Idle (bubbles)
GPUs waiting for another stage. The single most useful number to drive down.

The code. Every run emits a span per stage per step; the platform turns them into this breakdown and the "bubble" fraction (OpenTelemetry spans, exported like the traces in Observability).

import timefrom contextlib import contextmanagerfrom opentelemetry import trace, metrics tracer = trace.get_tracer("rl.step")stage_seconds = metrics.get_meter("rl").create_histogram("rl_stage_seconds", unit="s") @contextmanagerdef stage(name: str, step: int, run_id: str, gpus: int):    t0 = time.perf_counter()    with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"rl.{name}", attributes={"step": step, "run": run_id}):        yield    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0    stage_seconds.record(dt, {"stage": name, "run": run_id, "gpus": str(gpus)}) # in the training loopwith stage("rollout", step, run_id, rollout_gpus):     batch = rollout_pool.collect(prompts)with stage("reward", step, run_id, 0):                 rewards = reward_pool.score(batch)with stage("logprobs", step, run_id, train_gpus):      old_lp = trainer.logprobs(batch)with stage("train", step, run_id, train_gpus):         trainer.update(batch, rewards, old_lp)with stage("weight_sync", step, run_id, rollout_gpus): sync.push(trainer.state_dict_shards())
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure GPU-seconds, not seconds: a 60-second stage on 16 rollout GPUs and a 60-second stage on 128 training GPUs cost very different amounts. The breakdown is weighted by the GPUs each stage holds, including GPUs held while idle.
  • Profile the slowest step, not the average: the long tail is in the tail.

Long trajectories and the long tail

Scenario. At 64K-token answers, the median answer finishes in 4 minutes and the slowest 1% take 25. In synchronous RL, every step waits 25 minutes, and 90% of rollout GPUs sit idle for most of it.

What the picture shows. The long-tail problem and the techniques that tame it.

1Over-provision and cut off (active partial rollouts)
start more answers than the batch needs; when enough have finished, stop the rest and keep their partial output; resume them in the next step under the newer policy.
2Asynchrony with a staleness bound
separate rollout and training pools, so the trainer consumes whatever has finished; samples are at most k policy versions old, with importance-sampling corrections.
3Length-aware scheduling
route long-running requests to engines with free KV cache; rebalance during generation; speculative decoding for long answers.
4KV cache capacity
long contexts cap the number of concurrent sequences per rollout GPU; FP8 KV cache and prefix caching (group samples share the prompt) raise it.
5Training long sequences
context parallelism splits one sequence across GPUs; sequence packing and dynamic batch sizes by token count keep training balanced.
6Length dynamics
answer length usually grows during reasoning RL; the length cap, the overlong penalty and truncation masking (Design 06) decide how that interacts with the budget.

Production systems report that rollout can take 50–80% of step time and more, and that partial-rollout and asynchronous designs recover much of it, with the caveat that stale samples must be corrected or repaired.

The YAML. The rollout pool as a vLLM deployment sized for long contexts, separate from training (one group per engine with LeaderWorkerSet for multi-node engines).

apiVersion: leaderworkerset.x-k8s.io/v1kind: LeaderWorkerSetmetadata:  name: rollout-235b  namespace: rl-scale  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-rollout }spec:  replicas: 16                                    # 16 engines, 2 nodes each  leaderWorkerTemplate:    size: 2    restartPolicy: RecreateGroupOnPodRestart      # an engine is all-or-nothing    leaderTemplate:      spec:        containers:        - name: vllm          image: registry.example.com/rl/vllm:2026.11-rl          args:          - --model=/weights/current          - --tensor-parallel-size=8          - --pipeline-parallel-size=2          - --enable-expert-parallel          - --max-model-len=81920          - --kv-cache-dtype=fp8                  # more concurrent long sequences          - --enable-prefix-caching               # group samples share the prompt          - --max-num-seqs=256          resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }    workerTemplate:      spec:        containers:        - name: vllm-worker          image: registry.example.com/rl/vllm:2026.11-rl          resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Partial rollouts change the data: one answer may contain tokens from several policy versions. Record the version per token span so the importance-sampling correction uses the right probabilities.
  • The tail grows with training: as the model learns to think longer, a step-time budget that worked at step 500 fails at step 3,000. Re-check the breakdown regularly.

Larger models: two layouts and the weight sync between them

Scenario. The 235B MoE trains well with one parallel layout but needs a completely different layout to generate efficiently. Every step, the new weights have to get from one layout to the other, across 64 nodes, and that transfer alone takes four minutes.

What the picture shows. The training and rollout layouts, and the paths for moving weights between them.

1Training layout
tensor, pipeline, expert, context and data parallelism (Megatron or FSDP), optimized for memory and backward passes.
2Rollout layout
tensor and expert parallelism with many data-parallel engines, optimized for decoding throughput and KV cache.
3Resharding
each rollout engine needs the full model in its own layout; the trainer's shards must be gathered and re-split. Done naively, this is a full gather through one place.
4Colocated vs disaggregated
colocated (same GPUs, time-shared) reshards in GPU memory, no network; disaggregated (separate pools) must cross the network, but lets each pool scale and keeps both busy.
5Faster sync
bucketed broadcasts over NCCL on the fast fabric, overlapping sync with the next rollouts, sending only changed parameters or compressed deltas, and pipelining layer by layer so engines start before the whole model arrives.

The code. A bucketed, layer-pipelined push from trainer ranks to rollout engines, with the policy version recorded (sketch).

import torch, torch.distributed as dist BUCKET_BYTES = 1 << 30                                       # 1 GiB buckets def push_weights(named_shards, group, version: int, resharder):    """Gather each layer to rollout layout and broadcast in buckets over NCCL."""    bucket, size = [], 0    for name, shard in named_shards:                         # iterate layer by layer        full = resharder.to_rollout_layout(name, shard)      # TP/EP re-split for vLLM        bucket.append((name, full)); size += full.numel() * full.element_size()        if size >= BUCKET_BYTES:            _flush(bucket, group); bucket, size = [], 0    if bucket:        _flush(bucket, group)    dist.broadcast(torch.tensor([version], device="cuda"), src=0, group=group)  # engines tag tokens def _flush(bucket, group):    flat = torch.cat([t.flatten() for _, t in bucket])    dist.broadcast(flat, src=0, group=group)                 # rollout engines load in place
Going deeper2 points
  • Size the sync path like a serving path: a 235B model in BF16 is about 470 GB. At an effective 50 GB/s per receiving engine that's around 10 seconds; through one bottleneck link it's minutes. Use the GPU fabric (Design 05), not the pod network.
  • Measure sync as its own stage and set a budget (for example, under 5% of step time); above it, overlap sync with rollout or move to asynchronous training.

Numerics and MoE: the mismatch that grows with scale

Scenario. At 8B dense, the inference engine's token probabilities and the trainer's match closely. At 235B MoE with FP8 rollouts, a few percent of tokens have probability ratios above 10, and those tokens dominate the gradient. The run looks fine for a week, then collapses.

What the picture shows. Sources of train–inference mismatch, and how each is reduced.

1Different kernels and precision
the inference engine and trainer compute the same function in different ways; low-precision rollouts (FP8) widen the gap. Corrections: truncated or masked importance sampling at the token level, and keeping the final projection to logits in FP32 on both sides.
2MoE routing differences
a tiny numerical difference can send a token to different experts in the two engines, so the probabilities differ a lot. Routing replay records the experts chosen during rollout and reuses them in training.
3Staleness
asynchronous rollouts are from older policies; their ratios are expected to differ, and are corrected the same way.
4Watch the ratio distribution
track the fraction of tokens with ratio beyond a threshold, and the KL between rollout and trainer probabilities, per step. A widening tail is the earliest warning.
5Bitwise-consistent inference
where the engine offers kernels that exactly match the trainer, the mismatch disappears at some throughput cost; worth testing at each rung.

The code. Mismatch metrics and a truncated importance weight, computed from probabilities both engines already return.

import torch def mismatch_metrics(train_logp, rollout_logp, mask, cap: float = 3.0):    """Per-token log ratio between trainer and rollout engine, and a truncated IS weight."""    log_ratio = (train_logp - rollout_logp) * mask    ratio = log_ratio.exp()    n = mask.sum()    stats = {        "mismatch/kl": ((ratio - 1) - log_ratio).sum().item() / n.item(),   # k3 estimator        "mismatch/frac_ratio_gt_2": ((ratio > 2) & mask.bool()).sum().item() / n.item(),        "mismatch/max_ratio": ratio[mask.bool()].max().item(),    }    is_weight = ratio.clamp(max=cap).detach()               # truncated IS (TIS)    return stats, is_weight
Going deeper2 points
  • Precision is a ceiling choice, not just a speed choice. Published scaling work found that FP32 for the logit computation shifted the asymptotic performance, not only stability.
  • Test mismatch before the run: score the same rollouts with both engines on the target model and inspect the ratio histogram; it's a cheap pre-flight check at every rung.

Rewards and environments at scale

Scenario. Moving from math to multi-turn coding agents, each rollout calls tools 20–50 times. The sandbox pool that handled 2,000 test runs per step now gets 150,000 tool calls per step, and rollout GPUs sit idle waiting for sandboxes.

What the picture shows. The reward and environment tier as its own autoscaled service.

1Stateless verifiers
exact match, unit tests, schema checks; scale horizontally on CPU, batched per step.
2Judges and reward models
served on their own GPU pool with vLLM; sized for the step's token count, not for interactive latency.
3Stateful environments for agentic RL
sandboxes, browsers and terminals that live for a whole trajectory; pre-warmed pools and snapshots so starting one takes milliseconds (Design 01).
4Environment stragglers
one slow tool call blocks a trajectory; time out, retry or mark the turn failed, and count failures by environment.
5Back-pressure
rollout engines pause new trajectories when the environment queue is full, instead of piling up idle KV cache.

The YAML. The sandbox pool scales on queue depth, not CPU, so it grows before rollouts stall (KEDA).

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1kind: ScaledObjectmetadata:  name: rl-sandbox-pool  namespace: rl-scalespec:  scaleTargetRef: { name: sandbox-workers }  minReplicaCount: 200                           # pre-warmed for the step start  maxReplicaCount: 6000  cooldownPeriod: 300  triggers:  - type: prometheus    metadata:      serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090      query: sum(rl_env_queue_depth{run="assistant-v13-prod"})      threshold: "25"                            # pending tool calls per worker
Going deeper2 points
  • Environments are deterministic by contract: the same seed and actions give the same observations, so trajectories can be replayed for debugging and for importance-sampling checks.
  • Count environment cost per trajectory: at scale, CPU and sandbox minutes can rival GPU cost for agentic tasks.

Stability over thousands of steps

Scenario. The production run improves for 2,400 steps, then held-out scores start sliding. Entropy fell slowly the whole time, response length doubled since step 1,500, and 30% of prompts now have all-correct groups. Each signal was within its alert threshold; together they predicted the slide.

What the picture shows. Slow drifts that only matter on long runs, and the controls for each.

1Entropy decay
exploration fades over thousands of steps. Controls: clip-higher, temperature, entropy-targeted token selection, and resetting the reference point periodically if KL is used.
2Length growth
answers get longer as the model learns to think more; step time and memory grow with them. Controls: a length curriculum (raise the cap in stages), overlong penalties, and re-planning rollout capacity.
3Prompt exhaustion
the model solves more prompts and the informative set shrinks. Controls: refresh pass-rate estimates, add harder prompts, sample by difficulty, and remove mastered prompts.
4Mismatch accumulation
small ratio drift becomes large. Controls: IS corrections, routing replay, precision checks at intervals.
5Composite alerts
alert on combinations and trends (entropy slope × length slope × informative-prompt fraction), not single thresholds.
6Rollback with change
on a collapse, roll back to the last healthy checkpoint and change something (lower LR, tighter staleness, refreshed prompts); a plain restart usually collapses again at the same point.
Going deeper2 points
  • Keep checkpoints dense enough to roll back cheaply (every 25–50 steps for the latest, every few hundred kept long term), and record the health signals with each so "the last healthy checkpoint" is a query, not a guess.
  • Schedules over a long run: learning-rate decay, length-cap increases and data refreshes are planned in the recipe, so the curve fitted at rung 4 still applies.

Failures and recovery on multi-week runs

Scenario. A 2,048-GPU run on its eleventh day: one GPU throws an uncorrectable memory error. The whole job crashes; restarting takes 70 minutes (rescheduling, loading a 3 TB checkpoint, warming 64 rollout engines). It happens twice a week.

What the picture shows. Making failures cheap rather than rare.

1Separate the blast radius
a failed rollout engine is replaced while the run continues (rollouts are stateless and retryable); only trainer failures require a training restart.
2Fast checkpoints
asynchronous, sharded checkpoints to local NVMe first and object storage in the background, so saving takes seconds of training time (Design 04).
3Fast restarts
hot spare nodes reserved by the queue, pre-pulled images, checkpoints loaded in parallel from the nearest copy, rollout engines warm-started from the new weights.
4Health checks before admission
nodes run GPU, NVLink and network tests before joining; repeat offenders are drained automatically.
5Save the rollout buffer and data cursor
with the checkpoint, so a restart neither repeats nor skips prompts.

The YAML. The trainer as a JobSet with a failure policy that restarts the trainer group while rollout engines (a separate LeaderWorkerSet) keep running.

apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: JobSetmetadata:  name: assistant-v13-prod-trainer  namespace: rl-scale  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-production }   # reserved capacity, not preemptible  annotations:    alpha.jobset.sigs.k8s.io/exclusive-topology: network.example.com/fabric-block   # one fabric blockspec:  failurePolicy:    maxRestarts: 50                                   # weeks-long runs will restart    restartStrategy: Recreate  replicatedJobs:  - name: trainer    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        parallelism: 128        completions: 128        backoffLimit: 0        template:          spec:            containers:            - name: megatron              image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer:2026.11              command: ["python3", "-m", "rl.train", "--resume=latest", "--recipe=/recipes/prod.yaml"]              resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }              volumeMounts: [ { name: nvme, mountPath: /local-ckpt } ]            volumes:            - name: nvme              hostPath: { path: /mnt/nvme/ckpt }
Going deeper2 points
  • Track goodput: the fraction of reserved GPU-hours that produced training progress. Failures, restarts, sync and bubbles all subtract from it; it's the run-level metric leadership should see.
  • Rehearse a failure at rung 4: kill a trainer node and a rollout engine on purpose and time the recovery.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, measurement: step-time breakdown, goodput and mismatch metrics on every run, plus the curve-fitting service on eval history.
  • Phase 2, the ladder: rung recipes, exit criteria and the nightly reference rung.
  • Phase 3, systems for long trajectories and large models: disaggregated rollout pools, partial rollouts, bucketed weight sync, routing replay, autoscaled environment tier.
  • Phase 4, run operations: fast checkpoints, hot spares, composite alerts, rollback with change, failure rehearsals.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Spending 10–15% of the budget on the ladder, instead of starting the big run immediately.
  • Disaggregated rollout and training: better utilization and independent scaling, at the cost of network-bound weight sync and more moving parts.
  • Asynchrony and partial rollouts: large throughput gains, at the cost of off-policy samples that must be corrected and monitored.
  • Lower-precision rollouts: faster generation, at the cost of more mismatch; only adopted after the ratio histogram at the target scale is acceptable.

Open questions.

  • How far do curves extrapolate across model sizes? We fit per model size today; a joint fit would let rung 1 predict more.
  • Agentic RL at scale: environments with long, stateful, slow steps may need their own asynchronous design, decoupled from token generation.
  • Weight sync with sparse or delta updates: if only a small fraction of parameters change meaningfully per step, can we send much less?
  • Multi-cluster RL: rollout in one region and training in another, with weights crossing a WAN; viable only with large staleness tolerance.
Design 08 · 12 sections

Design 08: Training for long-horizon reasoning

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Why long horizons are hard
  3. The trajectory as data: turns, snapshots and branch points
  4. Credit assignment: a ladder of methods
  5. Branching rollouts: tree-shaped exploration
  6. Denser rewards without reward hacking
  7. Exploration: curricula over the horizon
  8. Verification for long tasks
  9. Context management: trajectories longer than the window
  10. The infrastructure: environments, trajectories and credit workers
  11. Measuring progress on long tasks
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we train models on tasks where success depends on many intermediate decisions (an 80-turn software fix, a multi-hour research task, a long proof), when the only reliable signal is often a single pass/fail at the very end? It covers how to give useful feedback to the decisions inside a trajectory (credit assignment), how to get more signal than one bit per trajectory (denser rewards), how to keep the model finding new strategies (exploration), and how to know a long task was really solved (verification). It builds on Design 06 (recipes and objectives), Design 07 (scale and long rollouts), Design 01 (environments) and Design 04 (snapshots and state).

The short version: the trajectory is the unit of storage, but the turn (or step) is the unit of credit. Every trajectory is recorded as a sequence of turns with environment snapshots at chosen points. Feedback moves from one end-of-task reward toward per-turn advantages through a ladder of methods: shared trajectory-level advantages, turn-level process rewards, and Monte Carlo value estimates from branching at snapshots. Exploration is helped by curricula over the horizon (start near the goal, then move the start back). Verification is layered, because the longer the task, the more ways a model has to look successful without being so.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The team trains a coding agent on real repository issues. A typical successful episode is 40–120 turns: read the issue, explore files, reproduce the bug, try a fix, run tests, revise, and submit. The reward is whether hidden tests pass at the end. After RL with trajectory-level GRPO, the agent improves on short issues but not on long ones: it learns to submit early, rarely recovers from a wrong first hypothesis, and on failed episodes every turn, including the excellent ones, gets the same negative signal.

What the platform must do.

  • Assign credit to turns: tell the model which decisions helped or hurt, not just whether the whole episode succeeded.
  • Get more signal per episode: use intermediate checks, milestones and value estimates where they're trustworthy, without teaching the model to game them.
  • Keep exploring: long tasks with a low success rate give almost no learning signal; the platform must create easier starting points and diverse attempts.
  • Verify long tasks robustly: final checks that can't be passed by shortcuts (editing tests, hard-coding outputs, faking progress).
  • Handle long contexts: trajectories longer than the context window, with summarization or memory, without breaking the training math.
  • Make it reproducible: every trajectory can be replayed and branched from any recorded point.

Out of scope: the base RL objective and scaling machinery (Designs 06 and 07), and sandbox security itself (Design 01).

Why long horizons are hard

Scenario. A researcher asks why the recipe that works on 4K-token math problems barely moves on 100-turn tasks. The answer is four problems that are minor for short tasks and dominant for long ones.

What the picture shows. The four problems and how each grows with the number of decisions.

1Sparse rewards
one bit at the end of hundreds of decisions. With a 5% success rate, most groups of attempts are all failures and give no signal at all in group-relative RL.
2Credit assignment
even when the outcome is informative, giving the same advantage to every token spreads the signal thinly across good and bad decisions alike. The useful information per decision shrinks as the trajectory grows.
3Exploration
a long task can fail in many more ways than it can succeed. Random variations rarely stumble onto a full solution, and the model's own habits (submitting early, repeating a failed command) reinforce themselves.
4Verification
final checks see only the end state, and there are more ways to fake an end state in a long task (editing tests, deleting failing code, claiming success). Intermediate checks are even harder to trust.
5Variance
all four combine into high-variance gradient estimates; training needs more samples per useful update, or better estimates of value.
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure success as a function of horizon: plot success rate against the number of turns a task needs. A recipe that only helps short tasks shows a steep drop-off; the goal of this design is to flatten that curve.
  • Most problems show up as "zero-variance groups": track the fraction of groups where every attempt failed or every attempt succeeded. On long tasks it's the clearest early sign that the signal is too sparse.

The trajectory as data: turns, snapshots and branch points

Scenario. To try a different credit method, a researcher needs to restart 1,000 failed episodes from turn 30 and try alternatives. The trajectories were stored as flat text, and the environments are gone. Nothing can be replayed.

What the picture shows. How a trajectory is recorded so it can be scored, replayed and branched.

1Turns
each turn is the model's output (reasoning and an action), the environment's response, and metadata (tokens, policy version, latency).
2Token log-probabilities
stored per turn from the rollout engine, for importance-sampling corrections later (Design 07).
3Snapshots at branch points
the environment's state (filesystem, process state or a VM snapshot) saved at selected turns, cheaply, so we can restart from there.
4Choosing branch points
not every turn. Good candidates are turns where the model's choice is uncertain (high entropy over the next action), where an important action happens (first edit, test run), or evenly spaced as a fallback.
5Outcome and checks
the final reward plus any intermediate verifier results and milestone flags, each with its verifier version.

The code. The trajectory schema shared by rollouts, reward workers, credit assignment and the trainer (Python).

from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclassclass Turn:    index: int    prompt_tokens: int                       # context the model saw (after any summarization)    output: str                              # reasoning + action    action: dict                             # parsed tool call, e.g. {"tool": "run_tests", ...}    observation: str                         # environment response (truncated for storage)    logprobs_ref: str                        # pointer to per-token rollout logprobs    policy_version: int    entropy_first_action_token: float        # used to choose branch points    snapshot_id: str | None = None           # set if this is a branch point    checks: dict[str, float] = field(default_factory=dict)   # e.g. {"repro_test_fails": 1.0} @dataclassclass Trajectory:    task_id: str    env_image: str                           # pinned environment version    seed: int    turns: list[Turn]    outcome: float | None = None             # final verified reward    verifier_version: str = ""    summary_boundaries: list[int] = field(default_factory=list)   # turns where context was compacted
Going deeper2 points
  • Snapshots must be cheap or branching won't happen: filesystem-level snapshots (copy-on-write volumes, container checkpoints) for code tasks; for browser or OS environments, VM-level snapshots (Design 01, Design 04).
  • Determinism by contract: the same snapshot, seed and actions give the same observations. Without it, branching estimates mix up the model's choices with environment noise.

Credit assignment: a ladder of methods

Scenario. On a failed 90-turn episode, the agent's first 30 turns were a careful, correct diagnosis; turn 31 applied the wrong fix and the rest was flailing. Trajectory-level RL punishes all 90 turns equally. The team wants the diagnosis reinforced and turn 31 discouraged.

What the picture shows. Methods for spreading feedback over turns, from cheapest to most precise.

1Trajectory-level (GRPO-style)
every token gets the episode's advantage. Simple, unbiased, high variance; works when trajectories are short or success rates are moderate.
2Turn-level rewards plus outcome
add verifiable or judged rewards for individual turns and combine them with the outcome advantage, so each turn gets its own advantage. Published multi-turn variants of GRPO and PPO built this way outperformed trajectory-level baselines on search agents.
3Monte Carlo values from branches
from a branch point, run several continuations to estimate how likely success is from that state. The difference in value before and after a turn is that turn's advantage. Unbiased and model-free; costs extra rollouts. This is the idea behind VinePPO, which showed that learned value networks barely beat random at ranking alternative reasoning steps, while Monte Carlo estimates trained faster and generalized better.
4Learned critics and process reward models
a model predicts value or step quality directly. Cheap at training time once trained, but it can drift from true outcomes and becomes something the policy can exploit.
5Hybrids
use Monte Carlo branches on a sample of trajectories to train or calibrate a process reward model, then use the cheaper model elsewhere and keep checking it against fresh branch estimates.

The code. Turn-level advantages from Monte Carlo branch values (Python sketch).

import numpy as np def branch_value(traj, turn_idx, k: int, rollout_from_snapshot) -> float:    """Estimate V(state at turn_idx) by k continuations from the saved snapshot."""    snap = traj.turns[turn_idx].snapshot_id    outcomes = [rollout_from_snapshot(snap, seed=traj.seed * 1000 + j).outcome for j in range(k)]    return float(np.mean(outcomes)) def turn_advantages(traj, branch_turns: list[int], k: int, rollout_from_snapshot):    """Advantage of each segment = value after it − value before it (outcome at the end)."""    points = [0] + branch_turns    values = [branch_value(traj, t, k, rollout_from_snapshot) for t in points] + [traj.outcome]    adv = np.zeros(len(traj.turns))    for (start, v0), v1, end in zip(zip(points, values), values[1:], points[1:] + [len(traj.turns)]):        adv[start:end] = v1 - v0                # a segment that raised the chance of success is credited    return adv                                  # broadcast to the tokens of each turn by the trainer
Going deeper2 points
  • Segment, don't go per token: branch every few turns, or at high-entropy decision points, rather than at every token. Segment-level values capture most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.
  • Check credit quality directly: on a held-out sample, compare each method's turn advantages with expensive Monte Carlo estimates (many branches). A credit method whose ranking of turns doesn't agree with ground truth is just adding noise.

Branching rollouts: tree-shaped exploration

Scenario. Monte Carlo credit needs extra rollouts. Done naively, each branch replays the whole prefix and re-creates the environment from scratch, which makes it 10× too expensive to use.

What the picture shows. Rollouts as a tree that shares prefixes, instead of independent attempts.

1Shared prefix, branching suffixes
several continuations from the same snapshot share the prefix's tokens (prefix caching in the inference engine) and its environment state (snapshot restore instead of replay).
2Branch where it matters
choose branch points by uncertainty (high entropy in the next action), after milestones, or before costly irreversible actions.
3Group-relative comparisons at each node
continuations from the same node form a natural group; their outcomes give a local baseline, so advantages compare alternatives at that decision, not across unrelated episodes.
4More signal from failures
a failing trajectory with one successful branch tells you exactly which decision turned failure into success.
5Budget
a fixed rollout budget per task split between new root attempts (exploration) and branches (credit); the split is a recipe hyperparameter.

The YAML. Branch points are filesystem snapshots of the environment's volume (Kubernetes CSI VolumeSnapshot); a branch restores from one into a new sandbox.

apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1kind: VolumeSnapshotmetadata:  name: traj-8f2c-turn-31                      # trajectory 8f2c, branch point at turn 31  namespace: rl-envs  labels:    rl.example.com/trajectory: 8f2c    rl.example.com/turn: "31"spec:  volumeSnapshotClassName: csi-fast-cow         # copy-on-write: seconds, not minutes  source:    persistentVolumeClaimName: env-8f2c-workspace---apiVersion: v1kind: PersistentVolumeClaimmetadata:  name: env-8f2c-b31-3-workspace                # branch 3 from turn 31  namespace: rl-envsspec:  storageClassName: fast-cow  dataSource:    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io    kind: VolumeSnapshot    name: traj-8f2c-turn-31                     # restore the exact state  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]  resources: { requests: { storage: 20Gi } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Snapshot cost sets the branching rate: measure snapshot and restore latency per environment type; a 30-second restore limits you to a few branches per task, a 1-second one to many.
  • Process state isn't on disk: for environments with running services or open shells, either snapshot the whole sandbox (container or VM checkpoint) or make the environment re-creatable from disk plus a short replay of recorded actions.

Denser rewards without reward hacking

Scenario. The team adds a reward for "tests run" to encourage the agent to test its fixes. Within 200 steps the agent runs the test suite after every single turn, triples episode length, and success doesn't improve.

What the picture shows. Sources of intermediate signal, ordered by how much to trust them.

1Verifiable milestones
checks against the environment's real state, such as "a failing test that reproduces the bug now exists" or "the project builds." Strong signals, but designed per task family.
2Process reward models and judges
a model scores each step's quality against a rubric. Flexible, but they learn and reward surface patterns.
3Intrinsic signals
for information-seeking tasks, the change in the model's own confidence in the right answer after a turn; research in 2026 used such belief-change rewards for turn-level credit.
4Potential-based shaping
reward the change in a progress measure, not its level, so the shaped reward sums to (nearly) zero over any loop. Running tests repeatedly doesn't add up.
5Guardrails
small weights relative to the outcome, caps per episode, rewards only for first achievement of a milestone, and dropping any shaping term whose correlation with final success declines during training.

The code. Milestone rewards as potential differences, paid once (Python).

def progress(state) -> float:    """A progress measure on the environment's real state (not the model's claims)."""    return (0.2 * state.reproduced_bug          # a failing repro test exists          + 0.3 * state.repro_test_passes       # ... and now passes          + 0.2 * state.builds_cleanly          + 0.3 * state.no_existing_tests_broken) def shaped_turn_rewards(states, gamma: float = 1.0, weight: float = 0.1) -> list[float]:    """Potential-based shaping: r_t = w * (γ·Φ(s_{t+1}) − Φ(s_t)). Loops earn nothing."""    phi = [progress(s) for s in states]    best, rewards = 0.0, []    for t in range(len(phi) - 1):        gain = gamma * phi[t + 1] - phi[t]        if phi[t + 1] <= best:                  # pay only for new progress, never repeated            gain = min(gain, 0.0)        best = max(best, phi[t + 1])        rewards.append(weight * gain)    return rewards                              # combined with the outcome advantage per turn
Going deeper2 points
  • Track each shaping term's correlation with final success across training. Once the policy learns to raise a term without raising success, the term is being gamed; reduce or remove it.
  • Process reward models drift: re-calibrate them periodically against Monte Carlo branch values on fresh trajectories from the current policy.

Exploration: curricula over the horizon

Scenario. On the hardest task family, the success rate is 1%. With 8 attempts per task, 92% of groups are all failures. The model gets almost no signal, and what it gets mostly reinforces the few lucky attempts.

What the picture shows. Ways to make long tasks learnable and keep the model trying new strategies.

1Reverse curriculum (start near the goal)
begin episodes from snapshots taken late in successful trajectories (from humans, a stronger model or earlier successes), where the remaining horizon is short. As success from those points rises, move the starting point earlier.
2Horizon curriculum
train first on task variants that need fewer steps, then longer ones, keeping each task's success rate in a learnable range.
3Hints and partial solutions
provide a plan or the first few steps for hard tasks, then remove them gradually.
4Diversity in attempts
sample with temperature, vary the first action, and use group sizes large enough that at least one attempt succeeds; objectives that reward pass@k (at least one success in k) keep exploration alive better than mean-reward objectives.
5Avoid collapse into habits
detect repeated actions and loops; cap identical tool calls; monitor entropy at decision points, not just averaged over all tokens.

The YAML. A curriculum spec the rollout scheduler reads: where to start episodes, and when to move the start back.

# recipes/swe-agent-v4/curriculum.yamltask_family: repo-issues-hardstart_points:  source: trajectories://swe-agent-v3/successful   # snapshots from earlier successes and demos  strategy: reverse                                # start near the end, move earlier  stages:  - { remaining_turns_max: 10,  promote_when: { success_rate_min: 0.6 } }  - { remaining_turns_max: 30,  promote_when: { success_rate_min: 0.5 } }  - { remaining_turns_max: 60,  promote_when: { success_rate_min: 0.4 } }  - { remaining_turns_max: null }                  # full task from the start  mix_full_tasks: 0.2                              # always keep some full episodestarget_success_band: [0.1, 0.9]                    # outside this, the task gives little signalgroup_size: 16loop_guard: { max_identical_actions: 3 }
Going deeper2 points
  • Starting mid-task changes the distribution: the model sees states it didn't create. Always mix in full episodes, and evaluate only on full episodes.
  • Track the success rate per remaining-horizon bucket as the curriculum advances; that curve is the learning signal for the curriculum itself.

Verification for long tasks

Scenario. The agent's success rate jumps from 34% to 51% in a week. Inspection shows a third of the "successes" modified the test files so the hidden tests import a patched helper. The verifier checked that tests passed, not that the right tests ran against unmodified code.

What the picture shows. Layers of verification, each catching what the previous one misses.

1Hidden outcome tests
run in a fresh environment built from the agent's final diff, not the agent's own environment; test files restored from the original task.
2State and diff checks
forbidden-file rules (tests, CI configs, lockfiles), diff size limits, no deleted assertions, no network calls the task didn't need.
3Behavior checks over the trajectory
did the agent claim to run tests it never ran? Did it stop early while saying the task was done? A judge reviews a sample of trajectories against a rubric.
4Regression tests
existing tests that passed before must still pass.
5Verifier versioning and audits
every reward is tagged with the verifier version; a sample of successes is reviewed by people each week; new exploits become new checks.

The YAML. A task's verification spec, run by the reward workers in a fresh sandbox.

task_id: repo-issue-48213verify:  fresh_environment: true                       # never verify in the agent's own sandbox  apply: agent_final_diff  restore_paths: ["tests/**", ".github/**", "pyproject.toml", "setup.cfg"]   # agent can't edit these  checks:  - { name: hidden_tests,      run: "pytest tests/hidden -q", weight: 1.0, required: true }  - { name: regression_tests,  run: "pytest tests/existing -q", required: true }  - { name: diff_size,         max_changed_lines: 400 }  - { name: no_skip_markers,   forbid_patterns: ["pytest.mark.skip", "assert True"] }  - { name: trajectory_honesty, judge: rubric://honest-claims@v3, sample_rate: 0.1 }  timeout_s: 900  network: noneverifier_version: swe-verify@2026.11.2
Going deeper2 points
  • The longer the task, the more the verifier is attacked: a model that takes 100 actions has 100 chances to find a weakness. Red-team verifiers with the current policy before large runs.
  • Separate training and evaluation verifiers: evaluate with checks the model never trained against, so a learned exploit shows up as a gap between training and held-out success.

Context management: trajectories longer than the window

Scenario. Long episodes exceed the 128K-token context. The agent's scaffold summarizes older turns, but the trainer was computing log-probabilities on the full, unsummarized history, which the model never actually saw. The training signal no longer matched the behavior.

What the picture shows. Keeping long trajectories trainable when context is compacted.

1Compaction strategies
drop or truncate old tool outputs, summarize earlier turns (by the model itself or a helper), or keep an external memory file the agent reads and writes.
2Train on what the model saw
each turn's log-probabilities are computed with exactly the context the model had at that turn, including summaries; store the compacted context per turn (or a recipe to rebuild it deterministically).
3The summary is an action too
when the model writes its own summary, it's part of the policy and gets credit like any other turn; a summary that drops the key fact leads to failure, and that failure is credited to it.
4Training cost
turns after compaction are separate sequences with different prefixes; pack them efficiently and use prefix sharing where turns share a context.
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure information loss: on held-out trajectories, ask the model questions about earlier turns from its compacted context; falling accuracy means compaction is losing what matters.
  • Keep compaction deterministic (fixed thresholds, recorded summary text) so replays and branches see the same context the original did.

The infrastructure: environments, trajectories and credit workers

Scenario. Long-horizon training needs thousands of concurrent environments, each living for an hour, with snapshots, branches, verifiers and a growing trajectory store. Today environments are created by the rollout scripts, and nobody knows how many exist or what they cost.

What the picture shows. The services that turn long rollouts into training data.

1Environment fleet
pre-warmed sandboxes per task family, created from pinned images; long-lived for an episode; snapshot and restore through the storage layer (Design 01).
2Rollout engines
generate turns; pause trajectories while environments respond; tag each turn with policy version and log-probabilities (Design 07).
3Trajectory store
turns, snapshots references and checks, in object storage with an index; trajectories are replayable and branchable.
4Credit workers
pick branch points, schedule branches, compute turn values and advantages, and calibrate process reward models; a separate queue so credit work can lag the rollout slightly.
5Verifier workers
fresh-environment verification, layered checks, versioned.
6Trainer
consumes turns with advantages; computes log-probabilities with the per-turn context.
7Snapshot garbage collection
snapshots expire once a trajectory's credit is computed, except those kept for curricula.

The YAML. Branch rollouts as a Kueue-admitted batch of short jobs, at lower priority than primary rollouts so they fill spare capacity.

apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: branches-8f2c-t31  namespace: rl-envs  labels:    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-branches    kueue.x-k8s.io/priority-class: branch-low       # yields to primary rolloutsspec:  completions: 8                                    # k = 8 continuations  parallelism: 8  completionMode: Indexed  backoffLimit: 2  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      runtimeClassName: gvisor                      # model-driven code runs sandboxed      containers:      - name: branch        image: registry.example.com/rl/branch-runner:2026.11        args: ["--trajectory=8f2c", "--from-turn=31", "--seed-index=$(JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX)",               "--policy=latest", "--max-turns=60"]        resources: { limits: { cpu: "2", memory: 4Gi } }        volumeMounts: [ { name: ws, mountPath: /workspace } ]      volumes:      - name: ws        ephemeral:          volumeClaimTemplate:            spec:              storageClassName: fast-cow              dataSource: { apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io, kind: VolumeSnapshot, name: traj-8f2c-turn-31 }              accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]              resources: { requests: { storage: 20Gi } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Environment cost can exceed GPU cost: an hour-long sandbox per episode, times thousands of episodes per step, times branches. Track environment-minutes per trajectory and per useful sample.
  • Rollouts wait on environments: the rollout engine should release KV cache for a trajectory waiting on a slow tool, and resume it later, so long tool calls don't hold GPUs.

Measuring progress on long tasks

Scenario. After a month of work, the overall success rate is up four points. Nobody can say whether long-horizon ability improved or the gain came from easy tasks.

What the picture shows. The metrics that show whether long-horizon reasoning, not just short-task performance, is improving.

1Success by horizon
success rate bucketed by the number of turns the reference solution needs; the slope of this curve is the headline metric.
2pass@1 and pass@k
pass@k shows whether the model can solve a task; pass@1 shows whether it reliably does. A widening gap means exploration is fine but consistency isn't.
3Partial progress
milestone completion on failed episodes; a model that gets further before failing is improving even when success is flat.
4Recovery rate
after an intermediate check fails (a test fails, a command errors), how often the agent recovers and still succeeds.
5Behavior pathologies
early stopping, loops, false claims of success, excessive length; each tracked per checkpoint.
6Credit quality
agreement between the training credit method and expensive Monte Carlo estimates on a held-out sample.
Going deeper2 points
  • Keep a fixed, private long-horizon eval set with fresh-environment verification and human-checked solutions; never train on it or on its environments.
  • Cost per solved task (GPU, environment and verifier minutes) is the efficiency metric that matters for long tasks.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, data foundations: the trajectory schema, per-turn log-probabilities, the trajectory store, layered verification and the horizon-bucketed eval.
  • Phase 2, credit: turn-level advantages from verifiable milestones; snapshots and branch rollouts for Monte Carlo values on a sample; credit-quality checks.
  • Phase 3, exploration: reverse and horizon curricula, pass@k-style objectives, loop guards.
  • Phase 4, efficiency: process reward models calibrated by branches; context compaction trained end to end; environment fleet autoscaling and snapshot garbage collection.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Branching costs extra rollouts (often 20–50% more environment time) for much better credit on the trajectories where it's used.
  • Shaped and process rewards add signal and risk: kept small, potential-based, and continuously checked against final success.
  • Curricula from snapshots speed up learning but train on states the model didn't produce; mitigated by mixing in full episodes and evaluating only on full ones.
  • Fresh-environment verification is slower and costlier than checking in place, and it's the only version we trust.

Open questions.

  • Learned critics at scale: can a value model trained on branch estimates become accurate enough to replace most branching?
  • Credit across compaction: how well does credit flow through summaries and memory writes, and should summarization be trained as a separate skill?
  • Horizon generalization: does training on 100-turn tasks transfer to 1,000-turn tasks, or does each horizon need its own curriculum?
  • Verification of open-ended work: for research or design tasks without tests, what combination of judges, rubrics and human review is trustworthy enough to train on?
Design 09 · 12 sections

Design 09: Off-policy and asynchronous training

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Where off-policy data comes from
  3. Three policies: behavior, proximal and target
  4. When off-policy data helps and when it hurts
  5. Bounded staleness in an asynchronous pipeline
  6. Filtering is off-policy too
  7. Replay buffers and data from other policies
  8. Diagnostics: measuring off-policyness
  9. Controlling instabilities automatically
  10. Building intuition: off-policy experiments
  11. The platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we train on data generated by older versions of the model, by different models, or by filtered selections of the model's outputs, and know when that data helps, when it hurts, and how to keep the resulting instabilities under control? Asynchronous RL (Design 07) makes almost every sample a little off-policy; replay buffers, teacher data and filtering (Design 06) make some samples very off-policy. This design builds the intuition, the metrics and the controls for all of them.

The short version: always know which policy produced each token, and measure how far it is from the policy being trained. Every token carries its behavior policy (who generated it, which version, its log-probability). The trainer separates three policies: the behavior policy that generated the data, a proximal policy that anchors the update, and the target policy being trained. Corrections are applied in two separate places (engine mismatch and staleness), and a small set of off-policy health metrics (importance-ratio quantiles, effective sample size, clipped and masked fractions, version age) drive automatic controls: lower the staleness limit, drop a batch, cut the learning rate, or roll back.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The RL team moved to fully asynchronous training to keep GPUs busy, and it's 2.4× faster. But the results are inconsistent: one run matches the synchronous baseline, another with "the same settings" collapses on day two, and a third quietly ends four points lower. At the same time, researchers want to reuse last month's expensive agent trajectories, mix in teacher solutions for hard problems, and keep dynamic sampling. Nobody can say how off-policy any of this data is, or which of it is safe.

What the platform must do.

  • Record provenance for every token: which model and version produced it, from which engine, with what log-probability and sampling settings.
  • Measure off-policyness per batch: how far the data is from the current policy, in numbers that predict trouble.
  • Correct consistently: one implementation of the corrections, applied the same way in every trainer, with the policies kept separate.
  • Control instability automatically: respond to warning signs during a run, not in a post-mortem.
  • Build intuition with experiments: make it cheap to sweep staleness, data age and data mixtures, and see where each recipe breaks.
  • Support reuse: replay buffers and other-policy data with explicit rules for what can be mixed in and how much.

Out of scope: the base objective and rewards (Design 06), the rollout systems themselves (Design 07).

Where off-policy data comes from

Scenario. In a design review, "off-policy" means six different things to six people. The team needs a shared vocabulary and a picture of how far from the current policy each source usually is.

What the picture shows. Sources of off-policy data, roughly ordered from mildly to strongly off-policy.

1Engine mismatch
same weights, different engines (vLLM or SGLang vs FSDP or Megatron). Technically off-policy even in synchronous training; small but always present.
2Staleness from asynchrony
samples generated by a policy that's k updates behind the trainer. Grows with k and with the learning rate.
3Partial rollouts
one answer generated across several policy versions (paused, then resumed under newer weights).
4Selection and filtering
dynamic sampling, rejection sampling and best-of-n change which samples are trained on. Each token is still the policy's own, but the batch no longer follows the policy's distribution.
5Replay of older data
trajectories from earlier in the run or from previous runs, possibly hundreds of updates old.
6Other policies
teacher models, other checkpoints, human demonstrations. Their tokens may be very unlikely under the current policy.
Going deeper2 points
  • Off-policyness is a distance, not a yes/no: it's measured per token as the log-ratio between the current policy and whatever produced the token, and it differs a lot between tokens in the same answer.
  • The same staleness can be harmless or fatal: five updates at a tiny learning rate on a stable run move the policy less than one update with a large learning rate during a fast phase. Measure the distance, not just the version gap.

Three policies: behavior, proximal and target

Scenario. The trainer computes PPO's ratio against "the old policy," which in the synchronous code meant "the policy that generated the data." In async mode that's the rollout engine's log-probability from four versions ago, so the clipping range now does two jobs at once (correcting staleness and limiting the update) and does neither well.

What the picture shows. Separating the policies so each correction does one job.

1Behavior policy (μ)
the policy that actually sampled the tokens, as seen by the inference engine, at some older version. Its log-probabilities are recorded at sampling time.
2Proximal policy (π_prox)
a recent version of the policy, computed by the training engine, used as the anchor for clipping. It defines the trust region: how far one update may move.
3Target policy (π_θ)
the parameters being updated now.
4Two ratios, two jobs
π_θ / π_prox is clipped (PPO's trust region); π_prox / μ is an importance weight that corrects for staleness and engine mismatch, truncated or masked when it's extreme.
5Decoupled objectives
this separation is the core of decoupled PPO, used by asynchronous systems such as AReaL. One reported ablation on a 1.5B reasoning model found naive PPO losing about 19 AIME24 points at a staleness of 4, while the decoupled objective stayed close to the synchronous result.
6The missing-old-logits problem
π_prox needs the training engine's log-probabilities for an older version. If those were never computed (weights already overwritten, partial rollouts spanning versions), staleness and engine-mismatch corrections get tangled together. Recent work names this failure and proposes repairs; the platform avoids it by computing π_prox log-probabilities on arrival.

The code. A decoupled, token-level loss with a truncated behavior weight (PyTorch).

import torch def decoupled_ppo_loss(logp_target, logp_prox, logp_behavior, advantages, mask,                       clip_low=0.2, clip_high=0.28, is_cap=3.0, mask_above=10.0):    """    logp_target:   log π_θ(token)      (requires grad)    logp_prox:     log π_prox(token)   training engine, recent version (no grad)    logp_behavior: log μ(token)        recorded by the rollout engine at sampling time    """    ratio = torch.exp(logp_target - logp_prox)                       # trust region    behavior_w = torch.exp(logp_prox - logp_behavior).detach()       # staleness + engine mismatch    keep = mask * (behavior_w < mask_above).float()                  # mask extreme tokens (MIS)    behavior_w = behavior_w.clamp(max=is_cap)                        # truncate the rest (TIS)     surr1 = ratio * advantages    surr2 = ratio.clamp(1 - clip_low, 1 + clip_high) * advantages    per_token = -behavior_w * torch.min(surr1, surr2)    loss = (per_token * keep).sum() / keep.sum().clamp(min=1)        # token-level mean     stats = {"offpolicy/masked_frac": 1 - keep.sum().item() / mask.sum().item(),             "offpolicy/clipped_frac": (((ratio - 1).abs() > clip_low) * mask).sum().item() / mask.sum().item()}    return loss, stats
Going deeper2 points
  • Choose π_prox by convenience and cost: the version that generated the data (needs one extra forward pass per sample on arrival) or the trainer's state at the start of the step (free, but further from the data). Record which one a run uses.
  • Sequence-level ratios (GSPO-style) are steadier for long answers and MoE models, because one extreme token can't dominate; they also hide which tokens are off. Keep token-level metrics even when the loss is sequence-level.

When off-policy data helps and when it hurts

Scenario. A researcher asks a simple question: "Can I set staleness to 8?" The honest answer depends on the learning rate, the correction, the task and how fast the policy is changing, and the platform should be able to show it.

What the picture shows. The trade-off between throughput and the quality of each sample, and where recipes typically land.

1It helps
throughput (no GPU waits for the slowest rollout), more samples per GPU hour, reuse of expensive trajectories, and access to behavior the current policy can't yet produce (teacher solutions to hard problems).
2It hurts through bias
uncorrected, the update optimizes the wrong policy's objective; the further the data, the larger the error.
3It hurts through variance
corrected, a few tokens with huge importance weights dominate the gradient; effective sample size falls, and the update becomes noisy even when unbiased.
4The safe region depends on how fast the policy moves
small learning rates and slow phases tolerate more staleness. Early training and sudden capability jumps tolerate less.
5Good corrections move the cliff
recent work describes a "prosperity before collapse" pattern, where stale data stays as useful as fresh data up to a point and then fails abruptly. A method that suppresses only the extreme importance weights (M2PO) reported stable training with data at least 256 updates old.

Data sources at a glance.

Data source Usually helps when Usually hurts when Control
Async staleness 1–4 Long tails waste GPU time LR high, fast-changing phase Decoupled loss, bounded staleness
Partial rollouts Very long answers Versions not recorded per span Per-span versions, behavior weights
Filtering / dynamic sampling Many zero-signal groups Filter correlates with a behavior you don't want Read capability from held-out evals
Replay buffer Rollouts are expensive (agents) Old data dominates; low ESS Age limits, mixing ratio, ESS floor
Teacher / other policy Policy can't solve hard prompts yet Tokens very unlikely under the policy Small ratio, SFT-style loss, anneal out
Going deeper2 points
  • Every recipe has a staleness curve: final held-out score versus allowed staleness, for each correction. That curve, measured at small scale, is the evidence for the staleness setting at large scale.
  • Distance, not age, predicts failure: across runs, the behavior KL and the importance-ratio tail predict collapse better than the version gap. Configure limits in both.

Bounded staleness in an asynchronous pipeline

Scenario. Rollout engines get new weights every few minutes, but one slow engine still serves version 112 while the trainer is at 131. Its samples are accepted because nothing checks.

What the picture shows. How versions flow through the pipeline and where staleness is enforced.

1Version tags
every weight push has a version; every token records the version that produced it (and partial rollouts record a list of spans).
2Admission at the buffer
samples older than the limit are rejected or sent to the replay pool, not into the main batch.
3Admission at the rollout scheduler
engines more than k versions behind stop receiving new prompts until they reload, so stale data isn't generated in the first place.
4Batch composition
the trainer can cap the share of a batch at each age (for example, at most 30% at the maximum allowed age).
5Adaptive limits
the limit can tighten automatically when the off-policy metrics degrade (see the controller below).

The YAML. The asynchronous pipeline's policy, read by the rollout scheduler, the buffer and the trainer.

# recipes/assistant-v13/async-policy.yamlasync:  max_staleness: 4                      # versions; hard limit at admission  max_behavior_kl: 0.02                 # distance limit, checked per batch  engine_stops_sampling_when_behind: 4  # don't generate what we'd reject  batch_age_mix: { "0-1": ">=0.5", "4": "<=0.3" }  partial_rollouts: { enabled: true, record_version_spans: true }correction:  objective: decoupled_ppo  proximal_policy: version_of_sample    # π_prox computed by trainer on arrival  behavior_weight: { truncate_at: 3.0, mask_above: 10.0, level: token }controller:  enabled: true  rules: recipes/assistant-v13/offpolicy-controller.yaml
Going deeper2 points
  • Compute π_prox on arrival: the trainer (or a dedicated log-prob worker on training-engine kernels) scores each sample with the weights of the version that generated it before those weights are discarded. This avoids the missing-old-logits problem and costs one forward pass per sample.
  • Keep a few old weight versions in memory or on fast storage for exactly this purpose, sized to the staleness limit.

Filtering is off-policy too

Scenario. Dynamic sampling keeps only prompts with mixed outcomes, and rejection sampling keeps only correct answers for an SFT step. Both "use the model's own outputs," so the team assumed they were on-policy. After a month, the model avoids a whole class of problems it used to attempt.

What the picture shows. How filters change the training distribution, and what to do about it.

1Prompt-level filters (dynamic sampling, pass-rate curation)
change which tasks are trained on. Usually benign for learning signal, but they shift what "average reward" means and can drop whole task types as they become easy or hard.
2Sample-level filters (rejection sampling, best-of-n)
train only on selected answers. Equivalent to a different behavior policy (the "policy plus filter"), biased toward whatever the filter favors, including length, style or verifier quirks.
3Token-level filters (masking extreme ratios, high-entropy tokens only)
change which tokens carry gradient. Useful for stability, but a large masked fraction means much of the data isn't being learned from.
4Controls
report filter rates per task type over time, cap how much any filter can remove, evaluate on unfiltered held-out sets, and treat a large rise in any filter rate as a signal, not just a mechanism.

The code. Logging what filters remove, by task type, so shifts are visible (Python).

from collections import Counter def filter_report(groups, step: int, log):    """groups: list of dicts with task_type and per-sample rewards; dynamic sampling drops all-equal groups."""    seen, dropped = Counter(), Counter()    kept = []    for g in groups:        seen[g["task_type"]] += 1        if len(set(g["rewards"])) == 1:                 # zero-variance group: no signal            dropped[g["task_type"]] += 1            continue        kept.append(g)    for t in seen:        log(f"filter/drop_rate/{t}", dropped[t] / seen[t], step)   # watch these drift    log("filter/kept_fraction", len(kept) / max(len(groups), 1), step)    return kept
Going deeper2 points
  • Best-of-n then SFT is a strong off-policy push: it moves the model toward its own best samples quickly, and toward the verifier's blind spots just as quickly. Keep the selected fraction and the verifier under review.
  • Masked fraction is a cost: if 5% of tokens are masked for extreme ratios, 5% of the rollout compute produced nothing. Track it alongside throughput.

Replay buffers and data from other policies

Scenario. Agent trajectories cost $3 each to generate. The team wants to reuse successful ones from last month and add teacher-written solutions for the hardest 5% of tasks. The first attempt mixes them in at 40% and the policy's entropy collapses within 300 steps.

What the picture shows. Rules for mixing in data the current policy didn't generate.

1Separate pools
fresh on-policy data, replay (own older data), and external (teacher, other checkpoints, human). Each has its own mixing ratio in the batch.
2Age and distance limits
replay samples are eligible only within an age limit and when their behavior KL to the current policy is below a threshold; the rest are retired.
3Prioritize informative samples
