successes on hard tasks and samples with large advantages, re-scored with current values where possible.
4External data with its own loss
teacher tokens can be very unlikely under the policy, so importance weights explode. Use a separate, small-weight SFT-style term (or on-policy distillation, Design 06) rather than pushing them through the RL loss, and reduce the weight as the policy learns to solve those tasks itself.
5ESS floor
if a batch's effective sample size falls below a set fraction of its size, the mixing ratio of off-policy pools drops automatically.

The code. A replay buffer with age and distance limits, sampled at a fixed ratio (Python).

import randomfrom dataclasses import dataclass @dataclassclass Sample:    tokens: list[int]    behavior_version: int    behavior_kl: float          # refreshed periodically vs the current policy    advantage: float    source: str                 # "fresh" | "replay" | "teacher" class MixedBuffer:    def __init__(self, max_age=64, max_kl=0.05, mix={"fresh": 0.8, "replay": 0.15, "teacher": 0.05}):        self.pools = {k: [] for k in mix}        self.max_age, self.max_kl, self.mix = max_age, max_kl, mix     def add(self, s: Sample):        self.pools[s.source].append(s)     def sample(self, n: int, current_version: int) -> list[Sample]:        self.pools["replay"] = [s for s in self.pools["replay"]                 # retire old/far data                                if current_version - s.behavior_version <= self.max_age                                and s.behavior_kl <= self.max_kl]        batch = []        for src, frac in self.mix.items():            pool = sorted(self.pools[src], key=lambda s: -abs(s.advantage))    # informative first            batch += pool[: int(n * frac)]        random.shuffle(batch)        return batch     def lower_offpolicy_share(self, factor=0.5):                               # called by the controller        moved = sum(v for k, v in self.mix.items() if k != "fresh") * (1 - factor)        for k in self.mix:            self.mix[k] = self.mix[k] * factor if k != "fresh" else self.mix[k] + moved
Going deeper2 points
  • Off-policy data can rescue exploration: when the policy solves 0% of a task family, a few teacher solutions provide the first positive signal. Anneal them out once the policy succeeds on its own.
  • Re-score replay rewards with the current verifier: a verifier fix should apply to old data too, or the buffer keeps teaching the old exploit.

Diagnostics: measuring off-policyness

Scenario. Two runs look identical on reward. One has 0.3% of tokens with importance ratio above 3; the other has 4%, rising. Only one of them will survive the week.

What the picture shows. The off-policy metrics every run reports per step, and what each predicts.

1Importance-ratio quantiles (p50, p99, max) and tail fraction
the share of tokens with ratio above 2 or 3. A growing tail is the earliest warning of collapse.
2Effective sample size (ESS)
how many samples the weighted batch is "worth." ESS / N near 1 means the weights are even; a falling ESS means a few samples dominate.
3Behavior KL
the estimated KL between the behavior and current policies, per source (fresh, replay, teacher) and per age bucket.
4Clipped fraction and masked fraction
how much of the batch is being cut by the trust region or dropped by the behavior weight.
5Version age histogram
the distribution of staleness actually trained on, versus the configured limit.
6Engine mismatch at zero staleness
the same metrics for samples with age 0, to separate engine mismatch from staleness.

The code. Effective sample size and ratio-tail metrics from the stored log-probabilities (PyTorch).

import torch def offpolicy_metrics(logp_prox, logp_behavior, mask, ages):    lr = (logp_prox - logp_behavior)[mask.bool()]    w = lr.exp()    ess = (w.sum() ** 2) / (w.pow(2).sum() * w.numel())            # ESS / N, in (0, 1]    m = {        "offpolicy/ess_frac": ess.item(),        "offpolicy/ratio_p99": w.quantile(0.99).item(),        "offpolicy/ratio_gt3_frac": (w > 3).float().mean().item(),        "offpolicy/behavior_kl": ((w - 1) - lr).mean().item(),     # k3 estimator    }    for a in sorted(set(ages.tolist())):                            # per-age KL: is staleness the cause?        sel = (ages == a).unsqueeze(-1).expand_as(mask).bool() & mask.bool()        if sel.any():            l = (logp_prox - logp_behavior)[sel]            m[f"offpolicy/behavior_kl_age{a}"] = ((l.exp() - 1) - l).mean().item()    return m
Going deeper2 points
  • Per-token ESS can mislead for long sequences; also compute it at the sequence level (product or mean of log-ratios per answer), which is what matters for sequence-level objectives.
  • Plot metrics against age: if the behavior KL grows steeply with age, the staleness limit is too loose for the current learning rate; if it's high even at age 0, the problem is engine mismatch, not staleness.

Controlling instabilities automatically

Scenario. At 3 a.m., the ratio tail fraction crosses 2% and keeps climbing. By the time someone looks at 9 a.m., the run has collapsed and the last healthy checkpoint is six hours old.

What the picture shows. A controller that reads the off-policy metrics and applies graduated responses.

1Level 1, tighten
lower the staleness limit, lower the share of replay and external data, or make engines reload sooner.
2Level 2, protect the update
skip a batch whose ESS or ratio tail is far outside the normal range; lower the learning rate temporarily.
3Level 3, recover
roll back to the last checkpoint whose metrics were healthy, apply the tighter settings, and continue; alert a person.
4Hysteresis
loosen settings again only after metrics have been healthy for a while, so the controller doesn't oscillate.
5Everything logged
every controller action is recorded as an event on the run's timeline, with the metric values that triggered it.

The YAML. The controller's rules, versioned with the recipe.

# recipes/assistant-v13/offpolicy-controller.yamlwindow_steps: 10rules:- name: ratio-tail-rising  when: { metric: offpolicy/ratio_gt3_frac, above: 0.01, for_steps: 5 }  then:  - { set: async.max_staleness, to: "max(1, current - 2)" }       # tighten first  - { set: buffer.mix.replay, multiply: 0.5 }- name: low-ess  when: { metric: offpolicy/ess_frac, below: 0.6 }  then:  - { action: skip_batch }  - { set: optim.lr, multiply: 0.5, restore_after_steps: 50 }- name: collapse-warning  when:    all:    - { metric: offpolicy/ratio_gt3_frac, above: 0.03 }    - { metric: health/entropy_slope, below: -0.002 }  then:  - { action: rollback, to: last_healthy_checkpoint }  - { action: page, team: rl-oncall }relax:  healthy_for_steps: 200  step_back: { async.max_staleness: +1, buffer.mix.replay: "*1.25" }

The code. The controller loop that applies those rules (Python sketch).

def control_step(step, metrics, rules, state, actions):    for rule in rules:        if rule.triggered(metrics, state.history):            for a in rule.then:                actions.apply(a)                                  # update recipe-live config                state.events.append({"step": step, "rule": rule.name, "action": a, "metrics": metrics})            state.last_trigger = step            return                                                # one rule per step    if step - state.last_trigger > state.relax_after:        actions.relax_one_notch()
Going deeper2 points
  • Healthy checkpoints are tagged automatically: a checkpoint is "healthy" if the off-policy and health metrics in the surrounding window were within limits; rollback targets only those.
  • Test the controller on purpose: inject staleness or a learning-rate spike in a small run and confirm the controller catches it before the reward moves.

Building intuition: off-policy experiments

Scenario. New team members learn the effects of staleness by breaking production runs. The team wants a cheap, repeatable way to see the effects instead.

What the picture shows. A small, standard experiment harness that turns off-policy questions into curves.

1Staleness injection
a synchronous run with an artificial delay: train on samples from k versions ago. Isolates staleness from every other async effect.
2Sweeps
staleness × correction method × learning rate, on a small model and a fixed task set; each cell is a short run.
3Outputs
the staleness curve (final held-out score vs k) for each correction, the steps-to-collapse, and the off-policy metrics at the moment each run broke.
4Data-source sweeps
the replay ratio and the teacher ratio, with the same outputs.
5A reference result library
every sweep's curves are stored with the recipe and model size, so "can I set staleness to 8?" is answered by a lookup.

The YAML. A staleness sweep as an Indexed Job: each index is one cell of the grid, admitted by Kueue at low priority.

apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: staleness-sweep-2026-11  namespace: rl-research  labels:    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: research-small    kueue.x-k8s.io/priority-class: sweep-lowspec:  completions: 24                      # 6 staleness × 2 corrections × 2 learning rates  parallelism: 8  completionMode: Indexed  backoffLimit: 0  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: cell        image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer:2026.11        command: ["python3", "-m", "rl.sweeps.staleness"]        args:        - --index=$(JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX)        - --grid=staleness:0,1,2,4,8,16;correction:naive,decoupled;lr:1e-6,3e-6        - --model=registry://small-1.5b@v3        - --inject=delayed-sync          # isolate staleness from other async effects        - --steps=400        resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Re-run the sweep when the recipe changes meaningfully: a new objective, a new model family or a much larger learning rate can move the cliff.
  • Check at one larger scale: confirm two or three cells of the sweep on the target model before trusting the small-scale curve.

The platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. The trainer, rollout engines, buffer, log-prob workers and controller were added piece by piece; nobody owns the versions flowing between them.

What the picture shows. The components and the data each passes on.

1Rollout engines (LeaderWorkerSet)
sample with version tags and record behavior log-probabilities; refuse new prompts when too far behind.
2Weight distribution
pushes versioned weights to engines and keeps the last k versions available for log-prob workers (Design 07).
3Log-prob workers
compute π_prox log-probabilities on arrival with the training engine's kernels and the sample's version.
4Sample buffer
fresh, replay and external pools; admission rules for age and distance; mixing ratios; persisted with checkpoints.
5Trainer (JobSet)
decoupled loss, off-policy metrics, checkpoints tagged healthy or not.
6Controller
reads metrics, changes live settings, triggers rollbacks, writes events.
7Experiment harness
staleness and mixing sweeps on the research queue.
Going deeper2 points
  • Live settings are versioned too: the controller's changes are written to a per-run settings record, so a run's effective configuration at any step can be reconstructed exactly.
  • One correction library: the loss, weights and metrics live in one shared package used by every trainer (TRL for small runs, verl or Megatron-based trainers for large ones), so "decoupled with truncation 3.0" means the same thing everywhere.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, provenance and metrics: per-token behavior version and log-probabilities, off-policy metrics on every run, version-age histograms.
  • Phase 2, consistent corrections: the shared correction library with decoupled loss; π_prox computed on arrival; bounded staleness at both the buffer and the scheduler.
  • Phase 3, control: the controller with graduated responses, healthy-checkpoint tagging and automatic rollback.
  • Phase 4, reuse and intuition: replay and external pools with limits; the sweep harness and reference result library.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Computing π_prox on arrival costs an extra forward pass per sample, in exchange for clean separation of staleness and engine mismatch.
  • Conservative default staleness (1–4) gives up some throughput for predictable training; larger limits are used only with evidence from the sweep library.
  • Automatic rollbacks sometimes discard good progress after a false alarm; we accept that over losing a whole run.
  • External data through a separate loss is less elegant than one unified objective, but much easier to keep stable.

Open questions.

  • Distance-adaptive staleness: should the limit be expressed only in behavior KL, letting the version gap float freely?
  • Better estimators for long sequences: token-level weights are noisy, sequence-level weights explode; which middle ground (segments, turns) works best for long-horizon agents (Design 08)?
  • Very old data: with outlier-only suppression reported to work at hundreds of updates of staleness, how much of last month's data can we safely reuse?
  • Filters as policies: can we model the "policy plus filter" explicitly and correct for selection bias, rather than just monitoring it?
Design 10 · 12 sections

Design 10: Verification and reward quality

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. How RL looks better than it is
  3. A verifier is a product: contract, interface and lifecycle
  4. Measuring verifier quality
  5. Hardening: fuzzing and differential testing
  6. Answer verification: strict contracts for math and short answers
  7. Code verification: tests that are hard to fool
  8. Model-based judges: useful, and fragile
  9. Detecting reward hacking during training
  10. Semi-automatic verification: people in the loop
  11. The platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build verification pipelines that we can trust as RL rewards, for tasks where correctness can be checked automatically or semi-automatically, and how do we detect and reduce reward hacking, false positives, brittle verifiers and the other failure modes that make RL look better than it really is? Rewards were introduced in Design 06, long-horizon verification in Design 08, and sandboxed execution in Design 01. This design treats the verifier itself as the product.

The short version: a verifier is production software that an optimizer is actively attacking. Every verifier has a written contract, a versioned implementation, a labeled test set, a fuzzing suite and measured precision and recall per task slice, and it may abstain when unsure. During training, a reward-quality monitor compares the training reward with independent checks (a stricter verifier, perturbed versions of the task, sampled human review) and treats any widening gap as reward hacking until proven otherwise. A verifier change re-scores the data it affected.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The team's math-and-code RL run reports +11 points on training reward and +9 on the internal benchmark. An external evaluation shows +2. Investigation finds three problems: the math verifier accepts answers that list several candidates, the code verifier counts a program as correct if its printed output matches even when it crashes afterwards, and the benchmark shares a verifier with training. RL learned all three.

What the platform must do.

  • Make verifiers trustworthy: precise contracts, measured error rates, and evidence before a verifier is used for training.
  • Prefer precision: a verifier that sometimes rejects correct answers slows learning; one that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior.
  • Find weaknesses before the model does: fuzzing, differential testing and adversarial cases on every verifier change.
  • Detect hacking during training: independent signals that diverge from the training reward when the policy exploits the verifier.
  • Use people where they matter: route uncertain and disputed cases to human review, within a budget.
  • Keep evaluation honest: evaluation verifiers that are independent of training verifiers.

Out of scope: the RL objective (Design 06), sandbox isolation itself (Design 01).

How RL looks better than it is

Scenario. Each failure was found by accident. The team wants a checklist of the ways a reward can lie, so each one has an owner and a test.

What the picture shows. The failure modes, grouped by where they come from.

1False positives
the verifier accepts a wrong answer. The most dangerous kind, because RL actively seeks them out and reinforces them.
2False negatives
the verifier rejects a correct answer (a different but equivalent form, unexpected formatting). Slows learning and pushes the model toward the verifier's preferred format.
3Brittle verifiers
results change with harmless variations (whitespace, units, 0.5 vs 1/2, key order in JSON). Both false positives and negatives hide here.
4Reward shortcuts
the model satisfies what the verifier checks without doing what the task intends. Recent work found RLVR-trained models abandoning rule induction because the verifier only checked whether the outputs were consistent with the examples.
5Judge exploits
model-based judges reward surface patterns; one study found that openers like "Let's solve this step by step," or even a lone colon, triggered false positive rewards from several LLM judges.
6Environment exploits
editing tests, reading answers from the environment, timing out the checker, or causing a crash that the harness misreads as success.
7Measurement leaks
evaluation sets contaminated by training data, or evaluated with the same verifier used for training, so exploits show up as gains.
Going deeper2 points
  • The optimizer finds what you didn't test: a verifier that's 99% precise on natural answers can be far less precise on answers produced by a policy trained against it. Measure precision on the policy's own outputs, not just on a static set.
  • Hacking grows with optimization: the 2026 study found hacking increased with task complexity and compute. A verifier that's good enough for a small run may not be good enough for a large one.

A verifier is a product: contract, interface and lifecycle

Scenario. The math verifier is a 40-line function written in an afternoon. Three teams copied it with small changes. Nobody knows which copy scored which run.

What the picture shows. The lifecycle every verifier goes through before and after it's used for training.

1Contract
a written definition of what counts as correct, including the answer format, accepted equivalences, what's forbidden (multiple answers, hedging) and when to abstain.
2Implementation
a versioned package with one interface: verdict (pass, fail, abstain), score, reasons and the verifier version.
3Test set
labeled examples, including tricky cases and past exploits, run in CI on every change.
4Fuzzing and differential tests
adversarial completions generated automatically, compared against a stricter reference verifier.
5Calibration
precision and recall measured per task slice on gold labels and on the current policy's outputs.
6Deployment and monitoring
served with a version; every reward is tagged with that version; quality is monitored during training.
7Change and re-score
a fix creates a new version, and data scored by the old one is re-scored.

The code. The interface every verifier implements (Python).

from dataclasses import dataclass, fieldfrom enum import Enum class Verdict(str, Enum):    PASS = "pass"    FAIL = "fail"    ABSTAIN = "abstain"          # unsure: no reward, routed to review @dataclassclass Result:    verdict: Verdict    score: float                 # 0..1; 1.0 only for PASS    reasons: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # machine-readable, e.g. "multiple_final_answers"    verifier: str = ""           # e.g. "math-final-answer@3.2.0" class Verifier:    name: str    version: str     def verify(self, task: dict, completion: str) -> Result:        raise NotImplementedError     def reward(self, task: dict, completion: str) -> float | None:        r = self.verify(task, completion)        return None if r.verdict is Verdict.ABSTAIN else r.score   # None = excluded from the loss
Going deeper2 points
  • Abstention is a feature: a verifier allowed to say "I don't know" can be strict without being wrong. Abstained samples are excluded from the loss (TRL reward functions, for example, accept None) and counted, so a rising abstention rate is visible.
  • Reasons are data: aggregated reasons ("multiple_final_answers" rising from 0.1% to 6%) are often the first sign of a policy probing the verifier.

Measuring verifier quality

Scenario. Asked "how good is our code verifier?", the team answers "it uses the official tests." That doesn't say how often it's wrong, or on what.

What the picture shows. How verifier quality is measured, and why precision gets the most attention.

1Gold labels
a sample of completions labeled by people or by a much stricter, slower reference check, refreshed regularly from the current policy's outputs.
2Confusion matrix per slice
precision (of what the verifier accepts, how much is correct) and recall (of what's correct, how much it accepts), by task type, difficulty and answer format.
3Precision first
a 2026 study of noisy rewards found that RL performance tracked the verifier's precision far more than its recall, and that moderate noise could even help exploration while false positives enabled hacking.
4Two populations
measure on a static gold set (regressions in the verifier) and on fresh policy outputs (exploits the policy has found). The second number is the one that drifts.
5Abstention rate and coverage
a verifier that abstains on 30% of a slice gives that slice little signal; track it per slice.

The code. Computing quality per slice from paired verifier and gold decisions (Python).

from collections import defaultdict def verifier_quality(rows):    """rows: dicts with slice, verdict ('pass'|'fail'|'abstain'), gold (True/False)."""    by = defaultdict(lambda: {"tp": 0, "fp": 0, "fn": 0, "tn": 0, "abstain": 0})    for r in rows:        c = by[r["slice"]]        if r["verdict"] == "abstain":            c["abstain"] += 1        elif r["verdict"] == "pass":            c["tp" if r["gold"] else "fp"] += 1        else:            c["fn" if r["gold"] else "tn"] += 1    out = {}    for s, c in by.items():        decided = c["tp"] + c["fp"] + c["fn"] + c["tn"]        out[s] = {            "precision": c["tp"] / max(c["tp"] + c["fp"], 1),      # the number that matters most            "recall": c["tp"] / max(c["tp"] + c["fn"], 1),            "abstain_rate": c["abstain"] / max(decided + c["abstain"], 1),            "n": decided + c["abstain"],        }    return out
Going deeper2 points
  • Gate training on precision: a verifier may be used for training on a slice only above a precision threshold (for example, 98% on fresh policy outputs); below it, the slice abstains or goes to review.
  • Report intervals, not points: with a few hundred labels per slice, a 99% precision estimate has a wide interval. Size the gold sample for the precision you need to prove.

Hardening: fuzzing and differential testing

Scenario. After a hack is found, the fix takes a day. But the policy found the hack in a few hundred steps; the team wants to find such holes before training does.

What the picture shows. Generating adversarial completions and comparing verifiers to find false positives automatically.

1Mutation-based fuzzing
take known wrong and right answers and apply transformations: list several answers, put the right answer first and a wrong one last, hedge ("either 3 or 4"), add the expected output in a comment, wrap answers in odd formatting, use equivalent forms.
2Model-based adversaries
prompt a model to produce answers that would pass the verifier without solving the task; or run a short RL run against the verifier on purpose (a "red-team run") and inspect what gets rewarded.
3Differential testing
run the production verifier and a stricter reference on the same cases; every disagreement is either a false positive, a false negative or a contract ambiguity, and each is triaged.
4Regression suite
every confirmed exploit becomes a permanent test case.
5Published evidence
a 2026 verifier-fuzzing study showed that realistic bugs (accepting the first number in a response, ignoring duplicate JSON keys, treating printed text as program correctness) create high-reward false positives, and stricter variants removed the measured false positives on the same generated cases.

The code. A small fuzzing harness that applies mutations and reports disagreements with a strict reference (Python).

import random MUTATIONS = {    "multi_answer":   lambda wrong, right: f"The answer is \\boxed{{{wrong}}} or \\boxed{{{right}}}",    "right_first":    lambda wrong, right: f"\\boxed{{{right}}} ... actually \\boxed{{{wrong}}}",    "hedge":          lambda wrong, right: f"It is either {right} or {wrong}.",    "number_soup":    lambda wrong, right: " ".join(str(x) for x in range(-5, 50)),    "equiv_form":     lambda wrong, right: f"\\boxed{{{to_equivalent_form(right)}}}",   # must PASS} def fuzz(verifier, reference, tasks, n_per_task=5, seed=0):    rng, findings = random.Random(seed), []    for task in tasks:        right, wrong = task["solution"], task["distractor"]        for name in rng.sample(list(MUTATIONS), k=min(n_per_task, len(MUTATIONS))):            completion = MUTATIONS[name](wrong, right)            a = verifier.verify(task, completion).verdict            b = reference.verify(task, completion).verdict            if a != b:                findings.append({"task": task["id"], "mutation": name, "prod": a, "ref": b,                                 "kind": "false_positive" if a == "pass" else "false_negative"})    return findings
Going deeper2 points
  • Fuzz on every verifier change in CI, and nightly against the current policy's outputs, since new policy behavior opens new attack surfaces.
  • A red-team run is cheap insurance: a few hundred RL steps on a small model against a new verifier often surfaces its worst holes before a large run does.

Answer verification: strict contracts for math and short answers

Scenario. The math verifier extracts "the last number in the response." The policy learns to end every answer with a short list of plausible values.

What the picture shows. A strict final-answer contract and the steps that enforce it.

1One designated final answer
exactly one marked final answer (for example, one \boxed{} after the reasoning). Zero or several means FAIL, not "take the last one."
2Parse into a narrow language
numbers, fractions, intervals, simple expressions; anything outside the accepted language abstains instead of guessing.
3Symbolic equivalence
compare with a computer algebra system (SymPy), not string matching, with explicit rules for units, rounding and ordering.
4Hedging detection
reject answers that say "or" around the final answer, or that give a range when a value was asked for.
5Abstain on ambiguity
when the reference answer itself has several valid forms that the parser can't settle, abstain and route to review.

The code. A strict final-answer verifier (Python, SymPy).

import reimport sympy as spfrom sympy.parsing.latex import parse_latex BOX = re.compile(r"\\boxed\{((?:[^{}]|\{[^{}]*\})*)\}") class StrictFinalAnswer(Verifier):    name, version = "math-final-answer", "3.2.0"     def verify(self, task, completion):        boxes = BOX.findall(completion)        if len(boxes) != 1:                                             # exactly one final answer            return Result(Verdict.FAIL, 0.0, [f"final_answers={len(boxes)}"], self.id)        if re.search(r"\b(or|either)\b", completion[completion.rfind("\\boxed"):][:80]):            return Result(Verdict.FAIL, 0.0, ["hedged_final_answer"], self.id)        try:            got, want = parse_latex(boxes[0]), parse_latex(task["solution"])        except Exception:            return Result(Verdict.ABSTAIN, 0.0, ["unparseable"], self.id)   # don't guess        try:            ok = sp.simplify(got - want) == 0        except Exception:            return Result(Verdict.ABSTAIN, 0.0, ["not_comparable"], self.id)        return Result(Verdict.PASS if ok else Verdict.FAIL, float(ok), [], self.id)     @property    def id(self):        return f"{self.name}@{self.version}"
Going deeper2 points
  • The prompt must state the contract: tell the model exactly how to give its final answer. A strict verifier with an unstated contract produces false negatives that look like capability problems.
  • Track the failure reasons per step: a policy that starts hitting "final_answers=2" more often is probing the contract.

Code verification: tests that are hard to fool

Scenario. A code task's tests check printed output. The policy learns to print the expected output and exit early; on some tasks it hard-codes outputs for the visible examples.

What the picture shows. Layers that make code verification robust.

1Hidden tests
visible examples in the prompt, separate hidden tests for the reward, so hard-coding visible cases fails.
2Stronger tests
property-based tests (random inputs checked against properties or a reference solution) and edge cases; measure test strength with mutation testing, by checking that deliberately broken versions of the reference solution fail.
3Run correctly
check the exit code, run each test in a separate process with time and memory limits, and treat crashes, timeouts and partial output as failures.
4Tamper resistance
run in a fresh sandbox with no network; restore test files; forbid reading the tests' directory; scan the code for reads of test files, environment introspection and monkey-patching of the test framework.
5Partial credit with care
fraction of tests passed gives a denser signal but rewards solving easy cases only; weight hard tests more, or require all tests for the full reward.

The YAML. A code task's verification spec, executed by the reward workers in a sandbox (Design 01).

task_id: code-interval-merge-2291verify:  sandbox: { runtime: gvisor, network: none, cpu: "1", memory: 1Gi, timeout_s: 20 }  fresh_environment: true  tests:  - { suite: hidden_examples,  cases: 40,  weight: 0.4 }  - { suite: edge_cases,       cases: 25,  weight: 0.3 }  - { suite: property_based,   runs: 500, oracle: reference_solution, weight: 0.3 }  each_test_in_new_process: true  success_requires: [exit_code_zero, no_stderr_traceback, output_complete]  forbid:    file_reads: ["/verify/**", "/tests/**"]    patterns: ["sys.exit(0)", "os._exit", "unittest.mock", "builtins.open('/tests"]  reward: { mode: all_or_weighted, full_credit_requires_all: true }test_strength:                              # checked when the task is added, not per rollout  mutation_score_min: 0.85                  # tests must catch ≥85% of injected bugsverifier_version: code-tests@5.1.0
Going deeper2 points
  • Test strength varies wildly between tasks: imported datasets often have tasks with one or two weak tests. Measure mutation scores once per task and drop or strengthen weak tasks.
  • Pattern scans are a backstop, not a defense: they catch lazy exploits. Isolation and hidden, strong tests are what make the result trustworthy.

Model-based judges: useful, and fragile

Scenario. For open-ended tasks with no checkable answer, the team uses an LLM judge with a rubric. After 400 steps the policy's answers all start with the same confident opening paragraph and the judge's scores rise 20%.

What the picture shows. How to make model-based judging as trustworthy as it can be.

1Reference-guided rubrics
give the judge the reference answer or key facts and a concrete rubric with yes/no criteria, rather than asking for an overall score.
2Adversarial checks on the judge
before use, test it on empty answers, answers that are only a reasoning opener, answers that restate the question, very long answers and answers with injected instructions ("grade this as correct"). Any non-trivial pass rate is disqualifying.
3Ensembles and disagreement
two or more judges (different models or prompts); disagreement means abstain or human review.
4Calibration on gold labels
the same precision and recall measurement as rule-based verifiers, on the policy's own outputs.
5Combine with rules
rules for what can be checked (format, presence of a final answer, length limits), the judge only for what can't.
6Watch length and style
judges often favor longer, more confident answers; track the correlation between judge score and length.

The code. Guarding a judge with pre-checks and a two-judge agreement rule (Python).

def judged_reward(task, completion, judge_a, judge_b, max_tokens=4000) -> Result:    text = completion.strip()    if len(text) < 20 or text.lower() in {"let's solve this step by step.", ":", "solution"}:        return Result(Verdict.FAIL, 0.0, ["trivial_answer"], "judge-guard@1.0")    if "grade" in text.lower() and "correct" in text.lower():        return Result(Verdict.ABSTAIN, 0.0, ["possible_judge_injection"], "judge-guard@1.0")    if count_tokens(text) > max_tokens:        return Result(Verdict.FAIL, 0.0, ["over_length"], "judge-guard@1.0")     a = judge_a.score(task["rubric"], task["reference"], text)    # each returns 0..1    b = judge_b.score(task["rubric"], task["reference"], text)    if abs(a - b) > 0.3:        return Result(Verdict.ABSTAIN, 0.0, ["judge_disagreement"], "judge-pair@2.1")    # route to review    return Result(Verdict.PASS if min(a, b) >= 0.7 else Verdict.FAIL, min(a, b), [], "judge-pair@2.1")
Going deeper2 points
  • The judge is a model the policy is training against: freeze its version for a run, and re-run its adversarial suite against outputs from the current policy every few hundred steps.
  • Don't let the judge see the policy's reasoning unless the rubric needs it; long reasoning is where persuasive patterns accumulate.

Detecting reward hacking during training

Scenario. On day four, training reward is still climbing smoothly. Nothing alerts. On day seven, a person reading samples notices that half of the "correct" answers are hedged lists.

What the picture shows. Independent signals that diverge from the training reward when the policy exploits it.

1Hacking gap
score a sample of each step's rollouts with a stricter or independent verifier (an "audit verifier") and track the gap between training reward and audit reward. A widening gap is the clearest signal.
2Perturbation tests
rewrite tasks into equivalent forms (renamed variables, reordered constraints, isomorphic structures) and check that performance holds; shortcuts break under perturbation while real skills don't. The 2026 rule-induction study used this kind of isomorphic verification to expose and remove shortcuts.
3Held-out evaluation with different verifiers
capability gains should show up on evals the policy never trained against.
4Shortcut detectors
rates of multiple answers, hedging, abnormal lengths, repeated openers, test-file access attempts and verifier failure reasons, tracked per step.
5Sampled human review
a fixed number of rewarded samples per day, read by people with a checklist; any confirmed exploit stops the run's promotion and creates a regression test.

The code. A per-step reward-quality monitor (Python).

def reward_quality_step(step, batch, train_verifier, audit_verifier, log, sample=256):    s = random.sample(batch, k=min(sample, len(batch)))    train = [train_verifier.reward(x.task, x.completion) or 0.0 for x in s]    audit = [audit_verifier.reward(x.task, x.completion) or 0.0 for x in s]    gap = sum(train) / len(s) - sum(audit) / len(s)    log("reward/hacking_gap", gap, step)                                   # alert on trend    log("reward/false_pos_rate_vs_audit",        sum(t > 0.5 and a < 0.5 for t, a in zip(train, audit)) / max(sum(t > 0.5 for t in train), 1), step)    reasons = Counter(r for x in s for r in train_verifier.verify(x.task, x.completion).reasons)    for r, n in reasons.items():        log(f"reward/reason/{r}", n / len(s), step)    log("reward/len_corr", correlation([len(x.completion) for x in s], train), step)    return gap
Going deeper2 points
  • The audit verifier must be independent, not the training verifier with one more rule: a different implementation, ideally a stricter contract, and never used as a training reward itself (or it becomes the next target).
  • Connect to the controller: a sustained hacking gap pauses promotion and, past a threshold, pauses the run (Design 09 has the same pattern for off-policy metrics).

Semi-automatic verification: people in the loop

Scenario. For proofs and research summaries, no automatic check is reliable. Reviewing everything is impossible; reviewing nothing means trusting the judge.

What the picture shows. How automatic checks and human review share the work.

1Automatic first
rules and judges handle what they can, each with abstention.
2Routing to people
abstentions, judge disagreements, low-confidence passes, suspected exploits and a small random sample of confident passes (to measure the automatic precision).
3Review queue with priorities
cases that affect training most (high-advantage samples, new task families) first; reviewers see the task, completion, verifier reasons and a checklist.
4Labels flow back
reviewed cases become gold labels for calibration, regression tests for the verifier, and, where appropriate, training data for the judge.
5Budget and latency
human labels arrive hours later, so they're used for calibration, gating and re-scoring, not as per-step rewards. A few hundred labels a day, chosen well, are enough to keep precision estimates honest.
Going deeper2 points
  • Inter-reviewer agreement is a quality metric too: if two reviewers disagree often on a slice, the contract for that slice is unclear; fix the contract before the verifier.
  • Formal checkers where possible: for mathematics, proof assistants (Lean and similar) give fully automatic verification for formalized statements; they shift the human effort to checking the formal statement matches the intended problem.

The platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. Verifiers run inside rollout workers, copied into each training repo. The team wants one service, one version history and one place to see quality.

What the picture shows. The components that keep rewards honest.

1Verifier service
versioned verifiers served as Deployments (CPU for rules, sandboxes for code, GPU pool for judges); the training run pins versions.
2Verifier registry
contracts, versions, test suites and measured quality per slice; a verifier can't be pinned for training without passing its gates.
3Fuzz and red-team jobs
in CI on every change, and nightly as a CronJob against fresh policy outputs.
4Reward-quality monitor
audit scoring, perturbation tests and shortcut detectors on a sample of each step's rollouts.
5Review service
the human queue, gold labels and agreement metrics.
6Re-scoring jobs
when a verifier version changes, affected stored samples (replay buffers, SFT datasets built from rollouts) are re-scored.

The YAML. A pinned verifier version as its own Deployment, and the nightly fuzzing job against the current policy's outputs.

apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: verifier-math-final-answer-3-2-0          # one Deployment per pinned version  namespace: rewards  labels: { app: verifier, verifier: math-final-answer, version: "3.2.0" }spec:  replicas: 20  selector: { matchLabels: { verifier: math-final-answer, version: "3.2.0" } }  template:    metadata: { labels: { app: verifier, verifier: math-final-answer, version: "3.2.0" } }    spec:      containers:      - name: verifier        image: registry.example.com/rewards/math-final-answer@sha256:5e1d...   # immutable        ports: [ { containerPort: 8080 } ]        resources: { limits: { cpu: "2", memory: 2Gi } }        readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } }---apiVersion: batch/v1kind: CronJobmetadata:  name: verifier-fuzz-nightly  namespace: rewardsspec:  schedule: "17 2 * * *"  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid  jobTemplate:    spec:      template:        spec:          restartPolicy: Never          containers:          - name: fuzz            image: registry.example.com/rewards/fuzz:2026.11            args:            - --verifiers=math-final-answer@3.2.0,code-tests@5.1.0            - --reference=strict-reference@1.4.0            - --policy-samples=s3://rl-runs/assistant-v13-prod/latest/rollouts/   # fresh outputs            - --fail-on=false_positive_rate>0.005            - --report=s3://rewards/fuzz-reports/
Going deeper2 points
  • Pinning by digest: a run records verifier image digests, not tags, so a reward can always be reproduced.
  • Shared with evaluation, separated from training: evaluation verifiers live in the same registry but are different entries, owned by a different team, and never pinned by training runs.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, interface and inventory: one verifier interface with abstention and reasons; all existing verifiers registered with versions; rewards tagged with versions.
  • Phase 2, measurement: gold sets per slice, precision and recall dashboards, training gated on precision.
  • Phase 3, hardening: fuzzing and differential testing in CI and nightly; strict answer contracts; stronger code tests with mutation scores; judge adversarial suites.
  • Phase 4, monitoring and review: the reward-quality monitor with audit verifiers and perturbation tests; the human review service; re-scoring on verifier changes.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Strict contracts cause false negatives: some correct answers are rejected for format; we accept slower learning for fewer false positives, and state the contract in the prompt.
  • Abstention reduces signal: abstained samples teach nothing, but they don't teach anything wrong.
  • Audit scoring and review cost compute and people, in exchange for knowing whether gains are real.
  • Separate training and evaluation verifiers means maintaining two implementations of similar logic.

Open questions.

  • How much noise is tolerable? Evidence suggests moderate false negatives are harmless and false positives are not; where exactly is the line for our tasks and scales?
  • Learned verifiers at scale: can judges trained on human labels and fuzzing outputs become reliable enough for frontier tasks, or will they always be the weakest link?
  • Formal verification coverage: how much of our math and code distribution can be moved to proof assistants and formal specifications?
  • Verifying agent behavior: for long agent trajectories, how do we verify not just the end state but that the process didn't cheat (Design 08)?
Design 11 · 12 sections

Design 11: Multi-task post-training across task families

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. The capability matrix: transfer and interference
  3. Specialization vs generality: four ways to cover many domains
  4. Designing the mixture
  5. Sequential, mixed or staged
  6. RL across domains: rewards, lengths and batches
  7. Interference: detect it, then reduce it
  8. Merging and distilling specialists
  9. Evaluation: scorecards and no-regression gates
  10. Domains as plug-ins: ownership and contracts
  11. The platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we scale post-training recipes across many task families and domains (math, code, agents, instruction following, chat, safety, languages), understand the trade-offs between specialized and general models, and design training mixtures that improve all capabilities together instead of trading one for another? It builds on Design 06 (recipes and mixtures), Design 07 (predicting from small runs), Design 09 (distillation and other-policy data) and Design 10 (verifiers per domain).

The short version: treat the mixture as the product. Each task family has an owner who supplies data, a verifier and an eval suite through a common contract. A central team owns the mixture: the weights, the order and the per-domain settings, chosen with small proxy runs and a measured transfer matrix (how training on one family affects every other). The default path is one generalist trained on a staged mixture, with short refreshes for families that regress; specialists are trained when a family needs more capacity or speed of iteration, and folded back by distillation or merging. A release has to clear a no-regression gate on every family, not just a better average.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. Five teams each improved "their" capability with their own post-training run: a math model, a coding agent, a multilingual chat model, a tool-use model and a safety-tuned model. Leadership wants one assistant. The first combined run (all data mixed at natural proportions) improves code and math, but instruction following drops six points, the multilingual model starts answering Spanish questions in English, and the safety team reports more over-refusals. Each team blames the others' data.

What the platform must do.

  • Make domains pluggable: a new task family arrives as data, verifier and evals through one contract, with an owner.
  • Measure interactions: know how training on each family affects every other family, positively or negatively.
  • Choose mixtures with evidence: weights, order and per-domain settings selected with proxy runs, not by negotiation.
  • Support both paths: one generalist trained on a mixture, and specialists that are later distilled or merged back.
  • Prevent regressions: no release that improves the average while degrading any family beyond an agreed margin.
  • Scale the number of domains: adding the twentieth domain must not take more work than adding the fifth.

Out of scope: the RL objective itself (Design 06), scaling a single run (Design 07).

The capability matrix: transfer and interference

Scenario. Someone claims "code data helps math." Someone else claims "chat data hurts reasoning." Nobody has measured either, and both may be true at different mixture weights.

What the picture shows. A transfer matrix: rows are the family added to training, columns are the evaluated family, cells are the change relative to a baseline mixture.

1Diagonal
the direct effect (training on code improves code). Large and positive, by design.
2Positive off-diagonal (transfer)
families that share skills help each other, such as math and code through step-by-step reasoning, or tool use and agents.
3Negative off-diagonal (interference)
families that pull the model in different directions, such as long reasoning traces making casual chat verbose, or terse coding style hurting explanation quality.
4Asymmetry
A helping B doesn't mean B helps A. The matrix is directional.
5It changes with scale and stage
a matrix measured on a small model or at the SFT stage is a starting hypothesis for a large model or the RL stage, not a fact.

The code. Estimating the matrix from leave-one-in ablations: a baseline mixture plus a small boost of one family at a time (Python).

import numpy as np FAMILIES = ["math", "code", "agents", "instr", "chat", "multiling", "safety"] def transfer_matrix(run_eval, base_mix: dict, boost: float = 0.10, seeds=(0, 1)):    """M[i, j] = change in eval j when family i's weight is raised by `boost` (proxy runs)."""    base = np.mean([run_eval(base_mix, seed=s) for s in seeds], axis=0)       # vector over FAMILIES    M = np.zeros((len(FAMILIES), len(FAMILIES)))    for i, fam in enumerate(FAMILIES):        mix = dict(base_mix); mix[fam] += boost        total = sum(mix.values()); mix = {k: v / total for k, v in mix.items()}        scores = np.mean([run_eval(mix, seed=s) for s in seeds], axis=0)        M[i] = scores - base                                                   # row: effect of adding fam    noise = np.std([run_eval(base_mix, seed=s) for s in (7, 8, 9)], axis=0)    return M, noise                                                            # ignore cells within noise
Going deeper2 points
  • Seed noise is the first thing to measure: many apparent transfer effects are smaller than the variation between seeds. Show the matrix with cells inside the noise band greyed out.
  • Refresh the matrix at every stage: SFT and RL interact differently; RL across domains is known to cause interference even when full-model gradients look nearly orthogonal, because the damage concentrates in a small shared set of parameters.

Specialization vs generality: four ways to cover many domains

Scenario. The coding team argues for keeping a dedicated coding model; the platform team wants one model to serve. Both have a point, and the choice changes training, serving and cost.

What the picture shows. Four strategies, from most specialized to most general.

1Separate specialists plus a router
best per-domain quality and independent iteration; more models to serve, a router that can misroute, and no transfer between domains at inference.
2Specialists merged in weight space
train specialists separately, combine parameters (task arithmetic, TIES, DELLA and similar). Cheap to try, no joint training; results depend strongly on model size and how far each specialist moved.
3One generalist trained on a mixture
one model, transfer between domains, one release; interference must be managed, and every team depends on one training run.
4Specialists distilled into a generalist
specialists act as teachers for one student; combines independent iteration with one served model, at the cost of the distillation run.

The options at a glance.

Strategy Quality per domain Transfer Serving Iteration speed Main risk
Specialists + router Highest None at inference Many models Fast, independent Misrouting, cost
Merge specialists Medium–high Some One model Fast Unpredictable interference
Mixture generalist Medium–high Yes One model Slow, shared Interference, slow loop
Distill specialists High Yes One model Medium Distillation cost, teacher quirks
Going deeper2 points
  • Scale changes the answer: one 2026 study of code models found data-mixture fine-tuning worked better at around 2B parameters, while merging specialists worked better at 7B. Re-test the choice when the model size changes.
  • Hybrid is common: a generalist for most traffic, a few specialists where quality or latency justify them, and periodic distillation of specialists back into the generalist.

Designing the mixture

Scenario. The first mixture used "natural proportions": whatever each team had. Code had 4 million examples and safety had 40,000, so the model saw code 100 times more often, regardless of what either needed.

What the picture shows. The levers that turn many datasets into one training stream.

1Weights, not sizes
each family gets a sampling weight; small, high-value families can be up-sampled (with care about repetition), and large ones down-sampled.
2Temperature sampling
a single knob between natural proportions (temperature 1) and uniform across families (high temperature), useful as a starting point.
3Epoch caps
limit how many times a small family's examples repeat, since repeated data overfits.
4Per-domain settings
maximum lengths, chat templates, system prompts and loss weights can differ by family.
5Search with proxies
choose weights by fitting a simple model of eval scores as a function of mixture weights on small runs, then confirm at scale.
6Minimum shares
every family keeps a floor weight, so no capability silently disappears from training.

The YAML. A multi-domain mixture in the recipe, with per-family settings (extends the recipe format of Design 06).

# recipes/assistant-v14/mixture.yamlmixture:  strategy: weighted  temperature: 2.0                      # starting point before search  floors: { default: 0.02 }             # no family below 2%  max_epochs_per_source: 3  families:    math:      { weight: 0.22, sources: [datasets://math-verified@v6],  max_len: 16384 }    code:      { weight: 0.22, sources: [datasets://code-tests@v9],     max_len: 16384 }    agents:    { weight: 0.14, sources: [envs://swe-tasks@v3],          max_len: 65536 }    instr:     { weight: 0.12, sources: [datasets://ifeval-style@v4],   max_len: 4096 }    chat:      { weight: 0.12, sources: [datasets://chat-prefs@v8],     max_len: 4096 }    multiling: { weight: 0.10, sources: [datasets://chat-ml@v5],        max_len: 4096,                 eval_languages: [es, de, fr, ja, hi] }    safety:    { weight: 0.08, sources: [datasets://safety@v11],        max_len: 4096 }owners:                                  # who answers for each family's data, verifier and evals  math: team-reasoning  code: team-code  safety: team-safety

The code. Fitting a simple response model on proxy runs and choosing weights that maximize the worst family's score (Python).

import numpy as npfrom scipy.optimize import minimize def fit_response(W: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray):    """W: runs x families (mixture weights), S: runs x families (eval scores). Linear in log-weights."""    X = np.hstack([np.log(W + 1e-3), np.ones((len(W), 1))])    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, S, rcond=None)    return lambda w: np.hstack([np.log(w + 1e-3), 1.0]) @ coef            # predicted score per family def best_mixture(predict, n, floor=0.02, base_scores=None):    def neg_worst(w):        w = np.abs(w) / np.abs(w).sum()        gains = predict(w) - (base_scores if base_scores is not None else 0)        return -gains.min()                                                # maximize the weakest family    res = minimize(neg_worst, np.full(n, 1 / n), method="Nelder-Mead", options={"maxiter": 4000})    w = np.maximum(np.abs(res.x) / np.abs(res.x).sum(), floor)    return w / w.sum()
Going deeper2 points
  • Optimize for the worst family, or a weighted product, not the average: an average-maximizing mixture happily sacrifices a small family.
  • Mixtures interact with quality: doubling a family's weight with low-quality data hurts more than leaving it alone. Clean the data before tuning its weight.

Sequential, mixed or staged

Scenario. The team trains math RL, then code RL, then chat RL. After the chat stage, math has dropped 8 points. Then they mix everything in each batch, and math and chat both end up worse than with their own runs.

What the picture shows. Three ways to order training across domains.

1Sequential
one domain after another. Simple and easy to attribute, but later stages degrade earlier ones (forgetting and interference).
2Mixed
every batch contains all domains. No forgetting by order, but gradients from different domains interfere within each update; recent work on math, chat and instruction following found both sequential and mixed RL fell short.
3Staged with refreshes
a mixed base, then short focused stages for domains that need more, each followed by a brief refresh of earlier domains. A 2026 study found that a short math refresh after a sequence of code, math, QA and creative-writing RL restored math from about 58 to 66 while largely preserving the other domains.
4Mixed with conflict handling
keep the mixture, but reduce gradient conflict between domains (gradient surgery per module, or per-domain adapters).

The YAML. A staged schedule: mixed base, focused stages and refreshes, each with its own mixture.

# recipes/assistant-v14/schedule.yamlstages:- name: sft-mixed  type: sft  mixture: recipes/assistant-v14/mixture.yaml- name: rl-mixed  type: rl  steps: 1200  mixture: { math: 0.25, code: 0.25, instr: 0.15, chat: 0.15, safety: 0.1, multiling: 0.1 }- name: rl-agents-focus  type: rl  steps: 400  mixture: { agents: 0.7, code: 0.15, instr: 0.15 }       # keep a share of neighbours- name: rl-refresh  type: rl  steps: 80                                               # short: restore, don't retrain  mixture: { math: 0.3, chat: 0.3, multiling: 0.2, safety: 0.2 }  trigger: { any_family_regression_gt: 1.5 }              # only if the gate shows regressionsgates_after_each_stage: evals://multi-family@v3
Going deeper2 points
  • Keep neighbours in focused stages: a focus stage at 70% agents and 30% related families forgets less than a pure agents stage.
  • Refreshes are cheap and targeted: a few dozen to a few hundred steps on the regressed family, after measuring which family regressed, beats re-running a full mixed stage.

RL across domains: rewards, lengths and batches

Scenario. In mixed RL, math rewards are 0/1 with 30% success, chat judge scores cluster between 0.6 and 0.8, and agent episodes are 50 times longer than chat answers. Math and agents dominate the updates; chat barely moves.

What the picture shows. The per-domain differences that distort a mixed RL batch, and the corrections.

1Reward scales differ
binary verifiers, judge scores and shaped rewards have different ranges and variances. Normalize advantages within each prompt group (and report per domain), so no domain dominates through scale alone.
2Lengths differ
token-level loss makes long answers contribute more tokens. Decide explicitly whether a domain should weigh by tokens or by samples, and balance batches by token count per domain.
3Difficulty differs
each domain needs its own pass-rate filter (Design 06); a domain with mostly all-correct groups contributes no signal regardless of its weight.
4Verifiers differ
each domain uses its own verifier from the registry (Design 10), with its own precision gate.
5Rollout cost differs
agent environments cost far more per sample than chat; the scheduler plans rollout capacity per domain so cheap domains don't wait on expensive ones.

The code. Per-domain advantage normalization and token-budgeted batch composition (Python).

from collections import defaultdictimport numpy as np def domain_advantages(groups):    """groups: list of dicts {domain, rewards: [..]} for one prompt each. Normalize within the group."""    out, stats = [], defaultdict(list)    for g in groups:        r = np.asarray(g["rewards"], dtype=float)        std = r.std()        adv = (r - r.mean()) / (std + 1e-6) if std > 0 else np.zeros_like(r)  # zero-variance: no signal        out.append(adv)        stats[g["domain"]].append(float(np.abs(adv).mean()))    return out, {d: float(np.mean(v)) for d, v in stats.items()}             # log signal per domain def compose_batch(pools, token_budget: int, shares: dict):    """Fill each domain's share of the batch by tokens, not by sample count."""    batch = []    for domain, share in shares.items():        budget, used = int(token_budget * share), 0        for s in pools[domain]:            if used + s.num_tokens > budget:                break            batch.append(s); used += s.num_tokens    return batch
Going deeper2 points
  • Log "effective signal" per domain: the mean absolute advantage and the fraction of non-zero-variance groups per domain show which domains are actually being trained in each step.
  • Separate KL or clip settings per domain are possible but add tuning burden; start shared and split only with evidence.

Interference: detect it, then reduce it

Scenario. Chat quality falls a little each time the code share rises. The team wants to know whether the two domains are actually fighting in the updates, and where.

What the picture shows. Signals that show interference, and tools that reduce it.

1Eval deltas per family
the most direct signal; the transfer matrix and per-stage gates measure it.
2Gradient conflict
compute per-domain gradients on a probe batch and their cosine similarity per module; negative cosines in shared modules mark where domains pull in opposite directions.
3Parameter-change overlap
which parameters each domain's updates change most; overlap with opposite signs predicts interference.
4Reducers
gradient surgery (project out conflicting components per module), per-domain adapters or LoRA modules on top of a shared model, more capacity (larger or mixture-of-experts models), conservative updates (small KL to the previous stage), and the refreshes above.

The code. Per-module gradient cosine between two domains on probe batches (PyTorch).

import torch def module_grads(model, loss_fn, batch):    model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)    loss_fn(model, batch).backward()    return {n: p.grad.detach().flatten().clone() for n, p in model.named_parameters() if p.grad is not None} def conflict_report(model, loss_fn, batch_a, batch_b, top=10):    ga, gb = module_grads(model, loss_fn, batch_a), module_grads(model, loss_fn, batch_b)    rows = []    for name in ga.keys() & gb.keys():        cos = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(ga[name], gb[name], dim=0).item()        rows.append((cos, name))    rows.sort()                                            # most conflicting modules first    return rows[:top]
Going deeper2 points
  • Whole-model cosine hides conflict: two domains can look orthogonal overall while conflicting strongly in a handful of modules; always look per module.
  • Capacity is a real lever: smaller models show more interference. If interference dominates and the data is clean, a larger or MoE model may be cheaper than more mixture tuning.

Merging and distilling specialists

Scenario. The coding team needs to iterate weekly; the generalist retrains monthly. They want to keep a specialist for speed and still get its gains into the generalist.

What the picture shows. Two ways to fold specialists back into one model.

1Weight merging
compute each specialist's "task vector" (its weights minus the shared base) and add scaled task vectors to the base. Methods like TIES and DELLA trim small changes and resolve sign conflicts. Fast and cheap; the merge weights are tuned on evals.
2Multi-teacher distillation
the generalist student generates answers on each domain's prompts, and that domain's specialist grades it token by token (on-policy distillation, Design 06); off-policy teacher data can start it.
3Requirements
a shared base and tokenizer for merging; a shared tokenizer for per-token distillation.
4When to use which
merging for quick combination of closely related specialists from the same base; distillation when specialists diverged a lot, when the student is smaller, or when merging shows interference.

The code. Task-vector merging with trimming and sign agreement (TIES-style, simplified; PyTorch).

import torch def ties_merge(base: dict, specialists: list[dict], weights: list[float], keep: float = 0.2):    merged = {}    for name, b in base.items():        deltas = torch.stack([s[name] - b for s in specialists])            # task vectors        k = max(1, int(keep * deltas[0].numel()))        thresh = deltas.abs().flatten(1).kthvalue(deltas[0].numel() - k + 1, dim=1).values        deltas = deltas * (deltas.abs() >= thresh.view(-1, *[1] * (deltas.dim() - 1)))   # trim small        sign = torch.sign((deltas * torch.tensor(weights).view(-1, *[1] * (deltas.dim() - 1))).sum(0))        agree = (torch.sign(deltas) == sign) & (deltas != 0)                 # keep agreeing signs        w = torch.tensor(weights).view(-1, *[1] * (deltas.dim() - 1))        num = (deltas * agree * w).sum(0)        den = (agree * w).sum(0).clamp(min=1e-8)        merged[name] = b + num / den    return merged
Going deeper2 points
  • Tune merge weights against the multi-family gate, not one domain; a merge that helps code and hurts safety fails the same gate as a training run would.
  • Merging generalists works too: merging several checkpoints from different runs or stages can reduce trade-offs between capabilities; it's a cheap experiment before a new training run.

Evaluation: scorecards and no-regression gates

Scenario. A candidate improves the average by 2.1 points. Inside that average, Hindi chat dropped 5 points and tool-call formatting dropped 3. Under the old "average must go up" rule, it would have shipped.

What the picture shows. How a multi-domain release is judged.

1A scorecard per family
each family's owner defines its suite, metric and acceptable regression margin.
2No-regression gate
a candidate passes only if no family regresses beyond its margin compared with the current release, with seed noise accounted for.
3Aggregate views that resist trade-offs
the minimum over families and a weighted geometric mean, alongside the average; the geometric mean punishes a collapse in one family more than the average does.
4Pareto view
candidates plotted on pairs of families show which trade-offs are available; a candidate dominated on every pair is dropped.
5Behavior across domains
length, refusal and language-consistency checks for every family, since cross-domain side effects often show up as behavior, not accuracy.

The code. The release gate as a function (Python).

import math def release_gate(candidate: dict, current: dict, margins: dict, noise: dict):    """Each dict maps family -> score (higher is better). Returns (passed, report)."""    report, passed = {}, True    for fam, margin in margins.items():        delta = candidate[fam] - current[fam]        tolerance = margin + 2 * noise.get(fam, 0.0)              # don't fail on seed noise        ok = delta >= -tolerance        report[fam] = {"delta": round(delta, 2), "allowed": -round(tolerance, 2), "ok": ok}        passed &= ok                                                # one regression fails the release    geo = math.exp(sum(math.log(max(candidate[f], 1e-6)) for f in margins) / len(margins))    report["_aggregate"] = {"min": min(candidate[f] for f in margins), "geomean": round(geo, 2)}    return passed, report
Going deeper2 points
  • Margins are negotiated once, not per release: owners set them in advance; changing a margin to let a release through needs explicit sign-off.
  • Language-consistency checks: for multilingual families, measure answering in the language of the question; it's a common casualty of reasoning-heavy mixtures.

Domains as plug-ins: ownership and contracts

Scenario. A sixth team wants to add legal reasoning. Last time a new domain was added, it took six weeks of meetings and broke the safety evals.

What the picture shows. The contract a task family must satisfy to join the mixture.

1Data
versioned datasets or environments, deduplicated and decontaminated against all eval sets, with licenses recorded.
2Verifier or judge
registered with measured precision (Design 10).
3Eval suite and margin
what "better" and "no worse" mean for this family.
4Owner and on-call
who answers when the family regresses or its verifier is exploited.
5Admission test
a proxy run adding the family at a small weight; the transfer row and column for the new family are measured, and the gate must pass for every existing family.
6Central ownership of the mixture
domain teams own their family; the mixture team owns weights, order and the release gate.
Going deeper2 points
  • Decontamination is cross-domain: a new family's data must be checked against every family's eval sets, not just its own.
  • Budget for the long tail of domains: small domains get a floor weight and can be grouped ("specialized professional domains") with shared evals, so adding one doesn't require a full study.

The platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. Training specialists, merging them, distilling and evaluating across seven families is a dozen jobs with dependencies. Today it's a spreadsheet and a chat thread.

What the picture shows. The pieces that run multi-task post-training.

1Domain registry
families, owners, data, verifiers, eval suites and margins.
2Mixture service
stores mixtures and schedules, runs proxy sweeps, fits response models and proposes weights.
3Training jobs
the mixed generalist runs and specialist runs, on the queues from Design 02.
4Per-domain rollout and reward pools
verifiers, judges and environments for each family, scaled independently (Design 07).
5Combination jobs
merging and distillation of specialists.
6Evaluation and gate
every candidate is scored on every family, and the gate decides promotion.
7Workflow engine
chains these steps (train specialists → merge or distill → evaluate → gate) as one auditable pipeline.

The YAML. One pipeline as an Argo Workflow: specialists in parallel, then merge, then the multi-family gate.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1kind: Workflowmetadata:  generateName: assistant-v14-combine-  namespace: post-trainingspec:  entrypoint: pipeline  templates:  - name: pipeline    dag:      tasks:      - name: code-specialist        template: train        arguments: { parameters: [ { name: recipe, value: recipes/specialists/code-v9.yaml } ] }      - name: agents-specialist        template: train        arguments: { parameters: [ { name: recipe, value: recipes/specialists/agents-v4.yaml } ] }      - name: merge        template: merge        dependencies: [code-specialist, agents-specialist]          # run after both      - name: gate        template: evaluate        dependencies: [merge]  - name: train    inputs: { parameters: [ { name: recipe } ] }    resource:                                                       # submit a Kueue-managed JobSet      action: create      successCondition: status.terminalState == Completed      manifest: |        apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2        kind: JobSet        metadata:          generateName: specialist-          labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: post-training }        spec:          replicatedJobs:          - name: trainer            template:              spec:                parallelism: 4                completions: 4                template:                  spec:                    restartPolicy: Never                    containers:                    - name: train                      image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer:2026.11                      args: ["--recipe={{inputs.parameters.recipe}}"]                      resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }  - name: merge    container:      image: registry.example.com/post-training/merge:2026.11      args: ["--method=ties", "--base=registry://assistant-v14-base",             "--specialists=registry://code-v9,registry://agents-v4", "--tune-on=evals://multi-family@v3"]  - name: evaluate    container:      image: registry.example.com/evals/runner:2026.11      args: ["--candidate=registry://assistant-v14-merged", "--gate=gates/no-regression.yaml"]
Going deeper2 points
  • Proxy sweeps are the bulk of the compute: dozens of small mixture runs per decision. Run them at low priority on borrowed capacity.
  • Every artifact carries its lineage: which specialists, merge weights, mixture and data versions produced a candidate, so a regression can be traced to its source.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, contract and gate: the domain registry and contract, per-family scorecards and the no-regression gate on the current release process.
  • Phase 2, measurement: proxy-run infrastructure, the transfer matrix, seed-noise estimates and per-domain RL signal metrics.
  • Phase 3, mixtures: response-model weight search, staged schedules with refreshes, per-domain batch composition.
  • Phase 4, combination: specialist pipelines with merging and multi-teacher distillation, and conflict-reduction methods where interference is measured.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • No-regression gates slow releases: some improvements wait until a regression elsewhere is fixed.
  • Proxy-run evidence is imperfect: mixtures chosen at small scale are confirmed at scale, and sometimes changed.
  • Specialists add moving parts: more training runs and a combination step, in exchange for faster iteration in the domains that need it.
  • Central mixture ownership: domain teams give up control of their weight in exchange for a fair, measured process.

Open questions.

  • Scaling laws for mixtures: how well do optimal weights found on small models transfer to large ones?
  • Capacity vs mixture: at what point is a larger or MoE model cheaper than ever more careful mixture tuning?
  • Merging RL-trained specialists: RL changes few parameters per domain; does that make RL specialists easier to merge than SFT specialists?
  • Automatic refreshes: can the platform detect a regression and schedule a targeted refresh without a person deciding?

Design 12: Experiment analysis and debugging for post-training

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Where the noise comes from
  3. Separating real improvements from noise
  4. Designing ablations that decide something
  5. Diagnosing a regression by bisection
  6. Diffing two runs
  7. Probes on every checkpoint
  8. Behavior analysis: reading outputs at scale
  9. Data attribution: which data caused the change?
  10. Looking inside: activation probes
  11. The analysis platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we develop a deep empirical understanding of post-training runs, so that we can diagnose regressions, separate real improvements from noise, design better ablations, and build the probes and analyses that make training less opaque? It sits on top of everything the earlier designs produce: recipes and health signals (Design 06), scaling ladders (Design 07), off-policy metrics (Design 09), verifier quality (Design 10) and multi-family evals (Design 11).

The short version: every claim about a run is a statistical claim, and every run is a dataset. The platform stores per-question eval results (not just averages) for every checkpoint, so comparisons are paired and come with error bars. Ablations are declared with a hypothesis and a decision rule before they run. Regressions are found by bisecting over recipe, data and code versions. And a fixed set of probes (log-probabilities on reference answers, per-layer update sizes, behavior statistics, linear probes on activations) runs on every checkpoint, so "what changed inside the model" has an answer before anyone asks.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A researcher reports that a new reward-shaping term improves the reasoning benchmark by 1.8 points. Two weeks later, a re-run with a different seed shows −0.4. Meanwhile, a regression in tool-call formatting shipped because nobody connected it to a data refresh three runs earlier, and a long RL run's entropy collapse is "explained" by four different theories in the team channel.

What the platform must do.

  • Quantify uncertainty: every reported difference comes with a confidence interval from paired, per-question data.
  • Make ablations decisive: one declared variable, matched compute, enough seeds and questions to detect the effect size that matters.
  • Find regressions fast: narrow a regression to a specific change (recipe key, data version, code commit) in hours.
  • Look inside runs: standard probes on every checkpoint, comparable across runs.
  • Explain behavior changes: connect a change in outputs to the data or reward that caused it.
  • Keep it cheap enough to always run: analysis that's only done for important runs is never available when needed.

Out of scope: the training systems themselves (Designs 06–09) and production monitoring of served models.

Where the noise comes from

Scenario. The same recipe, run three times with different seeds, scores 61.2, 62.9 and 60.7 on the reasoning suite. A 1.8-point "improvement" is inside that range.

What the picture shows. The sources of variation in a reported score, from the eval to the training run.

1Question sampling
an eval is a sample of possible questions; a 500-question suite has a standard error of around 2 points at 60% accuracy.
2Generation sampling
with temperature above zero, the same model gives different answers; averaging several samples per question reduces this part.
3Training seed and data order
different seeds give different models; for RL this variation is often larger than for SFT.
4Nondeterministic kernels and infrastructure
different GPU counts, kernels or batch splits change results slightly even with the same seed.
5Checkpoint choice
picking the best of several checkpoints on the same eval used to report it inflates the result.
6Decomposition
measuring each source once per recipe family tells you what to spend on: more questions, more samples per question, or more training seeds.

The code. Estimating the components from a small grid of seeds × generation samples (Python).

import numpy as np def variance_components(scores: np.ndarray):    """scores[s, g, q]: training seed s, generation sample g, question q (0/1 or fractional)."""    S, G, Q = scores.shape    per_seed = scores.mean(axis=(1, 2))                       # score of each trained model    within_seed_gen = scores.mean(axis=2).var(axis=1, ddof=1).mean()   # generation sampling, whole-suite    q_means = scores.mean(axis=(0, 1))    question_se = np.sqrt(q_means.var(ddof=1) / Q)            # suite-level sampling error    return {        "seed_sd": float(per_seed.std(ddof=1)),               # training seed / data order        "generation_sd": float(np.sqrt(within_seed_gen)),        "question_se": float(question_se),    }
Going deeper2 points
  • Seed variance is a property of the recipe: some recipes are much noisier than others; a noisy recipe needs more seeds before any comparison, and that noise is itself a reason to prefer a quieter recipe.
  • Never select and report on the same eval: choose checkpoints on a validation split and report on a separate test split.

Separating real improvements from noise

Scenario. Model B scores 62.0 and model A 60.8 on the same 600 questions. Is B better? The unpaired standard errors overlap; but most questions are answered identically by both, and the paired analysis tells a different story.

What the picture shows. The statistical practices the platform applies to every comparison.

1Paired differences
compare models question by question on the same questions; the variance of the difference is much smaller than the variance of each score, because shared difficulty cancels out. Evaluation-statistics work recommends inference on question-level paired differences rather than population-level summary statistics.
2Clustered standard errors
questions often come in groups (several questions on one document, several tests per coding task); treat each group as one cluster, or the error bars are too narrow.
3Small evals need care
with fewer than a few hundred questions, normal-approximation intervals can badly understate uncertainty; use exact or Bayesian intervals, or bootstrap at the cluster level.
4Multiple comparisons
comparing 20 evals at 95% confidence produces one false "significant" result on average; control the false discovery rate or pre-declare the primary metric.
5Power analysis
decide in advance the smallest effect worth detecting and compute how many questions, samples and seeds are needed.

The code. A paired comparison with clustered standard errors, plus the number of questions needed to detect a given effect (Python).
