import numpy as npfrom scipy import stats def paired_compare(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, clusters: np.ndarray | None = None):    """a, b: per-question scores of two models on the same questions (means over samples)."""    d = b - a    n = len(d)    if clusters is None:        se = d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)    else:                                                     # cluster-robust SE        ids = np.unique(clusters)        sums = np.array([d[clusters == c].sum() - d[clusters == c].size * d.mean() for c in ids])        se = np.sqrt((sums ** 2).sum()) / n * np.sqrt(len(ids) / (len(ids) - 1))    z = d.mean() / se    return {"diff": d.mean(), "ci95": (d.mean() - 1.96 * se, d.mean() + 1.96 * se),            "p": 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z))), "n": n} def questions_needed(effect: float, sd_diff: float, alpha=0.05, power=0.8) -> int:    """Questions needed to detect a paired mean difference `effect` (power analysis)."""    z = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(power)    return int(np.ceil((z * sd_diff / effect) ** 2))
Going deeper2 points
  • Report the interval, not the star: a result "+1.2 [−0.3, +2.7]" carries more information than "not significant", and stops both over- and under-claiming.
  • Seeds are the outer layer: paired question-level statistics handle eval noise; training-seed variance still needs several runs per arm. Compare arms with seeds as the unit, and questions within them.

Designing ablations that decide something

Scenario. An ablation changed the learning rate and the reward weight together, ran one seed each, and was evaluated on the suite the researcher happened to have open. Nobody can say what it showed.

What the picture shows. The elements of an ablation that produces a decision.

1Hypothesis and decision rule, declared first
what effect is expected, on which primary metric, and what result leads to which action.
2One declared variable
the launcher enforces that the recipe diff touches only the declared keys (Design 06).
3Matched compute
arms get the same tokens or GPU hours; otherwise "better" may just mean "trained longer".
4Enough seeds and questions
from the power analysis, not from habit.
5Proxy scale with a confirmation step
run at small scale; confirm the winner at the target scale before adopting it (Design 07).
6Factorial designs for interacting choices
when two settings plausibly interact (learning rate and batch size), a small 2×2 grid shows the interaction that two one-at-a-time ablations miss.

The YAML. An ablation declared with its hypothesis, budget and decision rule; the launcher refuses to run it without these.

# ablations/2026-11/overlong-penalty.yamlhypothesis: "An overlong penalty starting at 14K tokens improves math-hard without hurting length-sensitive chat evals."base_recipe: recipes/assistant-v14/rl-math-code.yamlvariable:  rewards.overlong_penalty: [off, {start: 14336, end: 16384}]   # the only key allowed to differbudget: { matched_by: tokens, tokens_per_arm: 2.0e9 }seeds: 3                                          # from the power analysis belowpower: { min_effect: 1.0, metric_sd_diff: 6.5, questions: 1200 }primary_metric: evals://math-hard@v5/pass@1guardrails:                                       # must not regress beyond these  evals://chat-length@v2/mean_tokens: { max_increase_pct: 5 }  evals://ifeval@v4/strict: { max_drop: 0.8 }decision:  adopt_if: "primary.ci95.low > 0 and all guardrails pass"  reject_if: "primary.ci95.high < 0.5"  otherwise: "extend seeds to 5, then decide"      # no open-ended 'interesting' outcomes
Going deeper2 points
  • Pre-registering doesn't forbid exploration: exploratory analysis is fine and often where insight comes from; it's labeled as exploratory, and a decision needs a confirmatory run.
  • Keep the ablation record even when it fails: a library of negative results stops the same idea from being re-tested every quarter.

Diagnosing a regression by bisection

Scenario. Tool-call formatting dropped 3 points between release candidates rc1 and rc5. In between: two data refreshes, a verifier version bump, a trainer upgrade and nine recipe changes. Reading diffs hasn't found it.

What the picture shows. Narrowing a regression to one change, the way git bisect narrows a bug.

1Enumerate the changes
every difference between the good and bad candidates as a list of atomic changes: recipe keys, data versions, verifier versions, code commits, image digests.
2Order them
by time, or group by kind (data, reward, code, recipe).
3Bisect with proxy runs
apply half the changes to the good recipe, run a short proxy, evaluate the regressed metric (with enough questions to see the effect), and keep the half that reproduces it.
4Check the checkpoint dimension too
within one run, evaluate intermediate checkpoints to find when the regression appeared; a sudden drop points to a data shard or a schedule event.
5Confirm by reverting
revert only the identified change on the bad recipe; the regression should disappear.

The code. Bisection over a list of changes with a proxy-run oracle (Python).

def bisect_changes(good_recipe, changes: list, regressed, apply):    """changes: atomic diffs between good and bad. regressed(recipe) runs a proxy and returns True if the    metric is significantly worse than the good recipe (paired test). apply(recipe, subset) applies diffs."""    lo, hi = 0, len(changes)                       # invariant: changes[:hi] reproduce, changes[:lo] don't    assert regressed(apply(good_recipe, changes)), "regression doesn't reproduce at proxy scale"    while hi - lo > 1:        mid = (lo + hi) // 2        if regressed(apply(good_recipe, changes[:mid])):            hi = mid        else:            lo = mid    culprit = changes[hi - 1]    return culprit                                  # confirm: revert only this on the bad recipe
Going deeper2 points
  • Interactions break bisection: if the regression needs two changes together, linear bisection points to the second one; when reverting it alone doesn't fully fix things, bisect the remaining changes with it applied.
  • Proxy fidelity first: before bisecting, confirm the regression reproduces at proxy scale; if it only appears at full scale, bisect over checkpoints and data shards of the full run instead.

Diffing two runs

Scenario. Two runs with "almost the same" config end 4 points apart. The team needs to see where, during training, they started to diverge, and on which signals.

What the picture shows. A run diff: two runs aligned on the same axis and compared on every signal.

1Config diff
the exact differences in recipe, data, code and image versions, from lineage.
2Aligned curves
all metrics aligned by tokens or samples seen (not wall-clock or step, which differ with batch size).
3First divergence
the earliest point where any signal's difference exceeds its seed-noise band; the signal that diverges first is usually closest to the cause.
4Eval-level diff
per-question paired differences at matched checkpoints; which question types moved.
5Sample diff
outputs of both runs on the same prompts at matched checkpoints, side by side.
Going deeper2 points
  • Seed-noise bands come from reference runs: keep two or three seeds of the reference recipe so every signal has a known spread to compare against.
  • Divergence in health signals often precedes divergence in evals by hundreds of steps: entropy, length or importance-ratio spread typically move first.

Probes on every checkpoint

Scenario. After an RL run, the model is better at math but worse at one style of instruction. Nobody can tell when that started or whether the model's knowledge changed or only its behavior.

What the picture shows. Cheap, fixed measurements run on every saved checkpoint.

1Reference log-probability probes
the model's log-probability of fixed reference answers (correct solutions, preferred responses, held-out text). A falling log-probability on held-out general text is an early sign of forgetting; on preferred responses, of a style shift.
2Distribution probes
entropy and top-token probabilities on a fixed prompt set; length and format statistics of generated answers.
3Distance probes
KL to the base model on fixed prompts; per-layer and per-module relative update size since the last checkpoint.
4Behavior probes
small, fast suites for refusals, language consistency, tool-call validity and verbosity.
5One table per run
every probe value per checkpoint, so runs can be compared at any point, not just at the end.

The code. A reference log-probability probe and per-module update sizes (PyTorch, Transformers).

import torch @torch.no_grad()def ref_logprob(model, tok, pairs, device="cuda"):    """pairs: [(prompt, reference_answer)]. Mean per-token log-prob of the reference answers."""    total, count = 0.0, 0    for prompt, ref in pairs:        p = tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(device)        r = tok(ref, return_tensors="pt", add_special_tokens=False).input_ids.to(device)        ids = torch.cat([p, r], dim=1)        logits = model(ids).logits[:, p.size(1) - 1:-1]        lp = torch.log_softmax(logits.float(), -1).gather(-1, r.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)        total += lp.sum().item(); count += r.numel()    return total / count def update_sizes(prev: dict, cur: dict) -> dict:    """Relative change per module between two checkpoints' state dicts."""    return {n: ((cur[n].float() - prev[n].float()).norm() / (prev[n].float().norm() + 1e-8)).item()            for n in cur if n in prev}
Going deeper2 points
  • Probes must be cheap: a probe set that takes an hour won't run on every checkpoint; keep each to minutes on one GPU and run them in parallel.
  • Version the probe sets like eval suites, and never train on them.

Behavior analysis: reading outputs at scale

Scenario. Users say the new model "feels different." Benchmarks are flat. Somebody needs to read thousands of outputs and say how.

What the picture shows. Turning many outputs into a description of behavior change.

1Paired samples
the same prompts answered by both models, at matched settings.
2Automatic statistics
length, formatting, hedging phrases, refusals, language, code-block use, tool calls, per prompt category.
3Model-assisted labeling
a model labels each pair against a taxonomy (more verbose, more cautious, different structure, wrong language), validated on a human-labeled sample.
4Clustering
embed the differences and cluster them, so unexpected changes appear as clusters nobody defined in advance.
5Human review of each cluster
a few examples per cluster read by people, who name the behavior and decide whether it matters.
Going deeper2 points
  • The taxonomy grows: every new behavior found by clustering becomes a label and, if it matters, a behavior eval (Design 11).
  • Check the labeler: model labels are measured against human labels like any verifier (Design 10).

Data attribution: which data caused the change?

Scenario. A run picked up a habit of ending answers with a summary table. The team suspects one of 40 data sources, but it could also be the reward model.

What the picture shows. Methods for tracing a behavior back to data, from cheapest to most precise.

1Search
find training examples (SFT data, high-reward rollouts) that show the behavior; often enough to spot the source.
2Rollout and reward analysis
in RL, compare the reward of outputs with and without the behavior; a reward model that prefers the behavior will teach it.
3Gradient similarity
compare the gradient of "produce this behavior" on probe prompts with gradients of training examples; examples with high similarity are candidates.
4Slice ablations
remove or down-weight a candidate source in a proxy run and check that the behavior goes away. This is the confirmation step.

The code. Ranking training examples by gradient similarity to a behavior probe, using a small set of parameters for speed (PyTorch).

import torch def grad_vec(model, loss, params):    g = torch.autograd.grad(loss, params, retain_graph=False)    return torch.cat([x.flatten() for x in g]) def attribute(model, behavior_loss_fn, examples, example_loss_fn, params, top=20):    """params: a few chosen modules (e.g. last layers' MLPs). Returns examples most aligned with the behavior."""    target = grad_vec(model, behavior_loss_fn(model), params)    target = target / target.norm()    scores = []    for ex in examples:        g = grad_vec(model, example_loss_fn(model, ex), params)        scores.append((torch.dot(g / (g.norm() + 1e-8), target).item(), ex["id"], ex["source"]))    scores.sort(reverse=True)    return scores[:top]                  # candidates: confirm with a slice ablation
Going deeper2 points
  • Attribution suggests, ablation confirms: gradient similarity is approximate; never remove data on attribution scores alone.
  • For RL, the reward is data too: many behavior changes come from what the verifier or reward model prefers, not from prompts.

Looking inside: activation probes

Scenario. Refusals rose after a safety-data update. The team wants to know whether the model's internal sense of "harmful request" changed, or only its threshold for acting on it.

What the picture shows. Simple tools for looking at internal representations across checkpoints.

1Linear probes
train a small classifier on hidden states at one layer to predict a property (harmful vs harmless request, language, task type); probe accuracy across checkpoints shows whether the property is still represented.
2Directions
the difference between mean activations of two groups (for example, requests that were refused vs answered) gives a direction; its projection shows how strongly each prompt activates it.
3Comparison across checkpoints
if the representation stays the same but the behavior changes, the change is in how the model acts on the representation; if the representation itself moves, the model now "sees" requests differently.
4Limits
these are coarse tools; they help form and test hypotheses, not prove mechanisms.

The code. A linear probe on one layer's activations, trained once and applied to several checkpoints (PyTorch, scikit-learn).

import numpy as npimport torchfrom sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression @torch.no_grad()def layer_acts(model, tok, prompts, layer: int, device="cuda"):    out = []    for p in prompts:        ids = tok(p, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(device)        hs = model(ids, output_hidden_states=True).hidden_states[layer]        out.append(hs[0, -1].float().cpu().numpy())          # last-token representation    return np.stack(out) def probe_across(checkpoints, tok, prompts, labels, layer=20):    X0 = layer_acts(checkpoints[0], tok, prompts, layer)    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X0, labels)   # train on the first checkpoint    return [clf.score(layer_acts(m, tok, prompts, layer), labels) for m in checkpoints]
Going deeper2 points
  • Use held-out prompts for probe accuracy, and compare with a probe trained on each checkpoint separately; the gap shows how much the representation moved.
  • Keep it in proportion: activation probes are a useful lens for post-training questions, but the decision still rests on behavior evals.

The analysis platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. Probes and evals run when someone remembers to start them, results live in personal notebooks, and per-question results are thrown away after the average is computed.

What the picture shows. The pieces that make analysis automatic.

1Checkpoint events
every registered checkpoint emits an event.
2Eval and probe jobs
triggered by the event, they run the standard suites and probes on low-priority capacity and store per-question and per-probe results.
3Results store
a columnar store keyed by run, checkpoint, suite, question and sample; everything comparisons need.
4Analysis service
paired comparisons, variance components, run diffs and bisection, as APIs and notebooks on the same data.
5Ablation registry
declared ablations, their outcomes and decisions, including negative results.

The YAML. An Argo Events sensor that runs probes and evals whenever a checkpoint is registered.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1kind: Sensormetadata:  name: checkpoint-analysis  namespace: analysisspec:  dependencies:  - name: ckpt-registered    eventSourceName: model-registry          # emits on every new checkpoint    eventName: checkpoint-registered  triggers:  - template:      name: probes-and-evals      k8s:        operation: create        source:          resource:            apiVersion: batch/v1            kind: Job            metadata:              generateName: analyze-              labels:                kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: analysis                kueue.x-k8s.io/priority-class: analysis-low      # borrows idle GPUs            spec:              backoffLimit: 1              template:                spec:                  restartPolicy: Never                  containers:                  - name: analyze                    image: registry.example.com/analysis/runner:2026.11                    args: ["CHECKPOINT_URI", "--suites=standard@v7", "--probes=standard@v3",                           "--store-per-question=true"]           # never keep only averages                    resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 1 } }        parameters:        - src: { dependencyName: ckpt-registered, dataKey: body.uri }          dest: spec.template.spec.containers.0.args.0      # replaces CHECKPOINT_URI          operation: overwrite
Going deeper2 points
  • Per-question storage is cheap, compared with the GPU time spent producing it; throwing it away makes paired analysis impossible later.
  • Analysis code is versioned too: a changed probe or statistic gets a new version, and dashboards say which version they show.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, data: per-question eval storage, checkpoint events, standard probes on every checkpoint.
  • Phase 2, statistics: paired comparisons and intervals in every report; variance components per recipe family; power analysis in the ablation launcher.
  • Phase 3, debugging: run diffing, change bisection, behavior clustering.
  • Phase 4, depth: data attribution, activation probes, and the ablation library.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • More seeds and questions cost compute, in exchange for fewer wrong decisions and fewer re-runs.
  • Declared ablations slow down quick tries: exploratory runs remain allowed but can't, by themselves, change a recipe.
  • Always-on probes take GPU time on every checkpoint, kept low by small, fast probe sets on borrowed capacity.

Open questions.

  • Cheaper seed variance: can a few short runs predict the seed variance of a long one?
  • Better attribution for RL: how to attribute behavior to rollouts and reward decisions, not just to prompts?
  • Early predictors: which probe values at 10% of a run best predict its final evals?
  • Automated diagnosis: can the platform propose the likely cause of a regression from run diffs and probes before a person looks?
Design 13 · 12 sections

Design 13: End-to-end execution, from idea to production-scale runs

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. From idea to production: stages and gates
  3. Contracts between teams
  4. Data quality: contracts, validation and lineage
  5. Verifier and environment readiness
  6. Capacity planning for big runs
  7. Reliable pipelines: pre-flight, failure classes and recovery
  8. Scaling a recipe up
  9. Running the run: reviews, incidents and decisions
  10. From successful run to repeatable recipe
  11. The platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do research, systems, infrastructure and data teams work together to get experiments from an idea to production-scale runs, with training pipelines that are reliable, data and verifiers whose quality is known, and successful experiments turned into repeatable, scalable recipes? It ties the earlier designs together: capacity and queues (Design 02), training infrastructure (Design 03), recipes (Design 06), scaling (Design 07), verifiers (Design 10), mixtures (Design 11) and analysis (Design 12).

The short version: the path from idea to production is a pipeline with explicit stages, contracts and gates, not a series of favours. Each stage (proxy, scale-up, production run, recipe release) has an entry checklist, an owner and a gate. The hand-offs between teams are contracts: a run spec for infrastructure, a data contract for data, a verifier contract for rewards, and a recipe manifest for whoever runs it next. Big runs start only after pre-flight checks pass; while they run, failures are classified and handled automatically; and a run that worked becomes a recipe release that CI can re-run.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A small-scale RL experiment shows a clear gain in March. It reaches a production-scale run in June. In between: the data it used turned out to include eval questions, its verifier couldn't handle the throughput of a large run, the first two large runs died on infrastructure problems nobody owned, and the final recipe existed only in a researcher's branch. When she went on leave, nobody could reproduce it.

What the platform must do.

  • Shorten idea-to-scale time: weeks, not months, for an experiment that has earned it.
  • Make hand-offs explicit: each team knows what it receives, what it promises and how quality is checked.
  • Make big runs reliable: problems found before the run starts, failures during the run handled in minutes.
  • Guarantee data and verifier quality: checked automatically at every stage, not discovered after training.
  • Turn experiments into recipes: a successful run becomes a versioned, reproducible recipe anyone can re-run.
  • Keep a record: decisions, incidents and results in one place.

Out of scope: the technical content of each component, which the earlier designs cover.

From idea to production: stages and gates

Scenario. Nobody can say what "ready for a big run" means. Some experiments jump straight to 512 GPUs; others sit at proxy scale for months waiting for someone to decide.

What the picture shows. The stages an experiment moves through, with a gate between each.

1Idea and proxy
a declared ablation at small scale (Design 12). Gate: a confirmed effect with an interval, on the primary metric and guardrails.
2Scale-up
the scaling ladder (Design 07): longer, larger, more steps. Gate: stable curve fit, understood step-time breakdown, pre-flight checks passing.
3Production run
the full budget on reserved capacity. Gate: multi-family no-regression evaluation (Design 11).
4Recipe release
the run's configuration, data and verifier versions packaged as a recipe that CI can reproduce. Gate: a reproduction at reference scale matches.
5Owners per stage
research leads the first two; the run's operational owner (from systems) leads the production run; the recipe owner keeps the release reproducible.
Going deeper2 points
  • Gates are light at the start and heavy at the end: a proxy run needs a recipe file; a production run needs everything. Heavy gates early kill exploration.
  • Time in each stage is a metric: where experiments wait is where the process needs work.

Contracts between teams

Scenario. Infrastructure learns about a 1,024-GPU run two days before it should start. The data team learns that their dataset is being used for RL when the run is already in progress. The verifier team learns its service is in the critical path when it falls over.

What the picture shows. The hand-offs between teams, each a document with a schema and an owner.

1Run spec (research → infrastructure)
size, duration, topology, storage and network needs, start window, priority. Submitted when the scale-up stage starts, not when the run starts.
2Data contract (data → research)
schema, versions, freshness, decontamination status, licenses, PII handling and validation results.
3Verifier contract (rewards → research)
versions, measured precision per slice, throughput limits and on-call (Design 10).
4Recipe manifest (research → everyone)
the complete, pinned description of how to run it again.
5Incident and decision log (everyone)
what went wrong, what was decided and why.

The YAML. A run spec submitted to infrastructure at the start of scale-up.

# runspecs/assistant-v14-rl-prod.yamlrun: assistant-v14-rl-prodowner: { research: alice, operations: rl-ops-oncall }stage: productionsize: { nodes: 128, gpus_per_node: 8, accelerator: h100 }duration_estimate: { gpu_hours: 180000, wall_days: 8 }topology: { same_fabric_block: true }                  # see Design 02storage: { checkpoint_tb: 4.2, checkpoint_interval_min: 30, dataset_tb: 1.1 }dependencies:  verifiers: [math-final-answer@3.2.0, code-tests@5.1.0]   # must meet throughput below  verifier_throughput_rps: 1800  sandbox_pool_peak: 4000window: { earliest_start: 2026-12-01, latest_start: 2026-12-08 }priority: production
Going deeper2 points
  • Contracts are versioned and validated by machines: a run spec missing a field or a data contract missing decontamination status is rejected by CI, not by a meeting.
  • Every contract names an on-call: a hand-off without a contact for 3 a.m. isn't a hand-off.

Data quality: contracts, validation and lineage

Scenario. The March experiment's gain was partly from eval contamination: a scraped dataset contained a third of the benchmark's questions, paraphrased.

What the picture shows. The checks every dataset passes before it can be used in a recipe.

1Schema and format
fields present, chat templates valid, lengths within limits, languages labeled.
2Deduplication
exact and near-duplicate removal within and across sources.
3Decontamination
n-gram and embedding-similarity checks against every eval set the organization uses, including paraphrase detection.
4Safety and compliance
PII detection and removal, license recorded, sensitive-content filters.
5Quality signals
per-source quality scores and spot-check samples reviewed by people.
6Versioned snapshots and lineage
every dataset version is immutable, with the code and inputs that produced it, so a recipe pins exact data.

The code. Validation run on every new dataset version before it's published (Python).

import hashlibfrom datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH def ngram_minhash(text, n=8, perm=128):    m = MinHash(num_perm=perm)    toks = text.lower().split()    for i in range(max(1, len(toks) - n + 1)):        m.update(" ".join(toks[i:i + n]).encode())    return m def build_eval_index(eval_texts, threshold=0.5):    lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=128)    for i, t in enumerate(eval_texts):        lsh.insert(f"eval-{i}", ngram_minhash(t))    return lsh def validate(rows, eval_index, max_len=32768):    report = {"rows": len(rows), "schema_errors": 0, "exact_dupes": 0, "contaminated": 0}    seen = set()    for r in rows:        if not r.get("messages") or r["messages"][-1]["role"] != "assistant":            report["schema_errors"] += 1        h = hashlib.sha256(str(r["messages"]).encode()).hexdigest()        report["exact_dupes"] += h in seen; seen.add(h)        text = " ".join(m["content"] for m in r["messages"])        if eval_index.query(ngram_minhash(text)):            report["contaminated"] += 1                                   # blocks publication    report["ok"] = report["schema_errors"] == 0 and report["contaminated"] == 0    return report
Going deeper2 points
  • Decontaminate against all evals, every time an eval is added: a new eval set triggers re-checking existing datasets, not just new ones.
  • Data bugs look like model behaviors: a wrong chat template in one source shows up as an odd habit after training; schema checks per source are cheap insurance.

Verifier and environment readiness

Scenario. The verifier that served a 32-GPU proxy run at 40 requests per second gets 1,800 per second in the production run. Latency rises from 200 ms to 9 s, rollouts stall, and GPU utilization falls to 20%.

What the picture shows. What must be true of rewards and environments before a big run.

1Quality gate
precision per slice above threshold on current policy outputs, fuzzing clean (Design 10).
2Throughput test
a load test at the run's expected peak request rate and payload sizes, with latency targets.
3Capacity reservation
sandbox pools and judge GPUs reserved and pre-warmed for the run's duration.
4Failure behavior
what happens when the verifier is slow or down: rollouts pause and retry, never default to "pass".
5Version pinning
the run pins verifier and environment image digests; no changes during the run without an explicit decision.

The code. A pre-flight check the launcher runs before a production run (Python).

import asyncio, time, statistics, httpx async def load_test(url, payloads, rps: int, seconds: int = 60):    lat, errors = [], 0    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30) as client:        async def one(p):            nonlocal errors            t0 = time.perf_counter()            try:                r = await client.post(url, json=p); r.raise_for_status()                lat.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)            except Exception:                errors += 1        for _ in range(seconds):            tick = time.perf_counter()            await asyncio.gather(*(one(payloads[i % len(payloads)]) for i in range(rps)))            await asyncio.sleep(max(0, 1 - (time.perf_counter() - tick)))    p99 = statistics.quantiles(lat, n=100)[98] if lat else float("inf")    return {"p99_s": p99, "error_rate": errors / (rps * seconds)} def preflight(runspec, verifier_registry):    results = {}    for v in runspec["dependencies"]["verifiers"]:        meta = verifier_registry.get(v)        results[v] = {            "precision_ok": all(s["precision"] >= s["gate"] for s in meta["slices"]),            "load": asyncio.run(load_test(meta["url"], meta["sample_payloads"],                                          rps=runspec["dependencies"]["verifier_throughput_rps"])),        }        results[v]["ok"] = results[v]["precision_ok"] and results[v]["load"]["p99_s"] < 2.0 \            and results[v]["load"]["error_rate"] < 0.001    return results
Going deeper2 points
  • Load-test with realistic payloads: policy outputs late in a run are longer than early ones; test with long outputs.
  • Fail closed: a reward service error must never be read as a pass; it's the cheapest reward hack there is.

Capacity planning for big runs

Scenario. A production run needs 1,024 GPUs for eight days. Two days in, the cluster's reserved block expires; nobody had checked the reservation's end date against the run's estimate.

What the picture shows. Turning a run spec into reserved, ready capacity.

1Estimate from the ladder
GPU hours and wall-clock from rung measurements (Design 07), plus a margin for restarts and evals.
2Match capacity sources
reserved blocks for the run's duration with margin, on-demand only for overflow (Design 02).
3Reserve in the queue
the run's queue gets guaranteed quota for the window; other work borrows around it.
4Reserve the dependencies
verifier, sandbox and judge capacity, storage throughput for checkpoints.
5Dry run
a short run on the actual reserved nodes before the window starts, to catch hardware and topology problems.

The code. A capacity estimate with margins from ladder measurements (Python).

def capacity_plan(tokens_total, tokens_per_gpu_hour, gpus, restart_rate_per_day=0.3,                  restart_cost_h=0.5, eval_overhead=0.06, safety_margin=0.15):    gpu_hours = tokens_total / tokens_per_gpu_hour    wall_h = gpu_hours / gpus    days = wall_h / 24    lost_h = days * restart_rate_per_day * restart_cost_h             # expected restart losses    wall_h = (wall_h + lost_h) * (1 + eval_overhead)    reserve_h = wall_h * (1 + safety_margin)                          # reservation must cover this    return {"gpu_hours": round(gpu_hours), "expected_wall_days": round(wall_h / 24, 1),            "reserve_days": round(reserve_h / 24, 1)} print(capacity_plan(tokens_total=4.0e11, tokens_per_gpu_hour=2.6e6, gpus=1024))
Going deeper2 points
  • Track estimate accuracy: compare each run's estimate with its actual; bias in estimates is fixed by calibrating tokens-per-GPU-hour from the latest rung, not by bigger margins.
  • Reservations are commitments: an unused reservation costs as much as a used one; release early if the run finishes early.

Reliable pipelines: pre-flight, failure classes and recovery

Scenario. The first production run died on day one: a typo in a data path that the 32-GPU proxy never hit. The second died on day three: a node's GPU fault was retried as if it were a code bug, failing the whole job after the retry limit.

What the picture shows. How a production run avoids preventable failures and handles the rest.

1Pre-flight smoke run
a few steps of the production configuration on a small slice of the reserved nodes, touching every code path: data loading from every source, a checkpoint save and load, a verifier call, a weight sync and an eval.
2Failure classes
infrastructure failures (GPU faults, node loss, network) are retried on other nodes without counting against the job; code and configuration errors fail fast and page the run owner; data errors quarantine the shard and continue or stop by policy.
3Checkpoint verification
every checkpoint is test-loaded once after it's written; a corrupt checkpoint is found then, not when needed.
4Watchdogs
stalled-step detection (no progress for N minutes), NaN detection and health-signal alerts (Design 06).
5On-call and runbooks
a named operations owner per production run, with runbooks for each failure class.

The YAML. A pod failure policy that separates infrastructure failures from code errors (Kubernetes Job API).

apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: assistant-v14-preflight  namespace: post-training  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-production }spec:  completions: 16  parallelism: 16  completionMode: Indexed  backoffLimit: 6  podFailurePolicy:    rules:    - action: Ignore                         # node drained / GPU fault: retry, don't count      onPodConditions:      - type: DisruptionTarget    - action: FailJob                        # exit code 42 = config or code error: stop now      onExitCodes:        containerName: trainer        operator: In        values: [42]    - action: Count                          # anything else counts against backoffLimit      onExitCodes:        containerName: trainer        operator: NotIn        values: [0, 42]  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: trainer        image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer@sha256:1f0c...        args: ["--recipe=/recipes/prod.yaml", "--preflight", "--steps=20",               "--touch-all-sources", "--test-checkpoint-roundtrip", "--test-verifiers"]        resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Exit codes are an API: the trainer exits with distinct codes for config errors, data errors and internal errors, so the platform can react correctly.
  • Count failures by class over time: a rising rate of one infrastructure class on certain nodes is a hardware problem to fix, not noise to retry.

Scaling a recipe up

Scenario. The recipe that worked at 64 GPUs used a batch of 256 prompts. At 1,024 GPUs, someone multiplied the batch by 16 and kept the learning rate. The run was stable and learned much less per sample.

What the picture shows. What has to change, and what must not, when a recipe moves from proxy to production scale.

1Keep the science fixed
objective, reward, data mixture and filtering stay the same unless the ladder showed a reason to change them.
2Change the systems deliberately
parallelism layout, micro-batch sizes, number of rollout engines and weight-sync configuration are re-tuned for the new size.
3Batch and learning rate together
if the global batch changes, the learning rate and number of steps are re-validated at a rung, not assumed.
4Length and time budgets
maximum response length, timeouts and checkpoint intervals reflect the longer, larger run.
5The scale-up diff is reviewed
every key that differs between the proxy recipe and the production recipe is listed and justified.

The code. A scale-up diff check that separates "systems" keys from "science" keys (Python).

SYSTEMS_KEYS = {"parallelism", "micro_batch", "rollout.engines", "weight_sync", "checkpoint_interval",                "timeouts", "resources"} def flatten(d, prefix=""):    out = {}    for k, v in d.items():        key = f"{prefix}.{k}" if prefix else k        out.update(flatten(v, key) if isinstance(v, dict) else {key: v})    return out def scale_up_review(proxy: dict, prod: dict, justified: set):    a, b = flatten(proxy), flatten(prod)    changed = {k for k in a.keys() | b.keys() if a.get(k) != b.get(k)}    science = {k for k in changed if not any(k.startswith(s) for s in SYSTEMS_KEYS)}    unjustified = science - justified                                    # science changes need a reason    return {"systems_changes": sorted(changed - science), "science_changes": sorted(science),            "blocked": sorted(unjustified)}
Going deeper2 points
  • Scale-up surprises go back down the ladder: if production behaves differently from the last rung, reproduce at the rung before adjusting the production run.
  • Systems changes can change science: different parallelism or precision changes numerics; the mismatch checks of Design 07 run after any layout change.

Running the run: reviews, incidents and decisions

Scenario. On day five of a production run, three people noticed entropy dropping. Each assumed someone else was handling it. On day seven, the run collapsed.

What the picture shows. The operational rhythm of a production run.

1Roles
a research owner (is it learning the right thing?) and an operations owner (is it running well?), both named in the run spec.
2Daily run review
fifteen minutes on health signals, evals at the latest checkpoints, throughput, cost and open issues.
3Incident process
any automatic alert or human concern opens an incident with an owner; decisions (pause, roll back, change a setting) are recorded with the evidence.
4Change control during the run
live changes (learning rate, staleness limit, mixture) go through the run's change log, never directly.
5Post-run review
what worked, what broke, what the next run should change; the results feed the recipe and the runbooks.
Going deeper2 points
  • The decision log is part of the recipe release: a recipe that needed three mid-run interventions isn't a recipe yet; those interventions become part of it or become fixed problems.
  • Automatic controls first: controllers from Design 09 handle common problems; people handle what's new.

From successful run to repeatable recipe

Scenario. The production run succeeded. Three months later, the next version starts from "what we did last time", and nobody can reconstruct the exact data mixture or the verifier version.

What the picture shows. What a recipe release contains, and how it stays reproducible.

1Pinned inputs
base checkpoint, dataset snapshots, verifier and environment versions, container image digests.
2Configuration
the full recipe and schedule, including the systems settings for each supported scale.
3Evidence
eval results with intervals, the scale-up record, the decision log and known issues.
4Runbook
how to run it, what to watch, what to do when known problems appear.
5Reproduction in CI
a scheduled job re-runs the recipe at reference scale on current infrastructure and compares with the recorded results, so infrastructure or library drift is caught.

The YAML. A recipe release manifest, the unit a future run starts from.

# releases/assistant-v14-rl@1.0.0/manifest.yamlrelease: assistant-v14-rlversion: 1.0.0base_checkpoint: registry://assistant-v14/sft@sha256:7c1e...data:  - datasets://math-verified@v6 # snapshot id: ds-2026-11-02-a91f  - datasets://code-tests@v9  - envs://swe-tasks@v3verifiers: [math-final-answer@3.2.0, code-tests@5.1.0]images: { trainer: "sha256:1f0c...", vllm: "sha256:88ab...", verifier-math: "sha256:5e1d..." }recipe: recipes/assistant-v14/rl-math-code.yaml@3f9a1c7scales:  reference: { gpus: 64,   steps: 300,  expected: { math-hard: [61.0, 63.4] } }   # CI reproduction band  production: { gpus: 1024, steps: 4200 }evidence:  evals: results://assistant-v14-rl-prod/final  decision_log: runs/assistant-v14-rl-prod/decisions.mdknown_issues: ["entropy dips at ~step 2,400; controller handles it (see runbook §3)"]owner: team-reasoning
Going deeper2 points
  • Reproduction bands come from seed variance: the CI check passes when the reference run lands inside the interval measured for that recipe (Design 12), not when it matches a single number.
  • Recipes have a lifecycle: active, superseded or deprecated; a deprecated recipe keeps its manifest so old results remain explainable.

The platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. Each stage of the path uses a different set of scripts, and the state of an experiment lives in a mix of tickets, chats and branches.

What the picture shows. The components that carry an experiment from idea to recipe.

1Experiment tracker
the stage, owners, contracts and gates for each experiment, linked to its runs.
2Contract validators in CI
run specs, data contracts, verifier contracts and recipe manifests checked on every change.
3Launcher
turns recipes and run specs into Kueue-managed jobs, runs pre-flight checks, and refuses launches that fail them.
4Data platform
versioned snapshots, validation and lineage.
5Reward platform
verifier registry and pools (Design 10).
6Training infrastructure
queues, reserved capacity, JobSets and RayJobs (Designs 02, 03).
7Run operations
dashboards, alerts, controllers, incident and decision logs.
8Recipe registry and reproduction CI
releases, manifests and scheduled reproduction runs.

The YAML. A scheduled reproduction of the recipe release at reference scale, triggered from CI (GitHub Actions).

# .github/workflows/reproduce-recipes.yamlname: reproduce-recipeson:  schedule: [ { cron: "23 3 * * 1" } ]          # weekly, Monday 03:23 UTC  workflow_dispatch: {}jobs:  reproduce:    runs-on: ubuntu-latest    strategy:      matrix: { release: [assistant-v14-rl@1.0.0, assistant-v14-sft@2.1.0] }    steps:    - uses: actions/checkout@v4    - name: Submit reference run      run: |        python3 tools/launch.py --release "releases/${{ matrix.release }}/manifest.yaml" \          --scale reference --queue research-small --wait    - name: Compare with expected band      run: |        python3 tools/compare_band.py --release "releases/${{ matrix.release }}/manifest.yaml" \          --run latest --fail-outside-band          # drift in infra or libraries fails the check
Going deeper2 points
  • One identifier everywhere: the experiment ID appears in run specs, jobs, checkpoints, eval results and recipe releases, so any artifact leads back to the decision that created it.
  • Dashboards per stage: how many experiments are in each stage, how long they wait, and why they fail gates.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, visibility: stages, owners and the experiment tracker; run specs submitted at scale-up; decision logs for production runs.
  • Phase 2, quality gates: data validation and decontamination in CI; verifier readiness checks; launcher pre-flight.
  • Phase 3, reliability: failure classes and pod failure policies, checkpoint verification, watchdogs, on-call and runbooks.
  • Phase 4, repeatability: recipe releases, scale-up reviews and reproduction CI.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Gates add steps: a few days of checks before a large run, in exchange for not losing weeks to preventable failures.
  • Reserved capacity costs money while idle, in exchange for runs that start on time and finish.
  • Contracts formalize relationships: some flexibility is lost, and much less is lost in miscommunication.
  • Reproduction CI uses compute weekly, in exchange for catching drift before a new version depends on an old recipe.

Open questions.

  • How light can early gates be while still catching the problems that are expensive later?
  • Automatic run reviews: can the analysis platform (Design 12) draft the daily run review?
  • Shared ownership at the boundary: who owns a failure that is half data and half verifier, and how is that decided quickly?
  • Recipes across model generations: how much of a recipe release carries over to the next base model, and how is that tested?
Design 14 · 12 sections

Design 14: Reliable infrastructure for large-scale RL training

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Anatomy of an RL system and its failure domains
  3. Reliability targets: failure rates, goodput and checkpoint intervals
  4. Node health: burn-in, continuous checks and automatic drain
  5. Trainer fault tolerance: from fast restarts to per-step recovery
  6. Rollout fleet resilience
  7. Weight synchronization you can trust
  8. The reward and environment tier: fail closed, degrade gracefully
  9. Checkpointing the whole RL state
  10. Stragglers, hangs and silent errors
  11. Observability, SLOs and fault injection
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we design and build infrastructure that keeps large-scale RL training running (thousands of GPUs, weeks of wall-clock time, many cooperating services) when hardware fails every few hours, services slow down, and some failures are silent? Design 07 covers what changes when RL scales and Design 13 covers how runs get from idea to production. This design is about the infrastructure underneath: failure domains, node health, fault tolerance for each RL component, whole-state checkpointing, stragglers and silent errors, and how reliability is measured and tested.

The short version: assume something is always broken, and make each break cost seconds of one component instead of hours of the whole run. The RL system is split into failure domains with different recovery strategies: the trainer is stateful and synchronous (fast checkpoint, fast restart, or per-step recovery across replica groups); rollout engines, verifiers and environments are stateless or cheaply restorable (retry, replace, route around). Nodes are continuously health-checked and drained before they break a job. All RL state (not only weights) is checkpointed asynchronously and verified. And reliability is a measured number, goodput, with an SLO, tested on purpose with fault injection.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The RL platform runs a 2,048-GPU training job with 512 more GPUs of rollout engines, a 6,000-pod sandbox pool and a judge fleet. In the first month: a GPU failure roughly every few hours, two silent NaN events from a bad GPU, a network flap that hung all NCCL collectives for 40 minutes, a verifier deploy that returned errors read as "fail" for an hour, and a checkpoint that couldn't be loaded when it was needed. Goodput was 61%.

What the platform must do.

  • Contain failures: a broken GPU, engine, verifier or sandbox affects the smallest possible part of the system.
  • Recover in minutes: automatic detection, replacement and resumption, without a person in the loop for common failures.
  • Lose little work: checkpoints frequent and cheap enough that a restart loses minutes, not hours.
  • Catch silent failures: slow nodes, numerical corruption and hung collectives are detected, not discovered from the loss curve.
  • Measure reliability: goodput and recovery times as tracked numbers with targets.
  • Prove it: fault injection in staging and during rehearsals, so recovery paths are known to work.

Out of scope: algorithmic stability (Designs 06–09) and the run's organizational process (Design 13).

Anatomy of an RL system and its failure domains

Scenario. One sandbox node's disk filled up. Rollouts that used it hung, the trainer waited for a full batch, and the whole 2,048-GPU job sat idle for 25 minutes. A failure in the cheapest component stopped the most expensive one.

What the picture shows. The components of a large RL system, grouped by how they fail and recover.

1Trainer (stateful, synchronous)
thousands of GPUs in collectives; one failed rank stops all of them. Recovery: restart from checkpoint, or per-step recovery across replica groups.
2Rollout engines (stateless, independent)
each engine can fail alone; in-flight requests are retried elsewhere. Recovery: replace.
3Reward and environment tier (stateless or snapshot-backed)
verifiers, judges and sandboxes. Recovery: retry, circuit-break, replace.
4Coordination state
the sample buffer, the controller, weight versions and the data cursor. Small but critical; must be durable and replicated.
5Storage and network
checkpoint storage, object storage, the GPU fabric and the pod network. Shared by everything; failures here are wide.
6The rule
failures flow toward the trainer as delays, never as stops. Every dependency of the trainer has a timeout, a fallback and a bound on how long the trainer will wait.
Going deeper2 points
  • Map the blast radius explicitly: for each component, write down what stops when it fails; anything that can stop the trainer, apart from the trainer itself, is a design bug.
  • Decoupling buys reliability as well as throughput: the asynchronous designs of Design 07 and Design 09 mean a slow rollout tier reduces fresh data instead of halting training.

Reliability targets: failure rates, goodput and checkpoint intervals

Scenario. Someone proposes checkpointing every 4 hours "to save storage." Someone else proposes every 5 minutes "to be safe." Neither has done the arithmetic.

What the picture shows. How failure rates turn into lost time, and how to choose the checkpoint interval.

1Failures scale with size
a job's failure rate is roughly the per-node rate times the number of nodes. Meta's Llama 3 405B run on 16,384 H100 GPUs saw 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days, about one every three hours, with GPUs or their memory responsible for about half.
2Lost time per failure
detection time + restart time + recomputation since the last checkpoint (on average half the interval).
3Checkpoint cost
the time training is paused to save; asynchronous checkpointing reduces it to seconds.
4Optimal interval
roughly the square root of (2 × checkpoint cost × mean time between failures), the Young–Daly approximation. Faster checkpoints allow shorter intervals.
5Goodput
the fraction of reserved GPU time that produced training progress. The target (for example, 90%+) is set per run and tracked daily.

The code. Expected goodput and the best checkpoint interval for a job (Python).

import math def plan(nodes, node_mtbf_h, ckpt_cost_s, restart_s, detect_s, step_overhead=0.0):    job_mtbf_s = node_mtbf_h * 3600 / nodes                       # failures add up across nodes    interval_s = math.sqrt(2 * ckpt_cost_s * job_mtbf_s)          # Young–Daly approximation    ckpt_overhead = ckpt_cost_s / interval_s    lost_per_failure = detect_s + restart_s + interval_s / 2    failure_overhead = lost_per_failure / job_mtbf_s    goodput = (1 - ckpt_overhead) * (1 - failure_overhead) * (1 - step_overhead)    return {"job_mtbf_h": round(job_mtbf_s / 3600, 2), "ckpt_interval_min": round(interval_s / 60, 1),            "goodput": round(goodput, 3)} # 256 nodes, a node fails every ~60 days on average; sync vs async checkpoint, slow vs fast restartprint(plan(256, 60 * 24, ckpt_cost_s=300, restart_s=1800, detect_s=300))   # sync, slow restartprint(plan(256, 60 * 24, ckpt_cost_s=8,   restart_s=240,  detect_s=30))    # async, hot spares
Going deeper2 points
  • Restart time matters as much as checkpoint interval: with failures every few hours, a 30-minute restart costs more than any checkpoint policy can recover.
  • Measure, don't assume, node MTBF: use the fleet's own failure history per hardware generation; it changes with age and firmware.

Node health: burn-in, continuous checks and automatic drain

Scenario. A node with a GPU throwing intermittent memory errors joins the training job. It doesn't fail outright; it fails the job twice a day for a week, each time looking like a new problem.

What the picture shows. The health lifecycle of a GPU node.

1Burn-in before admission
new or repaired nodes run GPU diagnostics, memory tests, NVLink and network bandwidth tests and a short multi-node collective test before they can join training pools.
2Continuous passive checks
GPU error counters (XID errors, ECC and row-remap events), thermals, PCIe and NIC errors, collected per node.
3Periodic active checks
short diagnostic runs during idle windows or between jobs.
4Automatic drain
a node that fails a check is tainted so no new pods land on it, its workloads are moved, and it goes to repair; a node that fails repeatedly is retired.
5Feedback from jobs
if one node appears in several job failures, it's drained even if its checks pass.

The YAML. A health-check DaemonSet that taints a node when its GPU checks fail (the check script uses NVIDIA DCGM; node tainting through the API).

apiVersion: apps/v1kind: DaemonSetmetadata:  name: gpu-health  namespace: gpu-opsspec:  selector: { matchLabels: { app: gpu-health } }  template:    metadata: { labels: { app: gpu-health } }    spec:      serviceAccountName: gpu-health            # RBAC: patch nodes (taints) only      nodeSelector: { nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true" }      tolerations: [ { operator: Exists } ]     # keep running on tainted nodes      priorityClassName: system-node-critical      containers:      - name: check        image: registry.example.com/gpu-ops/health:2026.11        args:        - --interval=60s        - --dcgm-level=1                        # quick passive checks; level 3 in idle windows        - --xid-fatal=48,63,64,74,79,94,95      # treat these XIDs as fatal        - --on-fail=taint:gpu-health=failed:NoSchedule        - --report=http://fleet-health.gpu-ops:8080/events        env:        - name: NODE_NAME          valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: spec.nodeName } }        securityContext: { privileged: true }   # DCGM needs device access        resources: { limits: { cpu: "500m", memory: 512Mi } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Drain gently during a run: a failing node in a running job is replaced at the next checkpoint or restart, not by killing the job immediately, unless the failure is already fatal.
  • Track node history: every node's failures and repairs are recorded; repeat offenders are retired before they fail another run.

Trainer fault tolerance: from fast restarts to per-step recovery

Scenario. Each trainer failure took the whole 256-node job down for 35 minutes: rescheduling pods, pulling images, re-forming NCCL groups and loading a 3 TB checkpoint. Four failures a day cost more than two hours of 2,048 GPUs.

What the picture shows. Three levels of trainer fault tolerance, each building on the previous.

1Fast full restart
hot spare nodes reserved in the queue, images pre-pulled, checkpoints loaded in parallel from local copies or peers; the whole job restarts in a few minutes.
2In-place restart
only the failed pod is replaced and the job restarts its processes without rescheduling the healthy pods, avoiding the pod-level work.
3Per-step recovery across replicas
with replicated data-parallel groups (DDP or HSDP), a failed replica group drops out, training continues with the rest, and the group rejoins by copying state from a healthy peer. Libraries like torchft implement this, allowing membership changes at the training step granularity instead of stopping the world.
4Collective timeouts
NCCL watchdog timeouts set so a hung collective fails in minutes, not hours; the failure is then handled like any other.

The YAML. A JobSet failure policy: infrastructure failures restart without using up the restart budget; configuration errors stop immediately.

apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: JobSetmetadata:  name: rl-trainer-prod  namespace: rl-scale  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: rl-production }spec:  failurePolicy:    maxRestarts: 20    restartStrategy: Recreate    rules:    - name: infra-disruption                       # node drained, GPU fault, preemption      action: RestartJobSetAndIgnoreMaxRestarts     # doesn't consume the budget      onJobFailureReasons: [PodFailurePolicy]    - name: config-error      action: FailJobSet                            # exit 42: don't retry a bad config      onJobFailureReasons: [BackoffLimitExceeded]      targetReplicatedJobs: [launcher]  replicatedJobs:  - name: trainer    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        parallelism: 256        completions: 256        backoffLimit: 0        podFailurePolicy:          rules:          - action: FailJob            onPodConditions: [ { type: DisruptionTarget } ]        template:          spec:            restartPolicy: Never            containers:            - name: trainer              image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer@sha256:1f0c...              env:              - { name: TORCH_NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING, value: "1" }              - { name: TORCH_NCCL_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT_SEC, value: "300" }   # hung collective → error              args: ["--resume=latest", "--ckpt-load=peer-first"]              resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }  - name: launcher    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        backoffLimit: 0        template:          spec:            restartPolicy: Never            containers:            - name: validate              image: registry.example.com/rl/trainer@sha256:1f0c...              args: ["--validate-config-only"]      # exits 42 on config errors
Going deeper2 points
  • Per-step recovery has requirements: replicated data-parallel groups, a coordination service, and enough memory headroom to run with one group missing; it pays off most at very large scale.
  • Measure each recovery phase: detection, scheduling, image, process start, collective setup, checkpoint load. The slowest phase is the one to fix.

Rollout fleet resilience

Scenario. One vLLM engine started returning garbled output after a driver error but kept passing its HTTP health check. For two hours, 1/64 of rollouts were nonsense with near-zero rewards.

What the picture shows. Keeping a large fleet of inference engines healthy and its failures invisible to the trainer.

1Stateless engines
any request can be retried on another engine; partial generations are discarded or resumed according to policy.
2Timeouts and hedging
each request has a deadline; requests in the slowest tail are re-issued on another engine and the first answer wins.
3Deep health checks
beyond "is it up," engines periodically answer a fixed canary prompt; output and log-probabilities are compared with expected values, catching silent corruption.
4Quarantine
an engine that fails a canary or produces abnormal statistics (rewards, lengths, log-probabilities far from its peers) is drained and replaced.
5Rolling weight updates
new weights are loaded engine by engine (or group by group), so the fleet never goes fully offline.

The code. A rollout client with deadlines, retries on another engine and hedged requests (Python, asyncio).

import asyncio, random async def generate(engines, request, deadline_s=600, hedge_after_s=120, max_attempts=3):    """Send to one engine; if slow, hedge on a second; retry elsewhere on failure."""    tried, attempt = set(), 0    while attempt < max_attempts:        attempt += 1        primary = random.choice([e for e in engines.healthy() if e not in tried]); tried.add(primary)        tasks = {asyncio.create_task(primary.generate(request))}        try:            done, _ = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=hedge_after_s)            if not done:                                            # slow: hedge on another engine                backup = random.choice([e for e in engines.healthy() if e not in tried]); tried.add(backup)                tasks.add(asyncio.create_task(backup.generate(request)))                done, _ = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=deadline_s - hedge_after_s,                                             return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)            for t in done:                if not t.exception():                    for other in tasks - {t}: other.cancel()                    return t.result()        except Exception:            pass        for t in tasks: t.cancel()        engines.report_failure(primary)                              # feeds quarantine decisions    raise TimeoutError("rollout failed on all attempts")             # the buffer skips this prompt
Going deeper2 points
  • Compare engines with their peers: per-engine reward, length and log-probability distributions should match the fleet; an outlier engine is suspect even when it responds.
  • Hedging costs capacity: hedge only the slowest few percent, and count hedged duplicates in the throughput budget.

Weight synchronization you can trust

Scenario. A weight push was interrupted halfway by a network flap. Half of one engine's layers were new and half were old. It served for an hour before anyone noticed.

What the picture shows. Making weight distribution atomic, verifiable and recoverable.

1Stage, then swap
new weights are written to a staging buffer on each engine; the engine switches versions only when the full set has arrived and verified.
2Checksums per bucket
each transferred bucket carries a checksum; a mismatch triggers a re-send of that bucket.
3Version handshake
after the swap, each engine reports its version and a fingerprint (for example, the log-probability of a canary prompt); the coordinator checks them.
4Timeouts and fallback path
if the fast path (NCCL over the GPU fabric) fails or times out, engines load the version from object storage instead.
5Version-tagged tokens
every generated token carries the version that produced it (Design 09), so a mistake is traceable and correctable.

The code. Staged, checksummed weight loading with an atomic swap on the engine side (Python sketch).

import hashlib, torch class WeightReceiver:    def __init__(self, model):        self.model, self.staging, self.expected = model, {}, {}     def begin(self, version: int, manifest: dict):          # manifest: bucket_id -> (names, sha256)        self.version, self.expected, self.staging = version, manifest, {}     def receive(self, bucket_id: str, tensors: dict[str, torch.Tensor]) -> bool:        h = hashlib.sha256()        for name in sorted(tensors):            h.update(tensors[name].contiguous().view(torch.uint8).cpu().numpy().tobytes())        if h.hexdigest() != self.expected[bucket_id][1]:            return False                                     # coordinator re-sends this bucket        self.staging.update({n: t.to("cuda", non_blocking=True) for n, t in tensors.items()})        return True     def commit(self) -> int:        if set(self.staging) != {n for names, _ in self.expected.values() for n in names}:            raise RuntimeError("incomplete weight set; keeping current version")        with torch.no_grad():            for name, p in self.model.named_parameters():                p.copy_(self.staging[name])                  # swap only when everything arrived        self.staging.clear()        return self.version
Going deeper2 points
  • Checksums on GPU: hashing large tensors on CPU is slow; compute a cheap GPU-side checksum (for example, sums over strided slices) per bucket and keep the full hash for the object-storage path.
  • Staging needs memory: a full staging copy doubles weight memory; with tight memory, stage per layer and swap layer by layer between requests.

The reward and environment tier: fail closed, degrade gracefully

Scenario. A verifier deploy started returning HTTP 500 for 30% of requests. The reward client treated errors as score 0. For an hour, the policy was punished for correct answers that happened to hit the broken pods.

What the picture shows. Patterns that keep reward failures from corrupting training or stalling it.

1Errors are not scores
a failed reward call is an error, retried or marked "no reward" (excluded from the loss), never a 0 or a 1 (Design 10).
2Circuit breakers
when a verifier's error rate crosses a threshold, calls stop for a cooling period; affected samples wait or are skipped.
3Back-pressure
when the reward queue is long, rollout engines slow down new trajectories instead of piling up work.
4Bulkheads
separate pools per verifier and per environment type, so one overloaded verifier doesn't starve the others.
5Sandbox hygiene
leaked or stuck sandboxes are reaped by age; pools are refilled before they run dry.
6Pinned versions during a run
verifier deploys during a run are explicit, canaried and reversible.

The code. A circuit breaker around reward calls that turns failures into "no reward", never into a score (Python).

import time class RewardBreaker:    def __init__(self, call, max_error_rate=0.05, window=200, cooldown_s=60):        self.call, self.max, self.window, self.cooldown = call, max_error_rate, window, cooldown_s        self.results, self.open_until = [], 0.0     def score(self, task, completion) -> float | None:        if time.time() < self.open_until:            return None                                   # breaker open: no reward, sample excluded        try:            r = self.call(task, completion)            self._record(ok=True)            return r        except Exception:            self._record(ok=False)            return None                                   # an error is never a score     def _record(self, ok: bool):        self.results = (self.results + [ok])[-self.window:]        errs = self.results.count(False) / len(self.results)        if len(self.results) >= 50 and errs > self.max:            self.open_until = time.time() + self.cooldown  # stop hammering a failing service            self.results.clear()
Going deeper2 points
  • Track "no reward" rate per verifier as a first-class metric; a rise means data is being lost even if training looks fine.
  • Graceful degradation is a policy: decide in advance whether a run pauses, continues with fewer domains, or slows down when a verifier is unavailable.

Checkpointing the whole RL state

Scenario. After a restart from checkpoint, the run repeated 40,000 prompts it had already trained on, the controller forgot that it had tightened the staleness limit, and the replay buffer was empty. The model was restored; the run wasn't.

What the picture shows. Everything a restart needs, and how it's saved without stopping training.

1Model and optimizer
sharded, saved asynchronously (copy to host memory, then write in the background).
2Data and sampling state
data cursors per source, curriculum position, RNG states.
3RL state
the sample buffer (or enough of it), in-flight rollout bookkeeping, weight version, controller settings and history.
4Two tiers
frequent saves to local NVMe or peer memory for fast restarts; less frequent copies to object storage for durability.
5Verification
every checkpoint is test-loaded (or checksum-verified against its manifest) once; only verified checkpoints are eligible for restart.
6Retention
keep the latest several, plus periodic ones for rollback (Design 07).

The code. Asynchronous sharded checkpointing of model, optimizer and RL state with PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint (sketch).

import json, torch.distributed as distimport torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcpfrom torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import get_state_dict pending = None def save_rl_checkpoint(step, model, optimizer, rl_state: dict, path_local: str):    """rl_state: data cursors, RNG, buffer index, weight version, controller settings (small, JSON-able)."""    global pending    if pending is not None:        pending.result()                               # at most one save in flight    model_sd, optim_sd = get_state_dict(model, optimizer)    state = {"model": model_sd, "optim": optim_sd}    pending = dcp.async_save(state, checkpoint_id=f"{path_local}/step-{step}")   # training continues    if dist.get_rank() == 0:        with open(f"{path_local}/step-{step}.rl.json", "w") as f:            json.dump({"step": step, **rl_state}, f)   # buffer contents saved separately by the buffer service    return pending
Going deeper2 points
  • The buffer service checkpoints itself: it persists its contents (or an index into stored rollouts) on the same step boundary, so trainer and buffer agree on what has been consumed.
  • Upload in the background, verify in the background: the trainer only waits for the copy to host memory; upload and test-load run on separate processes.

Stragglers, hangs and silent errors

Scenario. Step time crept from 41 to 52 seconds over two days. No failures, no alerts. One GPU was thermally throttling, and every collective waited for it.

What the picture shows. The failures that don't announce themselves, and how each is detected.

1Stragglers
one slow rank slows every synchronous step. Detect with per-rank step and collective timings; the outlier rank is the suspect.
2Hangs
a collective that never completes. Detect with collective watchdogs and "no progress for N minutes" monitors; dump stack traces from every rank before restarting.
3Silent data corruption
a faulty GPU computes wrong values without errors. Detect with loss and gradient-norm spikes, NaN and infinity checks, cross-replica checksum comparisons of parameters, and periodic re-computation of a fixed probe on every GPU.
4Silent rollout corruption
an engine producing wrong output (see the rollout section); detected by canaries and peer comparison.
5Response
isolate the suspect node, verify with a targeted diagnostic, roll back to a checkpoint from before the corruption started if it affected training.

The code. Finding straggler ranks from per-rank step timings gathered each step (PyTorch Distributed).

import torch, torch.distributed as dist def straggler_check(step_time_s: float, step: int, z_threshold=4.0, log=print):    """Gather every rank's compute time for this step; flag ranks far above the median."""    t = torch.tensor([step_time_s], device="cuda")    all_t = [torch.zeros_like(t) for _ in range(dist.get_world_size())]    dist.all_gather(all_t, t)    if dist.get_rank() == 0:        times = torch.cat(all_t)        med = times.median()        mad = (times - med).abs().median() + 1e-6        z = (times - med) / (1.4826 * mad)                      # robust z-score        slow = (z > z_threshold).nonzero().flatten().tolist()        if slow:            log({"step": step, "straggler_ranks": slow, "times": times[slow].tolist(), "median": med.item()})        return slow
Going deeper2 points
  • Time compute separately from communication: a rank that is slow in compute is the straggler; ranks that are slow in communication are often waiting for it.
  • Keep a known-good probe per GPU: a tiny fixed computation with a known result, run every few hundred steps on every GPU, catches many silent corruption cases cheaply.

Observability, SLOs and fault injection

Scenario. The platform team believes recovery takes "about five minutes." The last three real recoveries took 9, 31 and 47 minutes. Nobody had measured, and one recovery path had never been exercised.

What the picture shows. Measuring reliability, and testing it on purpose.

1SLOs per run
goodput, time to detect, time to recover, maximum work lost per failure, and "no reward" rate.
2Failure ledger
every interruption recorded with its class, component, node, detection time, recovery time and root cause; reviewed weekly.
3Dashboards by failure domain
trainer, rollout fleet, reward tier, storage, network, each with its own health and recovery metrics.
4Fault injection
in staging and in rehearsal runs, kill trainer pods, crash rollout engines, inject network delay, fail a verifier and corrupt a checkpoint; confirm each recovery path and time it.
5Game days before big runs
a scheduled exercise where the on-call team handles injected failures on a rehearsal run.

The YAML. Injecting failures with Chaos Mesh in a rehearsal namespace: kill a rollout engine every 15 minutes and add latency to the verifier.

apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1kind: Schedulemetadata:  name: kill-rollout-engine  namespace: rl-rehearsalspec:  schedule: "*/15 * * * *"  type: PodChaos  historyLimit: 5  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid  podChaos:    action: pod-kill    mode: one                                   # one random engine each time    selector:      namespaces: [rl-rehearsal]      labelSelectors: { app: rollout-engine }---apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1kind: NetworkChaosmetadata:  name: slow-verifier  namespace: rl-rehearsalspec:  action: delay  mode: all  selector:    namespaces: [rl-rehearsal]    labelSelectors: { app: verifier-math }  delay: { latency: "2s", jitter: "500ms" }     # does back-pressure hold?  duration: "20m"
Going deeper2 points
  • Untested recovery paths don't work: any recovery path that hasn't run in the last month is assumed broken until a rehearsal proves otherwise.
  • The failure ledger drives investment: the top three causes of lost goodput each quarter get engineering time; everything else waits.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, measure: goodput, failure ledger, per-phase recovery timing, node health history.
  • Phase 2, contain: timeouts and fallbacks on every trainer dependency, reward circuit breakers, rollout retries and hedging, node burn-in and automatic drain.
  • Phase 3, recover fast: asynchronous whole-state checkpointing with verification, hot spares, peer checkpoint loading, JobSet failure policies, verified weight sync.
  • Phase 4, harden: straggler and silent-corruption detection, per-step trainer recovery at the largest scales, regular fault injection and game days.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Hot spares cost GPUs that sit idle most of the time, in exchange for minutes-long restarts.
  • Deep health checks and canaries use capacity on every node and engine, in exchange for catching silent failures.
  • Per-step recovery adds complexity in the trainer and coordination; used only where restart cost justifies it.
  • Fault injection breaks things on purpose, in rehearsal namespaces only, in exchange for knowing that recovery works.

Open questions.

  • Silent corruption at scale: how much periodic verification is enough, and what does it cost?
  • Per-step recovery with expert and pipeline parallelism: replica-group recovery works best for data parallelism; how far can it extend to other parallel dimensions?
  • Predictive maintenance: can node telemetry predict failures early enough to drain nodes before they fail a run?
  • Cross-cluster resilience: should one RL run span clusters so a cluster-level failure only slows it down?
Design 15 · 12 sections

Design 15: Evaluation and benchmarking infrastructure

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Three questions, one platform
  3. Suite definitions and the harness
  4. Running evals at scale
  5. The results store and lineage
  6. Measuring model progress
  7. Training throughput benchmarks
  8. Inference throughput and latency benchmarks
  9. Uptime and availability
  10. Regression detection and benchmark CI
  11. The platform on Kubernetes and reporting
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build infrastructure that measures three things continuously and consistently: how much the models are improving (progress), how fast training and inference run (throughput), and how reliably training and serving stay up (uptime)? Design 12 covers the statistics for comparing runs, Design 10 covers verifier quality, and Design 14 covers what makes training reliable. This design is the measurement platform underneath them: suite definitions, eval execution at scale, the results store, performance benchmarks, uptime SLOs and regression detection.

The short version: one definition, one runner, one store per kind of measurement. Every eval suite and benchmark is a versioned definition (data, prompts, sampling, scorer, hardware); one scheduler runs them on shared capacity with caching; every result lands in one store with full lineage, per question or per request. Model progress, training throughput, inference throughput and uptime each have a small set of agreed metrics, measured the same way every time, and benchmark CI catches regressions from model changes and from software or hardware upgrades alike.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. On Monday, three dashboards disagree: the research tracker shows the new checkpoint 2 points better on reasoning, the release dashboard shows it 1 point worse (different prompt template), and the eval took three days because it waited behind training jobs. The serving team reports 2,300 tokens per second per GPU from a benchmark nobody else can reproduce; a driver upgrade quietly cost 12% of training throughput two weeks ago; and the platform's 99.9% uptime report disagrees with users' experience of two outages.

What the platform must do.

  • One definition per measurement: a suite or benchmark means exactly one thing, versioned, wherever it's run.
  • Fast, cheap evals: results for a new checkpoint within hours, not days, at predictable cost.
  • Full lineage: every number traceable to the model, data, code, harness and hardware that produced it.
  • Performance as a first-class measurement: training and inference throughput benchmarked the same way across models, versions and hardware.
  • Honest uptime: availability measured from the user's side for serving and as goodput for training.
  • Catch regressions automatically: from model changes, eval changes and infrastructure changes.

Out of scope: statistical methods (Design 12), verifier design (Design 10), production traffic monitoring beyond uptime SLIs.

Three questions, one platform

Scenario. Research, infrastructure and serving teams each built their own measurement tooling. The tools overlap in function and disagree in results.

What the picture shows. The three kinds of measurement, what each one measures and who uses it.

1Model progress
capability, behavior and safety eval suites run on checkpoints and release candidates. Used by researchers, release gates and leadership.
2Throughput
training performance (tokens per second per GPU, model FLOPs utilization, step time) and inference performance (time to first token, inter-token latency, throughput at a latency target). Used by infrastructure, serving and capacity planning.
3Uptime
serving availability measured as SLIs from the user's side, and training availability measured as goodput. Used by on-call, platform owners and customers.
4Shared foundation
a definition registry, a scheduler on shared GPU capacity, a results store with lineage, and benchmark CI. Built once, used by all three.
Going deeper2 points
  • Separate the question from the tool: "is the new checkpoint better?" and "did the driver upgrade slow us down?" share the same machinery (definitions, runs, comparisons against a baseline), even though the metrics differ.
  • Each metric has an owner: who defines it, who approves changes to its definition, and who is paged when it regresses.

Suite definitions and the harness

Scenario. The reasoning score differed by 3 points between two dashboards because one used a chat template with a system prompt and the other didn't. Both were labeled "math-hard".

What the picture shows. Everything that determines an eval result, captured in one versioned definition.

1Data
the exact dataset version and split, with a content hash.
2Prompting
template, system prompt, few-shot examples, chat formatting, tool definitions.
3Sampling
temperature, top-p, number of samples per question, maximum tokens, stop sequences, seeds.
4Scoring
