the verifier or judge and its version (Design 10), the metric (pass@1, pass@k, accuracy) and the aggregation (per-question mean, clusters).
5Harness version
the eval code itself, pinned by image digest.
6Any change makes a new version
"math-hard@v5" always means the same thing; dashboards say which version they show.

The YAML. A suite definition in the registry.

# suites/math-hard/v5.yamlsuite: math-hardversion: 5owner: team-reasoningdata:  source: datasets://math-hard-heldout@v3  sha256: 9b1e4c...  split: test  questions: 1200  clusters: problem_family              # for clustered standard errors (Design 12)prompt:  template: templates/math-cot@v2        # includes the final-answer contract  system: null  few_shot: 0sampling: { temperature: 0.6, top_p: 0.95, samples: 8, max_tokens: 16384, seed: 1234 }scoring:  verifier: math-final-answer@3.2.0  metric: pass@1                         # mean over 8 samples  report: [pass@1, pass@8, abstain_rate]harness: registry.example.com/evals/harness@sha256:41aa...cost_estimate: { gpu_hours_per_70b: 3.1 }
Going deeper2 points
  • Templates belong to the model family: the same suite runs with each model's own chat template; the definition references "the model's template", resolved and recorded at run time.
  • Deprecate, don't edit: when a suite saturates or has label errors, a new version replaces it; the old version stays runnable so historical results remain comparable.

Running evals at scale

Scenario. A release candidate needs 40 suites, each with several samples per question: about 2 million generations. Run naively, one suite at a time on one node, it takes three days.

What the picture shows. How the scheduler turns "evaluate this checkpoint" into fast, cheap work.

1Fan-out
each (checkpoint, suite) is split into shards of questions; shards run in parallel.
2Shared inference servers
shards send requests to vLLM servers for the checkpoint, sized to the work, instead of each shard loading the model itself.
3Generation cache
generations are cached by a key of (model weights hash, prompt, sampling settings, seed); re-scoring with a new verifier or re-running a dashboard doesn't regenerate.
4Priorities
release-candidate evals preempt routine checkpoint evals; both borrow idle GPUs from training queues at lower priority (Design 02).
5Retries and partial results
failed shards are retried; results stream in, so partial scores are visible early with their uncertainty.

The code. A shard worker: cached generation against a shared server, then scoring (Python).

import hashlib, json, asyncio, httpx def cache_key(weights_sha: str, prompt: str, sampling: dict, sample_idx: int) -> str:    raw = json.dumps([weights_sha, prompt, sampling, sample_idx], sort_keys=True)    return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()                     # same inputs → same key async def run_shard(questions, suite, model, cache, scorer, server_url, concurrency=64):    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=900) as client:        async def one(q, i):            key = cache_key(model["weights_sha"], q["prompt"], suite["sampling"], i)            text = cache.get(key)            if text is None:                async with sem:                    r = await client.post(f"{server_url}/v1/completions", json={                        "model": model["name"], "prompt": q["prompt"], "seed": suite["sampling"]["seed"] + i,                        **{k: v for k, v in suite["sampling"].items() if k not in ("samples", "seed")}})                    r.raise_for_status()                    text = r.json()["choices"][0]["text"]                cache.put(key, text)            res = scorer.verify(q, text)            return {"qid": q["id"], "sample": i, "score": res.score, "verdict": res.verdict, "cache_key": key}        jobs = [one(q, i) for q in questions for i in range(suite["sampling"]["samples"])]        return await asyncio.gather(*jobs)
Going deeper2 points
  • Determinism isn't guaranteed: batched inference can change outputs slightly even with fixed seeds. Store generations; recomputing is not the same as re-reading.
  • Cost per suite is tracked: GPU hours per suite per model size, so suites that cost more than they inform can be trimmed.

The results store and lineage

Scenario. A leadership slide quotes "71.4" for a model. Nobody can find which checkpoint, suite version or harness produced it.

What the picture shows. One store for all measurements, with the lineage that makes every number traceable.

1Granularity
evals per question and sample; inference benchmarks per request; training benchmarks per step; uptime per probe or per minute of SLI data.
2Lineage on every row
model or checkpoint ID and weights hash, suite or benchmark definition version, harness image digest, hardware type and count, software versions (driver, CUDA, framework), run ID.
3Columnar format
stored as partitioned Parquet (or a table format on top of it), so per-question analysis and dashboard aggregation read the same data.
4Derived tables
aggregates (scores with intervals, throughput curves, SLO compliance) computed from the raw rows by versioned jobs; dashboards read only derived tables.
5Immutability
rows are never edited; corrections are new rows with a new definition or scorer version.

The code. Writing eval rows with lineage as partitioned Parquet (Python, PyArrow).

import pyarrow as pa, pyarrow.parquet as pq SCHEMA = pa.schema([    ("run_id", pa.string()), ("checkpoint", pa.string()), ("weights_sha", pa.string()),    ("suite", pa.string()), ("suite_version", pa.int32()), ("harness_digest", pa.string()),    ("verifier", pa.string()), ("qid", pa.string()), ("cluster", pa.string()),    ("sample", pa.int16()), ("score", pa.float32()), ("verdict", pa.string()),    ("gen_cache_key", pa.string()), ("hardware", pa.string()), ("ts", pa.timestamp("s")),]) def write_results(rows: list[dict], root="s3://evals/results"):    table = pa.Table.from_pylist(rows, schema=SCHEMA)    pq.write_to_dataset(table, root_path=root,                        partition_cols=["suite", "suite_version", "checkpoint"])   # fast per-suite reads
Going deeper2 points
  • Every published number has a link: dashboards and reports render numbers with a link to the query that produced them.
  • Keep generations separately: generation text lives in object storage keyed by cache key; rows reference it, so the store stays small enough to query quickly.

Measuring model progress

Scenario. The team's flagship benchmark rose from 55% to 89% in a year. Half the remaining errors turn out to be label mistakes, and the top three models are within noise of each other. The benchmark no longer measures progress.

What the picture shows. Tracking progress over time, and checking that the evals can still measure it.

1Progress views
each family's score over checkpoints and releases, with intervals (Design 12); a capability index that combines families with stated weights, alongside the per-family scores.
2Held-out and public
private held-out suites (never trained on, rarely shown) next to public benchmarks; a gap that grows between them suggests contamination or overfitting to public benchmarks.
3Eval health
saturation (scores near the ceiling), discriminative power (can the suite separate models that differ?), label error rate (sampled human review of disagreements between strong models and labels), and contamination checks against training data.
4Suite lifecycle
new suites enter as experimental, become official once their health is measured, and retire when saturated.

The code. Eval health checks from the results store: saturation and how well a suite separates recent checkpoints (Python).

import numpy as np def suite_health(scores_by_model: dict[str, np.ndarray], ceiling=1.0):    """scores_by_model: model -> per-question mean scores on the same questions."""    models = sorted(scores_by_model, key=lambda m: scores_by_model[m].mean())    means = np.array([scores_by_model[m].mean() for m in models])    headroom = ceiling - means.max()                                   # saturation    separable = 0    for a, b in zip(models, models[1:]):                               # adjacent models        d = scores_by_model[b] - scores_by_model[a]        se = d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d))        separable += d.mean() > 2 * se    return {"best": round(means.max(), 3), "headroom": round(headroom, 3),            "adjacent_pairs_separated": f"{separable}/{len(models) - 1}"}   # low → retire or replace
Going deeper2 points
  • Saturation hides regressions too: near the ceiling, a real regression may look like noise; keep harder versions of saturated suites.
  • Label audits are cheap: reviewing the questions every strong model gets "wrong" finds most label errors with little effort.

Training throughput benchmarks

Scenario. After a routine driver upgrade, training throughput dropped 12%. It was found two weeks later, in a cost report, because the production run's slowdown was blamed on "the new data mix."

What the picture shows. Standard training benchmarks that make throughput comparable across time, hardware and software.

1Standard workloads
a small set of fixed training jobs (for example, a dense 8B and a MoE model at fixed parallelism and sequence length), run for a few hundred steps after warm-up.
2Metrics
tokens per second per GPU, model FLOPs utilization (MFU: achieved model FLOPs over hardware peak), step time and its breakdown (compute, communication, data loading), memory headroom.
3Matrix
each benchmark across hardware types and the software stack (driver, CUDA, NCCL, PyTorch, framework versions).
4Triggers
every software or image change to the training stack, every new hardware pool, and nightly on a reference pool.
5Production comparison
the production run's own throughput is compared with the benchmark on the same hardware and stack; a gap means the run (data, config) is the cause, not the platform.

The code. MFU from measured throughput for a dense transformer (Python).

def mfu(tokens_per_s_per_gpu: float, n_params: float, n_layers: int, seq_len: int, d_model: int,        peak_flops_per_gpu: float) -> float:    """Model FLOPs utilization: training FLOPs per token ≈ 6N + 12·L·s·d (attention), forward + backward."""    flops_per_token = 6 * n_params + 12 * n_layers * seq_len * d_model    return tokens_per_s_per_gpu * flops_per_token / peak_flops_per_gpu # 8B dense model, 8K sequence, BF16 dense peak ~989 TFLOP/s on H100 SXMprint(f"{mfu(4300, 8.0e9, 32, 8192, 4096, 989e12):.1%}")
Going deeper2 points
  • MFU and goodput answer different questions: MFU measures how efficiently a step runs; goodput (Design 14) measures how much of the reserved time produced steps. Report both.
  • Benchmark the RL loop too: for RL, also benchmark rollout throughput, weight-sync time and reward latency at fixed settings (Design 07).

Inference throughput and latency benchmarks

Scenario. The serving team reports 2,300 tokens per second per GPU. The capacity team measures 900. Both are right: one measured at maximum batch with no latency limit, the other at the product's latency target with real prompt lengths.

What the picture shows. Measuring inference performance as a curve, not a single number.

1Metrics
time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency or time per output token, end-to-end latency, requests and tokens per second, and their percentiles.
2Load sweep
run at increasing request rates; plot throughput against latency. Throughput only means something together with the latency at which it was measured.
3Throughput at the SLO
the headline number is the highest throughput at which p95 TTFT and p95 inter-token latency stay within the product's targets.
4Realistic traffic
prompt and output length distributions from production (or a replay), shared prefixes, multi-turn conversations; not uniform synthetic lengths.
5Same tool, same configs
a standard, model-server-agnostic load generator such as the Kubernetes community's Inference Perf (which supports vLLM, SGLang and other servers, and real or synthetic datasets) run from the same configs by every team.

The YAML. An Inference Perf load sweep against a serving deployment, run as a Kubernetes Job.

apiVersion: v1kind: ConfigMapmetadata: { name: perf-chat-70b, namespace: benchmarks }data:  config.yml: |    api: { type: chat, streaming: true }    data:      type: shareGPT                   # realistic conversation lengths; or a production replay    load:      type: constant      stages:                          # sweep request rates; 3 minutes each      - { rate: 5,  duration: 180 }      - { rate: 10, duration: 180 }      - { rate: 20, duration: 180 }      - { rate: 40, duration: 180 }    server:      type: vllm      model_name: assistant-70b-rc3      base_url: http://assistant-70b-rc3.serving.svc:8000    report:      request_lifecycle: { summary: true, per_stage: true, per_request: true }    storage:      google_cloud_storage: { bucket_name: perf-results, path: chat-70b/rc3 }---apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata: { name: perf-chat-70b-rc3, namespace: benchmarks }spec:  backoffLimit: 0  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: inference-perf        image: quay.io/inference-perf/inference-perf:latest   # pin by digest in practice        args: ["--config_file", "/cfg/config.yml"]        volumeMounts: [ { name: cfg, mountPath: /cfg } ]        resources: { limits: { cpu: "8", memory: 16Gi } }      volumes: [ { name: cfg, configMap: { name: perf-chat-70b } } ]
Going deeper2 points
  • The load generator can be the bottleneck: check its own CPU and network use; at high rates run several generator pods.
  • Benchmark the whole path: include the gateway and router in some runs (Design 03); the server alone and the full path give different, both useful, numbers.

Uptime and availability

Scenario. The platform reported 99.9% uptime for the month: every pod was running. Users experienced two outages: one where the gateway returned errors for 25 minutes while pods were healthy, and one where latency was ten times normal for an hour.

What the picture shows. Measuring uptime as users and training runs experience it.

1Serving SLIs
the fraction of requests that succeed and meet the latency target, measured at the gateway (real traffic) and by synthetic probes from outside the cluster (catches total outages with no traffic).
2SLOs and error budgets
for example, 99.5% of requests good over 30 days; the budget is the allowed bad fraction, and burn-rate alerts fire when it's being used up too fast.
3Training availability
goodput per run and the failure ledger (Design 14); "the cluster was up" isn't training uptime.
4Eval and benchmark availability
the measurement platform has its own SLO (results for a release candidate within N hours), since slow evals delay every decision.
5Reports from the same data
monthly uptime reports are computed from the SLI data, not from component health.

The YAML. Recording and alerting rules for a serving SLO with multi-window burn-rate alerts (Prometheus Operator).

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1kind: PrometheusRulemetadata: { name: chat-api-slo, namespace: monitoring }spec:  groups:  - name: chat-api-sli    rules:    - record: sli:chat_good_ratio:rate5m                   # good = success AND under latency target      expr: |        sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route="chat",code!~"5.."}[5m])            - rate(gateway_requests_slow_total{route="chat",threshold="ttft_2s"}[5m]))        / sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route="chat"}[5m]))    - record: sli:chat_good_ratio:rate1h      expr: |        sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route="chat",code!~"5.."}[1h])            - rate(gateway_requests_slow_total{route="chat",threshold="ttft_2s"}[1h]))        / sum(rate(gateway_requests_total{route="chat"}[1h]))  - name: chat-api-burn    rules:    - alert: ChatSLOFastBurn                                 # 99.5% SLO → budget 0.005      expr: |        (1 - sli:chat_good_ratio:rate5m) > (14.4 * 0.005)        and (1 - sli:chat_good_ratio:rate1h) > (14.4 * 0.005)   # burning 2% of budget per hour      for: 2m      labels: { severity: page }
Going deeper2 points
  • Synthetic probes catch silent outages: when the gateway is down, there may be no failed requests to count; an external probe every 30 seconds sees it.
  • Latency is part of availability: a 10× slower response is an outage for an interactive product; it counts against the SLO.

Regression detection and benchmark CI

Scenario. Every upgrade of vLLM, PyTorch or the GPU driver is "probably fine." Nobody runs the benchmarks before rollout because they take a day to set up.

What the picture shows. Benchmarks wired into change management.

1Triggers
a new model checkpoint (evals), a change to the serving or training image (performance benchmarks), a new hardware pool (both), and a nightly schedule (all, on reference hardware).
2Baselines
each benchmark compares with the rolling baseline for the same definition and hardware, using its known run-to-run variation.
3Gates
image changes can't roll out to production pools if a benchmark regresses beyond its threshold; model releases need the eval gate (Design 11).
4Trend detection
slow drifts (a 1% loss per week) are caught by change-point detection on the nightly series, not by single comparisons.
5Triage
a regression opens an issue with the diff between the two runs' lineage (what changed in model, image, driver, hardware).

The code. Comparing a new benchmark result with its rolling baseline using a robust threshold (Python).

import numpy as np def check_regression(history: list[float], new: float, higher_is_better=True,                     k: float = 4.0, min_rel: float = 0.02):    """history: recent results for the same benchmark + hardware + definition."""    h = np.asarray(history[-20:])    med = np.median(h)    mad = np.median(np.abs(h - med)) * 1.4826 + 1e-9                     # robust spread    delta = (new - med) if higher_is_better else (med - new)    regressed = delta < -max(k * mad, min_rel * abs(med))                # beyond noise AND material    return {"baseline": round(med, 2), "new": round(new, 2), "rel_change": round(delta / med, 4),            "regressed": bool(regressed)} print(check_regression([4310, 4295, 4322, 4301, 4318, 4290, 4307], 3790))   # driver upgrade: −12%
Going deeper2 points
  • Benchmarks need their own variance estimates: some are stable to 0.5%, others vary by 5% run to run; one threshold for all produces either noise or blindness.
  • Pin the benchmark itself: the benchmark harness and its configs are versioned; a change to the benchmark resets the baseline explicitly.

The platform on Kubernetes and reporting

Scenario. Measurements exist, but each audience reads a different spreadsheet. Leadership wants one page per week; on-call wants live SLOs; researchers want per-question drill-down.

What the picture shows. The components and the views built on them.

1Definition registry
eval suites, training and inference benchmarks, SLOs, all versioned with owners.
2Measurement scheduler
turns triggers into Kueue-managed jobs (sharded evals, benchmark jobs) on borrowed or reserved capacity; manages vLLM servers for evals and the generation cache.
3Collectors
Prometheus for SLIs and live metrics, benchmark tools writing raw results, eval shards writing per-question rows.
4Results store and derived tables
Parquet with lineage; versioned aggregation jobs.
5Views
a research view (per-question drill-down, comparisons with intervals), an infrastructure view (throughput matrices, regression history), an operations view (SLOs, error budgets, goodput) and a weekly report generated from derived tables.
Going deeper2 points
  • Generated reports, not hand-made ones: the weekly report is a template filled from derived tables, with each number linked to its query; hand-edited numbers are where disagreements start.
  • Measurement has a budget: evals and benchmarks get a fixed share of GPU capacity, and the platform reports what each suite and benchmark costs, so the budget is spent on what informs decisions.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, definitions and store: suite and benchmark registry, per-question and per-request results with lineage, one dashboard per audience reading derived tables.
  • Phase 2, scale: the sharded eval scheduler with shared inference servers, generation cache and priorities; release-candidate evals within hours.
  • Phase 3, performance and uptime: standard training and inference benchmarks with hardware and software matrices; serving SLIs, synthetic probes, SLOs and burn-rate alerts.
  • Phase 4, CI and health: benchmark gates on image and model changes, change-point detection on nightly series, eval health and suite lifecycle.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Versioned definitions slow down quick changes: a new prompt template means a new suite version and a new baseline, in exchange for numbers that mean the same thing everywhere.
  • Benchmark CI delays upgrades by hours, in exchange for not discovering a 12% slowdown in a cost report.
  • User-side uptime looks worse than component uptime, and is the number that matches what users experience.
  • Measurement capacity is reserved, so some GPUs aren't training; the measurement SLO justifies it.

Open questions.

  • Cheaper evals: how small can a suite be (via question selection) while keeping its ranking of models?
  • Evaluating agents: long, stateful agent evals need environments and much more compute per question (Design 08); how should they be scheduled and cached?
  • Comparable performance across generations: how to compare throughput across very different model architectures and hardware fairly?
  • Production signals as evals: which production metrics (user ratings, retries, abandonment) are reliable enough to sit beside offline evals in progress views?
Design 16 · 12 sections

Design 16: Data collection and feedback pipelines: from human signal to reward models to training

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. The feedback loop
  3. Kinds of human signal
  4. What to ask: active sampling
  5. Campaigns: task design and guidelines
  6. Rater quality and label quality
  7. Production feedback
  8. Training reward models
  9. Evaluating and calibrating reward models
  10. Using the signal in training, without over-optimizing
  11. Governance and the platform on Kubernetes
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build the data collection and feedback pipelines that close the loop between human signal, reward modeling and training, so that what people prefer reliably turns into better models, week after week? Design 10 covers rewards that can be checked automatically; this design covers the rewards that come from people: preference comparisons, ratings, edits and production feedback, and the reward models trained on them. It connects to Design 06 (how preferences and reward models are used in training), Design 11 (mixtures and gates) and Design 15 (measurement).

The short version: treat human signal as the scarcest and most expensive data in the system, and spend it where the model is most uncertain. Collection is organized as campaigns with versioned task definitions, guidelines and quality controls. Every label carries its rater, guideline version and quality scores, so bad labels can be found and re-weighted later. Active sampling chooses what to ask people: comparisons where the reward model is unsure, new domains and the current policy's own outputs. Reward models are trained, evaluated and calibrated against fresh human labels before use, and monitored for over-optimization during training. Production feedback flows back with consent, privacy filtering and bias correction. And the whole loop runs on a fixed cadence, so each model generation is trained on feedback about the previous one.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The team collects 40,000 preference comparisons a month from a vendor. Six months in: inter-rater agreement is 63% and nobody knows which raters are reliable; half the comparisons are between two answers from last year's model; the reward model prefers longer answers by a wide margin; RL against it improved the reward model's score by 30% while human win rate barely moved; and millions of thumbs-up and thumbs-down events from the product sit unused because nobody is sure they can be used.

What the platform must do.

  • Collect the right signal: decide which kinds of human feedback to collect for which goals, and what to ask about.
  • Control quality: measure rater reliability and label quality continuously, and use that in training.
  • Spend the budget well: direct labeling effort to the comparisons that improve the reward model most.
  • Build trustworthy reward models: trained on versioned data, evaluated on fresh human labels, calibrated, and checked for known biases.
  • Use production signal responsibly: with consent, privacy protection and correction for the biases of implicit feedback.
  • Close the loop on a cadence: each training round uses feedback on the current model, not the model from months ago.

Out of scope: automatic verifiers (Design 10) and the RL algorithms that consume rewards (Designs 06–09).

The feedback loop

Scenario. The data team, the reward-model team and the training team each run their part on their own schedule. A training run in May used a reward model trained in February on comparisons collected in December, about a model that no longer existed.

What the picture shows. The loop from human signal to a deployed model and back, and the latency of each step.

1Sample
choose prompts and pairs of responses from the current policy (and candidates) to show people.
2Collect
raters compare, rate or edit, following versioned guidelines; production users give explicit and implicit feedback.
3Curate
quality control, de-duplication, privacy filtering, and assembly into versioned preference datasets.
4Model
train and evaluate reward models; for some uses, the preferences go directly into DPO-style training.
5Train
RL against the reward model or preference optimization; gates before release (Design 11).
6Deploy and observe
production feedback and evals on the new model feed the next round.
7Cadence
a fixed cycle (for example, two weeks) with explicit freshness targets: most comparisons used in a round are about the current model.
Going deeper2 points
  • Staleness matters for human data too: comparisons between two outputs from an old model teach the reward model about mistakes the current model no longer makes (Design 09 for the same idea in RL data).
  • Each step has an owner and a latency target: the loop is only as fast as its slowest step, usually collection or reward-model evaluation.

Kinds of human signal

Scenario. The team asks raters for 1–7 quality ratings because they're quick. The ratings drift from week to week, and two raters' "5" mean different things. Pairwise comparisons of the same responses are far more consistent.

What the picture shows. The main kinds of human signal, what each is good for and what it costs.

1Pairwise preferences
"which response is better?", optionally with a strength and a reason. Consistent across raters; the standard input for reward models and DPO.
2Rubric ratings
yes/no or graded answers to specific criteria (correct, follows instructions, safe, concise). More informative than one overall score; good for diagnosing which property differs.
3Edits and corrections
a rater rewrites a response to be good. Expensive, but yields high-quality demonstrations and a natural preference pair (edited over original).
4Demonstrations
experts write the response from scratch. The most expensive; used for new capabilities and SFT.
5Production signal
thumbs up or down, regenerations, copies, edits, abandoned conversations. Cheap and plentiful; noisy, biased and subject to consent and privacy rules.

The signals at a glance.

Signal Cost per item Consistency Best for Main risk
Pairwise preference Low High Reward models, DPO Ties and weak preferences
Rubric ratings Medium Medium–high Diagnosis, multi-objective rewards Rubric drift
Edits High High Demonstrations + pairs Rater style imprinting
Demonstrations Highest Varies New capabilities, SFT Cost, rater skill
Production feedback Very low Low Coverage, real usage Bias, privacy, consent
Going deeper2 points
  • Collect reasons with preferences: a short reason or rubric tags on each comparison make the reward model debuggable and let you build per-property reward models later.
  • Match signal to expertise: coding and medical comparisons need domain experts; general helpfulness can use broader pools. Route tasks by required skill.

What to ask: active sampling

Scenario. Most of the monthly budget goes to comparisons where the reward model is already 95% confident and right. They add almost nothing. Meanwhile the reward model has never seen comparisons from the new agentic tool-use feature.

What the picture shows. Strategies for choosing which prompts and pairs go to human raters.

1Uncertainty
pairs where an ensemble of reward models disagrees, or where the predicted preference is near 50%.
2On-policy pairs
responses from the current policy (and from candidate checkpoints), so labels describe the mistakes the model makes now.
3Coverage
quotas per domain, language and feature, including new features with no data yet.
4Disagreement with other signals
pairs where the reward model disagrees with verifiers, judges or production feedback.
5Random slice
a fixed share sampled uniformly, to measure the reward model's accuracy without selection bias.
6Budget split
the mix of these strategies is a configuration of the campaign, reviewed each round.

The code. Selecting comparisons by reward-model ensemble disagreement, with per-domain quotas and a random slice (Python).

import numpy as np def pref_prob(rm, prompt, a, b) -> float:    """P(a preferred over b) under a Bradley–Terry reward model."""    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(rm.score(prompt, a) - rm.score(prompt, b)))) def select_pairs(candidates, ensemble, quotas: dict, random_share=0.15, seed=0):    """candidates: dicts with domain, prompt, a, b. Returns pairs to send to raters."""    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)    scored = []    for c in candidates:        p = np.array([pref_prob(rm, c["prompt"], c["a"], c["b"]) for rm in ensemble])        uncertainty = p.std() + (0.5 - abs(p.mean() - 0.5))       # disagreement + closeness to 50%        scored.append((uncertainty, c))    chosen = []    for domain, n in quotas.items():        pool = [x for x in scored if x[1]["domain"] == domain]        n_rand = int(n * random_share)        top = sorted(pool, key=lambda x: -x[0])[: n - n_rand]        rest = [x for x in pool if x not in top]        rand = [rest[i] for i in rng.choice(len(rest), size=min(n_rand, len(rest)), replace=False)]        chosen += [dict(c, selection="uncertainty") for _, c in top]        chosen += [dict(c, selection="random") for _, c in rand]           # unbiased accuracy estimate    return chosen
Going deeper2 points
  • Record why each pair was selected: the selection strategy is a column; reward-model accuracy is reported on the random slice, since uncertainty-selected pairs are hard by construction.
  • Don't over-mine hard pairs: many ambiguous pairs are ambiguous for people too; low agreement on a slice means the guideline, not the model, needs work.

Campaigns: task design and guidelines

Scenario. A vendor batch came back with 71% of comparisons marked "tie". The guideline said to mark a tie "when both answers are acceptable." Almost everything was acceptable.

What the picture shows. What a collection campaign defines before any rater sees a task.

1Task type and UI
side-by-side comparison with randomized order, rubric questions, optional edit box, and a required short reason.
2Guidelines
versioned, with worked examples and explicit rules for hard cases (both wrong, both fine but different, partially correct, unsafe content).
3Scale design
preference strength (for example, "much better / better / slightly better / tie") with ties discouraged and defined narrowly.
4Rater pool and routing
required expertise, languages and qualifications per task.
5Quality controls
gold questions, overlap for agreement, time limits and attention checks.
6Volume, deadline and budget,
and the sampling configuration from the previous section.

The YAML. A campaign definition, versioned like a suite or a recipe.

# campaigns/2026-11-coding-agent/campaign.yamlcampaign: coding-agent-prefs-2026-11owner: team-feedbacktask:  type: pairwise  ui: side_by_side  randomize_order: true                       # position bias control  scale: [much_better, better, slightly_better, tie]  tie_rule: "only when neither response is better on any rubric item"  rubric: [correct, follows_instructions, safe, concise, tool_use_appropriate]  require_reason: trueguidelines: guidelines/coding-agent@v4raters:  pool: experts-software  qualifications: [python-senior, guideline-coding@v4-quiz]sampling:  source: policies/assistant-v14-rc2 + policies/assistant-v14-rc3  strategy: { uncertainty: 0.6, coverage: 0.25, random: 0.15 }  quotas: { python: 3000, typescript: 1500, sql: 800, tool_use: 1700 }quality:  gold_rate: 0.05                             # 5% hidden gold comparisons  overlap: { rate: 0.15, raters_per_item: 3 } # for agreement  min_seconds_per_item: 45budget: { items: 7000, max_cost_usd: 84000, deadline: 2026-11-28 }
Going deeper2 points
  • Pilot every campaign: a few hundred items with internal experts first; measure agreement and tie rate, and fix the guideline before scaling.
  • Guidelines change labels: a guideline version is part of each label's lineage; mixing labels from different versions is a decision, not an accident.

Rater quality and label quality

Scenario. Agreement across all raters is 63%. When computed per rater, most agree with each other at about 75%, and four raters agree with nobody, at chance level. They had been labeling 18% of the data.

What the picture shows. Measuring and using label quality at the level of individual raters and items.

1Gold questions
comparisons with expert-agreed answers, mixed in without marking; accuracy per rater over time.
2Agreement
overlap items labeled by several raters; agreement per rater with the majority, and per slice.
3Behavior signals
time per item, position preference (always picking the left response), tie rate, reason length.
4Rater reliability weights
estimated from gold accuracy and agreement (or a latent-class model such as Dawid–Skene) and stored on each label.
5Actions
retrain or remove unreliable raters; down-weight or relabel their past items; route hard slices to experts.

The code. Per-rater gold accuracy, agreement with the majority and position bias (Python, pandas).

import pandas as pd def rater_report(labels: pd.DataFrame, gold: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:    """labels: item_id, rater, choice ('A'|'B'|'tie'), shown_left ('A'|'B'). gold: item_id, answer."""    g = labels.merge(gold, on="item_id")    gold_acc = (g.choice == g.answer).groupby(g.rater).mean().rename("gold_acc")    majority = labels.groupby("item_id").choice.agg(lambda s: s.mode().iat[0]).rename("majority")    m = labels.join(majority, on="item_id")    multi = m.groupby("item_id").rater.transform("count") >= 3    agree = (m[multi].choice == m[multi].majority).groupby(m[multi].rater).mean().rename("agree_majority")    left = (labels.choice == labels.shown_left).groupby(labels.rater).mean().rename("picks_left")    ties = (labels.choice == "tie").groupby(labels.rater).mean().rename("tie_rate")    rep = pd.concat([gold_acc, agree, left, ties], axis=1)    rep["weight"] = (rep.gold_acc.fillna(0.5) - 0.5).clip(lower=0) * 2      # 0 at chance, 1 at perfect    return rep.sort_values("weight")
Going deeper2 points
  • Low agreement is information: if experts disagree on a slice, the preference may be genuinely subjective; consider modeling it as such (or splitting by user need) rather than forcing a single label.
  • Use weights in training: the reward model's loss weights each comparison by rater reliability and preference strength, instead of dropping data with a hard threshold.

Production feedback

Scenario. The product records millions of thumbs-up and thumbs-down events, regenerations and edits each week. The data has never been used: nobody knows which users consented, the text contains personal data, and thumbs-down mostly come from a few heavy users.

What the picture shows. Turning product events into training signal safely.

1Consent first
only conversations from users and organizations whose settings allow training use are eligible; the consent state at the time of the conversation is recorded with each event.
2Privacy filtering
PII detection and removal, removal of secrets and credentials, exclusion of sensitive categories, and aggregation or minimum-count rules before anything is shown to raters.
3Signal extraction
explicit (thumbs, ratings, written feedback) and implicit (regenerate, edit, copy, abandon); each mapped to a weak preference with a known reliability.
4Bias correction
feedback comes from a skewed subset of users and situations; reweight by user and topic, cap each user's influence, and never treat absence of feedback as approval.
5Join with model lineage
each event carries the model version, system prompt and features active at the time.
6Use mainly for selection
production signal is best used to decide what to send to raters (which conversations went wrong) and as a weak auxiliary signal, not as ground truth.

The code. A production feedback event filtered for consent and privacy before entering the pipeline (Python).

import refrom dataclasses import dataclass EMAIL = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+")SECRET = re.compile(r"(?i)(api[_-]?key|token|password)\s*[:=]\s*\S+") @dataclassclass FeedbackEvent:    conversation_id: str    user_id_hash: str    org_training_opt_in: bool          # consent state at the time of the conversation    model_version: str    signal: str                        # thumbs_up | thumbs_down | regenerate | edit | abandon    prompt: str    response: str def admit(ev: FeedbackEvent, pii_detector, per_user_count: dict, cap_per_user=20):    if not ev.org_training_opt_in:        return None                                         # never enters the pipeline    if per_user_count.get(ev.user_id_hash, 0) >= cap_per_user:        return None                                         # limit any one user's influence    text = "\n".join([ev.prompt, ev.response])    if pii_detector.has_sensitive(text):        return None                                         # sensitive categories excluded    clean = SECRET.sub("[REDACTED]", EMAIL.sub("[EMAIL]", text))    per_user_count[ev.user_id_hash] = per_user_count.get(ev.user_id_hash, 0) + 1    return {"conversation_id": ev.conversation_id, "model_version": ev.model_version,            "signal": ev.signal, "text": clean, "weak_label_reliability": {"thumbs_down": 0.6,            "thumbs_up": 0.55, "regenerate": 0.65, "edit": 0.7, "abandon": 0.52}[ev.signal]}
Going deeper2 points
  • Privacy review is a gate, not a step: the privacy and legal owners approve each new use of production data, and the pipeline enforces their rules in code.
  • Implicit signals are confounded: a regeneration may mean a bad answer or curiosity; measure each signal's agreement with rater judgments before giving it weight.

Training reward models

Scenario. The reward model is retrained "when someone has time," on whatever comparisons are in the bucket, with no record of which data or which raters went into which version.

What the picture shows. A reward model as a versioned artifact with explicit data and objectives.

1Data
a versioned preference dataset: chosen and rejected responses, preference strength, rater weights, selection strategy and guideline version.
2Objective
the Bradley–Terry loss on score differences, with an optional margin from preference strength and a small term that keeps rewards centered near zero.
3Base model
usually initialized from a recent policy checkpoint of similar or larger size, so the reward model understands what the policy writes.
4Ensembles
several reward models (different seeds or data subsets) give uncertainty estimates for active sampling and for detecting over-optimization.
5Per-property models
when rubric data exists, separate reward heads for correctness, safety and style can be combined with explicit weights.

The code. Training a reward model with TRL's RewardTrainer on a preference dataset with margins from preference strength (Python).

from datasets import load_datasetfrom trl import RewardConfig, RewardTrainer STRENGTH_MARGIN = {"much_better": 1.0, "better": 0.5, "slightly_better": 0.2} prefs = load_dataset("parquet", data_files="s3://feedback/prefs/assistant-v14/v7/*.parquet")["train"]prefs = prefs.filter(lambda r: r["choice"] != "tie" and r["rater_weight"] > 0.2)prefs = prefs.map(lambda r: {"margin": STRENGTH_MARGIN[r["strength"]] * r["rater_weight"]})prefs = prefs.select_columns(["chosen", "rejected", "margin"])   # conversational chosen/rejected trainer = RewardTrainer(    model="registry/assistant-v14-sft",                  # start from a recent policy checkpoint    train_dataset=prefs,    args=RewardConfig(        output_dir="/checkpoints/rm/assistant-v14-rm-v7",        max_length=8192,        center_rewards_coefficient=0.01,                 # keep rewards centered near zero        learning_rate=1e-6,        num_train_epochs=1,                              # one pass: reward models overfit fast        per_device_train_batch_size=8,        bf16=True,    ),)trainer.train()
Going deeper2 points
  • One epoch is usually enough: reward models overfit preference data quickly; more data beats more epochs.
  • Version everything together: reward model version = base checkpoint + dataset version + training config; the RL recipe pins it (Design 06).

Evaluating and calibrating reward models

Scenario. The new reward model has 78% accuracy on its validation split. In RL it pushes answers to be 40% longer, and people prefer the RL model less than before. The validation split shared the length bias of the training data.

What the picture shows. What a reward model must pass before it's used in training.

1Accuracy on fresh, random-slice human labels
per domain and language, on the current policy's outputs, not only on a split of the training data.
2Calibration
when the model says 80% preference, people agree about 80% of the time; checked with reliability curves.
3Bias probes
length (does adding padding raise the score?), sycophancy (does agreeing with the user raise it?), formatting, position, confident tone; each measured with controlled pairs.
4Agreement with other signals
verifiers where available, LLM judges and production feedback, per slice.
5Best-of-n check
pick the best of n samples with the reward model and have people compare with random samples; a reward model that doesn't improve best-of-n for people isn't ready for RL.
6Release gate
thresholds on all of the above, tied to the model version.

The code. A length-bias probe: does padding a response with neutral text raise its reward? (Python).

import numpy as np FILLER = (" To summarize, the key points above address the question."          " Let me know if you need further detail.") def length_bias(rm, items, n_fill=(1, 2, 4)):    """items: (prompt, response). Score change when neutral filler is appended."""    out = {}    for k in n_fill:        deltas = [rm.score(p, r + FILLER * k) - rm.score(p, r) for p, r in items]        out[f"+{k}x filler"] = float(np.mean(deltas))    return out                                    # should be ≈ 0 or negative; positive → length bias
Going deeper2 points
  • Bias probes become training data: controlled pairs where the padded or sycophantic response is worse can be added to the preference data to teach the reward model the right direction.
  • Re-evaluate on the RL policy's outputs: a reward model accurate on the starting policy's outputs can be inaccurate on outputs from later in RL; evaluate on fresh samples during the run.

Using the signal in training, without over-optimizing

Scenario. RL against the reward model raised its score by 30%. Human evaluation found only a small win. Pushing further made people prefer the model less.

What the picture shows. The ways preference data reaches the model, and how to stop before over-optimization.

1RL against a reward model
flexible and strong; the reward model is a proxy, and optimizing it too hard hurts the true objective. A well-known study of reward model over-optimization found that the true (gold) score first rises and then falls as optimization against a proxy reward model increases.
2Direct preference optimization
DPO-style training on the preference pairs themselves; no separate reward model, less exposed to reward hacking, but offline (pairs not from the current policy) unless refreshed every round.
3Best-of-n and rejection sampling
pick high-reward samples and train on them; simple and robust, with its own over-optimization at large n.
4Controls
a KL penalty or trust region to the starting policy, early stopping on human or held-out-judge win rate (not reward-model score), reward-model ensembles (optimize a conservative combination such as the mean minus the spread), and reward models refreshed with on-policy labels each round.

The code. A conservative reward from a reward-model ensemble for RL (Python).

import numpy as np def conservative_reward(ensemble, prompt, response, k: float = 1.0) -> float:    """Mean minus k × std across reward models: uncertain regions get less reward."""    s = np.array([rm.score(prompt, response) for rm in ensemble])    return float(s.mean() - k * s.std())          # discourages exploiting one model's quirks
Going deeper2 points
  • The stopping rule uses people: a small, fresh human win-rate evaluation every few hundred steps decides when to stop, because the reward model can't tell you when it's being over-optimized.
  • Mix in verifiable rewards: where tasks are checkable, verifiers (Design 10) anchor the policy; preference rewards cover what they can't.

Governance and the platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. A legal request asks which training runs used conversations from a particular customer. Answering takes three weeks of manual searching.

What the picture shows. The components that run the loop, and the lineage that makes it auditable.

1Sampling service
generates candidate pairs from current policies and selects them with the campaign's strategy.
2Annotation platform
internal or vendor tools behind one API: tasks out, labels back, with rater IDs, timings and guideline versions.
3Quality service
gold scoring, agreement and rater weights; flags for relabeling.
4Feedback ingestion
production events filtered for consent and privacy.
5Preference datasets
versioned, immutable snapshots with lineage to every source item (campaign, rater, conversation, consent state).
6Reward model training and evaluation
Kueue-managed jobs; the evaluation gate before any RL recipe can pin a reward model.
7Retention and deletion
source data expires per policy, and deletion requests propagate to datasets (and are recorded for models trained on them).

The YAML. The loop's recurring part as an Argo CronWorkflow: every two weeks, sample from the current policy, create the campaign, then retrain and evaluate the reward model when labels arrive.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1kind: CronWorkflowmetadata:  name: feedback-loop  namespace: feedbackspec:  schedule: "17 6 * * 1"                     # Mondays; the template skips odd weeks  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid  workflowSpec:    entrypoint: loop    templates:    - name: loop      steps:      - - name: sample          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "sample --policy=current --campaign=next" } ] }      - - name: launch-campaign          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "campaign launch --from=sampled --wait-labels=10d" } ] }      - - name: quality          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "quality score --campaign=latest --reweight" } ] }      - - name: dataset          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "dataset snapshot --consent-check --pii-check" } ] }      - - name: train-rm          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "rm train --dataset=latest --ensemble=4" } ] }      - - name: eval-rm          template: run          arguments: { parameters: [ { name: cmd, value: "rm eval --gate=gates/rm-release.yaml" } ] }    - name: run      inputs: { parameters: [ { name: cmd } ] }      container:        image: registry.example.com/feedback/pipeline:2026.11        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]        args: ["feedbackctl {{inputs.parameters.cmd}}"]
Going deeper2 points
  • Lineage answers legal questions in minutes: every preference row points to its sources and consent state; every reward model and training run points to its datasets.
  • Rater welfare and fairness are part of the platform: clear guidelines, reasonable task times, and review of content that may be disturbing, with opt-outs and support.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, lineage and quality: campaign definitions, label lineage (rater, guideline, selection), gold questions and agreement, rater weights.
  • Phase 2, on-policy loop: sampling from the current policy, active selection with a random slice, a fixed cadence.
  • Phase 3, reward model discipline: versioned reward models, the evaluation gate (fresh labels, calibration, bias probes, best-of-n), ensembles and over-optimization stopping rules.
  • Phase 4, production signal: consent and privacy filtering, bias correction, production feedback for selection and as weak signal.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • On-policy collection costs more than reusing old comparisons, in exchange for labels about the mistakes the model makes now.
  • Gold and overlap items use budget (often 15–20% of items), in exchange for knowing label quality.
  • Strict consent and privacy rules leave production data unused, in exchange for trust and compliance.
  • Human stopping rules slow RL with periodic evaluations, in exchange for not over-optimizing a proxy.

Open questions.

  • AI feedback at scale: where can model-generated preferences (judges, constitutions) replace human labels, and how is their quality checked against people?
  • Pluralistic preferences: when people genuinely disagree, should reward models predict a distribution or condition on the user?
  • Long, agentic tasks: how do people give feedback on 100-step agent trajectories (Design 08) without reading all of them?
  • Feedback value: can we estimate, before collecting, how much a batch of labels will improve the trained model?
Design 17 · 12 sections

Design 17: Scheduling that keeps accelerators busy

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Where GPU-hours go
  3. Two layers: admission and placement
  4. Gang scheduling: all or nothing
  5. Topology-aware gang placement
  6. Bin-packing to reduce fragmentation
  7. Defragmentation and right-sizing
  8. Quotas: nominal, borrowing and lending
  9. Fair share: weighted shares and fairness over time
  10. Priority, preemption and backfill
  11. Measuring and tuning the scheduler
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we schedule a shared GPU fleet so that accelerators stay busy: distributed jobs start all at once or not at all (gang scheduling), small jobs don't fragment nodes that big jobs need (bin-packing), and many teams share the fleet fairly (quotas and fair share)? Design 02 covers the multi-cluster picture (which cluster a job goes to); this design goes inside one cluster, into the mechanics of admission, placement, preemption and measurement. For how kube-scheduler filters and scores nodes, see the scheduler deep dive; this design builds on it.

The short version: separate "when may this job start" from "where do its pods go", and measure where every GPU-hour went. Kueue decides admission: a job is admitted only when its whole gang fits its quota and, with topology-aware scheduling, the physical topology. kube-scheduler places pods with a bin-packing profile on GPU nodes, so partially used nodes fill up first and whole nodes stay free for big gangs. Teams get nominal quotas in cohorts with borrowing, lending limits and fair-share preemption; priorities and backfill keep idle quota working. And a GPU-hour accounting breaks idle time into causes (fragmented, reserved-but-idle, waiting for a gang, preempted work) so each one can be attacked.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A 1,024-GPU cluster (128 nodes × 8 H100) serves six teams. Finance reports 58% of GPU-hours doing useful work. A 256-GPU training job has waited three days; meanwhile 180 GPUs are free, scattered as 1–3 GPUs per node across 90 nodes. Last week two 64-GPU jobs (one GPU per pod) each got 40 of their pods running and then waited for each other for six hours, holding 80 GPUs idle. One team runs notebooks on 96 GPUs that are busy 8% of the time, and another team says the queue is unfair because "the same team always gets the GPUs."

What the platform must do.

  • Start distributed jobs atomically: all pods of a gang start together, or none hold resources.
  • Keep large jobs placeable: small jobs mustn't scatter across nodes that a large job needs whole.
  • Guarantee each team a share: a nominal quota that's available when the team needs it.
  • Lend idle capacity: unused quota works for others, and is reclaimed quickly when its owner returns.
  • Be fair over time: teams that used less recently get priority for borrowed capacity.
  • Explain idle time: every idle GPU-hour attributed to a cause.

Out of scope: which cluster a job runs in (Design 02), node health (Design 14), and GPU sharing inside one device beyond its role in bin-packing.

Where GPU-hours go

Scenario. "58% utilization" is the only number anybody has. It doesn't say whether to buy GPUs, fix the scheduler or talk to the notebook team.

What the picture shows. A breakdown of all GPU-hours in a period into categories with different fixes.

1Busy
allocated and doing useful work (measured by GPU activity, not just allocation).
2Allocated but idle
pods holding GPUs while idle: notebooks, jobs stuck in data loading, services sized for peak. Fix: idle culling, right-sizing, sharing smaller slices.
3Waiting for a gang
GPUs held by some pods of a job whose other pods can't start. Fix: all-or-nothing admission.
4Fragmented
free GPUs that no pending job can use because they're scattered. Fix: bin-packing and defragmentation.
5Free and unusable by policy
quota reserved for a team that isn't using it, not lent. Fix: borrowing and lending limits.
6Lost to preemption
work computed then discarded when a job was preempted before its next checkpoint. Fix: checkpoint-aware preemption.
7Truly free
nothing pending could use it. Fix: more demand, or fewer GPUs.

The code. Classifying each GPU-minute from scheduler and DCGM data (Python sketch).

from collections import Counter def classify(gpu_minute, pending_jobs, quota_state):    """gpu_minute: dict with allocated, util (0..1, DCGM), job_state, node_free_gpus, owner_queue."""    if gpu_minute["allocated"]:        if gpu_minute["job_state"] == "waiting_for_gang":            return "waiting_for_gang"                          # some pods up, others pending        if gpu_minute["util"] < 0.05:            return "allocated_idle"        if gpu_minute.get("discarded_by_preemption"):            return "lost_to_preemption"        return "busy"    fits = [j for j in pending_jobs if j["gpus_per_pod"] <= gpu_minute["node_free_gpus"]]    if pending_jobs and not fits:        return "fragmented"                                    # free, but no pending pod fits here    if fits and not quota_state.can_admit_any(fits):        return "blocked_by_quota_policy"    return "free" def breakdown(minutes, pending_at, quota_at):    c = Counter(classify(m, pending_at(m["t"]), quota_at(m["t"])) for m in minutes)    total = sum(c.values())    return {k: round(v / total, 3) for k, v in c.most_common()}
Going deeper2 points
  • Allocation is not utilization: a GPU can be allocated and idle; DCGM activity metrics (SM activity, tensor activity) say whether it's working.
  • Report the breakdown per team and per queue: the fix for "allocated but idle" is a conversation with a team; the fix for "fragmented" is a scheduler change.

Two layers: admission and placement

Scenario. When a job is pending, users look at pod events from kube-scheduler and see "0/128 nodes are available." The real reason is that the job's queue is out of quota, which kube-scheduler doesn't know about.

What the picture shows. Who decides what, from job submission to running pods.

1Admission (Kueue)
a job is created suspended and becomes a Workload in a LocalQueue. Kueue admits it when its whole request fits the ClusterQueue's quota (possibly by borrowing), in priority and fairness order, and optionally when it fits the physical topology. Admission is all-or-nothing for the whole job.
2Placement (kube-scheduler)
once admitted, pods are created and the scheduler filters and scores nodes for each pod (scheduler deep dive). Profiles decide scoring: bin-packing for GPU pools.
3Devices (device plugin or DRA)
the node assigns specific GPUs (or slices) to the container.
4One status per layer
"pending admission: queue over quota" and "admitted, pods unschedulable" are different problems with different owners.
Going deeper2 points
  • Kueue doesn't replace kube-scheduler: Kueue decides when a workload starts and against which quota; kube-scheduler still decides which node each pod lands on. Topology-aware scheduling is the point where Kueue also looks at nodes, so that what it admits can actually be placed together.
  • Upstream is moving toward workload-aware scheduling: kube-scheduler is gaining native awareness of pod groups; the admission/placement split in this design stays valid as that matures.

Gang scheduling: all or nothing

Scenario. Two 64-GPU jobs were created at the same time. The scheduler placed pods from both as GPUs freed up: 40 pods of each ran, and neither could start training without all 64. Both held 40 GPUs idle for six hours.

What the picture shows. Why per-pod scheduling deadlocks distributed jobs, and the two mechanisms that prevent it.

1The deadlock
distributed training can't make progress with some of its workers; per-pod scheduling lets two jobs each take part of the free capacity and wait forever.
2Quota-level all-or-nothing
Kueue admits a workload only if its full request fits the quota, so two jobs can't both be admitted into capacity that only fits one.
3Physical fit (topology-aware scheduling)
quota fit doesn't guarantee node fit; TAS checks that the pods can actually be placed (and placed close together) before admitting.
4Ready-pods timeout (waitForPodsReady)
after admission, if all pods aren't ready within a timeout, the workload is evicted, its pods deleted, and it's requeued with backoff. A recovery timeout handles pods that fail later.
5Workload types that know their gang
JobSet, LeaderWorkerSet, RayJob and PyTorchJob present all their pods as one workload with PodSets.

The YAML. Kueue configuration for ready-pods gang semantics and fair sharing (Configuration v1beta2).

apiVersion: config.kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: Configurationnamespace: kueue-systemwaitForPodsReady:  timeout: 10m                         # all pods ready within 10 min of admission, or requeue  recoveryTimeout: 5m                  # a pod failing later must recover within 5 min  blockAdmission: false                # TAS handles physical fit; don't serialize admissions  requeuingStrategy:    timestamp: Eviction    backoffBaseSeconds: 60    backoffMaxSeconds: 1800    backoffLimitCount: 10              # then the workload is deactivated for a human to look atfairSharing:  preemptionStrategies: [LessThanOrEqualToFinalShare, LessThanInitialShare]
Going deeper2 points
  • Choose the timeout from data: it must cover image pulls and model loading for large jobs; measure time-to-all-ready per job size and set the timeout above its 99th percentile.
  • blockAdmission trades throughput for safety: serializing admissions avoids deadlocks without TAS, but leaves capacity idle while each job starts; with TAS checking physical fit, it's usually unnecessary.

Topology-aware gang placement

Scenario. A 64-GPU job is admitted and placed across three network blocks; its all-reduce runs 30% slower than the same job in one block. A gang that fits but is spread out wastes accelerators too.

What the picture shows. Placing a gang within the smallest network domain that fits it.

1Topology levels
zone → block → rack → host, from node labels set by the cloud provider or a topology discovery tool.
2Required vs preferred
podset-required-topology waits until one domain can hold the whole PodSet; podset-preferred-topology tries the domain and falls back to wider ones.
3Slices
for very large jobs, split the PodSet into slices (for example, 16 pods each) that must each fit one rack, without requiring the whole job in one block.
4Groups
co-locate several PodSets of one workload (leader and workers of an inference server) in the same domain.
5Interaction with bin-packing
keeping whole racks and blocks free (next section) is what makes required topology placement possible without long waits.

The YAML. A Topology, a ResourceFlavor that uses it, and a JobSet requiring one block with racks of 16 pods.

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: Topologymetadata: { name: gpu-fabric }spec:  levels:  - nodeLabel: network.example.com/block  - nodeLabel: network.example.com/rack  - nodeLabel: kubernetes.io/hostname---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ResourceFlavormetadata: { name: h100-fabric }spec:  nodeLabels: { gpu.example.com/class: h100 }  topologyName: gpu-fabric                       # enables TAS for this flavor---apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: JobSetmetadata:  name: pretrain-ft-64  labels: { kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: llm-team }spec:  replicatedJobs:  - name: workers    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        parallelism: 8        completions: 8        completionMode: Indexed        template:          metadata:            annotations:              kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-required-topology: network.example.com/block      # whole job, one block              kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-slice-required-topology: network.example.com/rack              kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-slice-size: "4"                                  # 4 pods (32 GPUs) per rack          spec:            containers:            - name: trainer              image: registry.example.com/train:2026.11              resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Topology labels must be accurate: a wrong block label puts a "same block" job across the fabric. Validate labels against measured bandwidth during node burn-in (Design 14).
  • Required topology can wait forever: set a policy for how long a job may wait for its domain before it's offered a preferred (wider) placement, if its owner allows it.

Bin-packing to reduce fragmentation

Scenario. The default scoring spreads pods to the least-allocated nodes. Over a week, 1-, 2- and 4-GPU jobs land on almost every node, and no node has 8 free GPUs, though 180 GPUs are free in total.

What the picture shows. How scoring policy decides whether free GPUs end up usable or scattered.

1Spreading (least allocated)
good for CPU services' resilience; for GPUs, it scatters small jobs and destroys whole free nodes.
2Bin-packing (most allocated)
prefer the node that is already most used, so small jobs fill partly used nodes and whole nodes stay free.
3Weighted by resource
score GPU allocation most heavily, so the GPU dimension drives placement on GPU nodes.
4Separate profiles
a bin-packing scheduler profile for GPU pools, the default spreading profile for CPU services.
5Fragmentation metric
the share of free GPUs that sit on nodes with fewer than 8 free, and the largest gang that could start right now.

The YAML. A kube-scheduler profile that bin-packs GPUs (KubeSchedulerConfiguration v1).

apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1kind: KubeSchedulerConfigurationprofiles:- schedulerName: default-scheduler                 # CPU services keep spreading- schedulerName: gpu-binpack                       # GPU workloads set spec.schedulerName: gpu-binpack  pluginConfig:  - name: NodeResourcesFit    args:      scoringStrategy:        type: MostAllocated                        # prefer fuller nodes        resources:        - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, weight: 10 }     # GPUs dominate the score        - { name: cpu, weight: 1 }        - { name: memory, weight: 1 }  plugins:    score:      disabled:      - name: NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation      # balancing fights packing

The code. A fragmentation report: how much free capacity is usable by gangs of each size (Python).

def fragmentation(free_per_node: list[int], gpus_per_node: int = 8):    total_free = sum(free_per_node)    whole = sum(f for f in free_per_node if f == gpus_per_node)    report = {"free_gpus": total_free, "whole_free_nodes": whole // gpus_per_node,              "fragmented_share": round(1 - whole / total_free, 3) if total_free else 0.0}    for pod_gpus in (1, 2, 4, 8):        report[f"pods_of_{pod_gpus}_that_fit"] = sum(f // pod_gpus for f in free_per_node)    return report # 90 nodes with 1–3 free GPUs, 2 whole free nodesprint(fragmentation([2] * 60 + [1] * 15 + [3] * 15 + [8] * 2))
Going deeper2 points
  • Bin-packing has costs: packed nodes concentrate risk (a node failure hits more jobs) and can create noisy neighbours; keep packing for GPU batch work, not latency-critical services.
  • Your scheduler deep dive applies here: scoring plugins and weights interact (scheduler deep dive); test a new profile on a replay of real submissions before switching.

Defragmentation and right-sizing

Scenario. Even with bin-packing, long-running 1-GPU notebooks pin GPUs on dozens of nodes. Packing only affects new pods; the cluster needs a way to fix what's already scattered.

What the picture shows. Ways to recover whole nodes and avoid wasting whole GPUs on small work.

1Pool by job shape
a small-job pool (or partitioned GPUs) for notebooks and 1–2 GPU jobs, and a large-job pool kept for gangs of whole nodes.
2Partition GPUs for small work
MIG slices, time-slicing or MPS for notebooks and small inference, configured below Kueue with the device plugin or Dynamic Resource Allocation; the quota counts slices, not whole GPUs.
3Compaction
periodically migrate preemptible, checkpointable small jobs off sparsely used nodes (evict and requeue them), so their nodes become whole again; only when a pending gang needs whole nodes.
4Reserve whole nodes for waiting gangs
when a large job has waited beyond a threshold, stop placing small jobs on nodes that are about to become free, so the gang can start.
5Idle culling
notebooks idle beyond a limit are checkpointed and stopped (Design 03).

The code. Choosing nodes to drain to create whole nodes for a waiting gang, by fewest GPUs moved (Python).

def plan_compaction(nodes, needed_whole_nodes: int, gpus_per_node: int = 8):    """nodes: dicts with name, used_gpus, movable (all pods preemptible + checkpointable)."""    candidates = [n for n in nodes if 0 < n["used_gpus"] < gpus_per_node and n["movable"]]    candidates.sort(key=lambda n: n["used_gpus"])                  # cheapest to empty first    plan, moved = [], 0    for n in candidates:        if len(plan) == needed_whole_nodes:            break        plan.append(n["name"]); moved += n["used_gpus"]    free_elsewhere = sum(gpus_per_node - n["used_gpus"] for n in nodes if n["name"] not in plan                         and n["used_gpus"] < gpus_per_node) - moved    ok = len(plan) == needed_whole_nodes and free_elsewhere >= 0      # evicted pods must fit elsewhere    return {"drain": plan if ok else [], "gpus_moved": moved if ok else 0, "feasible": ok}
Going deeper2 points
  • Compaction costs work: evicted jobs lose progress since their last checkpoint; only move checkpointable, preemptible jobs, and only when a pending gang will use the freed nodes.
  • Partitioning changes the unit of quota: a team's quota for MIG slices is separate from its whole-GPU quota; model them as separate resources or flavors.

Quotas: nominal, borrowing and lending

Scenario. Each team had a hard limit on GPUs. The vision team's 96 GPUs sat idle on weekends while the LLM team's jobs waited, and nobody could lend them without an admin changing limits by hand.

What the picture shows. The quota model: guaranteed shares that can be lent and borrowed.

1ResourceFlavors
kinds of capacity (H100 on the fabric, H100 standalone, spot), each mapped to node labels.
2ClusterQueue per team
a nominal quota per flavor, the team's guaranteed share.
3Cohort
ClusterQueues in a cohort lend unused nominal quota to each other.
4Borrowing limit
the most a team can take beyond its nominal quota.
5Lending limit
the most of a team's unused quota others can borrow; the rest stays reserved for the team (for latency-sensitive work that must start immediately).
6Reclaim
when a team needs its nominal quota back, it can preempt borrowers (next sections).

The YAML. Two teams' ClusterQueues in one cohort, with borrowing and lending limits (v1beta2).

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ClusterQueuemetadata: { name: llm-team }spec:  cohortName: gpu-fleet  namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { team: llm } }  fairSharing: { weight: 2 }                     # larger share of borrowable capacity  resourceGroups:  - coveredResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu", "cpu", "memory"]    flavors:    - name: h100-fabric      resources:      - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, nominalQuota: 512, borrowingLimit: 256 }      - { name: cpu, nominalQuota: 6144 }      - { name: memory, nominalQuota: 48Ti }  preemption:    reclaimWithinCohort: Any                     # get nominal quota back from borrowers    borrowWithinCohort: { policy: LowerPriority, maxPriorityThreshold: 100 }    withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ClusterQueuemetadata: { name: vision-team }spec:  cohortName: gpu-fleet  namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { team: vision } }  resourceGroups:  - coveredResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu", "cpu", "memory"]    flavors:    - name: h100-fabric      resources:      - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, nominalQuota: 128, lendingLimit: 96 }   # 32 always kept for vision      - { name: cpu, nominalQuota: 1536 }      - { name: memory, nominalQuota: 12Ti }  preemption:    reclaimWithinCohort: Any    withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority
Going deeper2 points
  • Nominal quotas should add up to the fleet: quotas that sum to more than the hardware promise guarantees that can't all be kept; quotas that sum to less leave capacity owned by nobody.
  • Quota counts requests, not use: a notebook holding a GPU at 8% use consumes a whole GPU of quota; idle culling and right-sizing protect the quota as much as the hardware.

Fair share: weighted shares and fairness over time

Scenario. Borrowable capacity went to whichever team submitted first after it freed up. One team with an automated sweep generator got most of it every week.

What the picture shows. Two fairness mechanisms that work at different levels.

1Fair sharing between ClusterQueues (preemption-based)
borrowable capacity in a cohort is divided by weighted share; a queue below its fair share can preempt workloads of queues above theirs, using dominant resource fairness across resources. Weights express how much each team should get of what's shared; a weight of 0 means always last.
2Admission fair sharing between LocalQueues (usage-based)
within one ClusterQueue, workloads from LocalQueues (for example, projects within a team) that used fewer resources recently are admitted first. It reorders admission and doesn't evict running work.
3Preemption strategies
Kueue's fair-sharing strategies only preempt when it moves shares toward fairness (the preemptor's share after admission must not exceed the victim's), avoiding preemption cycles.
4What fairness can't fix
if total demand inside nominal quotas exceeds the fleet, fairness only decides who waits.

The YAML. Admission fair sharing for a team's ClusterQueue with several project LocalQueues (v1beta2).

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ClusterQueuemetadata: { name: research-team }spec:  cohortName: gpu-fleet  namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { team: research } }  fairSharing: { weight: 1 }  admissionScope:    admissionMode: UsageBasedAdmissionFairSharing   # projects that used less go first  resourceGroups:  - coveredResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu"]    flavors:    - name: h100-fabric      resources:      - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, nominalQuota: 128, borrowingLimit: 128 }---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: LocalQueuemetadata: { name: sweeps, namespace: research-sweeps }spec:  clusterQueue: research-team  fairSharing: { weight: 1 }                         # an automated sweep queue gets no extra weight
Going deeper2 points
  • Weights are a policy decision: write down why each team has its weight, and review weights quarterly against business priorities.
  • Show teams their share: a dashboard of each queue's share against its fair share ends most "the queue is unfair" debates with data.

Priority, preemption and backfill

Scenario. A release-candidate evaluation needed 64 GPUs immediately; all were busy with borrowed research jobs. Preempting them would discard four hours of work, because those jobs checkpointed every four hours.

What the picture shows. How urgent work gets capacity without wasting the work it displaces, and how gaps get filled.

1Workload priority classes
a small set (for example, production, release, standard, best-effort) set on workloads; Kueue orders and preempts by them, independently of pod priority.
2Preemption rules
reclaim nominal quota from borrowers, preempt lower priority within a queue, and borrow by preempting only below a priority threshold.
3Cheap preemption
preemptible work must checkpoint often (minutes, Design 14) and handle termination signals by saving state; preemption prefers victims with the most recent checkpoint.
4Backfill
while a large gang waits for whole nodes, short jobs that will finish before those nodes are needed can run in the gaps, if they declare a runtime limit (Kueue enforces a maximum execution time set on the workload).
5Guardrails
limits on how often a workload can be preempted, so best-effort jobs still finish eventually.

The YAML. Workload priority classes and a preemptible job that declares a maximum runtime for backfill (v1beta2).

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: WorkloadPriorityClassmetadata: { name: release }value: 1000description: "Release-candidate evals and production runs"---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: WorkloadPriorityClassmetadata: { name: best-effort }value: 10description: "Sweeps and exploration; preemptible, checkpoint every 10 minutes"---apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: sweep-lr-0042  namespace: research-sweeps  labels:    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: sweeps    kueue.x-k8s.io/priority-class: best-effort    kueue.x-k8s.io/max-exec-time-seconds: "5400"      # Kueue stops it after 90 min: a known bound makes it safe to backfillspec:  parallelism: 1  completions: 1  template:    spec:      schedulerName: gpu-binpack      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120              # time to save a checkpoint on preemption      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: train        image: registry.example.com/train:2026.11        resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 2 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Preemption cost is measurable: record the work lost per preemption (time since last checkpoint × GPUs) and include it in the GPU-hour breakdown.
  • Fewer priority classes are better: every extra class is a negotiation; most fleets need four or five.

Measuring and tuning the scheduler

Scenario. A proposed change to bin-packing weights is debated for weeks. Nobody can say what it would do to queue wait times or fragmentation, because the only way to find out is to deploy it.

What the picture shows. The metrics that describe scheduling quality, and how to test changes safely.

1Efficiency
busy share of GPU-hours, the GPU-hour breakdown, fragmentation share and the largest startable gang.
2Latency
queue wait per job size class (1, 8, 64, 256+ GPUs) and per priority; time from admission to all pods ready.
3Fairness
each queue's usage against its nominal quota and fair share over time; borrowing and reclaim events.
4Disruption
preemptions per day, work lost per preemption, evictions by waitForPodsReady timeouts.
5Trace replay
record submissions (size, runtime, queue, priority) and replay them against a scheduler simulator or a small test cluster with fake nodes, to compare policies before changing production.

The code. A fairness report per queue: usage against nominal quota and fair share (Python).

def fairness(usage_gpu_h: dict, nominal: dict, weights: dict, fleet_gpu_h: float):    """usage_gpu_h: queue -> GPU-hours used; nominal: queue -> guaranteed GPU-hours; weights: queue -> weight."""    borrowable = fleet_gpu_h - sum(min(usage_gpu_h[q], nominal[q]) for q in nominal)    wsum = sum(weights.values())    rows = {}    for q in nominal:        fair = nominal[q] + borrowable * weights[q] / wsum          # nominal + weighted part of the rest        rows[q] = {"used": round(usage_gpu_h[q]), "nominal": nominal[q], "fair_share": round(fair),                   "ratio_to_fair": round(usage_gpu_h[q] / fair, 2)}   # far below 1 while waiting = unfair    return rows
Going deeper2 points
  • Report wait time by size class: a scheduler that improves average wait by starving 256-GPU jobs looks better on average and worse where it matters.
  • Change one policy at a time: packing weights, preemption rules and fair-share weights interact; replay each change separately, then together.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, measure: the GPU-hour breakdown per team and queue, fragmentation, queue wait by size class.
  • Phase 2, gangs: all workloads through Kueue; waitForPodsReady with measured timeouts; topology-aware scheduling for jobs over one node.
  • Phase 3, packing: a bin-packing profile for GPU pools, pools by job shape, GPU partitioning for small work, idle culling.
  • Phase 4, sharing: cohorts with borrowing and lending limits, fair-share weights, admission fair sharing within teams, workload priority classes, checkpoint-aware preemption, backfill and compaction.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • All-or-nothing admission can leave capacity idle while a large job waits for its whole gang; topology-aware admission and backfill reduce it.
  • Bin-packing concentrates risk on fuller nodes, in exchange for whole free nodes for large jobs.
  • Preemption discards work since the last checkpoint; frequent checkpoints are required for preemptible work.
  • Lending limits leave some capacity idle on purpose, so teams with urgent work can start immediately.

Open questions.
