  • Native gang scheduling: kube-scheduler's workload-aware scheduling is beta in 1.37 but off by default, and AWS documents no way to turn it on in EKS (see the gang scheduling note). Once it is available, how much of the gang logic moves from Kueue into the scheduler?
  • Elastic jobs: can training jobs grow and shrink with free capacity (Design 14's per-step recovery) so fragments become useful instead of waiting?
  • Runtime prediction: can predicted job runtimes make backfill safe without users declaring limits?
  • Cost-aware sharing: should fair share count GPU-hours equally across GPU generations, or by cost?
Design 18 · 12 sections

Design 18: A multi-cloud GPU fleet that researchers don't have to think about

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Fleet architecture
  3. Sites and capacity sources
  4. One job API for researchers
  5. Placement: choosing the site
  6. The Kubernetes execution operator
  7. The Slurm execution operator
  8. A portable environment
  9. Data and checkpoints across sites
  10. Identity, secrets and access
  11. Fleet operations: onboarding, health and cost
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we stand up a GPU fleet that spans hyperscalers, GPU-focused clouds ("neoclouds") and on-premises clusters, orchestrated through custom Kubernetes and Slurm operators, so that researchers describe what their job needs and never have to think about where it lands? Design 02 covers a hub dispatching jobs to several Kubernetes clusters, Design 05 covers the network between sites, and Design 17 covers scheduling inside one cluster. This design adds what changes when the sites are different providers with different hardware, contracts, fabrics, storage and schedulers, including Slurm.

The short version: one job API, one placement brain, many execution sites behind adapters. Researchers submit a ResearchJob (image, command, GPUs, gang shape, data, checkpoints, deadline) through one CLI. A fleet control plane keeps an inventory of every site (provider, accelerator, fabric, storage, contract and price) and a placement service picks the site that can run the job soonest at the lowest true cost, using committed capacity first. Execution operators turn the job into native work: a JobSet under Kueue on Kubernetes sites, an sbatch job through slurmrestd on Slurm sites (including Slurm running on Kubernetes via operators such as Slinky or Soperator). Portable images, per-site runtime profiles, replicated data and cross-site checkpoints make the job behave the same wherever it lands, and a conformance suite decides when a new site may join.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A research lab's GPUs come from five places: an AWS account with capacity blocks of H100s, a Google Cloud reservation of A3 nodes, a three-year contract for 2,048 GPUs at a neocloud running managed Kubernetes, a second neocloud cluster delivered as Slurm, and an on-premises H100 cluster run by the university with Slurm. Researchers keep six sets of launch scripts, learn three schedulers and two container runtimes, and copy datasets by hand. Last quarter, the neocloud contract (paid whether used or not) averaged 61% utilization while 140 jobs queued for weeks on the on-premises cluster because "that's where the data is."

What the platform must do.

  • One way to submit: the same job definition and CLI regardless of provider or scheduler.
  • Automatic placement: the platform chooses the site; researchers state constraints (data residency, accelerator type) only when they matter.
  • Use what's paid for first: reserved and committed capacity before on-demand, without starving urgent work.
  • Same behavior everywhere: the same image, environment, data paths and checkpoint semantics on every site.
  • Move work when needed: a job interrupted at one site can resume at another from its checkpoint.
  • Onboard and retire sites safely: a new provider joins after passing tests; a contract that ends drains cleanly.
  • One view of cost, health and usage across all sites.

Out of scope: wide-area networking design (Design 05), in-cluster scheduling policy (Design 17).

Fleet architecture

Scenario. Each new provider brought its own console, scheduler and scripts. The lab needs a structure where adding a provider means adding an adapter, not teaching every researcher something new.

What the picture shows. The fleet as a control plane over heterogeneous execution sites.

1Fleet control plane
the job API and CLI, the site inventory, the placement service, policy (quotas, budgets, residency), and the execution operators. It runs in its own Kubernetes cluster, independent of any provider it schedules onto.
2Kubernetes sites
hyperscaler and neocloud managed Kubernetes clusters with Kueue; jobs arrive as JobSets (dispatched directly or through MultiKueue, Design 02).
3Slurm sites
bare-metal Slurm (on-premises) and Slurm running on Kubernetes (via Slinky or Soperator, often what neoclouds deliver); jobs arrive through slurmrestd.
4Shared services
container registry with per-site mirrors, object storage with replication, identity federation, observability and cost data.
5Adapters, not forks
everything provider-specific (instance types, fabric drivers, storage classes, auth) lives in a site profile and adapter; the job definition never changes.
Going deeper2 points
  • The control plane must not depend on one provider: if it runs only in one cloud, that cloud's outage stops the whole fleet. Keep its state replicated and a warm standby in a second location.
  • Sites keep local autonomy: each site's own scheduler (Kueue or Slurm) still decides placement inside the site; the fleet decides only which site, so a control-plane outage stops new dispatch but not running work.

Sites and capacity sources

Scenario. Nobody can answer "how many H100s do we have, at what price, until when?" The answer is spread across five contracts, three consoles and a spreadsheet.

What the picture shows. The inventory: every site described in one schema.

1Hardware
accelerator type and count, GPU memory, node shape, interconnect inside nodes and between nodes (InfiniBand, RoCE, EFA, or Ethernet only), and the largest gang that fits in one fabric domain.
2Scheduler and runtime
Kubernetes with Kueue, Slurm on Kubernetes, or bare-metal Slurm; container runtime (containerd, Enroot with Pyxis).
3Storage
parallel filesystem, object storage, local NVMe; measured throughput.
4Contract
reserved or committed (paid regardless of use), on-demand, or spot/preemptible; the price per GPU-hour, the commitment's end date and how much of it has been used.
5Constraints
region and jurisdiction, data residency classes the site may hold, export or compliance tags.
6Live state
free GPUs, queue length and estimated wait, health and recent reliability.

The YAML. A site described as a custom resource in the fleet control plane.

apiVersion: fleet.example.com/v1alpha1kind: Sitemetadata:  name: neocloud-a-us-eastspec:  provider: neocloud-a  region: us-east  jurisdiction: US  dataClasses: [public, internal]                 # may not hold restricted data  scheduler: { type: kubernetes, kueue: true, kubeconfigSecret: site-neocloud-a }  hardware:    accelerator: nvidia-h100-80gb    gpusPerNode: 8    nodes: 256    fabric: { type: infiniband, maxGangGPUsPerDomain: 1024 }  storage:    sharedFS: { type: vast, readGBps: 180 }    objectStore: { endpoint: https://s3.neocloud-a.example, region: us-east }  contract:    type: committed                              # paid whether used or not    gpuHourPrice: 2.10    committedGPUs: 2048    endsAt: "2028-06-30"  runtimeProfile: profiles/ib-mlx5-cuda12.yamlstatus:  freeGPUs: 312  estimatedWaitMinutes: { "8": 0, "64": 12, "512": 340 }  reliability30d: { jobFailureRate: 0.012, nodeMTBFHours: 1900 }
Going deeper2 points
  • Committed capacity has a "use it or lose it" value: idle committed GPU-hours cost money anyway; the placement service treats them as nearly free at the margin until the commitment is fully used.
  • Status is measured, not declared: estimated waits and reliability come from the site's own history, refreshed continuously.

One job API for researchers

Scenario. A researcher moving an experiment from the on-premises Slurm cluster to a cloud Kubernetes cluster rewrites a 60-line sbatch script into 140 lines of YAML, and gets the NCCL settings wrong.

What the picture shows. What a researcher declares, and what the platform fills in.

1The researcher declares
image, command, number of GPUs and how they're grouped (for example, 64 GPUs as 8 nodes of 8), accelerator class or minimum GPU memory, data inputs, checkpoint location, priority or deadline, and constraints only if needed (data residency, a specific accelerator).
2The platform fills in
the site, node selectors, fabric settings, mounts, credentials, queue names, the native job object and its scheduler settings.
3One CLI
submit, status, logs, attach, cancel and resume, with the same commands on every site; the CLI shows which site was chosen and why.
4Escape hatches
experts can pin a site or pass scheduler-specific options, recorded as constraints so the job remains portable by default.

The YAML. A ResearchJob: everything a researcher writes.

apiVersion: fleet.example.com/v1alpha1kind: ResearchJobmetadata:  name: rl-math-ablation-17  namespace: team-reasoningspec:  image: registry.example.com/reasoning/rl:2026.11       # mirrored to every site  command: ["python3", "-m", "rl.train", "--recipe=recipes/ablation-17.yaml"]  resources:    gpus: 64    shape: { nodes: 8, gpusPerNode: 8 }                    # gang: all 8 nodes or none    accelerator: { class: h100-class, minMemoryGB: 80 }    interconnect: high-bandwidth                           # needs IB/RoCE/EFA, not plain Ethernet  data:  - { name: prompts, uri: datasets://math-verified@v6, mount: /data/prompts }  checkpoints: { uri: ckpt://team-reasoning/rl-math-ablation-17, everyMinutes: 15 }  scheduling:    priority: standard    deadline: "2026-11-21T09:00:00Z"    preemptible: true                                      # may be moved between sites  constraints:    dataClass: internal                                    # sites allowed to hold this data
Going deeper2 points
  • The API is versioned and small: every field must have a meaning on every site type; anything that exists only on one site is a constraint, not a field.
  • "Why here?" is part of the answer: the CLI shows the placement decision (sites considered, scores, the winner) so researchers trust it instead of pinning sites by habit.

Placement: choosing the site

Scenario. Researchers pinned jobs to the on-premises cluster because their data lived there. Moving the 2 TB dataset once to the neocloud would have cost $40 in transfer and saved weeks of queueing.

What the picture shows. How the placement service picks a site.

1Feasibility filters
accelerator class and memory; a fabric domain large enough for the gang; data class and jurisdiction allowed; budget available; site healthy.
2Scores
estimated start time, true cost per GPU-hour (committed capacity costs almost nothing extra until used up), data movement cost and time, the site's recent reliability, and spreading risk across providers.
3Data gravity, measured
move the data if moving it is cheaper and faster than waiting; keep it where it is otherwise.
4Decisions are re-evaluated
a job still waiting after its estimated start can be re-placed at another site.

The code. A placement scorer over feasible sites (Python).

from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclassclass Option:    site: str    feasible: bool    wait_h: float              # estimated time to start    gpu_h_price: float         # marginal price per GPU-hour (≈0 for unused committed capacity)    data_move_usd: float       # transfer cost for inputs not already at the site    data_move_h: float    failure_rate: float        # recent job failure rate at this site def score(o: Option, gpus: int, est_runtime_h: float, deadline_h: float,          usd_per_wait_h: float = 50.0) -> float | None:    if not o.feasible:        return None    start_h = max(o.wait_h, o.data_move_h)                       # data can move while waiting    if start_h + est_runtime_h > deadline_h:        return None                                              # can't meet the deadline    compute = gpus * est_runtime_h * o.gpu_h_price    risk = o.failure_rate * gpus * est_runtime_h * 0.25 * max(o.gpu_h_price, 1.0)   # expected rework    delay = start_h * usd_per_wait_h                             # a researcher-hour of waiting has a cost    return compute + o.data_move_usd + risk + delay def place(options, **job):    scored = [(score(o, **job), o.site) for o in options]    scored = [(s, site) for s, site in scored if s is not None]    return min(scored)[1] if scored else None
Going deeper2 points
  • Price the wait: without a cost for waiting, placement always picks the cheapest site and queues there forever; the waiting cost is a policy knob per priority.
  • Burn commitments deliberately: track committed GPU-hours used against the plan; when a commitment is behind, lower its marginal price so more work flows there.

The Kubernetes execution operator

Scenario. The same JobSet worked on one cloud and failed on another: different GPU node labels, a different network device plugin, a different storage class, and NCCL needing a different transport plugin.

What the picture shows. How a ResearchJob becomes native work on a Kubernetes site.

1Render
the operator turns the ResearchJob into a JobSet (one replicated job of N pods for N nodes) with Kueue labels, topology annotations (Design 17) and the checkpoint and data mounts.
2Overlay the site profile
node selectors and tolerations, the fabric's device resources and environment (for example, EFA devices and the libfabric NCCL plugin on AWS, InfiniBand devices and RDMA settings on IB sites), storage classes, and image pull secrets or mirrors.
3Dispatch
create the JobSet in the site's cluster (directly, or through MultiKueue when the site is a MultiKueue worker), then watch it.
4Sync status back
queued, admitted, running, failed or succeeded, with the site's reason, into the ResearchJob status.

The YAML. A site runtime profile the operator merges into every pod it renders for that site.

# profiles/aws-p5-efa.yaml — overlay for AWS P5 sitesnodeSelector: { node.kubernetes.io/instance-type: p5.48xlarge }tolerations: [ { key: nvidia.com/gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoSchedule } ]resources:  perNode: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8, vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 32 }   # EFA interfaces per nodeenv:  FI_PROVIDER: efa  FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA: "1"  NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME: "^lo,docker"imageOverlay: registry.example.com/runtime/aws-ofi-nccl:1.14   # adds the libfabric NCCL pluginvolumes:  sharedFS: { storageClass: fsx-lustre }  scratch: { hostPath: /opt/dlami/nvme }---# profiles/ib-mlx5-cuda12.yaml — overlay for InfiniBand neocloud sitesnodeSelector: { gpu.nvidia.com/class: h100 }resources:  perNode: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8, rdma/ib: 8 }env:  NCCL_IB_HCA: "mlx5"  NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME: "eth0"volumes:  sharedFS: { storageClass: vast-rwx }  scratch: { hostPath: /mnt/local-nvme }
Going deeper2 points
  • Profiles are tested artifacts: a profile change runs the site conformance suite (below) before it's used for real jobs.
  • Same image, different overlay: keep the researcher's image identical everywhere; fabric-specific libraries come from a thin per-site layer or from the node, never from researchers rebuilding images per site.

The Slurm execution operator

Scenario. Two sites only offer Slurm. Researchers who never used Slurm can't use them, and those who did write scripts that only work on one of the two.

What the picture shows. How the same ResearchJob runs on a Slurm site.

1Render
the operator generates a batch script from the ResearchJob: node count, GPUs per node, time limit, partition and account from the site profile, and a containerized srun (with Pyxis and Enroot) running the same image and command.
2Submit through slurmrestd
the Slurm REST API, authenticated with a short-lived token for the mapped Slurm account; the operator stores the Slurm job ID.
3Watch and map states
PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, TIMEOUT and NODE_FAIL map to ResearchJob states; preemption and requeue map to the fleet's resume logic.
4Slurm on Kubernetes
where Slurm runs inside Kubernetes (Slinky, SchedMD's operator, or Nebius's Soperator, which also provides a shared root filesystem across nodes), the fleet still talks to Slurm through slurmrestd, so the operator doesn't care how Slurm is hosted.
5Same semantics
the job sees the same mounts, environment variables and checkpoint location as on Kubernetes sites.

The code. The rendered batch script and its submission through slurmrestd (Bash, Python).

#!/bin/bash#SBATCH --job-name=rl-math-ablation-17#SBATCH --nodes=8#SBATCH --gpus-per-node=8#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=8#SBATCH --time=36:00:00#SBATCH --partition=h100          # from the site profile#SBATCH --account=team-reasoning  # mapped from the researcher's team#SBATCH --requeue                 # fleet resumes from checkpoint on preemptionexport NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5           # from the site profilesrun --container-image=registry.example.com#reasoning/rl:2026.11 \     --container-mounts=/fs/datasets/math-verified-v6:/data/prompts,/fs/ckpt/rl-math-ablation-17:/ckpt \     python3 -m rl.train --recipe=recipes/ablation-17.yaml --ckpt-dir=/ckpt
import httpx def submit_slurm(site, script: str, job_name: str, token: str, user: str) -> int:    """Submit through slurmrestd; use the API version your Slurm release provides."""    body = {"job": {"name": job_name, "script": script,                    "current_working_directory": site.workdir,                    "environment": ["PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"]}}    r = httpx.post(f"{site.slurmrestd}/slurm/{site.api_version}/job/submit", json=body,                   headers={"X-SLURM-USER-NAME": user, "X-SLURM-USER-TOKEN": token}, timeout=30)    r.raise_for_status()    return r.json()["job_id"]
Going deeper2 points
  • Account mapping is policy: each team maps to a Slurm account with fair-share settings on each Slurm site, managed by the operator from the same quota data as Kueue (Design 17).
  • Don't hide Slurm from people who want it: experts can still log in to a Slurm site; the fleet just means nobody has to.

A portable environment

Scenario. A job that ran fine on one site crashed on another with a CUDA driver mismatch; on a third it ran 40% slower because NCCL fell back to TCP.

What the picture shows. The layers that make a job behave the same on every site.

1Base images
a small set of blessed base images (CUDA, NCCL, PyTorch versions) tested against every site's driver versions; researcher images build on them.
2Driver compatibility matrix
each site's GPU driver version and the CUDA versions it supports; placement rejects sites whose driver is too old for the image.
3Fabric layer
NCCL network plugins and settings per fabric, supplied by the site profile, not by researchers.
4Registry mirrors
images pushed once, replicated to a mirror or pull-through cache at each site; lazy-loading image formats for very large images.
5Runtime differences hidden
containerd on Kubernetes sites, Enroot with Pyxis on Slurm sites, both running the same OCI image.
6Startup check
every job's first seconds verify GPUs, driver, NCCL transport and mounts, and fail fast with a clear message if anything is wrong.

The code. A startup check that fails fast on environment problems (Python).

import os, sys, torch, torch.distributed as dist def startup_check(expect_transport: str | None = None):    problems = []    if not torch.cuda.is_available():        problems.append("no CUDA devices visible")    else:        need = int(os.environ.get("EXPECTED_GPUS_PER_NODE", "8"))        if torch.cuda.device_count() != need:            problems.append(f"expected {need} GPUs, found {torch.cuda.device_count()}")    for path in os.environ.get("REQUIRED_MOUNTS", "/data,/ckpt").split(","):        if not os.path.isdir(path):            problems.append(f"missing mount {path}")    # FLEET_NCCL_TRANSPORT is exported by the site's fabric layer after it loads the NCCL net plugin    if expect_transport and os.environ.get("FLEET_NCCL_TRANSPORT") != expect_transport:        problems.append(f"NCCL transport is not {expect_transport}: would fall back to TCP")    if problems:        print("STARTUP CHECK FAILED: " + "; ".join(problems), file=sys.stderr)        sys.exit(42)                    # config/environment error: fail fast, don't retry (Design 13)
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure, don't trust, the fabric: a short all-reduce bandwidth test at job start (a few seconds) catches silent TCP fallback that a configuration check can miss.
  • Keep the number of base images small: each base image multiplies the compatibility testing across sites.

Data and checkpoints across sites

Scenario. A job preempted at the neocloud should have resumed on AWS, but its checkpoints were on the neocloud's filesystem, unreachable from AWS. It waited a day to restart at the same site.

What the picture shows. Where data lives, how it moves and what it costs.

1Source of truth
datasets and checkpoints in object storage in a "home" region, with versioned snapshots (Design 13).
2Per-site caches
datasets replicated or cached at sites that run jobs on them, populated before the job starts (placement accounts for the copy time).
3Checkpoints
written locally first for speed, then copied to the site's object storage and replicated to home, so any site can resume.
4Data classes and residency
restricted data never leaves allowed jurisdictions; placement enforces it.
5Egress budgeting
transfer costs per provider and direction are part of placement and chargeback; large recurring transfers get dedicated links or are avoided.

The code. Estimating the cost and time of preparing a site for a job (Python).

EGRESS_USD_PER_GB = {("aws", "internet"): 0.09, ("gcp", "internet"): 0.12,                     ("neocloud-a", "internet"): 0.0, ("onprem", "internet"): 0.0}   # illustrative def staging_cost(inputs, site, link_gbps: float = 10.0):    """inputs: dicts with size_gb, home_provider, cached_at (set of sites)."""    usd, gb = 0.0, 0.0    for d in inputs:        if site in d["cached_at"]:            continue        gb += d["size_gb"]        usd += d["size_gb"] * EGRESS_USD_PER_GB.get((d["home_provider"], "internet"), 0.1)    hours = gb * 8 / (link_gbps * 3600)                       # GB → Gb, at the link rate    return {"gb": gb, "usd": round(usd, 2), "hours": round(hours, 2)}   # feeds placement
Going deeper2 points
  • Checkpoint replication is a recovery feature: replicate only the latest few checkpoints across sites; older ones stay at home.
  • Prefer pulling to pushing: a site fetches what its jobs need through its cache, so data movement follows placement decisions instead of predictions.

Identity, secrets and access

Scenario. Each site had its own long-lived keys in researchers' home directories. When a researcher left, it took two weeks to find and revoke them all.

What the picture shows. One identity for people and workloads across all providers.

1People
single sign-on to the fleet CLI; the fleet maps each person to their team and its accounts at each site. Nobody holds provider credentials to run jobs.
2Workloads
jobs authenticate to storage and services with short-lived tokens from workload identity federation (OIDC trust between the fleet's issuer and each provider), not static keys.
3Operators
the fleet's own credentials per site are scoped to job submission and status, rotated automatically and held in a secrets manager.
4Slurm sites
short-lived REST tokens for mapped Slurm accounts; no shared service account that can impersonate anyone.
5Offboarding
removing a person from the directory removes their access everywhere, because no site holds an independent credential for them.
Going deeper2 points
  • Audit in one place: every submission, data access and placement decision is logged in the fleet with the person and team, regardless of which site ran it.
  • Least privilege per site: a job at a neocloud gets read access to the datasets it declared and write access to its checkpoint path, nothing else.

Fleet operations: onboarding, health and cost

Scenario. A new neocloud contract started on Monday; the first real job ran on Thursday and failed because the storage was a tenth of the advertised throughput. Nobody had tested the site end to end.

What the picture shows. The lifecycle and daily operation of sites.

1Conformance suite before joining
GPU and node health (Design 14), NCCL all-reduce bandwidth at several gang sizes, storage read and write throughput, image pull time from the mirror, checkpoint write and cross-site restore, and an end-to-end ResearchJob on each scheduler path. A site joins only when results meet its profile.
2Site states
onboarding, active, degraded (no new large jobs), draining (contract ending or maintenance) and retired; placement respects the state.
3Normalized observability
the same GPU metrics (DCGM), job labels and logs from every site, so dashboards and the GPU-hour breakdown (Design 17) cover the whole fleet.
4Cost and commitments
spend per site, team and job; committed capacity burn against plan; alerts when a commitment is behind.
5Cross-site resume
jobs preempted or failed at one site, and flagged as movable, are re-placed and resume from the replicated checkpoint.

The YAML. The conformance suite run against a candidate site, as a ResearchJob pinned to it.

apiVersion: fleet.example.com/v1alpha1kind: ResearchJobmetadata:  name: conformance-neocloud-b-2026-11  namespace: fleet-opsspec:  image: registry.example.com/fleet/conformance:2026.11  command: ["python3", "-m", "conformance.run",            "--tests=gpu-health,nccl-allreduce,storage-throughput,image-pull,ckpt-roundtrip,cross-site-restore",            "--nccl-sizes=8,64,512", "--report=s3://fleet/conformance/neocloud-b/2026-11"]  resources:    gpus: 512    shape: { nodes: 64, gpusPerNode: 8 }    interconnect: high-bandwidth  constraints:    site: neocloud-b-eu-west                        # pinned: this is a test of the site itself  scheduling: { priority: fleet-ops }
Going deeper2 points
  • Re-run conformance after every site change: driver upgrades, firmware, scheduler versions and profile edits all re-run a subset; a regression puts the site in "degraded".
  • Exit plans are part of onboarding: for every contract, know how to drain it, where its data and checkpoints go, and how long that takes, before it starts.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, inventory and visibility: Site resources for every provider, normalized metrics and cost data, the GPU-hour breakdown across the fleet.
  • Phase 2, one job API on Kubernetes sites: ResearchJob, the CLI, the Kubernetes operator with site profiles, registry mirrors and placement across Kubernetes sites.
  • Phase 3, Slurm sites: the Slurm operator through slurmrestd, account mapping, Slurm-on-Kubernetes sites; startup checks and base images tested across all sites.
  • Phase 4, mobility and operations: dataset caches and checkpoint replication, cross-site resume, conformance-gated onboarding, commitment burn management.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • A lowest-common-denominator API: features only one site offers are reachable only as constraints, in exchange for jobs that run anywhere.
  • The fleet layer is another system to run, with its own availability, in exchange for researchers not learning five providers.
  • Data movement costs money, in exchange for using idle committed capacity instead of queueing next to the data.
  • Adapters lag new provider features by weeks, in exchange for stable behavior.

Open questions.

  • Gangs across sites: can large jobs span two sites (with very high staleness tolerance, as in asynchronous RL, Design 09), or must every gang fit one site?
  • Spot and preemptible capacity across providers: how much movable work can absorb interruptions without losing more than it saves?
  • Placement learning: can estimated waits, failure rates and runtimes be predicted well enough from history to make placement fully automatic?
  • Contract planning: how should next year's mix of commitments, on-demand and on-premises capacity be chosen from this year's fleet data?
Design 19 · 12 sections

Design 19: Building a scheduling layer that measurably raises accelerator utilization

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Defining utilization so it can't be argued with
  3. Baseline instrumentation
  4. Architecture of the scheduling layer
  5. Quotas as code
  6. Simulate before you ship
  7. Staged rollout with guardrails
  8. Proving the gain: separating policy from demand
  9. Idle reclamation: often the biggest lever
  10. Team scorecards that keep the gains
  11. Running the layer: SLOs and continuous tuning
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build a scheduling layer (gang scheduling, bin-packing and fair-share quotas) and prove, with numbers that survive scrutiny, that it raised accelerator utilization across teams? Design 17 explains the mechanisms: Kueue admission, topology-aware gangs, bin-packing profiles, cohorts and fair sharing. This design is about delivering them as a program: defining the metric, instrumenting a baseline, building the layer as code, simulating changes before rollout, rolling out in stages, attributing gains to each change, and reporting per team so the improvement lasts.

The short version: define utilization precisely, measure a baseline before touching anything, and ship each change as an experiment. Utilization is measured from GPU activity (not allocation), per team and per pool, from one pipeline. Quotas live in Git and generate the Kueue objects. Every policy change is first replayed against recorded jobs in a simulator, then rolled out to one pool while a comparable pool stays unchanged, so the gain can be separated from changes in demand. A per-change attribution shows which lever moved the number, and team scorecards keep the gains from eroding.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. Leadership has approved a scheduling project with a target: raise GPU utilization across the 1,024-GPU fleet from "about 58%" to 75% within two quarters, instead of buying 300 more GPUs. Three problems appear on day one. Nobody agrees on what "58%" measured. Two previous efforts claimed improvements that disappeared when demand dropped over the holidays. And team leads worry that "utilization" means their jobs will be preempted more.

What the program must deliver.

  • One agreed metric: a definition of utilization that teams, finance and the platform team accept, measured the same way every day.
  • A trustworthy baseline: several weeks of data before any change, by team and pool.
  • The scheduling layer as code: quotas, queues and scheduler profiles generated from versioned definitions.
  • Evidence before rollout: simulated impact of each change on utilization and on wait times.
  • Causal attribution: how much of the change came from the scheduler, separated from demand changes.
  • Guardrails: utilization gains that don't come at the cost of large-job wait times, preemption losses or fairness.
  • Lasting results: team-level reporting that keeps idle allocation from creeping back.

Out of scope: the mechanics of each scheduling feature (Design 17) and multi-cluster placement (Design 02, Design 18).

Defining utilization so it can't be argued with

Scenario. The platform dashboard said 58% (GPUs allocated to pods), the finance report said 71% (nodes powered on and assigned), and a team lead's notebook showed 34% (average SM activity). All three were "GPU utilization."

What the picture shows. A metric tree from raw capacity to useful work, with one headline number and the ones under it.

1Capacity
GPU-hours of healthy, schedulable GPUs. Nodes down for repair are reported separately, not hidden in the denominator.
2Allocation rate
the share of capacity requested by running pods (what Kueue and kube-scheduler control).
3Activity rate
the share of allocated GPU-hours where the GPU is actually working, measured from DCGM's graphics-engine activity (above a small threshold), not from nvidia-smi utilization alone.
4Headline: active utilization
= allocation rate × activity rate: the share of capacity doing work.
5Efficiency below that
SM activity and tensor-core activity show how hard the GPUs work while active; MFU belongs to training benchmarks (Design 15), not to the scheduler's target.
6The scheduler's target is active utilization;
the scheduler can raise allocation directly and activity indirectly (by reclaiming idle allocations), but it can't make a slow data loader faster.

The code. Computing the metric tree for one day and one team from per-GPU minute samples (Python).

import pandas as pd def utilization(samples: pd.DataFrame, active_threshold: float = 0.05) -> pd.Series:    """samples: one row per GPU per minute with columns       healthy (bool), allocated (bool), team (str|None), gr_engine_active (0..1 from DCGM)."""    healthy = samples[samples.healthy]    capacity = len(healthy)                                            # GPU-minutes    alloc = healthy[healthy.allocated]    active = alloc[alloc.gr_engine_active >= active_threshold]    return pd.Series({        "capacity_gpu_h": capacity / 60,        "allocation_rate": len(alloc) / capacity,        "activity_rate": len(active) / max(len(alloc), 1),        "active_utilization": len(active) / capacity,                  # the headline        "mean_engine_activity_when_active": active.gr_engine_active.mean(),        "unhealthy_gpu_h": (len(samples) - capacity) / 60,             # reported, not hidden    }) def by_team(samples):    return samples.groupby("team").apply(lambda g: utilization(g)).sort_values("active_utilization")
Going deeper2 points
  • Agree on the definition in writing before the project starts: the metric, threshold, denominator and data source, signed off by platform, finance and team leads; changing it later resets the baseline.
  • Report the tree, not just the headline: "allocation went up, activity went down" (jobs grabbing GPUs they don't use) is a different story from both rising.

Baseline instrumentation

Scenario. The previous effort measured "before" for one week in December and "after" for one week in February. Demand had doubled in between. The improvement was mostly demand.

What the picture shows. The data pipeline that produces the metric, the baseline and the context needed to interpret it.

1GPU activity
DCGM exporter on every GPU node, with pod and namespace labels, scraped every 30 seconds.
2Allocation
kube-state-metrics for GPU requests of running pods; Kueue metrics for quota usage, pending workloads and admission wait times.
3Demand context
submitted GPU-hours per team per day, pending GPU-hours, and job size mix; without these, utilization changes can't be interpreted.
4Recording rules and a warehouse
per-minute aggregates by team, pool and GPU type, stored long term so the baseline can be recomputed if definitions change.
5Baseline period
at least four weeks, covering normal variation (weekdays, weekends, deadlines), with no scheduler changes during it.

The YAML. Prometheus recording rules for allocation and activity per team (Prometheus Operator).

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1kind: PrometheusRulemetadata: { name: gpu-utilization, namespace: monitoring }spec:  groups:  - name: gpu-utilization    interval: 1m    rules:    - record: team:gpu_allocated:sum                       # GPUs requested by running pods (label_team from namespace labels)      expr: |        sum by (label_team) (          kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="nvidia_com_gpu"}          * on (namespace, pod) group_left() (kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Running"} == 1)          * on (namespace) group_left(team) kube_namespace_labels{label_team!=""}        )    - record: team:gpu_active:sum                          # allocated GPUs actually working      expr: |        sum by (label_team) (          (DCGM_FI_PROF_GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE > bool 0.05)          * on (namespace) group_left(team) kube_namespace_labels{label_team!=""}        )    - record: fleet:gpu_capacity_healthy:sum      expr: sum(kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="nvidia_com_gpu"} * on (node) group_left() (kube_node_spec_unschedulable == bool 0))    - record: fleet:gpu_active_utilization:ratio      expr: sum(team:gpu_active:sum) / fleet:gpu_capacity_healthy:sum
Going deeper2 points
  • Label hygiene matters: namespaces must carry a team label; unlabeled namespaces are a reported category, not silently dropped.
  • Recompute, don't edit: store raw per-minute aggregates, so a corrected definition can be applied to the whole history, including the baseline.

Architecture of the scheduling layer

Scenario. Previous changes were made by hand in the cluster: a ClusterQueue edited here, a scheduler flag there. Nobody could say which configuration was in effect on which date.

What the picture shows. The components the project builds, and how they connect.

1Policy source
team allocations, weights, priorities and pool definitions in Git, reviewed like code.
2Policy controller
generates ResourceFlavors, Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues and WorkloadPriorityClasses from the policy source and applies them; reports drift.
3Admission and placement
Kueue with gang semantics and topology-aware scheduling, kube-scheduler with a bin-packing profile for GPU pools (Design 17).
4Reclaimers
an idle reclaimer for allocations that aren't used, and a compaction controller for fragmented nodes.
5Measurement
the metric pipeline above, plus a change log of every policy version and when it was applied.
6Simulator
replays recorded jobs against candidate policies before they reach the cluster.
Going deeper2 points
  • Every policy version has a timestamp: attribution later needs to know exactly which configuration was active when; the controller writes each applied version to the change log.
  • The layer is Kubernetes-native: no custom scheduler fork; customization is configuration plus small controllers, so upgrades of Kueue and Kubernetes stay routine.

Quotas as code

Scenario. Quotas lived in a spreadsheet and were copied into ClusterQueues by hand. After a reorganization, the quotas added up to 1,180 GPUs on a 1,024-GPU fleet, and two teams had no LocalQueue at all.

What the picture shows. One reviewed file for team allocations, validated and turned into Kueue objects.

1Allocations file
each team's guaranteed GPUs per pool, borrowing and lending limits, fair-share weight and namespaces.
2Validation in CI
guaranteed quotas add up to the pool's healthy capacity (within a margin), every team has a queue, weights are positive, no namespace belongs to two teams.
3Generation
a small generator renders Cohorts, ClusterQueues and LocalQueues; a GitOps tool applies them.
4Change review
quota changes are pull requests with an owner's approval; the merge time becomes the change-log entry.

The code. Validating allocations and generating ClusterQueues (Python).

import yaml def validate(alloc: dict, capacity: dict, tolerance: float = 0.02):    errors = []    for pool, cap in capacity.items():        total = sum(t["pools"].get(pool, {}).get("guaranteed", 0) for t in alloc["teams"].values())        if abs(total - cap) > tolerance * cap:            errors.append(f"{pool}: guaranteed {total} vs capacity {cap}")          # 1,180 on 1,024    seen = {}    for team, t in alloc["teams"].items():        for ns in t["namespaces"]:            if ns in seen:                errors.append(f"namespace {ns} in {seen[ns]} and {team}")            seen[ns] = team    return errors def cluster_queue(team: str, t: dict, cohort: str) -> dict:    flavors = [{"name": pool, "resources": [{"name": "nvidia.com/gpu", "nominalQuota": p["guaranteed"],                **({"borrowingLimit": p["borrow"]} if "borrow" in p else {}),                **({"lendingLimit": p["lend"]} if "lend" in p else {})}]}               for pool, p in t["pools"].items()]    return {"apiVersion": "kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2", "kind": "ClusterQueue", "metadata": {"name": team},            "spec": {"cohortName": cohort, "namespaceSelector": {"matchLabels": {"team": team}},                     "fairSharing": {"weight": t.get("weight", 1)},                     "resourceGroups": [{"coveredResources": ["nvidia.com/gpu"], "flavors": flavors}],                     "preemption": {"reclaimWithinCohort": "Any", "withinClusterQueue": "LowerPriority"}}} alloc = yaml.safe_load(open("allocations.yaml"))errs = validate(alloc, {"h100-fabric": 1024})if errs:    raise SystemExit("\n".join(errs))print(yaml.safe_dump_all([cluster_queue(n, t, "gpu-fleet") for n, t in alloc["teams"].items()]))
Going deeper2 points
  • Allocations are a business decision: the platform team owns the mechanism, leadership owns the numbers; the file records who approved each allocation.
  • Generate LocalQueues too: a team that has quota but no queue in a namespace is the most common "my job is stuck" ticket.

Simulate before you ship

Scenario. The team argued for two weeks about whether bin-packing would hurt notebook users. A replay of the previous month's jobs answered it in an afternoon.

What the picture shows. Trace-driven simulation of scheduling policies.

1Traces
every job from the baseline period: submit time, team, GPUs and shape, runtime, priority, preemptibility, and whether it was a notebook or batch job.
2Simulator
a discrete-event model of the cluster's nodes, admission (quota, gangs) and placement (spread or pack), fast enough to replay a month in minutes.
3Candidate policies
each change on its own (gang admission, bin-packing, fair-share weights, idle reclaim) and combined.
4Outputs
allocation and active utilization, wait time by job size, fragmentation, preemptions; with a range from replaying with perturbed runtimes.
5Calibration
replay the baseline policy and check that the simulator reproduces the measured baseline within a few points; otherwise its predictions aren't trusted.

The code. A minimal discrete-event replay comparing spread and pack placement for gang jobs (Python).

import heapq def simulate(jobs, nodes=128, gpus_per_node=8, policy="pack"):    """jobs: sorted by submit; each dict has submit, runtime, pods, gpus_per_pod. Returns utilization, waits."""    free = [gpus_per_node] * nodes    events, queue, waits, busy_gpu_s = [], [], [], 0.0    t_end = max(j["submit"] + j["runtime"] for j in jobs) * 3    for j in jobs:        heapq.heappush(events, (j["submit"], 1, id(j), "submit", j))     def try_start(now):        nonlocal busy_gpu_s        for j in list(queue):            order = sorted(range(nodes), key=lambda n: free[n] if policy == "pack" else -free[n])            chosen, need = [], j["pods"]            for n in order:                                  # all pods placed, or none (gang)                k = min(need, free[n] // j["gpus_per_pod"])                chosen += [n] * k; need -= k                if need == 0:                    break            if need:                continue            for n in chosen:                free[n] -= j["gpus_per_pod"]            queue.remove(j); waits.append((j["pods"] * j["gpus_per_pod"], now - j["submit"]))            busy_gpu_s += j["runtime"] * j["pods"] * j["gpus_per_pod"]            heapq.heappush(events, (now + j["runtime"], 0, id(j), "end", (j, chosen)))     while events:        now, _, _, kind, payload = heapq.heappop(events)        if now > t_end:            break        if kind == "submit":            queue.append(payload)        else:            j, chosen = payload            for n in chosen:                free[n] += j["gpus_per_pod"]        try_start(now)    horizon = max(w for _, w in waits) + max(j["submit"] + j["runtime"] for j in jobs)    return {"allocation": busy_gpu_s / (nodes * gpus_per_node * horizon), "waits": waits}
Going deeper2 points
  • Simulators flatter policies they model and ignore what they don't: network contention, image pulls and failures are missing; treat predictions as ranges and confirm in the cluster.
  • Simulate the guardrails, not just the headline: a policy that adds 6 points of utilization and triples p90 wait for 256-GPU jobs is not an improvement.

Staged rollout with guardrails

Scenario. A fair-share change was rolled out to the whole fleet on a Friday. On Monday, preemptions had increased fivefold and two teams had lost a weekend of work.

What the picture shows. How each change reaches the fleet.

1Stage 1, shadow
compute what the new policy would have decided (from the simulator, or a dry-run mode), with no effect on jobs.
2Stage 2, one pool
apply to one pool or a set of volunteer teams; the rest of the fleet is the comparison group.
3Stage 3, fleet
apply everywhere after the guardrails held for an agreed period (for example, two weeks).
4Guardrails, checked daily
p90 wait by job size class, work lost to preemption, the fairness ratio per queue, and job failure rate; each with a threshold that triggers rollback.
5Rollback is a revert
the policy source is in Git; rolling back is reverting the change and letting the controller apply it.

The YAML. A change record that ties a policy version to its rollout stage, comparison group and guardrails.

# changes/2026-12-binpack-gpu-pools.yamlchange: binpack-gpu-poolspolicy_version: scheduling-policy@4f2a9c1hypothesis: "MostAllocated scoring on GPU pools raises allocation by 4–7 points by reducing fragmentation"simulated: { allocation_delta: [0.04, 0.07], p90_wait_256gpu_delta_h: [-6, -2] }stages:- { name: shadow,   start: 2026-12-01, scope: none }- { name: pool-a,   start: 2026-12-04, scope: { pools: [h100-a] }, comparison: { pools: [h100-b] } }- { name: fleet,    start: 2026-12-18, requires: guardrails_held_days >= 14 }guardrails:  p90_wait_hours: { "1-8": 2, "9-64": 8, "65-256": 36, "257+": 72 }  preemption_lost_gpu_h_per_day: 40  fairness_ratio_min: 0.7                  # every queue gets ≥ 70% of its fair share when it has demand  job_failure_rate_max_increase: 0.01rollback: "git revert; controller applies previous policy"
Going deeper2 points
  • Pick comparison pools that are alike: same GPU type, similar team mix and demand; otherwise the comparison measures the pools, not the policy.
  • One change per stage: two changes rolled out together can only be attributed together.

Proving the gain: separating policy from demand

Scenario. Utilization rose 9 points in December. Over the same month, a big project started and submitted three times its usual jobs. How much of the 9 points did the scheduler earn?

What the picture shows. Methods that attribute changes to policies rather than to demand.

1Difference in differences
compare the change in the treated pool with the change in the comparison pool over the same period; demand changes that affect both cancel out.
2Switchback
for policies that can be toggled safely, alternate them by week (or by day) in one pool and compare the periods; repeated switching averages out demand swings.
3Demand-adjusted views
utilization only means something when there's pending work; report utilization during hours when demand exceeded capacity, where the scheduler's choices matter most.
4Per-change waterfall
the total gain split into contributions from each rolled-out change, each from its own comparison, plus "demand and other".
5Uncertainty
daily values are correlated; use weekly blocks or block bootstrap for intervals (Design 12).

The code. A difference-in-differences estimate with a block-bootstrap interval (Python).

import numpy as np def did(treated_before, treated_after, control_before, control_after, block=7, n_boot=2000, seed=0):    """Each argument: daily active-utilization values (np.array) for one pool and period."""    est = (treated_after.mean() - treated_before.mean()) - (control_after.mean() - control_before.mean())    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)    def resample(x):        blocks = [x[i:i + block] for i in range(0, len(x) - block + 1, block)]        picks = rng.integers(0, len(blocks), size=len(blocks))        return np.concatenate([blocks[i] for i in picks])    boots = [(resample(treated_after).mean() - resample(treated_before).mean())             - (resample(control_after).mean() - resample(control_before).mean()) for _ in range(n_boot)]    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])    return {"effect": round(est, 4), "ci95": (round(lo, 4), round(hi, 4))}   # policy effect, net of demand
Going deeper2 points
  • Check the parallel-trends assumption: before the change, the treated and comparison pools should move together; plot them over the baseline period before trusting the estimate.
  • Claim the interval, not the point: "+5.5 points (3.4 to 7.6)" is the result to report to leadership.

Idle reclamation: often the biggest lever

Scenario. The baseline showed 12% of capacity allocated but idle: 96 GPUs held by notebooks that were busy 8% of the time, inference replicas sized for a peak that came once a week, and training jobs stuck waiting on data loaders.

What the picture shows. Recovering allocations that aren't doing work.

1Detect
per-pod GPU activity from DCGM over a window (for example, under 5% for 60 minutes) and the pod's kind (notebook, batch job, service).
2Policy by kind
notebooks are checkpointed and stopped after a warning; batch jobs that are idle for long are flagged to their owners, not killed; services are right-sized by their autoscalers (Design 03).
3Right-size requests
recommend smaller GPU slices for workloads that never use a full GPU (MIG or time-slicing, Design 17).
4Exemptions with expiry
a team can exempt a workload for a reason (a demo, a long debug session) for a limited time.
5Feedback
reclaimed GPU-hours per team appear on the team scorecard.

The YAML. An idle policy, read by a small reclaimer controller.

apiVersion: scheduling.example.com/v1alpha1kind: IdlePolicymetadata: { name: default-gpu-idle }spec:  selector: { matchLabels: { gpu.example.com/workload-kind: notebook } }  idle:    metric: DCGM_FI_PROF_GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE    below: 0.05    forMinutes: 60                         # 60 minutes with the GPU essentially unused  actions:  - { after: 0m,  do: notify, channel: owner }  - { after: 15m, do: checkpoint, command: ["/opt/notebook/save-state.sh"] }  - { after: 20m, do: stop }               # the notebook can be restarted from its saved state  exemptions: { annotation: gpu.example.com/idle-exempt-until, maxDays: 3 }---apiVersion: scheduling.example.com/v1alpha1kind: IdlePolicymetadata: { name: batch-gpu-idle }spec:  selector: { matchLabels: { gpu.example.com/workload-kind: batch } }  idle: { metric: DCGM_FI_PROF_GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE, below: 0.05, forMinutes: 120 }  actions:  - { after: 0m, do: notify, channel: owner }   # batch jobs: tell the owner, never kill automatically
Going deeper2 points
  • Idle reclaim has a social side: announce it, show each team its own idle numbers first, and give a grace period; surprise reclaim generates exemptions instead of savings.
  • Data-loader idle is a different problem: a training job at 30% activity needs a faster input pipeline, not a reclaimer; flag it as an efficiency issue for the team.

Team scorecards that keep the gains

Scenario. Six months after a previous push, idle allocation had crept back to where it started. Nobody had been looking at it per team.

What the picture shows. A weekly scorecard per team, generated from the same pipeline.

1Usage
guaranteed GPUs, average allocated, average active, and borrowed or lent GPU-hours.
2Efficiency
activity rate of the team's allocations, idle GPU-hours reclaimed, workloads with exemptions.
3Service received
p50 and p90 wait by job size, preemptions suffered and work lost, fairness ratio.
4Showback
the cost of allocated-but-idle GPU-hours, so idle capacity has a visible price; chargeback where the organization uses it.
5Trend
week over week, against the team's own baseline, not against other teams.

The code. Building a team's weekly scorecard from the warehouse (Python).

def scorecard(team, week, w):    """w: warehouse access returning per-minute aggregates for the team and week."""    m = w.team_minutes(team, week)                       # allocated, active, guaranteed, borrowed, lent    jobs = w.team_jobs(team, week)                       # waits, sizes, preemptions    gpu_h = lambda col: m[col].sum() / 60    return {        "team": team, "week": week,        "guaranteed_avg": m.guaranteed.mean(),        "allocated_avg": m.allocated.mean(),        "active_avg": m.active.mean(),        "activity_rate": gpu_h("active") / max(gpu_h("allocated"), 1e-9),        "idle_cost_usd": (gpu_h("allocated") - gpu_h("active")) * w.price_per_gpu_h,   # showback        "borrowed_gpu_h": gpu_h("borrowed"), "lent_gpu_h": gpu_h("lent"),        "p90_wait_h_by_size": jobs.groupby("size_class").wait_h.quantile(0.9).round(1).to_dict(),        "preemption_lost_gpu_h": jobs.lost_gpu_h.sum(),        "fairness_ratio": w.fairness_ratio(team, week),    }
Going deeper2 points
  • Show what the team gets, not just what it costs: wait times and borrowed capacity are on the same page as idle cost; scorecards that only criticize get ignored.
  • Lent GPU-hours are a contribution: teams whose idle quota helped others should see that credited.

Running the layer: SLOs and continuous tuning

Scenario. After the project ended, nobody owned the scheduler. A Kueue upgrade changed a default, and nobody noticed that 256-GPU jobs started waiting twice as long.

What the picture shows. The scheduling layer as a service with an owner and objectives.

1SLOs
active utilization during periods with pending demand, p90 wait per size class, work lost to preemption, and fairness ratio; reviewed monthly.
2Alerts
on guardrail breaches and sudden changes (a wait-time jump after an upgrade).
3Upgrade testing
Kueue and Kubernetes upgrades are replayed in the simulator and rolled out to one pool first, like policy changes.
4Tuning loop
each quarter, the attribution waterfall and scorecards pick the next lever: more idle reclaim, better packing, quota rebalancing or new capacity.
5Capacity decisions
the same data answers "do we need more GPUs?": if utilization during high-demand periods is near its ceiling and waits are long, the answer is yes.
Going deeper2 points
  • Utilization has a healthy ceiling: above roughly 85–90% active utilization, waits grow quickly for large gangs; the target is high utilization with acceptable waits, not 100%.
  • Keep the change log forever: months later, a question like "when did large-job waits get worse?" is answered by lining up the metric with the log.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, agree and measure (weeks 1–6): the metric definition signed off; the pipeline; a four-week baseline by team and pool; the simulator calibrated against the baseline.
  • Phase 2, quick wins (weeks 6–12): quotas as code; idle reclamation for notebooks; gang admission for all multi-node jobs. Each staged with a comparison pool and attributed.
  • Phase 3, structural changes (weeks 12–20): bin-packing profiles and pools by job shape; cohorts with borrowing and lending; fair-share weights.
  • Phase 4, keep it (ongoing): scorecards, SLOs, upgrade testing and the quarterly tuning loop.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • A slower start: six weeks of definitions and baseline before the first change, in exchange for results that hold up.
  • Comparison pools delay gains for some teams by a few weeks during staged rollout.
  • Idle reclamation inconveniences people: warnings, grace periods and exemptions soften it but don't remove it.
  • Active utilization below 100% by design: headroom keeps large-job waits acceptable.

Open questions.

  • Better activity signals: is graphics-engine activity the right threshold signal for all workloads, or should inference and training use different ones?
  • Elastic jobs: how much more utilization would jobs that grow and shrink with free capacity unlock, and how would we measure it?
  • Incentives: does showback change behavior, or is automatic reclamation the only thing that works?
  • Fleet-wide view: how to measure and attribute utilization across many clusters and providers (Design 18) with different contracts?
Design 20 · 12 sections

Design 20: Distributed training on PyTorch, Ray and Megatron with fast checkpointing and model loading

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Choosing the framework
  3. Launching PyTorch Distributed on Kubernetes
  4. Ray Train on KubeRay
  5. Megatron: mapping parallelism onto the topology
  6. Anatomy of a sharded checkpoint
  7. Fast checkpointing: stall only for the copy
  8. Tiered checkpoint storage
  9. Fast restarts: loading, resharding and the first step
  10. Fast model loading for evaluation and inference
  11. Measuring checkpoint and loading performance
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we run distributed training on Kubernetes with PyTorch Distributed, Ray or Megatron, while keeping checkpoint saves from stalling training and keeping restarts and model loads short? Each framework has its strengths: plain PyTorch with FSDP2 for most fine-tuning and mid-sized pre-training, Ray Train when training is one stage of a larger Python pipeline, and Megatron Core when a model needs tensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism together. The platform runs all three through one path: Kueue admission (Design 17), framework-specific launchers, and one checkpoint and model-loading layer that they share.

The short version: launch all three the same way, checkpoint in shards, asynchronously and in tiers, and treat loading as seriously as saving. Every rank writes its own shard of the model and optimizer state. Training only pauses while tensors are copied to pinned host memory, and a background process writes the copy to local NVMe and then uploads it to object storage. Restarts read from the nearest tier that has a complete checkpoint, and can reshard to a new world size. Evaluation and inference load weights from parallel streams or registry-mounted volumes, not from a single slow download. Two numbers, checkpoint stall per save and time from pod start to first training step, are tracked like any other SLO.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The platform runs three kinds of training. Fine-tuning teams use PyTorch FSDP2 on 8 to 64 GPUs. An RL team runs Ray, with rollout workers, reward models and a trainer in one program. The pre-training team runs Megatron Core on 1,024 H100s for a 70B model with tensor, pipeline and data parallelism. All three complain about the same things: saving a checkpoint pauses the 1,024-GPU job for 6 minutes every hour, a restart after a node failure takes 38 minutes before the first step, and loading a 140 GB checkpoint into an evaluation job takes 20 minutes.

What the platform must deliver.

  • One way to submit: all three frameworks go through Kueue, with gang admission and topology-aware placement.
  • Short checkpoint stalls: under 30 seconds of training time lost per save on the largest job.
  • Frequent checkpoints: an interval set by failure rate (Young–Daly), not by how much the stall hurts.
  • Fast restarts: under 8 minutes from failure to the first training step on the largest job.
  • Resharding: resume on a different number of GPUs or a different parallel layout.
  • Fast model loading: evaluation and inference jobs load a 70B model in under 2 minutes.
  • Durability: a checkpoint counts only once it is complete and verified in object storage.

Out of scope: in-job fault tolerance and failure handling (Design 14), and the scheduling policy itself (Design 17, Design 19).

Choosing the framework

Scenario. A new team asked which framework to use for a 13B fine-tune. They had seen a Megatron recipe, a Ray example and a plain PyTorch script, and they spent a week trying all three.

What the picture shows. A decision guide based on the model size and the shape of the program.

1PyTorch Distributed (torchrun + FSDP2)
the default. Sharded data parallelism with fully_shard covers most models up to tens of billions of parameters. It's plain PyTorch, so it's easy to debug.
2Ray Train on KubeRay
when training is one part of a Python program with other distributed parts, such as RL rollouts, data preprocessing or reward models. Ray starts the workers and sets up torch.distributed for you, and the training loop is still PyTorch.
3Megatron Core
when the model needs tensor, pipeline, context or expert parallelism to fit or to run efficiently. This usually means very large dense models, mixture-of-experts models or very long sequences. Its fused kernels and distributed optimizer give the best throughput at scale.
4The shared layer
all three use PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint (DCP) underneath. Megatron's torch_dist format builds on it, and Ray Train uploads whatever directory the training loop writes. So one checkpoint storage design serves all three.
Going deeper2 points
  • Combinations are normal: an RL system often runs Megatron or FSDP2 trainers inside Ray actors. The framework choice is per component, not per team.
  • Pick by parallelism needs, not by fashion: if FSDP2 fits the model with good throughput, adding tensor parallelism mostly adds complexity.

Launching PyTorch Distributed on Kubernetes

Scenario. Teams wrote their own StatefulSets for torchrun, each with a different way to find the master address. One of them hard-coded the rank-0 pod name, so every restart hung when that pod moved.

What the picture shows. One TrainJob per run, expanded by a shared runtime into a JobSet whose pods find each other through stable DNS.

1ClusterTrainingRuntime
maintained by the platform team. It defines the image, the torchrun launch, NCCL environment, volumes for local NVMe and pinned shared memory, and the failure policy.
2TrainJob
written by the team. It names the runtime, the number of nodes, GPUs per node and the command.
3JobSet and headless Service
created by the trainer controller, so rank 0 has a stable DNS name and torchrun's rendezvous works after restarts.
4Kueue
admits the whole TrainJob as one gang, with topology constraints so all nodes land in one fabric block.

The YAML. A team's TrainJob for a 64-GPU FSDP2 run (Kubeflow Trainer v2).

apiVersion: trainer.kubeflow.org/v1alpha1kind: TrainJobmetadata:  name: sft-13b-run42  namespace: team-finetune  labels:    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: finetune  annotations:    kueue.x-k8s.io/podset-required-topology: network.example.com/fabric-block   # one block for all 8 nodesspec:  runtimeRef:    apiGroup: trainer.kubeflow.org    kind: ClusterTrainingRuntime    name: torch-distributed-h100            # platform-maintained: NCCL env, /dev/shm, local NVMe, failure policy  trainer:    numNodes: 8    numProcPerNode: 8    image: registry.example.com/finetune/trainer:2026.11.3    command: ["python", "-m", "train.sft", "--config", "configs/13b.yaml"]    env:    - { name: CKPT_URI, value: "s3://ckpt-finetune/sft-13b-run42" }    - { name: CKPT_LOCAL, value: "/local-nvme/ckpt" }    resourcesPerNode:      limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 }
Going deeper3 points
  • Use elastic rendezvous (c10d) even for fixed-size jobs: torchrun's c10d backend handles a restarted pod rejoining, which a static master address doesn't.
  • Put platform defaults in the runtime: shared memory size, NCCL timeouts, the checkpoint volume and the preStop flush hook belong in the runtime, so a hundred TrainJobs don't each get them wrong.
  • Older guides use PyTorchJob. That is the API of Kubeflow's Training Operator v1, which Kubeflow's docs now file under "legacy v1" and replace with TrainJob and runtimes (migration guide). For all-or-nothing placement, a runtime can ask for Volcano groups with podGroupPolicy (Trainer guide). Since Trainer 2.4, its scheduling block can instead have the controller create the Kubernetes Workload and PodGroup objects, which needs the beta gate that is off by default (Trainer 2.4 post).

Ray Train on KubeRay

Scenario. The RL team ran a long-lived RayCluster shared by everyone on the team. Jobs competed for its GPUs without Kueue seeing them, and a crashed driver left GPUs reserved for days.

What the picture shows. One RayJob per run, with its own RayCluster, admitted by Kueue and deleted when the run ends.

1RayJob
creates the RayCluster from rayClusterSpec, submits the entrypoint, and deletes the cluster when the job finishes (shutdownAfterJobFinishes: true, which Kueue requires).
2Worker groups
separate groups for trainer GPUs, rollout GPUs and CPU-only data workers, each a pod set that Kueue accounts for.
3Ray Train
TorchTrainer starts one worker per GPU, sets up the process group, and handles reporting and checkpoint upload to storage_path.
4Checkpoints
the training loop writes a DCP checkpoint to local disk, and ray.train.report hands the directory to Ray, which uploads it to object storage.

The code. A Ray Train loop that saves sharded DCP checkpoints and resumes from the latest one (Python).

import os, tempfileimport ray.trainimport torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcpfrom ray.train import ScalingConfig, RunConfig, CheckpointConfig, Checkpointfrom ray.train.torch import TorchTrainerfrom torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import get_state_dict, set_state_dict def train_loop(cfg):    model, optim, loader = build(cfg)                     # FSDP2-wrapped model, optimizer, data loader    start = 0    if (ckpt := ray.train.get_checkpoint()):              # resume after a failure or preemption        with ckpt.as_directory() as d:            msd, osd = get_state_dict(model, optim)            state = {"model": msd, "optim": osd, "step": 0}            dcp.load(state, checkpoint_id=d)              # each rank reads only its shards            set_state_dict(model, optim, model_state_dict=state["model"], optim_state_dict=state["optim"])            start = state["step"]    for step in range(start, cfg["steps"]):        loss = train_step(model, optim, next(loader))        if step % cfg["ckpt_every"] == 0:            d = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir=os.environ.get("CKPT_LOCAL", "/tmp"))            msd, osd = get_state_dict(model, optim)            dcp.save({"model": msd, "optim": osd, "step": step}, checkpoint_id=d)            ray.train.report({"loss": loss.item(), "step": step}, checkpoint=Checkpoint.from_directory(d))        else:            ray.train.report({"loss": loss.item(), "step": step}) trainer = TorchTrainer(    train_loop, train_loop_config={"steps": 20_000, "ckpt_every": 500},    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=32, use_gpu=True),    run_config=RunConfig(name="rl-policy-run7", storage_path="s3://ckpt-rl/ray",                         checkpoint_config=CheckpointConfig(num_to_keep=3)),)trainer.fit()
Going deeper2 points
  • One cluster per job: long-lived shared Ray clusters hide GPU usage from the scheduler. Short-lived RayJobs make each run a gang that Kueue can admit, account for and preempt.
  • Ray's upload is synchronous by default: for large checkpoints, write with DCP's async path first (next sections) and report the directory once the local write completes.

Megatron: mapping parallelism onto the topology

Scenario. The 70B run used TP=8, PP=8, DP=16. A config change put tensor-parallel groups across two nodes, so every layer's all-reduce went over InfiniBand instead of NVLink. Throughput fell by 40%.

What the picture shows. How Megatron's parallel groups map onto nodes, racks and fabric blocks.

1Tensor parallelism (TP)
the most communication-heavy, so it stays inside one node over NVLink (TP ≤ 8 on 8-GPU nodes).
2Pipeline parallelism (PP)
point-to-point activation transfers between stages. It spans nodes, ideally within one rack or leaf switch.
3Data parallelism (DP), with the distributed optimizer
gradient reduce-scatter and parameter all-gather once per step. It spans the fabric block.
4Context and expert parallelism (CP, EP)
placed by communication volume. Expert all-to-all is often as heavy as TP.
5Rank order
Megatron assigns ranks so that TP is the innermost dimension. The platform's job is to make consecutive ranks land on the same node and the same rack. Topology-aware admission and a rank-ordered pod index do this.

The code. Checking that a parallel layout maps onto the hardware before launch (Python).

def check_layout(world: int, tp: int, pp: int, cp: int = 1, ep: int = 1,                 gpus_per_node: int = 8, nodes_per_rack: int = 16) -> list[str]:    errors = []    if world % (tp * pp * cp) != 0:        errors.append(f"world {world} not divisible by tp*pp*cp={tp*pp*cp}")    dp = world // (tp * pp * cp)    if tp > gpus_per_node or gpus_per_node % tp:        errors.append(f"TP={tp} crosses node boundaries (gpus_per_node={gpus_per_node})")   # NVLink only    if ep > 1 and dp * cp % ep:        errors.append(f"EP={ep} must divide dp*cp={dp*cp}")    stage_nodes = tp * cp * dp // gpus_per_node                # nodes holding one pipeline stage    if pp > 1 and stage_nodes > nodes_per_rack:        errors.append(f"one pipeline stage spans {stage_nodes} nodes: wider than a rack")    return errors or [f"ok: tp={tp} pp={pp} cp={cp} dp={dp} ep={ep}"] print(check_layout(world=1024, tp=8, pp=8))      # ok: tp=8 pp=8 cp=1 dp=16 ep=1print(check_layout(world=1024, tp=16, pp=4))     # TP=16 crosses node boundaries
Going deeper2 points
  • The layout is part of the checkpoint question: Megatron's default distributed-optimizer format (dp_reshardable) saves and loads fast but can't change TP or PP. Changing the layout means one save in the fully_reshardable format (--dist-ckpt-optim-fully-reshardable) and switching back afterwards.
  • Measure before scaling: run the layout for a few hundred steps on the target topology and compare tokens per second per GPU with the benchmark (Design 15) before committing a month of compute.

Anatomy of a sharded checkpoint

Scenario. The old checkpointing code gathered the full state on rank 0 and called torch.save. For the 70B model with Adam states (about 1.1 TB), rank 0 ran out of host memory, and the other 1,023 GPUs waited while one process wrote one file.

What the picture shows. What a distributed checkpoint contains and who writes what.

1Sharded state
each rank writes the shards it owns: its slice of the parameters, the optimizer moments and the master weights. Nothing is gathered.
2Deduplication
replicated tensors (for example, the same shard on several data-parallel replicas) are written once. The planner spreads the writing across the replicas so no rank does more than its share.
3Metadata
a small file mapping every logical tensor (name, global shape, offsets) to the files and byte ranges holding it. This is what makes resharding possible.
4Everything else needed to resume exactly
step, learning-rate scheduler, data-loader position and random-number-generator states, saved as small per-rank or global entries.
5Completion marker
written last, after every rank's files and the metadata are durable. A checkpoint without it doesn't exist.

The code. A complete, resumable training state with DCP and the Stateful protocol (Python).

import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcpfrom torch.distributed.checkpoint.stateful import Statefulfrom torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import get_state_dict, set_state_dict class TrainState(Stateful):    def __init__(self, model, optim, sched, loader, rng):        self.model, self.optim, self.sched, self.loader, self.rng = model, optim, sched, loader, rng        self.step = 0     def state_dict(self):        msd, osd = get_state_dict(self.model, self.optim)        # sharded DTensors, no gather        return {"model": msd, "optim": osd, "sched": self.sched.state_dict(),                "loader": self.loader.state_dict(), "rng": self.rng.state_dict(), "step": self.step}     def load_state_dict(self, sd):        set_state_dict(self.model, self.optim, model_state_dict=sd["model"], optim_state_dict=sd["optim"])        self.sched.load_state_dict(sd["sched"]); self.loader.load_state_dict(sd["loader"])        self.rng.load_state_dict(sd["rng"]); self.step = sd["step"] state = TrainState(model, optim, sched, loader, rng)dcp.save({"train": state}, checkpoint_id=f"/local-nvme/ckpt/step-{state.step:07d}")
Going deeper2 points
  • The data loader's position matters: resuming with the right weights but restarting the data stream replays the same examples. That's a quiet bias, not a crash.
  • Megatron's equivalent: --ckpt-format torch_dist builds on DCP and adds sharded-state metadata for TP, PP, EP and the distributed optimizer, so the same storage layer works for both.

Fast checkpointing: stall only for the copy

Scenario. Even with sharded saving, the 1,024-GPU job paused for 6 minutes per checkpoint because each rank wrote 1.1 GB directly to a network filesystem while training waited.

What the picture shows. Splitting a save into a short blocking stage and a long background stage.

1Stage (blocking)
copy the rank's shards from GPU memory to host memory. With a reused pinned-memory buffer this is a direct memory copy at tens of GB/s. For about 1.1 GB per rank it takes about a second.
2Persist (background)
a separate process writes the host copy to local NVMe. Training continues on the GPUs at the same time.
3Upload (background)
another background step copies the local checkpoint to object storage and writes the completion marker last.
4Back-pressure
at most one save in flight. If the previous save hasn't finished staging when the next is due, wait for it rather than piling up host-memory copies.
5Process, not thread
the background writer runs in a separate process, so Python's GIL doesn't slow the training loop.

The code. Asynchronous DCP saving with process-based execution and one save in flight (Python).

import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcpfrom torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict_saver import AsyncCheckpointerType class AsyncCheckpointer:    def __init__(self, local_root: str, uploader):        self.local_root, self.uploader, self.pending = local_root, uploader, None     def maybe_save(self, step: int, state, every: int):        if step % every:            return        if self.pending is not None:            self.pending.result()                                 # back-pressure: one save in flight        path = f"{self.local_root}/step-{step:07d}"        self.pending = dcp.async_save(            {"train": state}, checkpoint_id=path,            async_checkpointer_type=AsyncCheckpointerType.PROCESS,   # writer outside the training process        )        self.pending.add_done_callback(lambda f, p=path, s=step: self.uploader.enqueue(p, s))     def flush(self):                                              # call from the preStop / SIGTERM handler        if self.pending is not None:            self.pending.result()        self.uploader.drain()
Going deeper2 points
  • Pinned host memory has a cost: the staging buffer stays allocated between saves (about the size of the rank's shard). Budget it into the pod's memory request, and make sure the node's page-locked memory limit allows it.
  • Megatron: --async-save with the torch_dist format does the same staging and background persist. Newer Megatron Core versions use the NVIDIA Resiliency Extension for the async path.

Tiered checkpoint storage

Scenario. Every checkpoint went straight to a shared filesystem. With 1,024 ranks writing at once, the filesystem's metadata server became the bottleneck. Other teams' jobs slowed down every hour on the hour.

What the picture shows. Three tiers with different speeds, durability and cost.

1Tier 0, host memory (optional)
the staged copy, plus, in some designs, a copy in a peer node's memory. Fastest to restore, lost if both nodes fail.
2Tier 1, local NVMe
every save lands here first at several GB/s per node. Survives a process crash, lost when the node is replaced.
3Tier 2, object storage
every Nth checkpoint (or every checkpoint, uploaded in the background) is copied here with retries and checksums. Durable across node, rack and cluster failures.
4Retention
keep the last 2 on NVMe, the last 5 plus daily and milestone checkpoints in object storage, and expire the rest by lifecycle rules.
5Restore order
the newest complete checkpoint across tiers. Local NVMe if every rank still has its shards there, otherwise object storage.

The YAML. Runtime volumes and the uploader sidecar for tiered checkpoints (fragment of the ClusterTrainingRuntime pod template).

spec:  initContainers:  - name: ckpt-uploader                       # native sidecar: starts first, stops after the trainer    image: registry.example.com/platform/ckpt-uploader:1.8    restartPolicy: Always    args: ["--watch=/local-nvme/ckpt", "--dest=$(CKPT_URI)", "--parallel=32",           "--marker=COMPLETE", "--keep-local=2"]          # upload shards, then write the marker last    volumeMounts: [{ name: local-nvme, mountPath: /local-nvme }]  containers:  - name: node    volumeMounts:    - { name: local-nvme, mountPath: /local-nvme }    - { name: dshm, mountPath: /dev/shm }    lifecycle:      preStop: { exec: { command: ["/opt/train/flush-checkpoint.sh"] } }   # finish in-flight save on eviction  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 300  volumes:  - name: local-nvme    ephemeral:      volumeClaimTemplate:        spec: { storageClassName: local-nvme-raid0, accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce], resources: { requests: { storage: 3Ti } } }  - name: dshm    emptyDir: { medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 64Gi }
Going deeper2 points
  • Object storage likes many parallel streams: 1,024 ranks each uploading their own files with multipart uploads use the aggregate bandwidth well. The limits to watch are request rates per prefix, so spread checkpoint keys by rank.
  • Verify before you trust: the uploader records checksums, and a periodic job loads a sample of checkpoints in a small cluster to prove they restore (Design 14).

Fast restarts: loading, resharding and the first step

Scenario. After a node failure, the 70B job took 38 minutes to take its first step again: 6 minutes rescheduling, 9 minutes pulling a 22 GB image, 18 minutes reading the checkpoint from the shared filesystem, and 5 minutes compiling and warming up.

What the picture shows. The restart timeline before and after, and what removes each part.

1Rescheduling
a hot-spare node or a warm reservation means Kueue re-admits the job immediately (Design 14).
2Image pull
images pre-pulled on GPU nodes, lazy-loading snapshotters, or a node-local registry mirror. The 22 GB image is already there.
3Checkpoint read
the surviving 127 nodes read their shards from local NVMe. Only the replacement node reads from object storage, with many parallel range requests.
4Peer restore
where data-parallel replicas hold identical shards, the new node can receive its shard from a peer over the fabric, faster than from object storage.
5Warm-up
cached compilation artifacts (for example, a shared torch.compile or Triton cache) cut the first-step compile time.
6Resharding
when the job resumes on a different world size, DCP's metadata lets each new rank read the byte ranges it now owns, so no conversion job is needed.

The code. Choosing the restore source per rank and resuming on a different world size (Python).
