import os, torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp def newest_complete(local_root: str, remote, required_step: int | None = None) -> str:    """Newest checkpoint that is complete for *every* rank; prefer local NVMe when all ranks have it."""    local = sorted(p for p in os.listdir(local_root) if p.startswith("step-"))    have = local[-1] if local else ""    t = torch.tensor([int(have.split("-")[1]) if have else -1], device="cuda")    dist.all_reduce(t, op=dist.ReduceOp.MIN)                       # all ranks must have it locally    remote_step = remote.latest_with_marker()    if t.item() >= 0 and t.item() >= remote_step:        return f"{local_root}/step-{t.item():07d}"    return remote.uri(remote_step)                                  # read shards with parallel range GETs def resume(state, local_root, remote):    path = newest_complete(local_root, remote)    dcp.load({"train": state}, checkpoint_id=path)    # works on a new world size: planner reads by offsets    return path
Going deeper2 points
  • Track restart time as a budget: schedule, pull, read, warm-up, each with a target. The slowest part changes after every fix.
  • Resharding costs read bandwidth: a world-size change means every rank reads from many files. Prefer object storage with high concurrency over a shared filesystem for this case.

Fast model loading for evaluation and inference

Scenario. Every evaluation job downloaded the 140 GB checkpoint from object storage with a single-threaded client, converted it to Hugging Face format on one CPU, then loaded it. Twenty minutes per job, and 200 evaluation jobs per week.

What the picture shows. The path from a training checkpoint to a model that serves in under 2 minutes.

1Export once
a post-checkpoint job converts milestone checkpoints to safetensors (sharded by tensor-parallel rank if the server needs it) and records the export in the model registry. Evaluation jobs never convert.
2Stream, don't download
a model streamer reads tensors from object storage with many concurrent readers straight into host buffers and then GPU memory. In vLLM this is --load-format runai_streamer.
3Or mount from a registry
weights packaged as an OCI artifact and mounted with an image volume, cached on the node by the container runtime. This is useful for models that many pods load repeatedly.
4Node-local cache
a DaemonSet-managed cache on NVMe holds recently used models, so the second job on a node loads from local disk.
5Pre-sharded weights
for tensor-parallel servers, each GPU reads only its own shard (runai_streamer_sharded) instead of reading everything and slicing.

The YAML. An evaluation server that streams pre-sharded weights from object storage (vLLM).

apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata: { name: eval-70b-step120k, namespace: eval }spec:  replicas: 1  selector: { matchLabels: { app: eval-70b } }  template:    metadata: { labels: { app: eval-70b } }    spec:      serviceAccountName: eval-reader                     # read-only access to the export bucket      containers:      - name: vllm        image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0        args:        - s3://model-exports/llm-70b/step-120000-tp8        - --tensor-parallel-size=8        - --load-format=runai_streamer_sharded             # each GPU streams only its own shard        - --model-loader-extra-config={"concurrency":32}        resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Loading time is bandwidth arithmetic: 140 GB in 2 minutes needs about 1.2 GB/s sustained. A single stream rarely does that, and 32 parallel streams from object storage usually do. Measure the node's NIC and the bucket's limits first.
  • Version the export, not just the checkpoint: the registry records which training checkpoint, which conversion code and which sharding produced each export, so evaluation results trace back to exact weights (Design 15).

Measuring checkpoint and loading performance

Scenario. After the async change, the team said checkpoints were "basically free". A month later, a model-size increase doubled host-memory staging time, and nobody noticed for three weeks.

What the picture shows. The metrics that make checkpointing and loading visible.

1Checkpoint stall
training time blocked per save (the stage step plus any back-pressure wait), per job. The SLO is under 30 seconds on the largest job.
2Background duration
time to local completion and to durable upload. If upload takes longer than the save interval, saves queue up.
3Recovery point
the age of the newest durable checkpoint. It bounds how much work a total failure loses.
4Restart time
from failure detection to first step, broken down by phase.
5Model load time
from pod start to ready, by model size and load method.
6Goodput
productive training time divided by wall-clock time, net of stalls, restarts and lost work (Design 14).

The code. Choosing the checkpoint interval from measured stall time and failure rate (Young–Daly) and reporting the expected overhead (Python).

import math def checkpoint_plan(stall_s: float, mtbf_h: float, restart_s: float) -> dict:    """stall_s: training time lost per save; mtbf_h: job-level mean time between failures."""    mtbf_s = mtbf_h * 3600    interval = math.sqrt(2 * stall_s * mtbf_s)                 # Young–Daly optimum    save_overhead = stall_s / interval    expected_rework = (interval / 2 + restart_s) / mtbf_s      # half an interval lost per failure, plus restart    return {"interval_min": round(interval / 60, 1),            "save_overhead_pct": round(100 * save_overhead, 2),            "failure_overhead_pct": round(100 * expected_rework, 2),            "goodput_ceiling_pct": round(100 * (1 - save_overhead - expected_rework), 1)} print(checkpoint_plan(stall_s=360, mtbf_h=4, restart_s=38 * 60))   # before: sync saves, slow restartsprint(checkpoint_plan(stall_s=20,  mtbf_h=4, restart_s=7 * 60))    # after: async saves, fast restarts
Going deeper2 points
  • The interval follows the stall: with a 6-minute stall the best interval is about 54 minutes. With a 20-second stall it's about 13 minutes, so each failure costs about a quarter as much rework.
  • Alert on trends, not just thresholds: stall time growing with model size or with host-memory pressure is the early warning.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, one launch path (weeks 1–4): ClusterTrainingRuntimes for torchrun and Megatron, RayJob templates, all through Kueue with topology-aware gangs.
  • Phase 2, sharded and async checkpoints (weeks 4–8): DCP everywhere, async process-based saves, completion markers, and stall and recovery-point metrics.
  • Phase 3, tiers and restarts (weeks 8–12): local NVMe tier, the uploader sidecar, restore-from-nearest-tier, pre-pulled images, compile caches and the restart-time breakdown.
  • Phase 4, model loading (weeks 10–14): export jobs, the model registry, streamed and sharded loading, and node caches for evaluation and inference.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • More host memory per node for pinned staging buffers.
  • Local NVMe can lose the newest checkpoint when a node dies before upload. The recovery point is the last durable checkpoint, not the last save.
  • Megatron's fast checkpoint format isn't reshardable. Changing the layout costs one slower save.
  • Exports duplicate storage: milestone checkpoints exist in training format and serving format.

Open questions.

  • In-memory checkpointing: how far can peer replication in host memory cut the recovery point before object-storage upload becomes the only durability guarantee?
  • Checkpoint-free recovery: can fault-tolerant training (replica groups that continue without a failed member) replace most restarts (Design 14)?
  • One format for training and serving: could exports be avoided if serving engines read DCP checkpoints directly?
  • Cross-cluster restarts: what's the fastest way to resume a job in another cluster or cloud (Design 18) when the newest checkpoint is in the wrong region?
Design 21 · 12 sections

Design 21: Deploying and tuning high-throughput LLM serving

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Characterize the workload and the SLO
  3. Parallelism for dense models
  4. Expert parallelism for mixture-of-experts models
  5. Engine tuning: batching, scheduling and caching
  6. Prefill/decode disaggregation
  7. Routing: cache-aware and phase-aware
  8. KV cache offload
  9. FP8 and FP4 quantization with an accuracy gate
  10. Benchmarking and the tuning loop
  11. Autoscaling and operations
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we deploy LLMs on Kubernetes so they serve as many tokens per GPU as possible while still meeting latency targets? The levers are well known: tensor, data and expert parallelism; splitting prefill from decode; offloading KV cache to host memory; and FP8 or FP4 quantization. The hard part is knowing which lever helps which workload, applying them together without breaking each other, and proving the result with benchmarks that reflect real traffic. vLLM is the engine here. SGLang and TensorRT-LLM offer the same levers under different names.

The short version: start from the workload and the SLO, not from the features. Measure input and output lengths and how much prompt prefix requests share. Define throughput as goodput: tokens per second per GPU from requests that met their time-to-first-token and inter-token-latency targets. Pick parallelism by model shape: tensor parallelism within a node for dense models, data-parallel attention with expert parallelism for large mixture-of-experts models. Quantize with an accuracy gate. Add KV offload when prefix reuse is high, and prefill/decode disaggregation when long prompts hurt decode latency. Route requests with a cache-aware endpoint picker. Every change is a benchmarked experiment against the same traffic replay.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The platform serves two models. A 70B dense model handles chat and a coding assistant on 64 H100s. A large mixture-of-experts model (about 670B total parameters, about 37B active per token) serves agent workloads on 32 B200s. Traffic doubled in a quarter. Coding requests carry 20,000-token prompts that share most of their prefix, and during spikes their prefills make chat's token streaming stutter. Finance asks for 40% more requests per GPU before any new hardware.

What the platform must deliver.

  • Latency SLOs per product: for chat, p95 time to first token (TTFT) under 1 s and p95 inter-token latency (ITL) under 50 ms. For the coding assistant, p95 TTFT under 3 s with 20k-token prompts.
  • Goodput as the throughput metric: tokens per second per GPU from requests that met their SLO.
  • Model-aware parallelism: a layout per model and GPU type, checked before deployment.
  • Quantization with an accuracy gate: no quantized model ships unless it passes the evaluation suite within agreed deltas.
  • KV cache that lasts: shared prefixes stay cached beyond GPU memory.
  • Isolation of prefill from decode where long prompts hurt streaming latency.
  • Repeatable tuning: every configuration change benchmarked against replayed production traffic.

Out of scope: model loading speed (Design 20), training-side model export, and multi-cluster routing (Design 02).

Characterize the workload and the SLO

Scenario. The team tuned the 70B deployment with a benchmark of 512-token prompts and 128-token answers. Production chat had a median prompt of 3,000 tokens and answers of 600, so the tuned settings were wrong for real traffic.

What the picture shows. The measurements that decide which levers matter.

1Input and output length distributions per product
long inputs make prefill dominant. Long outputs make decode and KV memory dominant.
2Prefix sharing
the fraction of each prompt's tokens that already appeared in a recent request (system prompts, documents, repository context). High sharing makes prefix caching and KV offload valuable.
3Arrival pattern
bursts determine queueing, and so the headroom needed to meet TTFT.
4KV bytes per token
from the model's architecture. This sets how many tokens fit on a GPU and so the batch size decode can sustain.
5SLO per product
TTFT and ITL percentiles. Goodput counts only requests that meet both.

The code. KV-cache size per token and the token capacity of a deployment (Python).

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers: int, kv_heads: int, head_dim: int, dtype_bytes: float) -> float:    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes          # K and V for every layer def kv_capacity_tokens(gpus: int, hbm_gb: float, weights_gb: float, kv_per_token: float,                       util: float = 0.90, activation_gb_per_gpu: float = 6.0) -> int:    free = gpus * (hbm_gb * util - activation_gb_per_gpu) - weights_gb    return int(free * 1e9 / kv_per_token) # 70B dense model: 80 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), head_dim 128bf16 = kv_bytes_per_token(80, 8, 128, 2)       # 327,680 B ≈ 320 KiB per tokenfp8 = kv_bytes_per_token(80, 8, 128, 1)        # half thatprint(kv_capacity_tokens(4, 80, 140, bf16))    # BF16 weights + BF16 KV on 4 × H100print(kv_capacity_tokens(4, 80, 70, fp8))      # FP8 weights + FP8 KV: about 4× the tokens
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure from logs, not guesses: gateway logs with token counts and prefix hashes give the distributions. Replay them for every benchmark (Design 15).
  • Goodput keeps tuning honest: raw tokens per second always improves with bigger batches until latency collapses. Goodput peaks where the SLO starts to break.

Parallelism for dense models

Scenario. The 70B model ran with tensor parallelism of 8 on every node, because "more GPUs per replica is faster". At production load, eight TP=2 replicas would have served 50% more requests per node within the SLO.

What the picture shows. How tensor, pipeline and data parallelism trade latency for throughput.

1Tensor parallelism (TP)
splits each layer across GPUs in a node, with an all-reduce per layer over NVLink. Higher TP lowers per-token latency and frees memory for KV cache, but adds communication and cuts the number of replicas.
2Data parallelism (DP), meaning more replicas
each replica serves its own requests. This scales throughput linearly with no communication between replicas.
3Pipeline parallelism (PP)
only when a model doesn't fit in one node. It adds latency per stage and needs enough concurrent requests to keep stages busy.
4The rule of thumb
use the smallest TP that fits the weights plus enough KV cache for the target batch, then add replicas. Increase TP only when ITL misses the SLO.
5Quantization changes the answer
FP8 halves weight memory, so a 70B model fits on fewer GPUs with more KV room.

The code. Choosing the smallest TP that leaves enough KV cache for the target concurrency (Python).

def choose_tp(weights_gb, kv_per_token, target_concurrency, mean_context,              hbm_gb=80, options=(1, 2, 4, 8)):    need = target_concurrency * mean_context                     # tokens resident at the target load    for tp in options:        cap = kv_capacity_tokens(tp, hbm_gb, weights_gb, kv_per_token)        if cap >= need * 1.2:                                     # 20% headroom for bursts            return {"tp": tp, "kv_tokens": cap, "replicas_per_node": 8 // tp}    return {"tp": None, "reason": "use PP across nodes or quantize"} print(choose_tp(70, fp8, target_concurrency=64, mean_context=3600))   # FP8 70B, chat traffic
Going deeper2 points
  • Benchmark the two closest layouts: the sizing gives a candidate. A replayed-traffic benchmark of TP=2 and TP=4 decides.
  • Pin the layout to the GPU type: the same model may use TP=4 on H100 and TP=2 on B200, so the deployment templates are keyed by both.

Expert parallelism for mixture-of-experts models

Scenario. The MoE model ran with TP=8 per node across 4 nodes, splitting every expert across 32 GPUs. Expert layers spent most of their time in all-reduce, and the batch per GPU was tiny.

What the picture shows. Data-parallel attention with expert parallelism (wide EP).

1Attention layers
replicated in data-parallel ranks (TP=1 or a small TP), each rank handling its own requests and KV cache. Latent-attention models have small KV caches, which favors this.
2Expert layers
each GPU holds a subset of experts. Tokens are sent to the GPUs holding their chosen experts and back with all-to-all (dispatch and combine). The EP size is TP × DP.
3Communication kernels
DeepEP high-throughput kernels suit prefill, and low-latency kernels with CUDA-graph support suit decode. Multi-node NVLink systems have their own all-to-all backends.
4Expert load balancing (EPLB)
popular experts are replicated and placement is rebalanced from observed load, so one hot GPU doesn't set the step time.
5On Kubernetes
a LeaderWorkerSet runs each serving group (leader plus workers across nodes) as a unit that's created, restarted and scaled together, with topology constraints so the group stays on one fabric block.

The YAML. A 32-GPU wide-EP serving group as a LeaderWorkerSet (vLLM, 4 nodes × 8 GPUs).

apiVersion: leaderworkerset.x-k8s.io/v1kind: LeaderWorkerSetmetadata: { name: moe-decode, namespace: serving }spec:  replicas: 1  leaderWorkerTemplate:    size: 4                                                # 1 leader + 3 workers = 32 GPUs    restartPolicy: RecreateGroupOnPodRestart               # one failed pod restarts the whole group    leaderTemplate:      metadata: { labels: { role: leader, app: moe-decode } }      spec:        containers:        - name: vllm          image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0          command: ["vllm", "serve"]          args: ["deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3-0324",                 "--tensor-parallel-size=1", "--data-parallel-size=32", "--data-parallel-size-local=8",                 "--data-parallel-address=$(LWS_LEADER_ADDRESS)", "--data-parallel-rpc-port=13345",                 "--enable-expert-parallel", "--all2all-backend=deepep_low_latency",   # EP = 32                 "--enable-eplb", "--kv-cache-dtype=fp8"]          resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }    workerTemplate:      spec:        containers:        - name: vllm          image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0          command: ["sh", "-c"]          args: ["vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3-0324 --headless --tensor-parallel-size=1                  --data-parallel-size=32 --data-parallel-size-local=8                  --data-parallel-start-rank=$((LWS_WORKER_INDEX * 8))                  --data-parallel-address=$LWS_LEADER_ADDRESS --data-parallel-rpc-port=13345                  --enable-expert-parallel --all2all-backend=deepep_low_latency --enable-eplb --kv-cache-dtype=fp8"]          resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Prefill and decode want different EP setups: prefill uses large batches and high-throughput kernels, decode uses small per-step batches and low-latency kernels. This is one of the strongest reasons to disaggregate MoE serving.
  • The fabric matters as much as the GPUs: all-to-all over RDMA needs GPUDirect RDMA and a non-blocking fabric. Check the topology placement (Design 17) before tuning kernels.

Engine tuning: batching, scheduling and caching

Scenario. The engine ran with defaults. With 20k-token prompts arriving, each prefill took over a whole engine step, and all the decoding requests in the batch waited for it.

What the picture shows. The engine settings that matter most, and what each trades.

1Chunked prefill and the token budget
--max-num-batched-tokens caps the tokens per step. Long prompts are split into chunks mixed with decode tokens. A smaller budget protects ITL, and a larger one improves prefill throughput and TTFT.
2Concurrency cap
--max-num-seqs limits running requests. Too high and KV pressure causes preemptions. Too low and the GPU is underused.
3Memory split
--gpu-memory-utilization sets how much HBM goes to weights, activations and KV cache.
4Prefix caching
reuses KV blocks for shared prefixes. It's nearly free when there's no sharing and large when there is.
5CUDA graphs, compilation and async scheduling
reduce CPU overhead per step. This matters most for small decode batches and fast GPUs.
6Speculative decoding
a draft model or multi-token-prediction head proposes tokens that the main model verifies. It lowers ITL at low load, but its benefit shrinks at high batch sizes.

The YAML. Engine configuration for the 70B chat deployment (vLLM config file, mounted from a ConfigMap).

# /etc/vllm/chat-70b-h100.yamlmodel: nvidia/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-FP8tensor-parallel-size: 2gpu-memory-utilization: 0.92kv-cache-dtype: fp8max-model-len: 32768max-num-seqs: 192max-num-batched-tokens: 4096          # protects ITL during long prefills; tuned by sweepenable-prefix-caching: trueasync-scheduling: truespeculative-config: '{"method": "eagle3", "model": "registry.example.com/drafts/llama-70b-eagle3", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}'
Going deeper2 points
  • Tune one setting at a time against replayed traffic: the token budget, max sequences and speculative decoding interact. Changing all three at once makes the result impossible to explain.
  • Watch preemptions: vLLM reports preempted requests when KV cache runs out. A rising count means the concurrency cap is too high for the memory.

Prefill/decode disaggregation

Scenario. Even with chunked prefill, chat ITL spiked during coding-assistant bursts. The two phases shared every GPU, and a 4096-token budget couldn't satisfy both a 3-second TTFT for 20k-token prompts and a 50 ms ITL for chat.

What the picture shows. Separate pools for prefill and decode, with KV cache transferred between them.

1Prefill pool
processes prompts with large token budgets and the parallelism best for compute-heavy work. It produces the KV cache and the first token.
2KV transfer
the decode worker pulls the prompt's KV blocks from the prefill worker over RDMA (NIXL with UCX), asynchronously, without staging through CPUs.
3Decode pool
generates tokens with large batches and settings that minimize ITL, never interrupted by prefills.
4Independent tuning and scaling
TTFT is tuned on the prefill pool and ITL on the decode pool. The prefill-to-decode ratio (for example, 1:2 or 2:3) follows the input/output mix.
5When it doesn't pay
short prompts, small models or slow networks. Then the transfer costs more than the interference it removes. The vLLM docs note that disaggregation targets latency control, not raw throughput.

The YAML. The prefill and decode engine arguments (vLLM with NixlConnector; deployed as two Deployments or LeaderWorkerSets).

# prefill poolcommand: ["vllm", "serve"]args: ["nvidia/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-FP8", "--tensor-parallel-size=4",       "--max-num-batched-tokens=32768", "--enable-prefix-caching", "--kv-cache-dtype=fp8",       "--kv-transfer-config", '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_both"}']---# decode poolcommand: ["vllm", "serve"]args: ["nvidia/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-FP8", "--tensor-parallel-size=2",       "--max-num-seqs=256", "--max-num-batched-tokens=2048", "--kv-cache-dtype=fp8",       "--kv-transfer-config", '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_both"}']   # same connectorenv:- { name: UCX_TLS, value: "rc,cuda_copy,cuda_ipc" }     # RDMA + GPU memory transports
Going deeper2 points
  • Different TP sizes on each side work: the connector handles layout differences, which allows prefill at TP=4 for TTFT and decode at TP=2 for replica count.
  • Measure transfer time: KV size per request (prompt tokens × KV bytes per token) divided by network bandwidth is the minimum added to TTFT. A 20k-token prompt in FP8 is about 3.3 GB for the 70B model.

Routing: cache-aware and phase-aware

Scenario. A round-robin Service spread requests evenly, so each coding session's 20k-token prefix was recomputed on whichever replica it landed on. The prefix-cache hit rate was 9% even though 80% of tokens were shared.

What the picture shows. An inference-aware gateway that picks the endpoint per request.

1InferencePool
a Gateway API inference-extension resource grouping the model-server pods, with an endpoint picker (EPP) that chooses one per request.
2Signals the picker uses
which pod likely holds the request's prefix in its KV cache, queue depth, KV-cache usage and, with disaggregation, which prefill and decode pods to pair.
3Session affinity by prefix, not by user
the same document or repository prefix lands on the same pods, keeping hit rates high without pinning users.
4Priority and fairness
critical traffic (interactive chat) is admitted ahead of sheddable traffic (batch evaluation) when the pool is saturated.
5llm-d
packages this pattern (vLLM, the inference gateway's endpoint picker, P/D-aware scheduling and KV-cache indexing) as a Kubernetes-native stack.

The YAML. An InferencePool with an endpoint picker, behind an HTTPRoute (Gateway API Inference Extension).

apiVersion: inference.networking.k8s.io/v1kind: InferencePoolmetadata: { name: chat-70b, namespace: serving }spec:  selector: { matchLabels: { app: chat-70b } }  targetPorts: [{ number: 8000 }]  endpointPickerRef:                                   # prefix-cache, load and P/D-aware picking    name: chat-70b-epp    port: { number: 9002 }---apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1kind: HTTPRoutemetadata: { name: chat-70b, namespace: serving }spec:  parentRefs: [{ name: inference-gateway }]  rules:  - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /v1 } }]    backendRefs: [{ group: inference.networking.k8s.io, kind: InferencePool, name: chat-70b }]
Going deeper2 points
  • Prefix-aware routing and load balancing pull in opposite directions: sending everything with the same prefix to one pod overloads it. The picker scores both and spills over when queues grow.
  • Hash prefixes the way the engine does: routing by block hashes that match the engine's prefix-cache blocks gives accurate hit predictions. Routing by raw text approximations gives looser ones.

KV cache offload

Scenario. The coding assistant's sessions came back every few minutes with the same repository context. By then the prefix had been evicted from GPU memory, so every return meant recomputing 20,000 tokens of prefill.

What the picture shows. KV cache in tiers beyond GPU memory.

1GPU HBM
the working set for running requests.
2Host memory (CPU DRAM)
evicted blocks are copied to pinned host memory instead of being discarded. A later hit reloads them over PCIe or NVLink-C2C, much faster than recomputing a long prefill.
3Shared or local storage
a larger, slower tier for long-lived prefixes across replicas (LMCache, shared filesystems or a KV store).
4When it pays
long shared prefixes that return after eviction, such as agent sessions, coding context and RAG documents. When nothing is reused, it's pure overhead.
5Routing must know about the tiers
a picker that only sees GPU blocks undervalues pods with the prefix in host memory.

The YAML. Native CPU offload in vLLM for the coding deployment.

command: ["vllm", "serve"]args: ["nvidia/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-FP8", "--tensor-parallel-size=2",       "--enable-prefix-caching",                       # offload builds on prefix caching       "--kv-offloading-backend=native",       "--kv-offloading-size=400"]                      # GiB of host memory for KV, across TP ranksresources:  limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 2, memory: 560Gi }          # budget pinned host memory in the pod limit
Going deeper2 points
  • Size host memory per pod: with FP8 KV at about 160 KiB per token, 400 GiB holds about 2.6 million tokens, or about 130 cached 20k-token prefixes per replica.
  • Mind PCIe bandwidth: reloading many blocks per step competes with other traffic. Watch offload store and reload rates against throughput.

FP8 and FP4 quantization with an accuracy gate

Scenario. An FP4 version of the 70B model doubled throughput on B200s in a benchmark. A week after release, the coding team found it failed noticeably more unit tests on long functions. Nobody had evaluated it on code.

What the picture shows. The quantization options and how a quantized model earns its way to production.

1FP8 (W8A8) on Hopper and Blackwell
weights and activations in FP8 with per-tensor or per-channel scales. Typically near-lossless for large models. Halves weight memory and uses FP8 tensor cores.
2FP4 (NVFP4, W4A4) on Blackwell
4-bit values with fine-grained block scales. About a quarter of BF16 weight memory, with the largest throughput gains. Accuracy needs checking per task, and some layers are often kept at higher precision.
3FP8 KV cache
halves KV memory, doubling the tokens that fit. Its accuracy effect is separate from weight quantization and is tested on its own.
4Producing checkpoints
with calibration data that looks like production traffic (NVIDIA ModelOpt, LLM Compressor), recorded in the registry with the recipe used.
5The gate
the full evaluation suite, per product and per task family, against the BF16 reference, with agreed maximum deltas. A model that fails any family doesn't ship for that product.

The code. An accuracy gate comparing a quantized model with its reference, per task family (Python).

GATES = {"chat_quality": -0.5, "math": -1.0, "code_pass@1": -1.0, "long_context_recall": -1.5, "tool_use": -1.0} def quantization_gate(reference: dict, candidate: dict, ci: dict) -> dict:    """reference/candidate: score per task family (points); ci: 95% half-width of the difference."""    results = {}    for family, max_drop in GATES.items():        delta = candidate[family] - reference[family]        worst = delta - ci[family]                         # pessimistic bound        results[family] = {"delta": round(delta, 2), "worst_case": round(worst, 2), "pass": worst >= max_drop}    results["ship"] = all(r["pass"] for k, r in results.items() if k in GATES)    return results
Going deeper2 points
  • Calibrate on your traffic: calibration sets of generic web text under-represent code and long contexts. Sample them from production prompts with privacy filters applied.
  • Gate per product, not globally: an FP4 model can ship for chat and stay FP8 for the coding assistant. The registry and routing support different variants per product.

Benchmarking and the tuning loop

Scenario. Three teams each reported a different "best" configuration for the same model. Each had used a different benchmark tool, prompt set and concurrency, and none had measured latency percentiles.

What the picture shows. One benchmark procedure for every serving change.

1Traffic replay
sampled production request shapes (lengths, prefix sharing, arrival bursts) per product, versioned like a dataset.
2Sweep
request rate or concurrency from low to past saturation, recording TTFT and ITL percentiles and throughput at each point.
3Goodput curve
tokens per second per GPU from requests within SLO. The configuration's score is the peak of this curve.
4Comparison
the candidate against the current production configuration on the same hardware and replay, repeated to estimate noise.
5Tools
an inference-benchmark harness (for example, Inference Perf or vLLM's serving benchmark) driven by the replay (Design 15).

The code. Finding the goodput peak from a load sweep (Python).

import numpy as np def goodput(results, ttft_slo_s, itl_slo_ms, gpus):    """results: list of dicts per load level, each with per-request ttft_s, itl_ms_p95, output_tokens, duration_s."""    curve = []    for level in results:        ok = [r for r in level["requests"] if r["ttft_s"] <= ttft_slo_s and r["itl_ms_p95"] <= itl_slo_ms]        tokens = sum(r["output_tokens"] for r in ok)        curve.append({"rate": level["rate"], "goodput_tok_s_gpu": tokens / level["duration_s"] / gpus,                      "slo_attainment": len(ok) / len(level["requests"])})    best = max(curve, key=lambda c: c["goodput_tok_s_gpu"] if c["slo_attainment"] >= 0.95 else 0)    return best, curve
Going deeper2 points
  • Report the curve, not one number: a configuration that peaks higher but falls off faster past its peak is risky under bursty traffic.
  • Benchmark on the target GPUs and network: disaggregation and wide EP results depend on the fabric. Numbers from a different cluster don't transfer.

Autoscaling and operations

Scenario. The HPA scaled on GPU utilization, which stays near 100% on a busy LLM server at any load. Replicas never scaled down overnight, and during the morning spike new replicas took 9 minutes to become ready.

What the picture shows. Scaling on signals that track latency, with pools scaled separately.

1Scaling signals
queue depth (waiting requests), KV-cache usage and observed TTFT. GPU utilization doesn't track load for LLM servers.
2Scale pools independently
the prefill pool on prompt-token arrival rate and TTFT, the decode pool on running requests and KV usage.
3Fast readiness
streamed or cached model loading and pre-pulled images keep scale-up within minutes (Design 20).
4Rollouts
a new configuration or quantized variant gets a slice of traffic through the gateway, with SLO and quality canaries before it takes all traffic.
5Dashboards
TTFT and ITL percentiles per product, goodput, prefix-cache hit rate by tier, preemptions, KV transfer time and expert load balance.
Going deeper4 points
  • Keep warm capacity for bursts: scale-up is never instant for a 70B model. A small buffer of ready replicas, sized from the arrival pattern, protects TTFT.
  • Scale-down must drain: in-flight streams finish before a pod stops, and for disaggregated pools the decode side drains last.
  • How KServe does this today (checked November 2026): its LLMInferenceService scales either through the Workload Variant Autoscaler, which reads KV-cache use and queue depth, or through KEDA triggers you write yourself. Since KServe 0.21, KEDA can take it to zero replicas on either path; the HPA option stops at one (autoscaling guide, 0.21 release). Zero replicas frees the pods, not the machines. The GPU node goes away only if the node autoscaler removes it, and the next request then pays a full cold start.
  • A canary with KServe: run the old and the new version as two LLMInferenceServices in the same routing group, each with a weight. Weights are proportions, so 9 and 1 give a 90/10 split, and you change only the version you're moving. KServe's own guide starts the new version at weight 1 rather than 0, because raising a weight from 0 later may cause brief connection failures. Each version also has a direct path for test traffic, and stopping the old version promotes the new one while keeping the old one for rollback (canary guide). KServe moves the traffic; the quality and latency checks that decide each step are still yours.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, measure (weeks 1–3): request-shape logging, replay datasets per product, goodput definition and the benchmark harness. Baseline every deployment.
  • Phase 2, quick wins (weeks 3–6): FP8 weights and KV cache with the accuracy gate, right-sized TP and more replicas, engine settings tuned by sweep, and cache-aware routing.
  • Phase 3, MoE (weeks 6–10): data-parallel attention with wide EP and EPLB on LeaderWorkerSets, with topology-aware placement.
  • Phase 4, structural (weeks 8–14): prefill/decode disaggregation for the coding assistant and MoE, KV offload for long-context products, and NVFP4 variants where the gate passes.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • More moving parts: disaggregation, offload and an endpoint picker each add components to operate and debug.
  • Per-product variants: different quantizations and layouts per product cost registry, testing and capacity planning effort.
  • Host memory for KV offload makes serving nodes more expensive to configure.
  • Benchmarks before every change slow down tuning, and make it explainable.

Open questions.

  • Dynamic P/D ratios: can the prefill-to-decode split adjust automatically as the traffic mix shifts during the day?
  • Cross-replica KV sharing: when does a shared KV store across replicas beat cache-aware routing with per-pod offload?
  • Lower precision KV cache: how far can FP4 KV go before long-context recall degrades?
  • Speculative decoding with disaggregation: where should the draft model run, and how does it change the P/D ratio?
Design 22 · 12 sections

Design 22: Benchmarking and traffic replay for LLM serving, with per-config baselines

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Defining the metrics precisely
  3. Capturing production traffic as shapes
  4. Open-loop replay and coordinated omission
  5. Load generation at scale on Kubernetes
  6. Percentiles done right
  7. Sweeps, saturation and goodput curves
  8. Server-side metrics next to client metrics
  9. Configuration fingerprints and the baseline store
  10. Regression gates in CI
  11. Running the benchmark service
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build tools that measure LLM serving latency correctly, replay real traffic against any configuration, and keep a trusted performance baseline for every configuration we run? Design 21 relies on a benchmark procedure to choose parallelism, quantization and engine settings. Design 15 covers evaluation and benchmarking across the whole program. This design is the serving benchmark toolkit itself: metric definitions, traffic capture, open-loop replay, percentile statistics, sweeps, configuration fingerprints, the baseline store and regression gates.

The short version: measure from the client, replay open-loop, and attach every number to a fingerprint. TTFT, TPOT, inter-token latency and end-to-end latency are computed per request from streaming timestamps on the client, with exact definitions everyone uses. Production traffic is captured as request shapes (arrival times, token counts, prefix structure), not as prompt text, and replayed on its original schedule so a slow server can't hide its queueing. Percentiles come from merged histograms with confidence intervals. Every result is stored under a fingerprint of the model, engine, flags, hardware and replay dataset. A change ships only if its result is within noise of, or better than, the baseline for its fingerprint.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The serving team runs 14 configurations across 3 models, 2 GPU types and 2 engine versions. When a vLLM upgrade went out, chat p99 TTFT doubled in production, yet the pre-release benchmark had shown "a 12% improvement". It turned out the benchmark used a fixed concurrency of 32. The server's slowdown just meant fewer requests were sent, so the queueing never showed up in the numbers.

What the tools must deliver.

  • One set of metric definitions: TTFT, TPOT, ITL and end-to-end latency, computed the same way in every tool and dashboard.
  • Realistic load: replay of production arrival times and request shapes per product, at any speed multiple.
  • Correct latency under overload: an open-loop load generator that sends on schedule regardless of how the server responds.
  • Trustworthy percentiles: p50, p90, p99 with confidence intervals, merged correctly across load-generator pods.
  • Baselines per configuration: a stored, versioned result for every fingerprint, refreshed on a schedule.
  • Regression gates: engine upgrades, config changes and new model variants are blocked when they're worse than the baseline beyond noise.
  • Privacy: no customer prompt text leaves the production boundary.

Out of scope: model quality evaluation (Design 15), and how to tune configurations (Design 21).

Defining the metrics precisely

Scenario. One dashboard computed "TPOT" as total time divided by output tokens, and another as the average gap between tokens after the first. For long prompts they differed by 3×, and two teams argued for a week about whether a change had helped.

What the picture shows. One streamed request on a timeline, and the metrics computed from it.

1TTFT (time to first token)
from the client sending the request to the first content token arriving. It includes network, gateway queueing, scheduling and prefill.
2TPOT (time per output token)
(end-to-end latency − TTFT) ÷ (output tokens − 1). One number per request, the average decode pace that user saw.
3ITL (inter-token latency)
each gap between consecutive tokens. Its percentiles across all gaps show stalls that TPOT averages away.
4End-to-end latency
from send to the last token.
5Token counts from the tokenizer
streamed chunks can carry several tokens, so output tokens are counted with the model's tokenizer (or the server's usage field), not by counting chunks.
6Client-side timestamps with a monotonic clock
measured where the user experiences them. Server-side metrics explain the numbers but don't replace them.

The code. Per-request metrics from streaming timestamps (Python).

from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclassclass StreamRecord:    sent: float                     # time.perf_counter() when the request was sent    chunk_times: list[float]        # arrival time of every content chunk    chunk_tokens: list[int]         # tokens in each chunk (tokenizer or usage deltas) def request_metrics(r: StreamRecord) -> dict:    ttft = r.chunk_times[0] - r.sent    e2e = r.chunk_times[-1] - r.sent    out = sum(r.chunk_tokens)    tpot = (e2e - ttft) / (out - 1) if out > 1 else None          # one value per request    itl = []                                                        # per-token gaps    for prev, t, n in zip(r.chunk_times, r.chunk_times[1:], r.chunk_tokens[1:]):        itl += [(t - prev) / n] * n                                 # spread a multi-token chunk evenly    return {"ttft_s": ttft, "tpot_s": tpot, "e2e_s": e2e, "output_tokens": out, "itl_s": itl}
Going deeper2 points
  • Publish the definitions as a library: the benchmark tools, the gateway's metrics and the dashboards import the same functions, so the definitions can't drift apart.
  • Report TPOT and ITL percentiles together: a good TPOT p99 with a bad ITL p99 means requests stall in the middle, often because of prefill interference.

Capturing production traffic as shapes

Scenario. To build a realistic benchmark, someone asked to copy a day of production prompts into the benchmark cluster. Legal said no, and the team fell back to a public chat dataset whose lengths looked nothing like their coding traffic.

What the picture shows. What the gateway records, and how replays are built from it without prompt text.

1Per request
arrival time, product, model, input and output token counts, the max-tokens setting, whether it streamed, and a session ID.
2Prefix structure
a chain of hashes of fixed-size token blocks (for example, 256 tokens), salted per capture. Matching hashes show which requests shared which prefix, and for how long, without revealing content.
3Synthesis
replays generate prompts with the same lengths and the same prefix-sharing structure. Requests whose hash chains match share identical synthetic blocks, so prefix-cache behavior is preserved.
4Output length control
the replay sets max tokens to the recorded output length and ignores end-of-sequence tokens, so decode work matches production.
5Versioned datasets
each capture window becomes a replay dataset with a version, and its summary statistics are stored next to it.

The code. Synthesizing prompts that preserve lengths and prefix sharing from hash chains (Python).

import random def synthesize(trace: list[dict], vocab_size: int, block: int = 256, seed: int = 0) -> list[dict]:    """trace rows: arrival_s, input_tokens, output_tokens, block_hashes (list of str)."""    blocks: dict[str, list[int]] = {}                                 # same hash -> same synthetic tokens    rng = random.Random(seed)    out = []    for row in trace:        ids = []        for h in row["block_hashes"]:            if h not in blocks:                blocks[h] = [rng.randrange(1000, vocab_size) for _ in range(block)]            ids += blocks[h]        tail = row["input_tokens"] - len(ids)                          # unshared remainder        ids += [rng.randrange(1000, vocab_size) for _ in range(max(tail, 0))]        out.append({"arrival_s": row["arrival_s"], "prompt_token_ids": ids[: row["input_tokens"]],                    "max_tokens": row["output_tokens"], "ignore_eos": True})    return out
Going deeper2 points
  • Random tokens aren't natural text: acceptance rates for speculative decoding and some MoE routing patterns depend on content. For those experiments, use a licensed or internal corpus sliced to the recorded lengths.
  • Salt and rotate the hashes: a hash chain without a salt can be checked against guessed prompts. Salting per capture keeps the structure while protecting content.

Open-loop replay and coordinated omission

Scenario. The upgrade benchmark used 32 concurrent clients, each sending its next request when the previous one finished. When the new version slowed down, the clients slowed down too. Arrival rate dropped, queues never formed, and TTFT looked fine.

What the picture shows. Closed-loop and open-loop load, and why only one reveals queueing.

1Closed loop (fixed concurrency)
each client waits for a response before sending. A slower server automatically receives less load. This hides queueing, a problem known as coordinated omission.
2Open loop (scheduled arrivals)
requests are sent at their scheduled times (from a trace, a Poisson process or a ramp) whether or not earlier ones have finished. A slower server builds a queue, and TTFT shows it.
3Lateness tracking
the generator records how late each send was compared with its schedule. If the generator itself falls behind, the run is invalid.
4Speed multiples
a trace can be replayed at 1×, 1.5× or 2× its original rate to probe headroom while keeping its burst structure.
5When closed loop is right
measuring the maximum throughput of a server at a fixed batch, as one point in a sweep, but never for latency SLOs.

The code. An open-loop replayer that sends on schedule and records lateness (Python, asyncio and httpx).

import asyncio, json, time, httpx async def send(client, url, req, t0, results):    sched = t0 + req["arrival_s"]    await asyncio.sleep(max(0.0, sched - time.perf_counter()))    sent = time.perf_counter()    rec = {"lateness_s": sent - sched, "sent": sent, "chunk_times": [], "chunk_tokens": []}    body = {"model": req["model"], "prompt": req["prompt_token_ids"], "max_tokens": req["max_tokens"],            "ignore_eos": True, "stream": True, "stream_options": {"include_usage": True}}    try:        async with client.stream("POST", url, json=body, timeout=600) as r:            async for line in r.aiter_lines():                if line.startswith("data: ") and line != "data: [DONE]":                    chunk = json.loads(line[6:])                    if chunk.get("choices") and chunk["choices"][0].get("text"):                        rec["chunk_times"].append(time.perf_counter()); rec["chunk_tokens"].append(1)                    if chunk.get("usage"):                        rec["usage"] = chunk["usage"]           # authoritative token count    except httpx.HTTPError as e:        rec["error"] = type(e).__name__    results.append(rec) async def replay(url, requests, speed=1.0, max_inflight=4096):    limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=max_inflight, max_keepalive_connections=max_inflight)    results, t0 = [], time.perf_counter() + 2.0                  # 2 s to schedule everything    async with httpx.AsyncClient(limits=limits, http2=False) as client:        tasks = [asyncio.create_task(send(client, url, {**r, "arrival_s": r["arrival_s"] / speed}, t0, results))                 for r in requests]                              # all scheduled up front: open loop        await asyncio.gather(*tasks)    late = sorted(r["lateness_s"] for r in results)    assert late[int(0.99 * len(late))] < 0.05, "generator fell behind: run invalid"    return results
Going deeper2 points
  • Errors and timeouts are results: a request that timed out at 600 s counts as a 600 s (or worse) latency in percentiles and fails goodput. Dropping it flatters the run.
  • Connection limits can reintroduce closed-loop behavior: if the HTTP client caps connections below the in-flight count, sends wait for free connections. Size limits above the expected peak, and check lateness.

Load generation at scale on Kubernetes

Scenario. A single benchmark pod generating 2,000 requests per second for a 64-GPU deployment ran out of CPU parsing streams. Its timestamps were delayed by its own event loop, and the "server latency" it reported was mostly its own.

What the picture shows. Distributed load generation that the benchmark itself doesn't distort.

1Indexed Job of generators
N pods, each replaying a deterministic shard of the trace (requests where index mod N equals its index), so the combined schedule equals the trace.
2Placement
generators run on dedicated CPU nodes in the same cluster and zone as the gateway, never on the GPU nodes under test.
3Through the real path
requests go through the same gateway and endpoint picker as production, so routing and cache-aware placement are measured too.
4Start barrier
all generators start at the same wall-clock time (synchronized clocks), and each uses a monotonic clock for its own measurements.
5Self-checks
each generator reports its CPU usage, event-loop lag and send lateness. A run where any generator was saturated is discarded.
6Results
per-request records and histograms written to object storage, then merged by a collector.

The YAML. A benchmark run as an Indexed Job. Each pod runs the team's replayer image (the open-loop replayer above, packaged with its shard logic) on one shard of the trace.

apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata: { name: bench-chat70b-h100-tp2-r20261119, namespace: bench }spec:  completionMode: Indexed  completions: 8  parallelism: 8                                         # 8 generators, one shard of the trace each  template:    spec:      nodeSelector: { node-pool: bench-loadgen }         # CPU nodes, never the GPUs under test      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: loadgen        image: registry.example.com/bench/replayer:1.4          # platform image: replayer + metrics library        args: ["--trace", "s3://bench-replays/chat/2026-11-w46", "--speed", "1.0", "--out", "s3://bench-results/$(JOB_NAME)"]        env:        - { name: SHARD, valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: "metadata.annotations['batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index']" } } }        - { name: SHARDS, value: "8" }        - { name: JOB_NAME, value: bench-chat70b-h100-tp2-r20261119 }        - { name: START_AT, value: "2026-11-19T22:00:00Z" }   # start barrier; clocks synced by chrony        resources: { requests: { cpu: "8", memory: 16Gi }, limits: { cpu: "8", memory: 16Gi } }        volumeMounts: [{ name: config, mountPath: /config }]      volumes: [{ name: config, configMap: { name: bench-chat70b-run } }]
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure the generator's ceiling once: benchmark the generators against a stub server that returns instant streams, and record the maximum rate per pod with acceptable lateness. Plan shards so no pod exceeds half of it.
  • Benchmark the path you care about: for engine tuning, send directly to a pod. For product SLOs, go through the gateway. Record which one in the result.

Percentiles done right

Scenario. Eight generators each reported their own p99 TTFT, and the summary averaged them into "p99 = 0.84 s". The true p99 across all requests was 1.31 s, because one generator's shard happened to include most of the long coding prompts.

What the picture shows. How latency distributions are aggregated and reported.

1Never average percentiles
merge the raw measurements (or mergeable histograms such as HDR histograms or DDSketch) and compute percentiles once.
2Enough samples for the tail
a p99 from 1,000 requests rests on 10 requests. Each load level runs long enough for at least a few thousand requests per product.
3Confidence intervals
bootstrap over sessions (not individual requests, which are correlated within a session) to get an interval for each percentile.
4Warm-up and cool-down excluded
the first and last minutes of each stage are dropped, so cold caches and draining queues don't skew results.
5Per product and per length bucket
a mixed p99 hides that long prompts behave differently. Report both the mix and each bucket.

The code. Merged percentiles with a session-level bootstrap interval (Python).

import numpy as np def percentile_ci(values_by_session: dict[str, list[float]], q: float, n_boot=2000, seed=0):    """values_by_session: session id -> TTFT samples from all generators, already merged."""    sessions = list(values_by_session)    allv = np.concatenate([values_by_session[s] for s in sessions])    point = np.percentile(allv, q)    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)    boots = []    for _ in range(n_boot):        pick = rng.choice(len(sessions), size=len(sessions), replace=True)   # resample sessions        boots.append(np.percentile(np.concatenate([values_by_session[sessions[i]] for i in pick]), q))    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])    return {"q": q, "value": float(point), "ci95": (float(lo), float(hi)), "n": int(allv.size)}
Going deeper2 points
  • Use log-scaled histograms for latency: they keep relative precision from milliseconds to minutes in small, mergeable structures, which matters at millions of requests.
  • Report the n: a percentile without its sample count and interval can't be compared with another one.

Sweeps, saturation and goodput curves

Scenario. Each configuration was benchmarked at one request rate, chosen by whoever ran it. Comparisons were meaningless, because one config was measured below its knee and the other above it.

What the picture shows. The standard sweep every configuration gets.

1Find saturation first
a short ramp finds the rate at which throughput stops increasing.
2Stages around it
fixed-duration stages from low load to past saturation, spaced more densely near the knee.
3Per stage
TTFT, TPOT, ITL and end-to-end percentiles with intervals, throughput, error rate and goodput against the product's SLO.
4The headline numbers
maximum goodput, and the highest rate at which every SLO percentile holds (the SLO capacity). These go into the baseline.
5Replay speed as the load knob
with trace replay, stages are speed multiples of the trace, which keeps the mix and bursts realistic at every level.

The YAML. A saturation sweep with Inference Perf (fragment of its config file). The same stages are applied as speed multiples when replaying a trace.

load:  type: poisson  interval: 15  sweep:    type: geometric          # stages clustered around the detected saturation point    timeout: 60    num_stages: 8    stage_duration: 300api:  type: completion  streaming: truedata:  type: shared_prefix         # synthetic prefix sharing; use the team's replayer for trace replays
Going deeper2 points
  • Stop at the knee for SLO capacity: past saturation, queues grow for the whole stage and latency depends on stage length, which isn't a property of the configuration.
  • Keep the stage duration fixed across configs: a 5-minute stage and a 15-minute stage past saturation produce different p99s from the same server.

Server-side metrics next to client metrics

Scenario. Client TTFT p99 rose from 0.9 s to 1.6 s after a gateway change, but the engine's own TTFT histogram didn't move. The extra time was spent in a new authentication filter at the gateway.

What the picture shows. Breaking client latency into where the time went.

1Client
the TTFT and TPOT users experience.
2Gateway and endpoint picker
time from receiving a request to forwarding it, queueing and routing decisions.
3Engine
vLLM's own histograms for TTFT, inter-token latency, queue time and prefill and decode time (vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds, vllm:request_queue_time_seconds and related metrics), plus running and waiting requests and KV-cache usage.
4GPU
DCGM activity, memory bandwidth and power, to see whether the engine was compute-bound or waiting.
5The breakdown
client TTFT minus engine TTFT minus gateway time is network plus unaccounted time. When it grows, the problem is outside the engine.

The code. Pulling engine histograms for the run window and comparing them with client percentiles (Python, Prometheus HTTP API).

import requests PROM = "http://prometheus.monitoring:9090/api/v1/query" def server_quantile(metric: str, q: float, selector: str, window: str) -> float:    expr = f'histogram_quantile({q}, sum by (le) (rate({metric}_bucket{{{selector}}}[{window}])))'    r = requests.get(PROM, params={"query": expr}).json()    return float(r["data"]["result"][0]["value"][1]) def breakdown(client_ttft_p99: float, selector: str, window: str = "5m") -> dict:    engine = server_quantile("vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds", 0.99, selector, window)    queue = server_quantile("vllm:request_queue_time_seconds", 0.99, selector, window)    return {"client_ttft_p99": client_ttft_p99, "engine_ttft_p99": engine, "engine_queue_p99": queue,            "outside_engine_s": round(client_ttft_p99 - engine, 3)}      # gateway + network
Going deeper2 points
  • Server histograms have coarse buckets: their quantiles are interpolated, so use them to locate time, not to replace client percentiles.
  • Capture engine and GPU metrics into the result: a stored benchmark with its server-side context can be explained months later.

Configuration fingerprints and the baseline store

Scenario. A dashboard showed "chat-70b: 1,450 tok/s/GPU" from three months ago. Nobody could say which engine version, flags or replay dataset produced it, so it couldn't be compared with anything.

What the picture shows. What identifies a configuration, and what a baseline record holds.

1Fingerprint inputs
model and revision (weights hash), quantization, engine and version, all engine flags (normalized and sorted), parallelism, GPU type and count, driver and CUDA versions, and node type.
2Workload identity
replay dataset and version, speed multiples, SLO definitions and the path benchmarked (pod or gateway).
3Baseline record
fingerprint, workload, per-stage percentiles with intervals, SLO capacity, maximum goodput, server-side context and links to raw data.
4Lineage
each new baseline references the one it replaced and the change that caused it, so a configuration's history reads as a list of changes and their effects.
5Storage
a table in the warehouse for querying, and raw records in object storage for re-analysis.

The code. Computing a stable fingerprint from a deployment's effective configuration (Python).

import hashlib, json IGNORED_FLAGS = {"--port", "--host", "--served-model-name", "--disable-log-requests"} def fingerprint(model_rev: str, engine: str, engine_version: str, flags: list[str],                gpu: str, gpus: int, driver: str, cuda: str) -> str:    norm = sorted(f for f in flags if f.split("=")[0] not in IGNORED_FLAGS)   # order-independent    doc = {"model": model_rev, "engine": f"{engine}=={engine_version}", "flags": norm,           "hw": {"gpu": gpu, "count": gpus, "driver": driver, "cuda": cuda}}    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(doc, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:16] fp = fingerprint("llama-3.3-70b-fp8@sha256:9c1e", "vllm", "0.32.0",                 ["--tensor-parallel-size=2", "--kv-cache-dtype=fp8", "--max-num-batched-tokens=4096"],                 "H100-SXM-80GB", 2, "580.95", "13.0")
Going deeper2 points
  • Read the effective configuration from the running server, not the manifest: defaults change between engine versions. Record the resolved configuration the engine logs at startup.
  • Fingerprint the replay dataset too: the same configuration measured on two different replays has two baselines.

Regression gates in CI

Scenario. The vLLM upgrade had passed CI. The CI benchmark ran once, closed-loop, on whatever GPUs were free, and accepted anything within 20% of a number typed into a YAML file a year earlier.

What the picture shows. How a change is compared with its baseline before it ships.

1Triggers
engine or image upgrades, engine flag changes, new quantized variants, gateway and endpoint-picker changes, and driver updates on the benchmark pool.
2Runs
the candidate and the current baseline configuration both run on the same benchmark pool, back to back, with repeats (for example, 3 each) to measure run-to-run noise.
3Comparison
each headline metric (SLO capacity, maximum goodput, TTFT and TPOT p99 at the production rate) is compared with a noise-aware threshold derived from the repeats.
4Verdicts
pass, regression (block with a report), or improvement (propose a new baseline for review).
5Reports
the goodput curves overlaid, the per-metric deltas with intervals, and the server-side breakdown for any regression.

The code. A noise-aware comparison of candidate and baseline repeats (Python).

import numpy as np def compare(baseline: list[float], candidate: list[float], higher_is_better: bool, min_effect: float = 0.03):    """Each list: one headline metric from repeated runs (e.g., SLO capacity in req/s)."""    b, c = np.mean(baseline), np.mean(candidate)    noise = max(np.std(baseline, ddof=1), np.std(candidate, ddof=1), 1e-9)    rel = (c - b) / b if higher_is_better else (b - c) / b       # positive = better    if abs(c - b) < 2 * noise or abs(rel) < min_effect:        return {"verdict": "within_noise", "rel_change": round(rel, 3)}    return {"verdict": "improvement" if rel > 0 else "regression", "rel_change": round(rel, 3)} print(compare([18.2, 18.6, 18.4], [15.1, 15.4, 15.0], higher_is_better=True))   # regression
Going deeper2 points
  • Run the baseline again rather than reusing the stored number: the benchmark pool's hardware, drivers and neighbors drift. A same-day baseline run removes that drift from the comparison.
  • Keep a small and a full gate: a 20-minute gate on every engine-flag change, and the full sweep for upgrades and new variants.

Running the benchmark service

Scenario. Benchmarks ran on whatever GPUs were idle, often next to a training job saturating the same network switch. Results varied by 15% from run to run, so no change smaller than that could be detected.

What the picture shows. The benchmark service as a platform component.

1Dedicated benchmark pool
a small set of GPU nodes per GPU type, isolated from training traffic, admitted through Kueue with exclusive placement (Design 17).
2Scheduled baselines
every production fingerprint is re-run weekly, so slow drift (drivers, firmware, kernel) is caught even without a change.
3Production comparison
live production percentiles, at similar request rates, are compared with the baseline's predictions. A gap means the replay no longer represents production, so a new capture is due.
4Self-service
teams submit a benchmark by naming a fingerprint and a replay dataset. Results land in the store with a report link.
5Noise budget
the service tracks its own run-to-run variation per configuration and publishes the smallest change it can detect.
Going deeper2 points
  • Refresh replays on a schedule: traffic changes as products evolve. A monthly capture, with a diff of its length and sharing distributions against the previous one, shows when baselines need to be rebuilt.
  • Treat the benchmark service like production: its own versions, change log and on-call. A broken benchmark silently approves regressions.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, definitions and capture (weeks 1–3): the metrics library, gateway capture of request shapes and salted prefix hashes, and the first replay datasets per product.
  • Phase 2, the replayer (weeks 3–6): open-loop distributed replay on Kubernetes, generator self-checks, merged histograms and bootstrap intervals.
  • Phase 3, baselines (weeks 6–9): fingerprints, the baseline store, standard sweeps and server-side breakdowns for every production configuration.
  • Phase 4, gates and service (weeks 9–12): CI regression gates, the dedicated benchmark pool, weekly re-baselining and production-versus-baseline drift alerts.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Synthetic content: replays preserve shape but not text, so content-dependent effects (speculative decoding acceptance, expert routing) need separate corpora.
  • Dedicated benchmark GPUs cost capacity that could serve or train.
  • Slower releases: full sweeps with repeats take hours for engine upgrades.
  • Strict validity rules discard runs: generator lateness or saturation invalidates a run instead of producing a doubtful number.

Open questions.

  • Agentic traffic: multi-turn sessions where each request depends on the previous answer need dependency-aware replay, not independent arrivals.
  • Cost per token as a first-class metric: should baselines carry dollars per million tokens at SLO capacity, using each GPU type's price?
  • Benchmarks across clusters: can baselines from one cluster predict another with different networking (Design 18)?
  • Smaller detectable changes: what isolation (fixed clocks, pinned firmware, reserved switches) would bring run-to-run noise from 3% to 1%?
Design 23 · 12 sections

Design 23: Health checks across layers and automated remediation that survives fault storms

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. The health model: layers, signals and failure domains
  3. Passive detection: Xid, DCGM and logs
  4. Active checks: from preflight to burn-in
  5. Network health: finding the bad link
  6. Software health and configuration conformance
  7. From signals to verdicts
  8. The remediation ladder
  9. Handling fault storms
  10. Safety rails for automation
  11. Measuring the health system
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we detect faults in GPU nodes across hardware, network and software, fix them automatically, and keep that automation from making things worse when many things fail at once? Design 14 covers how training jobs survive failures: checkpoints, restarts and hot spares. This design is about the fleet underneath: the checks that find bad GPUs, links and nodes, the remediation that repairs them without a human, and the safety mechanisms that stop remediation when a single shared cause (a switch, a power feed, a bad driver rollout) makes a hundred nodes look broken at once.

The short version: detect at every layer, decide with evidence, repair by a ladder, and treat many simultaneous failures as one problem. Passive signals (Xid errors, DCGM fields, logs, link counters) and active checks (diagnostics, bandwidth and NCCL tests) feed one event pipeline. It turns signals into node conditions with evidence, and taints a node before anything runs on it. Remediation climbs a ladder from the least disruptive action (restart the workload, reset one GPU) to the most (reimage, replace, send to the vendor), checking after each step. Before acting, a storm guard checks whether failures cluster in a shared failure domain or exceed rate limits. If they do, it stops node-level remediation, holds affected nodes in quarantine, and raises one domain-level incident instead of a hundred reboots.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The fleet has 256 nodes with 2,048 GPUs. Most days, one to three nodes develop a fault, and an engineer finds it hours later from a failed job. Then a top-of-rack switch firmware bug made links flap in three racks. The old remediation script saw 96 nodes failing their network check and rebooted all of them within 20 minutes. That killed every job in those racks, including ones that had been running fine, and the reboots didn't fix the switch.

What the platform must deliver.

  • Coverage of every layer: GPU, memory, PCIe, NVLink and NVSwitch, power and thermals, NICs and the fabric, and the software stack (driver, fabric manager, container runtime, kubelet, device plugin).
  • Fast detection: most faults detected within minutes, before a job is placed on a bad node.
  • Automatic repair: most single-node faults remediated without a human, from detection to a node back in service.
  • Least-disruptive action first: don't reboot a node when one GPU reset fixes it, and don't kill healthy jobs to repair a component they don't use.
  • Storm safety: correlated failures across a failure domain trigger one incident and a hold, not mass remediation.
  • Low false positives: the health system itself is measured, because wrong verdicts cost capacity.
  • A repair loop that closes: nodes that keep failing go to a repair queue and, if needed, the vendor, with evidence attached.

Out of scope: job-level fault tolerance (Design 14) and capacity planning for spares.

The health model: layers, signals and failure domains

Scenario. Each team wrote its own checks. The training team checked GPUs, the network team checked switches, and nobody checked whether the device plugin still advertised 8 GPUs after a driver crash. Faults between layers went unnoticed until jobs failed.

What the picture shows. One catalog of what can fail, how each failure is observed, and which shared domains link nodes.

1Hardware layer
GPU compute and memory (ECC, row remapping), PCIe, NVLink and NVSwitch, power and thermals, host memory and disks, NICs or InfiniBand HCAs, and optics.
2Network layer
link state and error counters, fabric routing, congestion and pause storms, and the paths to storage and the API server.
3Software layer
driver and firmware versions, fabric manager, container runtime and toolkit, kubelet, CNI, device plugin and DRA driver, and mounted filesystems.
4Passive signals
what the system reports by itself (Xid events, DCGM fields, kernel logs, link counters, node conditions). Cheap and continuous.
5Active signals
what a test shows (diagnostics, bandwidth tests, NCCL collectives, file I/O). More conclusive, but they need the node or the link.
6Failure domains
rack, top-of-rack switch, spine group, power distribution unit, cooling loop, and software rollout cohort (nodes that got the same driver or firmware). The storm guard uses these.

The YAML. The check catalog: what each check covers, how often it runs and what it costs (a platform convention, read by the health agents).

# health/catalog.yamlchecks:- { name: xid-watch,        layer: hardware, kind: passive, source: kernel-log,  interval: continuous }- { name: dcgm-fields,      layer: hardware, kind: passive, source: dcgm,        interval: 30s,    fields: [ECC_DBE_VOL_TOTAL, ROW_REMAP_PENDING, ROW_REMAP_FAILURE, NVLINK_CRC_FLIT_ERROR_COUNT_TOTAL, GPU_TEMP, POWER_VIOLATION] }- { name: ib-counters,      layer: network,  kind: passive, source: sysfs,       interval: 60s,    fields: [symbol_error, link_downed, port_rcv_errors, link_error_recovery] }- { name: sw-conformance,   layer: software, kind: passive, source: node-agent,  interval: 5m }- { name: dcgm-diag-r1,     layer: hardware, kind: active,  needs: idle-gpu,     interval: between-jobs, duration: 1m }- { name: dcgm-diag-r3,     layer: hardware, kind: active,  needs: idle-node,    interval: after-repair, duration: 30m }- { name: nvbandwidth,      layer: hardware, kind: active,  needs: idle-node,    interval: between-jobs, duration: 2m }- { name: nccl-allreduce-rack, layer: network, kind: active, needs: idle-rack,   interval: weekly-or-after-repair, duration: 10m }domains: [rack, tor_switch, spine_group, pdu, cooling_loop, driver_cohort, firmware_cohort]
Going deeper2 points
  • Every check names its layer and domain: a verdict can then say "GPU 3 on node r12n07" or "every node on tor-12", which decides between a node-level repair and a domain incident.
  • Use what exists before building: DCGM, Node Problem Detector and packaged systems such as NVIDIA's NVSentinel already implement much of the detection, quarantine and remediation pipeline. The design here works the same way whether these are adopted or built.

Passive detection: Xid, DCGM and logs

Scenario. A GPU logged Xid 79 ("fallen off the bus") at 02:14. The node stayed schedulable, Kueue placed a 64-GPU job on it at 02:30, and the job hung at initialization until someone noticed at 09:00.

What the picture shows. How continuous signals become classified events within seconds.

1Sources
kernel logs (Xid, PCIe AER, machine checks), DCGM fields and health watches, InfiniBand and Ethernet counters, kubelet and container runtime logs.
2Classification
each signal maps to a fault class, a scope (one GPU, the node, a link) and a recommended first action, following NVIDIA's GPU debug guidelines for Xids.
3Thresholds and rates
counters matter as rates and trends. A few correctable errors are normal, but a rising rate or pending row remaps are not.
4Immediate quarantine
fatal classes taint the node at once, so no new pods land on it while the rest of the pipeline decides what to do.
5Context with the event
the job running on the GPU at the time, recent changes to the node, and earlier events, all attached as evidence.

The code. Classifying Xid events into fault classes and first actions (Python, simplified; follow the vendor's current guidance per GPU generation).

XID_CLASSES = {    # xid: (fault class, scope, first action)    13:  ("app-or-hw",       "gpu",  "restart-workload"),   # graphics engine exception; often the application    31:  ("app-or-hw",       "gpu",  "restart-workload"),   # memory page fault; usually the application    43:  ("app",             "gpu",  "none"),               # GPU stopped processing; the application's error    48:  ("memory-dbe",      "gpu",  "drain-then-reset-gpu"),    63:  ("row-remap",       "gpu",  "drain-then-reset-gpu"),    64:  ("row-remap-fail",  "gpu",  "drain-then-reboot"),     # remapping failed: replacement candidate    74:  ("nvlink",          "node", "drain-then-reset-gpu"),    79:  ("fell-off-bus",    "node", "drain-then-reboot"),  # fatal: taint immediately    92:  ("sbe-rate",        "gpu",  "watch"),              # informational    94:  ("contained-ecc",   "gpu",  "restart-workload"),    95:  ("uncontained-ecc", "gpu",  "drain-then-reset-gpu"),    119: ("gsp-timeout",     "node", "drain-then-reboot"),    120: ("gsp-error",       "node", "drain-then-reboot"),}FATAL = {"fell-off-bus", "uncontained-ecc", "gsp-timeout", "gsp-error", "row-remap-fail"} def classify(xid: int, gpu_index: int, node: str, repeats_24h: int) -> dict:    cls, scope, action = XID_CLASSES.get(xid, ("unknown", "node", "investigate"))    if cls.startswith("app") and repeats_24h >= 3:            # same GPU, different jobs: likely hardware        cls, action = "suspect-hw", "drain-then-reset-gpu"    return {"node": node, "gpu": gpu_index, "xid": xid, "class": cls, "scope": scope,            "action": action, "taint_now": cls in FATAL}
Going deeper2 points
  • Application errors look like hardware errors: Xid 13 or 31 from one job is usually that job. The same Xid on the same GPU across different jobs is the GPU. Keep per-GPU history to tell them apart.
  • Watch pending row remaps: a GPU with pending remaps needs a reset to activate them. A GPU whose remapping failed needs replacement.

Active checks: from preflight to burn-in

Scenario. A node passed every passive check but delivered 60% of normal NVLink bandwidth on one GPU. Every 512-GPU job that included it ran at the speed of its slowest rank. Nothing reported an error.

What the picture shows. Active checks in tiers, by cost and by when the node can spare the time.

1Preflight (seconds, at job start)
each pod checks its GPUs are visible, healthy and not in use, and that a small collective with its neighbors completes. A failure releases the job's placement before it wastes a gang (Design 17).
2Between jobs (minutes, on idle nodes)
quick diagnostics (dcgmi diag -r 1 or -r 2) and GPU-to-GPU bandwidth tests. These catch degraded but not failed hardware.
3After repair and periodically (30 minutes or more)
long diagnostics (-r 3 or -r 4), memory and stress tests, and multi-node NCCL tests across the rack. A node returns to service only after passing these.
4Performance baselines, not just pass/fail
bandwidth and collective results are compared with the fleet's distribution for that node type. A node in the bottom 1% is flagged even without an error.
5Scheduling the checks
idle-node checks run as low-priority, preemptible workloads through Kueue, so they use gaps instead of taking capacity from jobs.

The code. Flagging degraded nodes from bandwidth results against the fleet distribution (Python).

import numpy as np def degraded(results: dict[str, list[float]], fleet: list[float], z: float = -4.0, floor: float = 0.85) -> list[dict]:    """results: node -> per-GPU NVLink bandwidth (GB/s); fleet: all healthy GPUs of this type."""    med, mad = np.median(fleet), np.median(np.abs(np.array(fleet) - np.median(fleet))) * 1.4826    flags = []    for node, per_gpu in results.items():        for gpu, bw in enumerate(per_gpu):            score = (bw - med) / mad            if score < z or bw < floor * med:                       # robust z-score or 15% below median                flags.append({"node": node, "gpu": gpu, "bw": bw, "fleet_median": med, "z": round(score, 1)})    return flags
Going deeper2 points
  • A slow GPU is a fault: in synchronous training, one GPU at 60% bandwidth slows the whole job. Performance outliers are remediated like errors.
  • Keep preflight short: a 30-second preflight on 1,024 pods is cheap compared with a job that hangs for an hour. A 10-minute preflight isn't.

Network health: finding the bad link

Scenario. A 256-GPU job ran 30% slower than the day before. Every node passed its checks. The cause was one optical transceiver with a high symbol-error rate, retransmitting quietly on a single rail.

What the picture shows. Network checks that localize problems to a link, a switch or a domain.

1Counters per port
symbol errors, link-down events, receive errors and error-recovery counts on hosts and switches, tracked as rates.
2Link flaps
a link that goes down and up is a different fault from a link that's slow. Both are recorded with timestamps.
3Congestion signals
for RoCE, pause-frame (PFC) rates and ECN marks. A pause storm from one host can slow a whole switch.
4Pairwise tests
bandwidth tests between pairs of nodes, per rail, arranged so every link is covered. The pattern of slow pairs identifies the common link.
5Domain view
when many links on one switch degrade together, the switch is the suspect, not the nodes. This feeds the storm guard.

The code. Localizing a bad link from a pairwise bandwidth matrix (Python).

from collections import Counter def suspect_links(pairs: dict[tuple[str, str], float], paths: dict[tuple[str, str], list[str]],                  expected: float, slow: float = 0.8) -> list[tuple[str, int, int]]:    """pairs: (src, dst) -> measured GB/s; paths: (src, dst) -> links traversed (host port, switch ports)."""    bad_pairs = [p for p, bw in pairs.items() if bw < slow * expected]    on_bad = Counter(l for p in bad_pairs for l in paths[p])    on_all = Counter(l for p in pairs for l in paths[p])    ranked = sorted(on_bad, key=lambda l: on_bad[l] / on_all[l], reverse=True)    return [(l, on_bad[l], on_all[l]) for l in ranked if on_bad[l] / on_all[l] > 0.9]   # slow on ~every path
Going deeper2 points
  • The network team owns the switches, the health system owns the evidence: a ticket with the suspect link, its counters and the failing pair tests gets fixed faster than "job is slow".
  • Drain the rail, not the node: with multi-rail networks, a bad link can be excluded from NCCL's topology while it's repaired, if the job framework supports it.

Software health and configuration conformance
