Scenario. After a partial driver upgrade, 14 nodes ran a driver that didn't match their fabric manager version. The fabric manager failed to start, NVLink was unavailable, and jobs fell back to PCIe. Every hardware check passed.

What the picture shows. The software stack checked against a golden configuration per node type.

1Versions
driver, CUDA compatibility, fabric manager, firmware (GPU, NIC, BMC), OFED or NIC drivers, kernel, container toolkit.
2Services
fabric manager running, persistence mode, the device plugin or DRA driver advertising the expected GPUs, kubelet and runtime healthy, and the CNI ready.
3Allocatable vs physical
a node with 8 physical GPUs that advertises 7 has a problem, even if every visible GPU is healthy.
4Mounts and paths
shared filesystems mounted and responsive, local NVMe healthy, and reachability of the API server, registry and object storage.
5Conformance as a check
the node agent reports drift from the golden configuration. Drift is a fault with a scope (a rollout cohort) and a fix (finish or roll back the rollout).

The code. A conformance check against the golden configuration for the node type (Python, node agent).

GOLDEN = {"h100-sxm": {"driver": "580.95.05", "fabricmanager": "580.95.05", "gpus": 8,                       "nic_fw": "28.43.1014", "kernel": "6.8.0-60", "persistence_mode": True}} def conformance(node_type: str, observed: dict) -> list[dict]:    want, issues = GOLDEN[node_type], []    for key, value in want.items():        if observed.get(key) != value:            issues.append({"check": key, "want": value, "got": observed.get(key)})    if observed.get("driver") != observed.get("fabricmanager"):        issues.append({"check": "driver==fabricmanager", "severity": "fatal"})       # NVLink unusable    if observed.get("allocatable_gpus") != observed.get("gpus"):        issues.append({"check": "allocatable", "want": observed.get("gpus"), "got": observed.get("allocatable_gpus")})    return issues
Going deeper2 points
  • Rollouts are failure domains: conformance drift usually comes from a rollout that stopped halfway. The fix is at the rollout, not at each node.
  • Version the golden configuration: it changes with every planned upgrade, and checks must know which version a node is meant to be on during the rollout window.

From signals to verdicts

Scenario. Three tools watched the same node: one set a custom node condition, one added a taint, and one paged the on-call. They disagreed about whether the node was healthy, and the remediation script acted on whichever it read first.

What the picture shows. One pipeline from raw signals to a single verdict per node, with evidence.

1Ingest
agents send events (signal, class, scope, timestamp, evidence) to one pipeline.
2Deduplicate and correlate
repeats of the same fault are merged, and related events (an Xid and a failed diagnostic on the same GPU) are joined.
3Verdict
healthy, degraded (usable, but flagged for maintenance), quarantined (no new work) or failed (evacuate), with the evidence that led to it.
4Expressed in Kubernetes
node conditions say why (for example, GpuXidFatal, NvlinkDegraded, SoftwareDrift), taints say what the scheduler must do. Only the pipeline writes them.
5Consumers
the scheduler (taints), remediation (verdicts), dashboards and tickets (evidence). Nothing acts on raw signals directly.

The YAML. What a quarantined node looks like after the pipeline's verdict (node conditions and taint).

status:  conditions:  - type: GpuXidFatal    status: "True"    reason: Xid79FellOffBus    message: "GPU 3 (PCI 0000:9a:00.0) Xid 79 at 02:14:07Z; evidence: health-evt-7f2c"    lastTransitionTime: "2026-11-19T02:14:09Z"spec:  taints:  - key: health.example.com/quarantine            # written only by the health pipeline    value: gpu-fatal    effect: NoSchedule  - key: health.example.com/evacuate    value: gpu-fatal    effect: NoExecute                             # added later by remediation, after the storm guard allows it
Going deeper2 points
  • Separate "don't schedule" from "evict": quarantine (NoSchedule) is cheap and safe to apply immediately. Eviction (NoExecute or a drain) affects running work and goes through the storm guard.
  • Evidence IDs everywhere: every condition, taint, ticket and remediation record references the same event IDs, so an engineer can reconstruct the reasoning.

The remediation ladder

Scenario. The old policy for every fault was "reboot the node". For a single GPU with a pending row remap, that cost a 20-minute reboot and a 64-GPU job restart. A GPU reset would have taken 30 seconds and touched one rank.

What the picture shows. Remediation as a ladder, climbed one step at a time with a check after each.

1Step 0, workload
the job restarts from its checkpoint on the remaining healthy capacity (Design 14). Used for application-class faults.
2Step 1, reset the GPU
for recoverable GPU faults (pending row remaps, contained errors). The node stays up and other GPUs keep working, where the hardware supports single-GPU reset.
3Step 2, reboot the node
for driver, GSP or PCIe faults, after draining the node's workloads (with a checkpoint request first).
4Step 3, reimage
for software corruption or repeated failures after reboot.
5Step 4, replace or repair
cloud nodes are replaced through the provider API. On-premises nodes go to a repair queue and, with evidence, to the vendor for RMA.
6Verification gate
after each step, the node runs the post-repair checks. It returns to service only if they pass. Otherwise the ladder climbs one step.
7Retry limits
a node that needs the same step three times in a week skips straight to repair, instead of cycling.

The code. The ladder as a small state machine (Python, remediation controller).

LADDER = ["restart-workload", "reset-gpu", "reboot", "reimage", "replace"] def next_step(fault: dict, history: list[dict]) -> str:    """fault: classified event; history: this node's remediations in the last 7 days."""    start = {"restart-workload": 0, "drain-then-reset-gpu": 1, "drain-then-reboot": 2}.get(fault["action"], 2)    tried = [h["step"] for h in history if h["fault_class"] == fault["class"]]    if tried.count(LADDER[start]) >= 3:        return "replace"                                            # repeat offender: stop cycling    if tried and not history[-1]["verified"]:        last = LADDER.index(history[-1]["step"])        return LADDER[min(last + 1, len(LADDER) - 1)]               # previous step failed verification    return LADDER[start]
Going deeper2 points
  • Drain politely: before evicting a training pod, signal the job to checkpoint (or wait for its next checkpoint within a deadline), so the repair doesn't throw away hours of work.
  • Collect diagnostics before fixing: a reboot erases evidence. Gather logs, nvidia-bug-report output and counters first, and attach them to the repair record.

Handling fault storms

Scenario. The switch firmware bug from the first scenario: 96 nodes failed network checks within ten minutes, all in three racks under one spine group. Node-level remediation rebooted them all. The real fix, rolling back the switch firmware, came three hours later from the network team.

What the picture shows. The storm guard between verdicts and remediation.

1Correlation by failure domain
before remediating, the guard groups recent failures by rack, switch, spine group, power feed, cooling loop and rollout cohort. If one domain holds far more failures than its share, the cause is probably the domain.
2Rate limits
a maximum number of nodes in remediation at once, per pool and per domain, and a maximum per hour. Above them, new remediations wait.
3Minimum healthy capacity
remediation that would leave a pool below a healthy floor is held. (The medik8s NodeHealthCheck operator's minHealthy setting implements the same idea for node remediation.)
4Storm mode
when the guard trips, affected nodes stay quarantined (no new work) but aren't drained or rebooted. Running jobs that still work keep running. One incident is raised for the domain, with the evidence, and it pages a human.
5Leaving storm mode
a person, or the domain's own health returning, clears it. Nodes are then re-checked and remediated individually at the normal rate.

The code. Detecting a domain-level storm before acting (Python, storm guard).

from collections import Counter def storm_check(failing: list[dict], fleet: list[dict], window_min: int = 15,                max_concurrent: int = 8, domain_share: float = 0.3) -> dict:    """failing: nodes with new failure verdicts in the window; fleet: all nodes with their domains."""    if len(failing) <= 2:        return {"storm": False}    for dim in ("tor_switch", "spine_group", "pdu", "cooling_loop", "driver_cohort", "firmware_cohort", "rack"):        counts = Counter(n[dim] for n in failing)        domain, hits = counts.most_common(1)[0]        size = sum(1 for n in fleet if n[dim] == domain)        if hits >= 3 and hits / size >= domain_share:                       # a third of the domain failing            return {"storm": True, "reason": f"{dim}={domain}", "hits": hits, "domain_size": size,                    "action": "hold-remediation-and-open-domain-incident"}    if len(failing) > max_concurrent:        return {"storm": True, "reason": "rate", "hits": len(failing), "action": "queue-remediation"}    return {"storm": False}
Going deeper2 points
  • A storm is often caused by the health system: a bad check, a monitoring outage or a new threshold can make healthy nodes look failed. Storm mode protects against that too.
  • Keep quarantine cheap and remediation expensive: in a storm, stopping new placements is almost always right. Evicting and rebooting rarely is.

Safety rails for automation

Scenario. A new health check with a wrong threshold went live on a Monday. It marked 40% of nodes as degraded and queued them all for reboot. The rate limit slowed it down, but nobody noticed until 30 nodes had rebooted.

What the picture shows. How changes to the health system itself are made safe.

1Shadow mode for new checks and rules
they produce verdicts that are logged but not acted on, and are compared with existing checks for a week before enforcement.
2Staged enforcement
a new rule enforces on one pool first, like any other change (Design 19).
3Budgets
a daily remediation budget per pool (for example, 3% of nodes). Exceeding it pauses automation and pages a human.
4Kill switch
one setting pauses all remediation while keeping detection and quarantine running.
5Audit
every action records its trigger, evidence, rule version and result.
6Check the checks
a small set of known-good nodes and known-bad parts (kept for the purpose) verifies that checks pass and fail when they should.

The YAML. A NodeHealthCheck with a minimum-healthy floor and pause support (medik8s), for the generic not-ready case alongside the GPU-specific pipeline.

apiVersion: remediation.medik8s.io/v1alpha1kind: NodeHealthCheckmetadata: { name: gpu-workers-notready }spec:  selector:    matchLabels: { node-pool: h100 }  minHealthy: "90%"                                  # never remediate below 90% healthy in the pool  unhealthyConditions:  - { type: Ready, status: "False",   duration: 300s }  - { type: Ready, status: "Unknown", duration: 300s }  pauseRequests: []                                  # the kill switch: add a reason to pause new remediations  remediationTemplate:    apiVersion: self-node-remediation.medik8s.io/v1alpha1    kind: SelfNodeRemediationTemplate    name: self-node-remediation-automatic-strategy-template    namespace: medik8s
Going deeper2 points
  • Automation that can't be paused will eventually do damage: the kill switch is tested in drills, not discovered during an incident.
  • Version the rules like code: a remediation record that names the rule version makes it possible to find every action a bad rule took.

Measuring the health system

Scenario. The team believed automated remediation "handled most things". The data showed 35% of remediated nodes failed again within a week, and the same 11 nodes accounted for half of all remediations.

What the picture shows. The metrics that show whether health checks and remediation work.

1Time to detect
from fault to verdict, by fault class.
2Time to repair
from verdict to back in service, by ladder step.
3Automation rate
the share of faults fixed without a human.
4Recurrence
the share of repaired nodes that fail again within 7 days. High recurrence means the ladder stops too low.
5Repeat offenders
nodes and parts with the most remediations, sent to the repair queue with their history.
6False positives
verdicts later shown wrong (a node that passed every deep check after quarantine). Each costs capacity.
7Capacity lost
GPU-hours in quarantine, repair and drained-but-healthy states, per week.

The code. Weekly health-system metrics from remediation records (Python).

import pandas as pd def health_metrics(r: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:    """r: one row per remediation with fault_ts, verdict_ts, in_service_ts, node, step, human, refail_7d, false_positive."""    detect = (r.verdict_ts - r.fault_ts).dt.total_seconds() / 60    repair = (r.in_service_ts - r.verdict_ts).dt.total_seconds() / 60    offenders = r.node.value_counts()    return {        "mttd_min_p50": detect.median(), "mttr_min_p50_by_step": repair.groupby(r.step).median().round(0).to_dict(),        "automation_rate": round(1 - r.human.mean(), 3),        "recurrence_7d": round(r.refail_7d.mean(), 3),                      # 35% means the ladder stops too low        "false_positive_rate": round(r.false_positive.mean(), 3),        "top_offenders": offenders.head(10).to_dict(),        "offender_share": round(offenders.head(11).sum() / len(r), 3),    }
Going deeper2 points
  • Recurrence decides the ladder: if reboots fix a fault class for a day and then it returns, start that class one step higher.
  • Share the evidence with vendors: RMA requests with diagnostics, Xid history and counters are approved faster, and fleet-wide data shows batch problems with a part.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, detect and quarantine (weeks 1–4): passive detection on every node, the event pipeline, verdicts as node conditions and quarantine taints. No automatic remediation yet.
  • Phase 2, active checks (weeks 3–8): preflight, between-job diagnostics and bandwidth checks, post-repair burn-in, pairwise network tests and software conformance.
  • Phase 3, remediation (weeks 6–12): the ladder for the most common fault classes, with the storm guard, budgets and kill switch, in shadow mode first and then pool by pool.
  • Phase 4, close the loop (weeks 10–16): repair queue and vendor RMA integration, metrics and recurrence-driven ladder tuning.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Quarantine before certainty: some healthy nodes are held for minutes while evidence is gathered.
  • Storm mode leaves faults unrepaired until a human confirms the cause, by design.
  • Active checks cost GPU time on idle nodes and at job start.
  • More components to operate: agents, the pipeline, the storm guard and the repair queue are a system of their own, with their own failure modes.

Open questions.

  • Predicting failures: can trends in correctable errors, temperatures and link counters predict failures well enough to drain nodes before they fail?
  • Partial nodes: should a node with one bad GPU keep serving 7-GPU or smaller jobs instead of going to repair?
  • Cross-cluster domains: how to detect a storm whose cause spans clusters, such as a firmware cohort deployed across providers (Design 18)?
  • Learning from incidents: can past storm incidents tune domain thresholds automatically, or should they stay hand-set?
Design 24 · 12 sections

Design 24: Instrumenting fleet utilization with DCGM, Prometheus and Grafana

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. The pipeline from GPU to dashboard
  3. Choosing fields and the interval
  4. Labels and joins: who used this GPU?
  5. Cardinality and scale
  6. The recording rule hierarchy
  7. Testing rules and alerts
  8. Alerts teams rely on
  9. Routing, ownership and noise control
  10. Dashboards as code
  11. Trusting the alerts: measuring alert quality
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we instrument a GPU fleet so that utilization numbers are correct, dashboards are fast, and alerts are ones teams act on instead of muting? Design 19 defined the utilization metric the scheduling program is judged on. Design 23 uses many of the same signals to find faults. This design is the observability layer under both: which DCGM fields to collect, how to attach team and job labels, how to keep Prometheus within its limits, the recording rules every dashboard reads, the alerts with their owners and runbooks, and the tests that keep all of it correct.

The short version: collect deliberately, join labels once, and make recording rules the only interface. DCGM exporter collects a reviewed set of fields at a fixed interval, with pod mapping on. Recording rules do the expensive joins (GPU to pod to namespace to team, GPU to node to pool) once per minute and publish a small set of named series in a fixed hierarchy: GPU, node, team and pool, fleet. Dashboards and alerts read only those series. Every rule and alert lives in Git with unit tests, every alert has an owner label that routes it, a runbook link and a measured precision, and alerts that aren't acted on are fixed or deleted.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The fleet has 2,048 GPUs across 3 clusters and 14 teams. Each team built its own Grafana dashboard with its own PromQL, so "utilization" had five definitions. The fleet dashboard took 40 seconds to load because every panel joined raw DCGM series with kube-state-metrics on the fly. One Prometheus ran out of memory twice in a month. The GPU alerts paged the platform on-call about low utilization in jobs that were simply loading data, so people muted them, and a real thermal-throttling problem went unnoticed for a week.

What the platform must deliver.

  • One definition per metric: utilization, allocation, activity and the rest come from shared recording rules, matching Design 19.
  • Attribution: every GPU sample attributed to node, pool, GPU model, pod, namespace, team and job.
  • Fast dashboards: fleet and team views load in under 3 seconds, at 30-day ranges.
  • Bounded cost: a known, budgeted number of series per GPU, and Prometheus instances that stay within memory.
  • Alerts teams rely on: each alert has an owner, a runbook and a severity that matches what the owner must do, and its precision is measured.
  • Correctness under change: rules and alerts are tested in CI against synthetic series before they deploy.
  • Long-term history: a year of aggregates for capacity planning and before-and-after comparisons.

Out of scope: application-level metrics (serving latency in Design 22, training throughput in Design 15) and fault remediation (Design 23).

The pipeline from GPU to dashboard

Scenario. DCGM exporter had been installed three different ways in three clusters: by the GPU Operator, by a standalone Helm chart, and by hand. The clusters exposed different metric sets, at different intervals, with different label names.

What the picture shows. One pipeline, the same in every cluster.

1DCGM exporter
deployed by the GPU Operator on every GPU node, with a shared metrics ConfigMap and Kubernetes pod mapping enabled.
2Prometheus per cluster
run by the Prometheus Operator, scraping the exporter through a ServiceMonitor, plus kube-state-metrics and node exporter.
3Recording rules
evaluated in each cluster's Prometheus, producing the shared series with a cluster label.
4Long-term store
recording-rule outputs (not raw DCGM series) are remote-written to a central store such as Mimir or Thanos for fleet views and a year of history.
5Grafana and Alertmanager
dashboards query the long-term store for fleet views and the cluster Prometheus for detail. Alerts are evaluated close to the data and routed by Alertmanager.

The YAML. The GPU Operator settings for DCGM exporter: a shared field list, a fixed interval and a ServiceMonitor (ClusterPolicy fragment).

apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1kind: ClusterPolicymetadata: { name: cluster-policy }spec:  dcgmExporter:    enabled: true    config:      name: fleet-dcgm-metrics                 # ConfigMap with key dcgm-metrics.csv, same namespace as the operator    env:    - { name: DCGM_EXPORTER_COLLECTORS, value: /etc/dcgm-exporter/dcgm-metrics.csv }    - { name: DCGM_EXPORTER_INTERVAL, value: "30000" }          # 30 s everywhere    - { name: DCGM_EXPORTER_KUBERNETES, value: "true" }         # pod, namespace, container labels    serviceMonitor:      enabled: true      interval: 30s      honorLabels: false      additionalLabels: { release: kube-prometheus-stack }
Going deeper2 points
  • Remote-write the rules, not the raw series: raw per-GPU DCGM data stays in the cluster for a short retention. The long-term store receives the much smaller recording-rule outputs, which is what fleet dashboards and capacity planning need.
  • The same pipeline everywhere is the feature: clusters added later get the same fields, labels and rules by installing the same GPU Operator values and rule bundle.

Choosing fields and the interval

Scenario. The teams' dashboards relied on DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL. A data-loading job that touched the GPU once a second showed 100% "utilization". SM activity, the field that would have shown the GPU was mostly idle, wasn't being collected at all.

What the picture shows. The reviewed field list, grouped by purpose, and the interval trade-off.

1Activity (profiling fields)
graphics engine active (the headline activity signal), SM active, SM occupancy, tensor pipe active and DRAM active. Several are commented out in the exporter's default list and must be enabled.
2Memory and interconnect
framebuffer used and free, PCIe and NVLink transmit and receive bytes.
3Power and thermals
power usage, GPU and memory temperature, and clock event (throttle) reasons.
4Errors
Xid errors, ECC counts, row-remap status and failures, and NVLink error counters, which Design 23 uses.
5Identity
driver version and GPU model as labels.
6Interval
30 seconds for the fleet. Profiling fields cost GPU-side sampling. Faster intervals multiply storage, and the questions asked (minutes to months) don't need them.

The YAML. The shared field list (ConfigMap read by DCGM exporter; three columns: field, Prometheus type, help).

apiVersion: v1kind: ConfigMapmetadata: { name: fleet-dcgm-metrics, namespace: gpu-operator }data:  dcgm-metrics.csv: |    # activity    DCGM_FI_PROF_GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE,    gauge,   Ratio of time the graphics engine is active    DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE,           gauge,   Ratio of cycles an SM has at least one warp assigned    DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_OCCUPANCY,        gauge,   Ratio of resident warps to maximum warps per SM    DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE,  gauge,   Ratio of cycles the tensor pipe is active    DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE,         gauge,   Ratio of cycles device memory is sending or receiving    DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL,             gauge,   Kept for compatibility; not used in rules    # memory and interconnect    DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED,              gauge,   Framebuffer used (MiB)    DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_FREE,              gauge,   Framebuffer free (MiB)    DCGM_FI_PROF_NVLINK_TX_BYTES,     counter, NVLink bytes transmitted    DCGM_FI_PROF_NVLINK_RX_BYTES,     counter, NVLink bytes received    DCGM_FI_PROF_PCIE_TX_BYTES,       counter, PCIe bytes transmitted    DCGM_FI_PROF_PCIE_RX_BYTES,       counter, PCIe bytes received    # power and thermals    DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE,          gauge,   Power draw (W)    DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP,             gauge,   GPU temperature (C)    DCGM_FI_DEV_MEMORY_TEMP,          gauge,   Memory temperature (C)    DCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCK_THROTTLE_REASONS, gauge, Clock throttle reasons bitmask    # errors    DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS,           gauge,   Last Xid error    DCGM_FI_DEV_ECC_DBE_VOL_TOTAL,    counter, Volatile double-bit ECC errors    DCGM_FI_DEV_ROW_REMAP_FAILURE,    gauge,   Row remapping failed    DCGM_FI_DEV_UNCORRECTABLE_REMAPPED_ROWS, counter, Rows remapped for uncorrectable errors    DCGM_FI_DEV_NVLINK_CRC_FLIT_ERROR_COUNT_TOTAL, counter, NVLink flit CRC errors
Going deeper3 points
  • Profiling fields and profilers compete: when a user runs Nsight Compute or Nsight Systems with GPU metrics on a node, DCGM's profiling fields can conflict with it. DCGM can pause profiling collection (dcgmi profile --pause) for the session. Document this for users, and expect gaps rather than errors.
  • When fleet metrics say "busy" but one job is slow, profile that job: Nsight Systems records a timeline of one process, with its GPU kernels, memory copies and any phases you label, so you can see whether the GPU waits for data. Run it inside the job's pod. That needs access to the kernel's performance interface (in container terms, the SYS_ADMIN capability or privileged mode, and a host setting that allows it), and sampling GPU metrics needs elevated permissions (Nsight Systems guide). Grant that only to a short-lived debug pod, not to every job, and pause DCGM's profiling fields on the node first, as above. In the current guide the option that samples GPU metrics is spelled --gpu-metrics-devices.
  • Field names change between DCGM versions: the throttle-reasons field has a newer name (DCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCKS_EVENT_REASONS). Pin the exporter version with the field list and test both together.

Labels and joins: who used this GPU?

Scenario. DCGM series carried the pod and namespace, but not the team, the node pool or the job. Every team dashboard joined three metrics in every panel, and teams whose namespaces lacked a team label silently disappeared from the totals.

What the picture shows. Where each label comes from and where the join happens.

1From DCGM exporter
GPU index, UUID, model name, hostname, and (with pod mapping) pod, namespace and container, read from the kubelet's pod-resources API.
2From kube-state-metrics
namespace labels (team, cost center), node labels (pool, rack, GPU product) and pod labels (job name, workload kind). These must be allow-listed in kube-state-metrics to appear at all.
3MIG
with MIG enabled, the exporter adds GPU-instance labels. Each instance is a separate series, and rules must count instances rather than whole GPUs.
4Join once, in recording rules
the first rule level attaches team, pool and job to every GPU sample. Everything above reads the joined series.
5Unattributed is a category
GPUs whose namespace has no team label are reported as team="unlabeled", not dropped.

The YAML. The first-level recording rules that attach team and pool to GPU activity (Prometheus Operator).

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1kind: PrometheusRulemetadata: { name: gpu-joins, namespace: monitoring }spec:  groups:  - name: gpu-joins    interval: 1m    rules:    - record: namespace:team:info                      # one series per namespace with its team      expr: |        max by (namespace, team) (          label_replace(kube_namespace_labels{label_team!=""}, "team", "$1", "label_team", "(.*)")        )        or max by (namespace, team) (          label_replace(kube_namespace_labels{label_team=""}, "team", "unlabeled", "", "")   # never dropped        )    - record: node:pool:info      expr: |        max by (node, pool, gpu_product) (          label_replace(label_replace(kube_node_labels, "pool", "$1", "label_node_pool", "(.*)"),                        "gpu_product", "$1", "label_nvidia_com_gpu_product", "(.*)")        )    - record: gpu:engine_active:ratio                  # one series per GPU, with team and pool attached      expr: |        label_replace(DCGM_FI_PROF_GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE, "node", "$1", "Hostname", "(.*)")        * on (namespace) group_left (team) namespace:team:info        * on (node) group_left (pool, gpu_product) node:pool:info
Going deeper2 points
  • Idle GPUs have no pod: a GPU not assigned to any pod has empty pod and namespace labels, so a join on namespace drops it. A parallel rule records unassigned GPUs with team="none", so fleet totals still add up.
  • Hostname is not always the node name: on some platforms DCGM's Hostname differs from the Kubernetes node name. Set the exporter's node name from the downward API, or keep a mapping rule, and test it.

Cardinality and scale

Scenario. One Prometheus ran out of memory twice. It held 3.1 million active series. More than half came from DCGM series that inherited every pod label, including a per-run hash, through a well-meant relabeling rule.

What the picture shows. The series budget and the controls that keep it.

1Budget per GPU
about 25 DCGM fields times one series per GPU (more with MIG and NVLink per link) gives roughly 30 series per GPU. At 2,048 GPUs, that's about 60,000 series. That's cheap, unless labels multiply it.
2Label churn is the danger
every new pod creates new series. Per-run labels (hashes, run IDs) on raw DCGM series turn each job into a new set of series, and they pile up across the retention window.
3Controls
don't copy pod labels onto DCGM series. Attach job identity only in recording rules, and only labels on an allow-list. Drop unused fields at scrape time.
4Retention by level
raw DCGM series kept 7 days in the cluster. Recording-rule outputs kept 13 months in the long-term store.
5Watch it
active series per job and per metric name, with an alert when the budget is exceeded.

The code. Estimating active series for DCGM data under different label policies (Python).

def dcgm_series(gpus: int, fields: int, nvlink_fields: int = 2, links_per_gpu: int = 18,                mig_instances: int = 1, churn_jobs_per_gpu_per_day: float = 0.0, retention_days: int = 7) -> dict:    per_gpu = fields * mig_instances + nvlink_fields * links_per_gpu        # per-link fields add up fast    steady = gpus * per_gpu    churn = gpus * per_gpu * churn_jobs_per_gpu_per_day * retention_days    # series kept alive in the TSDB    return {"steady_series": steady, "with_label_churn": int(steady + churn)} print(dcgm_series(2048, 25, nvlink_fields=0))                                   # ~51k: pod labels onlyprint(dcgm_series(2048, 25, nvlink_fields=0, churn_jobs_per_gpu_per_day=6))     # per-run labels on raw series
Going deeper2 points
  • Per-link NVLink fields are opt-in: 18 links per GPU times a few fields doubles the DCGM series count. Collect the per-GPU totals by default and per-link data only on demand.
  • Shard by cluster, not by metric: one Prometheus per cluster (or per few hundred nodes) keeps joins local. Fleet views come from the long-term store.

The recording rule hierarchy

Scenario. Five dashboards computed fleet utilization five ways: averaging GPU utilization, summing SM activity, counting allocated GPUs. They disagreed by up to 20 points, and each team believed its own.

What the picture shows. One set of rules, named by level, that every consumer reads.

1Naming
Prometheus's level:metric:operations convention. The prefix says what the series is aggregated by (gpu:, node:, team:, pool:, fleet:), and the suffix says what was done (:ratio, :sum, :avg1h).
2GPU level
joined activity, allocation (is any pod assigned to this GPU) and health per GPU, every minute.
3Node, team and pool levels
sums and averages of the GPU level, with counts so ratios can be recomputed correctly at higher levels.
4Fleet level
the headline numbers of Design 19: allocation rate, activity rate and active utilization.
5Time aggregates
hourly averages for dashboards with long ranges. Daily values computed in the long-term store.
6Ratios from sums, never averages of ratios
a team-level ratio is the sum of active GPUs divided by the sum of allocated GPUs, not the average of per-GPU ratios.

The YAML. The core utilization rules from GPU level to fleet level (Prometheus Operator).

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1kind: PrometheusRulemetadata: { name: gpu-utilization, namespace: monitoring }spec:  groups:  - name: gpu-utilization    interval: 1m    rules:    - record: gpu:allocated:bool                       # 1 if a pod holds this GPU      expr: max by (cluster, node, gpu, UUID, team, pool, gpu_product, namespace, pod) (gpu:engine_active:ratio{pod!=""} >= bool 0)    - record: gpu:active:bool                          # 1 if allocated and the engine is working      expr: max by (cluster, node, gpu, UUID, team, pool, gpu_product, namespace, pod) (gpu:engine_active:ratio{pod!=""} > bool 0.05)    - record: team:gpu_allocated:sum      expr: sum by (cluster, team, pool) (gpu:allocated:bool)    - record: team:gpu_active:sum      expr: sum by (cluster, team, pool) (gpu:active:bool)    - record: pool:gpu_capacity:sum                    # healthy, schedulable GPUs      expr: |        sum by (cluster, pool) (          kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="nvidia_com_gpu"}          * on (cluster, node) group_left (pool) node:pool:info          * on (cluster, node) group_left () (kube_node_spec_unschedulable == bool 0)   # 0 if cordoned        )    - record: pool:gpu_active_utilization:ratio        # the headline, from sums      expr: sum by (cluster, pool) (team:gpu_active:sum) / pool:gpu_capacity:sum    - record: fleet:gpu_active_utilization:ratio      expr: sum(team:gpu_active:sum) / sum(pool:gpu_capacity:sum)    - record: team:gpu_active:avg1h      expr: avg_over_time(team:gpu_active:sum[1h])
Going deeper2 points
  • Rules are an API: renaming or redefining a recording rule breaks dashboards and alerts that depend on it. Version them, deprecate old names for a release before removing them, and list consumers.
  • Evaluation time matters: rule groups that depend on other groups' outputs see them one interval late. Keep dependent rules in the same group, where they're evaluated in order.

Testing rules and alerts

Scenario. A refactor changed > 0.05 to > 5 in the activity rule, because someone assumed the field was a percentage. Fleet utilization dropped to zero on every dashboard, and the low-utilization alert fired for every team at once.

What the picture shows. Rules and alerts tested like code before they deploy.

1Unit tests with synthetic series
promtool test rules feeds hand-written series into the rules and checks the outputs and alerts at given times.
2Test the edge cases
unlabeled namespaces, idle GPUs without pods, MIG instances, a node going unschedulable, missing data.
3Lint in CI
promtool check rules, plus checks that every alert has an owner label, a severity, a summary and a runbook URL.
4Shadow evaluation
a changed rule runs under a new name next to the old one for a few days, and the difference is reviewed before switching.
5Contract tests for dashboards
a script checks that every query in every dashboard only references recording rules that exist.

The YAML. A unit test for the activity and utilization rules, and for a team alert (promtool).

# tests/gpu-utilization.test.yamlrule_files: [../rules/gpu-utilization.yaml]evaluation_interval: 1mtests:- interval: 1m  input_series:  - series: 'gpu:engine_active:ratio{cluster="c1",node="n1",gpu="0",UUID="u0",team="llm",pool="h100",gpu_product="H100",pod="p1"}'    values: '0.62x10'  - series: 'gpu:engine_active:ratio{cluster="c1",node="n1",gpu="1",UUID="u1",team="llm",pool="h100",gpu_product="H100",pod="p2"}'    values: '0.01x10'                                  # allocated but idle  - series: 'kube_node_status_allocatable{resource="nvidia_com_gpu",node="n1",cluster="c1"}'    values: '8x10'  - series: 'node:pool:info{node="n1",pool="h100",gpu_product="H100",cluster="c1"}'    values: '1x10'  - series: 'kube_node_spec_unschedulable{node="n1",cluster="c1"}'    values: '0x10'  promql_expr_test:  - expr: team:gpu_active:sum{team="llm"}    eval_time: 5m    exp_samples: [{ labels: 'team:gpu_active:sum{cluster="c1",team="llm",pool="h100"}', value: 1 }]  - expr: pool:gpu_active_utilization:ratio    eval_time: 5m    exp_samples: [{ labels: 'pool:gpu_active_utilization:ratio{cluster="c1",pool="h100"}', value: 0.125 }]   # 1 of 8
Going deeper2 points
  • A test per bug: every rule bug found in production gets a test that reproduces it, so it can't come back.
  • Test alerts with time: alert tests check that an alert is not firing before its for duration has passed and is firing after, which catches wrong durations.

Alerts teams rely on

Scenario. The platform on-call received 140 GPU pages a week, mostly "GPU utilization below 10%" for jobs that were loading data or waiting at a barrier. They were muted. A cooling fault that throttled 64 GPUs for a week never paged anyone, because throttling had no alert.

What the picture shows. The alert catalog, split by who owns the fix.

1Platform alerts (page the platform)
exporter down or data stale, fatal Xid or row-remap failure (also feeding Design 23), sustained thermal or power throttling across a domain, NVLink error rates, and the observability pipeline itself (rule evaluation failures, remote-write lag).
2Team alerts (ticket to the team, not a page)
GPUs allocated but idle for hours, jobs holding GPUs with no activity since start, quota near exhaustion, and team utilization trends.
3Principles
each alert says what is wrong for whom, has a for duration longer than normal transient behavior, carries an owner label, a severity (page or ticket), and a runbook, and is tested.
4Symptoms over causes for pages
"64 GPUs throttled for 30 minutes" pages. "One GPU at 85 °C" doesn't.
5No utilization pages
low utilization isn't an emergency. It's a ticket with numbers, sent to the team that can fix it.

The YAML. Representative platform and team alerts (Prometheus Operator).

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1kind: PrometheusRulemetadata: { name: gpu-alerts, namespace: monitoring }spec:  groups:  - name: gpu-platform    rules:    - alert: DcgmExporterDataStale      expr: |        max by (cluster, node) (          label_replace(time() - timestamp(DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE), "node", "$1", "Hostname", "(.*)")        ) > 180      for: 5m      labels: { severity: page, owner: platform }      annotations:        summary: "No DCGM data from {{ $labels.node }} for 3+ minutes"        runbook_url: https://runbooks.example.com/gpu/dcgm-stale    - alert: GpuThermalThrottlingWidespread      expr: |        count by (cluster, pool) (          (DCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCK_THROTTLE_REASONS % 64 >= 32)                     # thermal slowdown bit          or (DCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCK_THROTTLE_REASONS % 128 >= 64)                  # hardware thermal slowdown bit        ) > 16      for: 30m      labels: { severity: page, owner: platform }      annotations:        summary: "{{ $value }} GPUs in {{ $labels.pool }} thermally throttled for 30 minutes"        runbook_url: https://runbooks.example.com/gpu/thermal-throttling  - name: gpu-team    rules:    - alert: GpusAllocatedButIdle      expr: |        sum by (cluster, team, namespace, pod) (gpu:allocated:bool - gpu:active:bool) >= 1        and on (cluster, team, namespace, pod)        (max by (cluster, team, namespace, pod) (max_over_time(gpu:active:bool[2h])) == 0)        and on (cluster, team, namespace, pod)        (max by (cluster, team, namespace, pod) (count_over_time(gpu:allocated:bool[2h])) >= 110)   # held ~2 h      for: 15m      labels: { severity: ticket, owner: team }        # routed to the team, never a page      annotations:        summary: "{{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} holds GPUs with no activity for 2 hours"        runbook_url: https://runbooks.example.com/gpu/idle-allocation
Going deeper2 points
  • Bitmask alerts need care: throttle reasons are bit flags. Test each bit with modulo arithmetic as above, and check the bit values against the DCGM version in use.
  • Alert on the pipeline too: a dashboard showing zero because the exporter died is worse than no dashboard. Staleness alerts come first.

Routing, ownership and noise control

Scenario. All GPU alerts went to one Slack channel. When a top-of-rack switch failed, 200 alerts arrived in five minutes (exporter stale, Xid, NVLink errors for every node behind it), and the one alert that explained the cause was on the second page.

What the picture shows. Alertmanager configuration that sends each alert to its owner, once.

1Route by owner and severity
platform pages go to the platform's paging service. Team tickets go to each team's queue, found from the team label.
2Group by domain
alerts are grouped by cluster and pool (or rack), so a domain-wide problem arrives as one notification listing the affected nodes.
3Inhibition
when a node is down or its exporter is stale, alerts that depend on that node's data are suppressed. A domain-level alert (from Design 23's storm detection) inhibits the node-level ones beneath it.
4Maintenance silences
planned drains and upgrades create silences automatically from the maintenance system, with an expiry.
5Repeat intervals by severity
pages repeat hourly until acknowledged. Tickets are sent once a day.

The YAML. Alertmanager routing, grouping and inhibition (fragment).

route:  receiver: platform-tickets  group_by: [cluster, pool, alertname]  group_wait: 60s  group_interval: 5m  routes:  - matchers: [owner="platform", severity="page"]    receiver: platform-pager    repeat_interval: 1h  - matchers: [owner="team"]    receiver: team-queues                     # webhook that files a ticket in the team's queue by label    group_by: [cluster, team, alertname]    repeat_interval: 24hinhibit_rules:- source_matchers: [alertname="DcgmExporterDataStale"]  target_matchers: [owner="platform", severity="page"]  equal: [cluster, node]                      # no GPU alerts from a node whose data is stale- source_matchers: [alertname="DomainIncident"]  target_matchers: [severity="page"]  equal: [cluster, pool]receivers:- name: platform-pager  pagerduty_configs: [{ routing_key_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/pd-platform }]- name: platform-tickets  webhook_configs: [{ url: http://alert-router.monitoring/tickets/platform }]- name: team-queues  webhook_configs: [{ url: http://alert-router.monitoring/tickets/by-team }]
Going deeper2 points
  • Every team label must route somewhere: a CI check compares team labels in the namespace inventory with the router's team list, so no alert lands nowhere.
  • Inhibition hides information: keep inhibited alerts visible in the alert UI and attached to the parent notification. Suppress the notifications, not the knowledge.

Dashboards as code

Scenario. Grafana had 230 dashboards, 180 of them copies of each other with small edits. Fixing a query meant finding every copy, and the fleet dashboard took 40 seconds because its panels queried raw DCGM series over 30 days.

What the picture shows. A small set of generated dashboards that only read recording rules.

1Four standard dashboards
fleet (pools, utilization tree, trends), team (allocation, activity, idle cost, wait times), node and GPU (fields, errors, thermals for one node), and job (the GPUs of one job over its lifetime).
2Generated from code
dashboards are generated by a script (or Grafonnet) from shared panel definitions, committed to Git, and provisioned by the Grafana Operator.
3Only recording rules
fleet and team panels query team:, pool: and fleet: series, so they're fast at any range. Raw DCGM queries appear only on the node and job dashboards, at short ranges.
4Variables, not copies
cluster, pool and team are dashboard variables. Each team uses the same dashboard filtered to its label.
5Links between levels
fleet links to pool, pool to team, team to job, job to node.

The code. Generating the team dashboard's panels from recording rules (Python).

import json PANELS = [    ("Allocated GPUs",        'sum(team:gpu_allocated:sum{team="$team", cluster=~"$cluster"})', "stat"),    ("Active GPUs",           'sum(team:gpu_active:sum{team="$team", cluster=~"$cluster"})', "stat"),    ("Activity rate",         'sum(team:gpu_active:sum{team="$team"}) / sum(team:gpu_allocated:sum{team="$team"})', "timeseries"),    ("Idle allocated (1h avg)", 'sum(team:gpu_allocated:sum{team="$team"}) - sum(team:gpu_active:avg1h{team="$team"})', "timeseries"),] def team_dashboard(uid: str = "gpu-team") -> dict:    panels = []    for i, (title, expr, kind) in enumerate(PANELS):        assert "DCGM_" not in expr, f"{title}: team panels must read recording rules only"        panels.append({"id": i + 1, "type": kind, "title": title,                       "gridPos": {"x": (i % 2) * 12, "y": (i // 2) * 8, "w": 12, "h": 8},                       "targets": [{"expr": expr, "refId": "A"}]})    return {"uid": uid, "title": "GPU · Team", "schemaVersion": 39, "panels": panels,            "templating": {"list": [                {"name": "cluster", "type": "query", "query": "label_values(team:gpu_allocated:sum, cluster)", "multi": True, "includeAll": True},                {"name": "team", "type": "query", "query": "label_values(team:gpu_allocated:sum, team)"}]}} print(json.dumps(team_dashboard())[:200])
Going deeper2 points
  • Provision, don't click: dashboards edited in the UI drift from Git. Make provisioned dashboards read-only and give teams a sandbox folder for experiments.
  • Show definitions on the dashboard: a text panel that links to the metric definitions settles most "why does this say 58%?" questions.

Trusting the alerts: measuring alert quality

Scenario. Nobody knew which alerts were useful. Some fired daily and were always ignored. Others had never fired, and nobody knew whether they still worked.

What the picture shows. Alerts treated as a product with quality metrics.

1Precision
the share of an alert's notifications that led to action (an acknowledgment followed by a change, ticket or incident). Alerts below a threshold are reworked or deleted.
2Volume per owner
pages per on-call shift and tickets per team per week, with targets.
3Time to acknowledge
by alert and severity. Slow acknowledgment of a page means it isn't trusted or isn't urgent.
4Coverage
incidents that no alert caught, found in postmortems, become new alerts with tests.
5Silent alerts
alerts that haven't fired in 90 days are tested by injecting a synthetic series, to prove they still work.
6Monthly review
owners review their alerts' metrics and decide whether to keep, tune or delete each one.

The code. Alert quality from Alertmanager notification history and ticket outcomes (Python).

import pandas as pd def alert_quality(n: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:    """n: one row per notification with alertname, owner, severity, fired_at, acked_at, actioned (bool)."""    n = n.assign(tta_min=(n.acked_at - n.fired_at).dt.total_seconds() / 60)    q = n.groupby(["alertname", "owner", "severity"]).agg(        notifications=("actioned", "size"), precision=("actioned", "mean"),        tta_p50_min=("tta_min", "median"))    q["verdict"] = "keep"    q.loc[(q.precision < 0.3) & (q.notifications >= 10), "verdict"] = "rework-or-delete"   # mostly ignored    q.loc[(q.severity == "page") & (q.tta_p50_min > 30), "verdict"] = "not-urgent: make it a ticket"    return q.sort_values("precision")
Going deeper2 points
  • Deleting alerts is a success: a smaller set of alerts that are always acted on protects attention better than a large set that's mostly ignored.
  • Track what the alerts protect: for each page, record the impact it prevented or shortened. That makes the case for keeping it.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, one pipeline (weeks 1–3): the same GPU Operator exporter settings and field list in every cluster, ServiceMonitors, kube-state-metrics label allow-lists and a series budget.
  • Phase 2, rules (weeks 3–6): the join and utilization rule hierarchy with unit tests, remote write of rule outputs, and retention by level.
  • Phase 3, dashboards (weeks 5–8): the four generated dashboards, provisioning through the Grafana Operator, and retirement of copied dashboards.
  • Phase 4, alerts (weeks 6–10): the alert catalog with owners and runbooks, Alertmanager routing and inhibition, deletion of the utilization pages, and monthly alert-quality reviews.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • 30-second resolution: short spikes are averaged away. Job-level profiling tools cover that need.
  • Raw DCGM data kept only 7 days: older questions are answered from aggregates.
  • Fewer, centrally owned rules: teams can't define their own utilization, which is the point but costs flexibility.
  • Utilization never pages: some teams wanted it to. They get tickets with numbers instead.

Open questions.

  • Per-job efficiency: should the platform publish model FLOPs utilization per job by combining DCGM tensor activity with the job's own throughput metrics?
  • MIG and time-slicing: how should "active" be defined for a GPU shared by several pods?
  • OpenTelemetry: when should the pipeline move from Prometheus scraping to OpenTelemetry collectors, and what changes for rules?
  • Cost attribution: how to turn the same series into chargeback that finance trusts as much as the platform does?
Design 25 · 12 sections

Design 25: A warehouse for utilization and spend: attribution to teams and workloads, and capacity planning

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Data sources and the model
  3. Ingestion: landing, staging and marts
  4. Cost per GPU-hour, comparable across providers
  5. Attribution: direct use, idle capacity and shared costs
  6. Workload costs and unit economics
  7. Reconciliation and data quality
  8. Statements, budgets and forecasts for teams
  9. Capacity planning: forecasting demand
  10. Commitments: how much to reserve
  11. Running it: the operating cadence
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we combine utilization, scheduler and billing data in one warehouse, so that every GPU dollar is attributed to a team and a workload, the totals match the invoices, and capacity decisions rest on the same numbers? Design 24 produces the utilization series. Design 19 uses them for team scorecards. This design takes them to finance: ingestion of metrics, workload records and billing exports from every provider (Design 18), a cost per GPU-hour for each pool, attribution rules for direct and shared costs, reconciliation against invoices, monthly statements, and the forecasts and commitment decisions of capacity planning.

The short version: one hourly fact table of GPU-hours, one cost per GPU-hour per pool, and attribution that always adds up to the invoice. Hourly GPU-hours come from recording rules and scheduler events, joined to teams and workloads with ownership valid at that time. Billing arrives in FOCUS format where providers support it, and on-premises cost is amortized into the same shape. Each pool-hour's cost is split among the workloads that held its GPUs, and idle capacity is a visible line, not hidden in everyone's rate. A reconciliation check proves that attributed cost equals billed cost, month by month. Capacity planning uses the same tables: demand forecasts from submitted and pending GPU-hours, a utilization ceiling, and commitment levels chosen from the demand distribution.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The fleet spends about $4.1 million a month across on-premises H100s, a hyperscaler (part committed, part on demand) and a neocloud's B200s. Finance gets three invoices and a depreciation schedule, and divides the total by headcount to charge teams. Teams dispute the numbers because they can't see what they used. Meanwhile, the platform team is asked whether to sign a two-year commitment for 512 more GPUs, and nobody can say how much of today's demand is steady.

What the platform must deliver.

  • Complete attribution: every dollar assigned to a team and, where possible, a workload (a training run, a serving deployment, an evaluation), or to an explicit shared or idle bucket.
  • Reconciliation: attributed totals per provider and month match the invoices (and the on-premises cost model) within 0.5%.
  • One cost per GPU-hour per pool: comparable across providers, including commitments, amortized hardware and operating costs.
  • Statements teams can check: monthly per-team reports that link to the workloads and hours behind each line.
  • Workload unit costs: cost per training run and cost per million tokens served.
  • Capacity planning: demand forecasts with uncertainty, required capacity at a target utilization, and commitment recommendations.
  • History: at least three years, with ownership changes handled correctly.

Out of scope: how utilization is measured (Design 24) and how jobs are placed across providers (Design 18).

Data sources and the model

Scenario. The first attempt joined monthly invoice totals with monthly average utilization. A team that used 400 GPUs for one week appeared to use 100 for the month, and the cost of the idle three weeks went to everyone else.

What the picture shows. The sources, at the grain each one arrives, and the hourly model they're reshaped into.

1Utilization
hourly GPU-level allocation and activity, from the recording rules of Design 24 (exported from the long-term store).
2Scheduler
Kueue workload records (admission, finish, preemption, queue, priority, requested resources) and Kubernetes ownership (pod → job → workload → namespace → team).
3Inventory
nodes, pools, GPU models, provider, region and purchase or contract references.
4Billing
provider exports in FOCUS format where available (the FinOps Foundation's common billing schema), provider-native exports otherwise, neocloud invoices, and commitment purchases.
5On-premises cost
depreciation of hardware, power, colocation, support contracts and operating staff, entered by finance per pool and month.
6The grain
one row per GPU per hour is the core fact. Costs arrive daily or monthly and are spread to hours. Ownership changes are effective-dated.

The code. The core tables (warehouse SQL, simplified).

-- one row per GPU per hourCREATE TABLE fact_gpu_hour (  hour_ts        TIMESTAMP,      -- start of the hour, UTC  gpu_uuid       VARCHAR,  node           VARCHAR,  pool_id        VARCHAR,        -- joins to dim_pool (provider, model, region, contract)  workload_uid   VARCHAR,        -- NULL when no pod held the GPU in this hour  allocated_frac DOUBLE,         -- share of the hour the GPU was held (0..1)  active_frac    DOUBLE,         -- share of the hour the GPU was active (0..1)  healthy_frac   DOUBLE          -- share of the hour the GPU was schedulable);-- one row per workload, with ownership as of its startCREATE TABLE dim_workload (  workload_uid VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, kind VARCHAR, name VARCHAR, namespace VARCHAR,  team_id VARCHAR, project VARCHAR, experiment VARCHAR, priority VARCHAR,  started_at TIMESTAMP, finished_at TIMESTAMP);-- team ownership of namespaces over time (slowly changing dimension, type 2)CREATE TABLE dim_namespace_owner (  namespace VARCHAR, team_id VARCHAR, valid_from TIMESTAMP, valid_to TIMESTAMP   --);-- billing lines, FOCUS-shapedCREATE TABLE fact_cost_line (  provider VARCHAR, charge_period_start TIMESTAMP, charge_period_end TIMESTAMP,  billed_cost DECIMAL(18,6), effective_cost DECIMAL(18,6), resource_id VARCHAR,  sku VARCHAR, charge_category VARCHAR, commitment_discount_id VARCHAR, tags JSON);
Going deeper2 points
  • Hourly is the right grain: jobs start and stop within days, and prices differ by hour (on-demand burst vs committed). Monthly averages hide exactly the variation attribution needs.
  • Effective-dated ownership: when a namespace moves from one team to another, past hours stay with the old team. A type-2 dimension makes historical statements reproducible.

Ingestion: landing, staging and marts

Scenario. Billing exports were loaded by a script that appended each day's file. When the hyperscaler restated three days of charges, the restated rows were added on top of the originals, and that month's cost was overstated by $180,000.

What the picture shows. Three layers, with partition replacement instead of appends.

1Landing
raw files and API extracts as received, in object storage, partitioned by source and date, never modified.
2Staging
typed, cleaned and conformed tables (FOCUS columns for billing, one schema for metrics). Each load replaces whole partitions (a day of metrics, a month of billing), so reloading is always safe.
3Marts
the hourly GPU fact, unit costs, attributed cost and capacity tables, rebuilt from staging by versioned SQL models (for example, dbt).
4Late and restated data
billing for a month keeps changing for weeks after it closes. The open month and the previous one are reloaded daily, and statements are final only after the provider's invoice closes.
5Lineage
every mart row can be traced to its staging partitions and landing files.

The code. Extracting hourly GPU-level allocation and activity from the metrics store for one day, replacing that day's partition (Python).

import datetime as dt, requests, pandas as pd PROM = "https://mimir.example.com/prometheus/api/v1/query_range" def extract_day(day: dt.date, store) -> int:    start = dt.datetime.combine(day, dt.time(), tzinfo=dt.timezone.utc)    q = {"start": start.timestamp(), "end": (start + dt.timedelta(days=1)).timestamp() - 1, "step": 3600}    frames = []    for name, expr in {        "allocated_frac": "avg_over_time(gpu:allocated:bool[1h])",        "active_frac":    "avg_over_time(gpu:active:bool[1h])",    }.items():        r = requests.get(PROM, params={**q, "query": expr}, timeout=300).json()["data"]["result"]        rows = [{**s["metric"], "hour_ts": pd.to_datetime(float(t), unit="s", utc=True) - pd.Timedelta(hours=1),                 name: float(v)} for s in r for t, v in s["values"]]        frames.append(pd.DataFrame(rows))    df = frames[0].merge(frames[1], on=["hour_ts", "UUID", "node", "pool", "namespace", "pod", "cluster"], how="outer")    store.replace_partition("stg_gpu_hour", partition=str(day), frame=df.fillna({"active_frac": 0.0}))    return len(df)
Going deeper2 points
  • Use recording-rule outputs, not raw series: extracting raw DCGM data for a month is slow and repeats the joins. The rule outputs already carry team, pool and pod.
  • Keep both billed and effective cost: billed cost matches the invoice, and effective cost spreads commitment purchases over their term. Attribution uses effective cost, and reconciliation checks both.

Cost per GPU-hour, comparable across providers

Scenario. A comparison showed the neocloud at $3.80 per GPU-hour and on-premises at "$0.15". That number was the power bill alone. Once depreciation, colocation, support and staff were added, it was $1.65.

What the picture shows. How each pool's cost per GPU-hour is built, so that pools can be compared and attributed the same way.

1Hyperscaler committed
the commitment's amortized (effective) cost per hour, divided by the GPUs it covers. Unused commitment hours stay in the pool's cost.
2Hyperscaler on-demand
the billed hourly rate for the instances that ran, including attached storage and network charged per instance.
3Neocloud
the contract price per GPU-hour, plus any separately billed storage and egress.
4On-premises
hardware depreciated over its expected life, plus power (measured or modeled per node), colocation, support contracts and an allocation of operating staff.
5All-in, per healthy GPU-hour
the pool's total monthly cost divided by its healthy GPU-hours. The cost of repair time is part of the rate, not a separate charge.

The code. On-premises cost per GPU-hour from finance inputs (Python).

def onprem_gpu_hour(capex_per_node: float, life_months: int, node_kw: float, kwh_price: float, pue: float,                    colo_per_node_month: float, support_per_node_month: float, staff_per_node_month: float,                    gpus_per_node: int = 8, healthy_share: float = 0.97) -> dict:    hours = 730    parts = {        "depreciation": capex_per_node / life_months,        "power": node_kw * pue * hours * kwh_price,        "colocation": colo_per_node_month,        "support": support_per_node_month,        "staff": staff_per_node_month,    }    per_node_month = sum(parts.values())    per_gpu_hour = per_node_month / (gpus_per_node * hours * healthy_share)        # healthy hours only    return {"per_gpu_hour": round(per_gpu_hour, 2), **{k: round(v / (gpus_per_node * hours * healthy_share), 3) for k, v in parts.items()}} print(onprem_gpu_hour(capex_per_node=300_000, life_months=48, node_kw=10.2, kwh_price=0.09, pue=1.3,                      colo_per_node_month=1_100, support_per_node_month=600, staff_per_node_month=500))
Going deeper2 points
  • The life assumption dominates: depreciating over 36 or 60 months changes the on-premises rate by 40% or more. Agree it with finance once and record it in the pool dimension.
  • Compare like with like: a B200 hour isn't an H100 hour. For planning, normalize by delivered work (tokens per second or training throughput from Design 15) as well as by GPU-hour.

Attribution: direct use, idle capacity and shared costs

Scenario. Splitting the total by headcount charged a three-person research team with one notebook GPU the same as the 40-person pre-training team. Switching to "by GPU-hours used" hid a 22% idle share inside everyone's rate, and nobody had a reason to reduce it.

What the picture shows. How each pool-hour's cost is split.

1Direct use
each workload is charged for the GPU-hours it held (allocated fraction × pool rate), whether or not it used them. Holding a GPU idle is a cost the team controls.
2Idle capacity
healthy GPU-hours that nobody held. Reported as its own line, owned by the platform. Optionally redistributed to teams in proportion to their guaranteed quota, because quotas are what the capacity was bought for.
3Unhealthy hours
GPUs in repair. Part of the pool rate (as above), so not a separate line.
4Shared costs
platform services (control planes, monitoring, registries), shared storage and network egress. Allocated by a driver that fits each cost: storage by bytes stored per namespace, egress by bytes sent, platform overhead as a percentage of direct cost.
5Unattributed
GPU-hours whose namespace had no owner at that time. A visible bucket with a target of zero.

The code. Hourly attribution of pool cost to workloads, with idle capacity as its own line (warehouse SQL).

WITH pool_hour AS (  SELECT g.pool_id, g.hour_ts,         SUM(g.healthy_frac)   AS healthy_gpu_h,         SUM(g.allocated_frac) AS allocated_gpu_h,         MAX(r.cost_per_gpu_h) AS rate  FROM fact_gpu_hour g JOIN mart_pool_rate r ON r.pool_id = g.pool_id AND r.month = DATE_TRUNC('month', g.hour_ts)  GROUP BY 1, 2),direct AS (  SELECT g.hour_ts, g.pool_id, g.workload_uid,         COALESCE(o.team_id, 'unattributed') AS team_id,         SUM(g.allocated_frac) * MAX(p.rate) AS cost  FROM fact_gpu_hour g  JOIN pool_hour p USING (pool_id, hour_ts)  LEFT JOIN dim_workload w ON w.workload_uid = g.workload_uid  LEFT JOIN dim_namespace_owner o         ON o.namespace = w.namespace AND g.hour_ts >= o.valid_from AND g.hour_ts < o.valid_to   -- owner at that hour  WHERE g.workload_uid IS NOT NULL  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4),idle AS (  SELECT hour_ts, pool_id, NULL AS workload_uid, 'platform:idle' AS team_id,         GREATEST(healthy_gpu_h - allocated_gpu_h, 0) * rate AS cost                              --  FROM pool_hour)SELECT * FROM direct UNION ALL SELECT * FROM idle;
Going deeper2 points
  • Showback first, chargeback later: publish attributed cost for a quarter before it affects budgets. Teams find attribution errors faster when nothing is at stake yet.
  • Preempted work is still use: a workload preempted after 3 hours held the GPUs for 3 hours. If the platform's policy caused the waste, credit it from the platform's line, by explicit rule.

Workload costs and unit economics

Scenario. A research lead asked what the last 70B training run cost. The answer took a week of spreadsheet work and still left out the 41 evaluation jobs and the failed first attempt.

What the picture shows. Costs rolled up from workloads to the things people ask about.

1Runs and experiments
workloads carry labels for project, experiment and run (set by the launchers of Design 20), so a training run's cost includes its restarts, its evaluation jobs and its data-preparation jobs.
2Serving
cost per deployment per day, divided by tokens served (from the serving metrics of Design 21), gives cost per million tokens, by model and product.
3Waste views
cost of failed runs, cost of GPU-hours held but idle, and cost lost to preemption, per team.
4Label coverage
the share of cost whose workloads carry project and experiment labels, reported per team with a target.

The code. Cost per run and cost per million tokens served (warehouse SQL).

-- cost of each training run, including restarts, evals and data prep labeled with the same runSELECT w.project, w.experiment, COUNT(DISTINCT w.workload_uid) AS workloads,       SUM(a.cost) AS cost_usd,       SUM(CASE WHEN w.kind = 'eval' THEN a.cost ELSE 0 END) AS eval_cost_usd,       SUM(CASE WHEN w.status = 'Failed' THEN a.cost ELSE 0 END) AS failed_cost_usdFROM mart_attributed_cost a JOIN dim_workload w USING (workload_uid)WHERE w.project = 'llm-70b'GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY cost_usd DESC; -- cost per million output tokens, per serving deployment and daySELECT a.day, w.name AS deployment, SUM(a.cost) AS cost_usd, MAX(t.output_tokens) AS tokens,       SUM(a.cost) / NULLIF(MAX(t.output_tokens), 0) * 1e6 AS usd_per_m_tokens               --FROM mart_attributed_cost_daily aJOIN dim_workload w USING (workload_uid)JOIN fact_serving_tokens_daily t ON t.deployment = w.name AND t.day = a.dayWHERE w.kind = 'serving'GROUP BY 1, 2;
Going deeper2 points
  • Labels are the bottleneck: cost per experiment is only as good as the labels on workloads. Make the launchers set them by default, and reject workloads without a project label in production queues.
  • Unit costs move with utilization: cost per million tokens falls as a deployment gets busier. Report it with the deployment's utilization next to it.

Reconciliation and data quality

Scenario. The first statements attributed $3.62 million in a month whose invoices and cost model totaled $4.08 million. The $460,000 gap was a neocloud invoice line for storage that no GPU-hour carried, and two days of missing metrics.

What the picture shows. Checks that make the numbers trustworthy before anyone sees them.

1Totals
attributed cost (direct + idle + shared + unattributed) per provider and month equals billed or effective cost within 0.5%. A larger gap blocks publication.
2Coverage
every healthy GPU-hour in the inventory has a fact row. Missing hours are filled from scheduler records where possible and flagged otherwise.
3Freshness
metrics within 6 hours, scheduler records within 1 hour, billing within the provider's export delay.
4Integrity
allocated fraction ≤ healthy fraction ≤ 1, every workload resolves to an owner, no GPU allocated to two workloads in one hour.
5Anomalies
day-over-day changes in a team's cost beyond a threshold are flagged for review before statements go out.

The YAML. Data tests on the marts (dbt).

models:- name: fact_gpu_hour  tests:  - dbt_utils.expression_is_true: { expression: "allocated_frac <= healthy_frac + 0.001" }  - dbt_utils.expression_is_true: { expression: "healthy_frac BETWEEN 0 AND 1" }  - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns: { combination_of_columns: [hour_ts, gpu_uuid] }  - dbt_utils.recency: { datepart: hour, field: hour_ts, interval: 6 }- name: mart_reconciliation_monthly  columns:  - name: abs_gap_pct    tests:    - dbt_utils.accepted_range: { max_value: 0.005, config: { severity: error } }   # blocks statements  - name: unattributed_share    tests:    - dbt_utils.accepted_range: { max_value: 0.01, config: { severity: warn } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Reconcile to the invoice, not to a forecast: the check compares with the provider's own billed total. When they disagree, the warehouse is wrong until shown otherwise.
  • Missing metrics aren't zero: an hour with no data means "unknown", not "idle". Fill from scheduler allocation records, and mark the activity as unknown.

Statements, budgets and forecasts for teams

Scenario. Teams received a single number per month in an email. When the vision team's cost doubled, it took two weeks to find that a forgotten evaluation sweep had held 64 GPUs over a holiday.

What the picture shows. What each team gets, and when.

1Monthly statement
direct cost by pool and workload kind, share of idle and shared costs (if chargeback applies), and the top workloads by cost, each linked to its GPU-hours.
2Daily view
month-to-date cost, forecast to month end and budget, in a dashboard backed by the same marts.
3Budget alerts
a forecast above budget, or a single workload costing more than a threshold per day, notifies the team's owner (the routing of Design 24).
4Explanations
month-over-month changes are broken down into usage change, rate change (pool mix) and idle share change, so a doubling has a reason attached.

The code. Explaining a team's month-over-month cost change by volume, rate and idle (Python).

def explain_change(prev: dict, cur: dict) -> dict:    """prev/cur: {'gpu_h': held GPU-hours, 'rate': blended $/GPU-h, 'idle_share_cost': $}."""    volume = (cur["gpu_h"] - prev["gpu_h"]) * prev["rate"]                 # more or fewer hours    rate = (cur["rate"] - prev["rate"]) * cur["gpu_h"]                      # pool mix, prices    idle = cur["idle_share_cost"] - prev["idle_share_cost"]    total = (cur["gpu_h"] * cur["rate"] + cur["idle_share_cost"]) - (prev["gpu_h"] * prev["rate"] + prev["idle_share_cost"])    return {"total": round(total), "volume": round(volume), "rate": round(rate), "idle": round(idle)} print(explain_change({"gpu_h": 61_000, "rate": 2.31, "idle_share_cost": 18_000},                     {"gpu_h": 118_000, "rate": 2.44, "idle_share_cost": 21_000}))
Going deeper2 points
  • Statements are reproducible: a closed month's statement is stored with the versions of the SQL models and rates that produced it. Corrections are issued as adjustments in a later month, not silent rewrites.
  • Show what the team can change: held-but-idle hours and failed runs are the controllable parts. Put them at the top.

Capacity planning: forecasting demand

Scenario. The platform added 256 GPUs after a quarter of long queues. Two months later, queues were long again. The forecast had used last quarter's consumed GPU-hours, which were capped by the capacity that existed, not by what teams wanted.

What the picture shows. Demand measured without the capacity cap, forecast with uncertainty, and turned into a capacity requirement.

1Demand, not consumption
consumed GPU-hours plus pending GPU-hours (admitted later or never) from Kueue, plus demand turned away (jobs not submitted because quotas were full, estimated from team plans).
2Known plans
large planned runs and launches from team roadmaps, added as discrete events on top of the trend.
3Forecast
a trend with weekly seasonality on weekly demand, with prediction intervals, per GPU type.
4Required capacity
forecast demand divided by the target utilization (for example, 80%, from the healthy ceiling of Design 19), plus headroom for repairs.
5Lead times
on-premises hardware takes months, commitments take weeks, on-demand takes minutes. The plan says what must be ordered now to cover the 80th-percentile demand at each lead time.

The code. A simple demand forecast with intervals and the resulting capacity requirement (Python).

import numpy as np def forecast_capacity(weekly_demand_gpu_h: np.ndarray, weeks_ahead: int = 26,                      target_util: float = 0.80, repair_share: float = 0.03, planned: dict | None = None) -> dict:    """weekly_demand_gpu_h: consumed + pending GPU-hours per week (not capped by capacity)."""    t = np.arange(len(weekly_demand_gpu_h))    y = np.log(weekly_demand_gpu_h)    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(t, y, 1)                                  # log-linear growth    resid = y - (intercept + slope * t)    sigma = resid.std(ddof=2)    future = np.arange(len(t), len(t) + weeks_ahead)    mean = np.exp(intercept + slope * future)    spread = sigma * np.sqrt(1 + (future - t.mean()) ** 2 / ((t - t.mean()) ** 2).sum())    p50, p80 = mean, np.exp(intercept + slope * future + 0.84 * spread)    for week, gpu_h in (planned or {}).items():        p50[week] += gpu_h; p80[week] += gpu_h                              # known large runs    to_gpus = lambda gpu_h: gpu_h / (7 * 24) / target_util / (1 - repair_share)    return {"weekly_growth_pct": round((np.exp(slope) - 1) * 100, 2),            "gpus_needed_p50": np.ceil(to_gpus(p50)).astype(int), "gpus_needed_p80": np.ceil(to_gpus(p80)).astype(int)}
Going deeper2 points
  • Forecast per GPU type and pool: demand for H100s and B200s grows differently, and some workloads can't move between them.
  • Compare forecasts with outcomes: each quarter, score the previous forecasts. Persistent under-forecasting usually means hidden demand isn't being counted.

Commitments: how much to reserve

Scenario. The hyperscaler offered a two-year commitment for 512 GPUs at about a third of the on-demand price. Half of the platform team wanted all 512. The other half pointed out that demand had swung by 300 GPUs within a single month.

What the picture shows. Choosing a commitment level from the distribution of hourly demand.

1The trade-off
a committed GPU-hour is paid whether used or not. An on-demand (or neocloud burst) GPU-hour costs more but only when used.
2The rule
one more committed GPU pays off if demand exceeds it in more than (committed price ÷ on-demand price) of the hours. With committed at $2.50 and on-demand at $6.90, that's 36%, so commit up to the 64th percentile of hourly demand.
3Inputs
hourly demand for the pool's GPU type over the commitment horizon (from the forecast, as a distribution), prices, and constraints (minimum commitment sizes, regions).
4Layering
on-premises and existing commitments cover the base, new commitments the next layer, and on-demand or neocloud burst the peaks (Design 18).
5Review
each commitment's realized utilization is tracked. Unused commitment hours are idle capacity in the attribution.

The code. Choosing a commitment level from simulated hourly demand (Python).

import numpy as np def commitment_level(hourly_demand: np.ndarray, committed_price: float, on_demand_price: float,                     already_covered: int = 0) -> dict:    """hourly_demand: GPUs needed per hour over the horizon (forecast samples); already_covered: base capacity."""    beyond_base = np.maximum(hourly_demand - already_covered, 0)    critical = (on_demand_price - committed_price) / on_demand_price           # 0.64 for $2.50 vs $6.90    level = int(np.quantile(beyond_base, critical))                             # demand exceeds it 36% of hours    def cost(c):        return (c * committed_price * len(beyond_base)                + np.maximum(beyond_base - c, 0).sum() * on_demand_price)    return {"commit_gpus": level, "critical_ratio": round(critical, 2),            "cost_at_level": round(cost(level)), "cost_commit_none": round(cost(0)),            "cost_commit_512": round(cost(512))}
Going deeper2 points
  • The forecast's uncertainty matters more than its mean: two forecasts with the same mean but different spread give different commitment levels. Use the full distribution.
  • Flexibility has value: commitments that can move between instance types or regions reduce the risk, and are worth a slightly higher price. The same calculation shows how much.

Running it: the operating cadence

Scenario. The first version of the warehouse answered every question, but only when a data engineer ran the right query. Finance still waited until mid-month for numbers, and the capacity review happened when someone remembered.

What the picture shows. What runs when, and who owns it.

1Daily
ingestion, reloads of open months, data tests and reconciliation, month-to-date and forecast views per team, and budget alerts.
2Monthly
the close after providers' invoices arrive, frozen statements per team, and a review of pool rates with finance.
3Quarterly
a new demand forecast scored against the previous one, the capacity plan per GPU type, and commitment recommendations, reviewed with finance and team leads.
4Ownership
finance owns rates, budgets and the on-premises cost inputs. The platform team owns the data pipeline, the attribution rules and the idle line.
5One set of tables
run costs, bill explanations, idle capacity and commitment decisions are all queries over the same marts, so answers agree.
Going deeper2 points
  • Publish the rules with the numbers: attribution drivers, rates and their versions are documented next to the statements, and changes are announced before they apply.
  • Close the loop with scheduling: idle capacity found here becomes the next lever in the scheduling program (Design 19), and long queues found there feed the demand forecast.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, the model (weeks 1–4): the hourly GPU fact from recording rules and scheduler records, inventory and ownership dimensions, and billing ingestion in FOCUS shape for each provider.
  • Phase 2, rates and attribution (weeks 4–8): pool rates (with finance's on-premises inputs), direct and idle attribution, shared-cost drivers, reconciliation checks.
  • Phase 3, showback (weeks 8–14): monthly statements and daily views per team, workload and unit costs, and a quarter of showback before any chargeback.
  • Phase 4, planning (weeks 10–16): demand forecasts, capacity requirements and commitment recommendations, reviewed quarterly with finance.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Hourly grain: more data and compute than monthly, needed for correct attribution.
  • Idle as a visible line: uncomfortable for the platform team, and the reason idle capacity gets reduced.
  • Allocation, not activity, is charged: teams pay for GPUs they hold, even if their code leaves them idle.
  • Statements are final only after invoices close: teams see estimates for the current and previous month.

Open questions.

  • Charging for priority: should high-priority or preempting workloads pay more per GPU-hour than preemptible ones?
  • Carbon: should statements include energy and emissions per team, from the same power data?
  • Cross-provider normalization: how should a B200 hour be compared with an H100 hour for planning, by throughput on representative workloads or by price?
  • Token-level billing: as billing standards add AI and token-level units, should serving cost move from GPU-hours to tokens end to end?
Design 26 · 12 sections

Design 26: Autoscaling, rightsizing and idle-capacity recovery with measurable cost results

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Sizing the opportunity
  3. The savings ledger and how savings are measured
  4. Serving autoscaling: following traffic
  5. GPU node autoscaling and consolidation in the cloud
  6. Batch and development: provision for the queue, scale to zero
  7. Rightsizing GPU workloads
  8. Rightsizing the serving fleet
  9. Recovering idle capacity, commitments and orphans
  10. Guardrails: savings that don't cost service
  11. Running the program and sustaining the results
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we run autoscaling, rightsizing and idle-capacity recovery as programs whose savings are measured well enough that finance books them? The mechanisms appear in earlier designs: serving autoscaling in Design 21, idle reclamation in Design 19, and the attributed cost data in Design 25.
