This design turns them into a portfolio: sizing each opportunity in dollars, choosing the levers, building them (KEDA, Karpenter, Kueue provisioning, recommenders), protecting service levels, and measuring each saving against a counterfactual in a ledger that finance trusts.

The short version: size from the warehouse, measure against a counterfactual, and book only what holds. Every initiative starts with a dollar estimate from attributed cost, a named owner and a measurement method chosen before the change. Savings are computed as what the same work would have cost without the change (from unit costs such as GPU-hours per million tokens) minus what it did cost, so growth in demand doesn't hide savings and a drop in demand doesn't inflate them. Initiatives run behind service-level guardrails, and savings during a guardrail breach aren't booked. A monthly ledger reports projected, realized and sustained savings, and flags initiatives whose savings decay.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The fleet spends $4.08 million a month (Design 25). Leadership asks for a 15% reduction within two quarters without slowing research. A previous "cost push" claimed $900,000 a month of savings. Finance could confirm about $200,000 on the invoices, because most of the claims were requests reduced on paper, nodes stopped for a week and then restarted, and lower spend in a month when demand happened to fall.

What the program must deliver.

  • A sized backlog: every opportunity estimated in dollars per month from attributed cost, with an owner.
  • Measurement chosen up front: each initiative has a baseline, a counterfactual method and the metric it's judged on, agreed before any change.
  • Levers built as platform features: autoscaling for serving and GPU node pools, queue-driven provisioning, scale-to-zero for development, rightsizing recommendations, idle and orphan recovery.
  • Service levels protected: each initiative names the SLOs it might affect, and breaches stop it.
  • A ledger finance accepts: projected, realized and sustained savings per initiative, reconciled with spend.
  • Savings that last: sustained savings are re-measured monthly, and decay is visible.

Out of scope: scheduling policy (Design 17), serving engine tuning (Design 21) and commercial negotiations with providers.

Sizing the opportunity

Scenario. The team started with the idea everyone liked best, a custom autoscaler for training jobs. Sizing later showed that idle capacity and serving replicas left running overnight were each worth five times more.

What the picture shows. A waste taxonomy, sized in dollars per month from the attributed-cost marts.

1Idle capacity
healthy GPU-hours nobody held (the platform's idle line in Design 25).
2Held but idle
GPU-hours allocated to workloads with no activity: notebooks, forgotten jobs, oversized reservations.
3Serving over-provisioning
replica-hours beyond what traffic needed at the SLO, especially overnight and on weekends.
4Oversized hardware
workloads on larger or more GPUs than they use (small models on full H100s, jobs that never exceed half their GPU memory).
5Expensive capacity at the wrong time
on-demand burst while committed or on-premises capacity sat idle.
6Unused commitments and orphans
committed hours with nothing scheduled, and resources nobody owns (stopped instances still billed, detached volumes, forgotten reservations).
7Addressable share
each category gets a realistic recoverable share (not all idle capacity can be recovered), giving the backlog's expected value.

The code. Sizing the waste categories for a month from the attributed-cost marts (warehouse SQL).

WITH m AS (SELECT DATE '2026-10-01' AS month_start, DATE '2026-11-01' AS month_end)SELECT 'idle capacity' AS category, SUM(cost) AS usdFROM mart_attributed_cost, m WHERE team_id = 'platform:idle' AND hour_ts >= month_start AND hour_ts < month_endUNION ALLSELECT 'held but idle', SUM(g.allocated_frac - g.active_frac) * MAX(r.cost_per_gpu_h)            --FROM fact_gpu_hour g JOIN mart_pool_rate r ON r.pool_id = g.pool_id AND r.month = DATE_TRUNC('month', g.hour_ts), mWHERE g.workload_uid IS NOT NULL AND g.hour_ts >= month_start AND g.hour_ts < month_endUNION ALLSELECT 'serving over-provisioning', SUM(cost * (1 - needed_replicas / NULLIF(running_replicas, 0)))FROM mart_serving_hourly, m WHERE hour_ts >= month_start AND hour_ts < month_endUNION ALLSELECT 'on-demand while base idle', SUM(od.cost)FROM mart_attributed_cost od JOIN mart_pool_idle_hourly base  ON base.hour_ts = od.hour_ts AND base.gpu_product = od.gpu_product AND base.idle_gpus >= 8, mWHERE od.pool_kind = 'on-demand' AND od.hour_ts >= month_start AND od.hour_ts < month_end;
Going deeper2 points
  • Size before you build: the backlog is ordered by expected dollars recovered per week of engineering, not by how interesting the lever is.
  • Overlaps are real: recovering held-but-idle hours turns them into idle capacity, which saves money only if capacity then shrinks or absorbs demand that would have bought more. The ledger counts each dollar once.

The savings ledger and how savings are measured

Scenario. One team reported savings as "requests reduced × list price". Another reported "this month's bill minus last month's". In a month when demand grew 12%, the second method showed a cost increase despite real efficiency gains, and the first claimed savings on GPUs that had never been paid for.

What the picture shows. How each initiative's savings are defined, measured and booked.

1Baseline period
usage and unit cost before the change (for example, four weeks), from the warehouse.
2Counterfactual
what the current period's work would have cost at baseline efficiency: current output (tokens served, GPU-hours of demand, jobs run) × baseline unit cost (GPU-hours per output) × current price.
3Realized saving
counterfactual cost minus actual cost, per month.
4Cash vs avoided cost
savings that reduce the invoice (fewer on-demand hours, cancelled reservations) are cash. Savings that absorb growth without buying more are avoided cost, recognized only when a planned purchase is actually deferred.
5States
proposed (sized), committed (measurement agreed), realized (measured for a month), sustained (holding after three months), decayed (fallen below half).
6Finance sign-off
cash savings reconcile with invoice changes, and avoided cost needs a deferred purchase order or capacity plan line.

The code. A ledger entry measured against a unit-cost counterfactual (Python).

from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclassclass Initiative:    name: str    owner: str    kind: str                         # "cash" or "avoided"    baseline_gpu_h_per_unit: float    # e.g. GPU-hours per million tokens, measured before the change    unit: str def realized(i: Initiative, month_output_units: float, month_gpu_h: float, price_per_gpu_h: float) -> dict:    counterfactual_gpu_h = month_output_units * i.baseline_gpu_h_per_unit           # same work, old efficiency    saved_gpu_h = counterfactual_gpu_h - month_gpu_h    return {"initiative": i.name, "kind": i.kind,            "counterfactual_usd": round(counterfactual_gpu_h * price_per_gpu_h),            "actual_usd": round(month_gpu_h * price_per_gpu_h),            "realized_usd": round(saved_gpu_h * price_per_gpu_h),            "efficiency_gain_pct": round(100 * saved_gpu_h / counterfactual_gpu_h, 1)} serving = Initiative("serving autoscaling: chat-70b", "serving-platform", "cash", 0.92, "M tokens")print(realized(serving, month_output_units=118_000, month_gpu_h=71_500, price_per_gpu_h=2.50))
Going deeper2 points
  • Pick the output unit carefully: tokens served, training steps, jobs completed or GPU-hours of admitted demand. It must measure the work the user cares about, or an "efficiency gain" can be less work done.
  • Prices change separately: a provider price cut isn't an initiative's saving. The counterfactual uses current prices, so price changes don't leak into the ledger.

Serving autoscaling: following traffic

Scenario. The chat deployments ran 32 replicas around the clock, sized for the weekday peak. At 03:00 they served 15% of peak traffic. Nobody had changed the replica count since launch, because the last attempt to autoscale scaled on GPU utilization and never scaled down.

What the picture shows. Replica counts that follow load, scaled on signals that track latency.

1Scaling signals
waiting requests and KV-cache usage per replica, from the engine's metrics (Design 21), not GPU utilization.
2KEDA ScaledObject
reads the signals from Prometheus and drives the HPA, with a minimum for burst headroom and a maximum for cost control.
3Asymmetric behavior
scale up fast (a burst can't wait), scale down slowly (avoid oscillation and repeated model loads).
4Fast readiness makes it pay
replicas that load weights in under two minutes (Design 20) let the minimum stay low.
5Where freed GPUs go
on cloud capacity, node autoscaling returns them. On committed or on-premises capacity, a preemptible batch queue absorbs them, otherwise nothing is saved.

The YAML. A KEDA ScaledObject for a chat deployment, scaling on queued requests per replica.

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1kind: ScaledObjectmetadata: { name: chat-70b, namespace: serving }spec:  scaleTargetRef: { name: chat-70b }  minReplicaCount: 6                                   # burst headroom; was a fixed 32  maxReplicaCount: 40  cooldownPeriod: 900  advanced:    horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig:      behavior:        scaleUp:   { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0,   policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 50, periodSeconds: 60 }] }        scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 900, policies: [{ type: Pods,    value: 2,  periodSeconds: 300 }] }  triggers:  - type: prometheus    metadata:      serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090      query: sum(vllm:num_requests_waiting{namespace="serving", model_name="chat-70b"})      threshold: "4"                                    # target waiting requests per replica  - type: prometheus    metadata:      serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090      query: avg(vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc{namespace="serving", model_name="chat-70b"}) * 100      threshold: "75"
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure with GPU-hours per million tokens: the ledger entry for autoscaling compares this unit cost before and after, at current traffic.
  • Test scale-up under replayed bursts: the benchmark replay of Design 22 at 2× speed shows whether the minimum and the scale-up policy hold the TTFT SLO.

GPU node autoscaling and consolidation in the cloud

Scenario. Cloud GPU node pools were sized by hand for the busiest week of the quarter. On an average day, 30% of on-demand GPU nodes ran nothing but DaemonSets, and the few that ran one small pod each couldn't be removed.

What the picture shows. Node capacity that follows pending pods, and consolidation that empties underused nodes.

1Provision on demand
Karpenter (or the cluster autoscaler) adds GPU nodes when pods are pending, choosing instance types from the NodePool's allowed list.
2Consolidate
nodes that are empty, or whose pods fit elsewhere, are drained and removed after a delay. Disruption budgets limit how many go at once.
3Layers stay separate
committed and on-premises nodes are never scaled down (they're paid for anyway). Only on-demand pools scale, and they fill only after the base is full.
4Protect long jobs
training pods carry a do-not-disrupt annotation, so consolidation never interrupts a gang. Serving and batch pods are disruptable.
5Limits
a NodePool's GPU limit caps spend if something misbehaves.

The YAML. An on-demand GPU NodePool with consolidation and a spend cap (Karpenter v1).

apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1kind: NodePoolmetadata: { name: gpu-on-demand }spec:  template:    metadata: { labels: { pool-kind: on-demand } }    spec:      nodeClassRef: { group: karpenter.k8s.aws, kind: EC2NodeClass, name: gpu }      requirements:      - { key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: ["on-demand"] }      - { key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type, operator: In, values: ["p5.48xlarge", "g6e.12xlarge", "g6e.48xlarge"] }      taints: [{ key: nvidia.com/gpu, effect: NoSchedule }]      expireAfter: 720h  limits:    nvidia.com/gpu: "256"                                # spend cap for the pool  disruption:    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized    consolidateAfter: 10m    budgets:    - nodes: "10%"    - nodes: "0"      schedule: "0 9 * * mon-fri"                        # no voluntary disruption during the weekday peak      duration: 8h
Going deeper2 points
  • Prefer the base first: a scheduling preference (or Kueue flavor order, Design 17) places work on committed and on-premises capacity before on-demand. Otherwise autoscaling adds expensive nodes while cheap ones sit idle.
  • Watch for churn: nodes that are added and removed within an hour cost startup time and money. A consolidation delay of minutes, not seconds, avoids it.

Batch and development: provision for the queue, scale to zero

Scenario. Each research team kept a "dev pool" of 4 GPU nodes always on, so that notebooks started instantly. Across 14 teams, 56 nodes averaged 11% activity. Batch jobs, meanwhile, held on-demand nodes while they waited for their full gang to be placed.

What the picture shows. Capacity created for work that's admitted, and released when it's gone.

1Queue-driven provisioning
Kueue asks the autoscaler for the whole gang's capacity (a ProvisioningRequest) before admitting a workload. Nodes appear for a job that will start, and no partial gang holds on-demand nodes while waiting. While it waits, the workload already holds its quota. If the request fails, Kueue releases that quota and the workload tries again after a backoff, three times by default (Kueue docs).
2Scale to zero for development
notebooks and dev environments run on a pool with a minimum of zero, with a warm buffer of one node per GPU type during working hours.
3Idle stop
notebooks are checkpointed and stopped after an idle period (Design 19's idle policy), and their node is consolidated away.
4Start-time budget
the trade-off is explicit. A notebook may take 3 to 5 minutes to start from zero, and the program publishes that number.
5Shared, not per team
one dev pool with fair sharing replaces 14 team pools.

The YAML. Kueue admission that provisions capacity for the whole workload before admitting it (ProvisioningRequest admission check).

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ProvisioningRequestConfigmetadata: { name: gpu-gang-capacity }spec:  provisioningClassName: check-capacity.autoscaling.x-k8s.io   # all-or-nothing capacity for the gang  managedResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu"]---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: AdmissionCheckmetadata: { name: gpu-gang-capacity }spec:  controllerName: kueue.x-k8s.io/provisioning-request  parameters: { apiGroup: kueue.x-k8s.io, kind: ProvisioningRequestConfig, name: gpu-gang-capacity }---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ClusterQueuemetadata: { name: batch-on-demand }spec:  admissionChecksStrategy:    admissionChecks: [{ name: gpu-gang-capacity, onFlavors: [h100-on-demand] }]  resourceGroups:  - coveredResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu"]    flavors: [{ name: h100-on-demand, resources: [{ name: nvidia.com/gpu, nominalQuota: 256 }] }]
Going deeper2 points
  • Development savings are the easiest to book: always-on dev nodes are cash, and their removal shows on the next invoice.
  • Keep the experience good: a published start time, a warm buffer during working hours and saved notebook state make scale-to-zero acceptable to users.

Rightsizing GPU workloads

Scenario. A team's inference service for a 7B model ran on full H100s, using 18 GB of 80 GB and 9% of compute. Elsewhere, a 4-GPU training pod requested 96 CPUs on 8-GPU nodes with 112 CPUs, so three of the node's four remaining GPUs couldn't be used by anyone.

What the picture shows. Recommendations from observed usage, by type of mismatch.

1GPU count
jobs whose GPUs are mostly idle or whose memory never exceeds a fraction of the allocation, recommended to request fewer.
2GPU type
small-model inference and light workloads recommended to smaller GPUs (for example, L40S instead of H100) or MIG slices, where latency allows.
3Stranding by CPU and memory
pods whose CPU or memory requests leave a node's other GPUs unschedulable, with the number of GPUs stranded and their cost.
4Evidence and savings with each
the recommendation shows the usage behind it, the projected monthly saving and the risk (for example, "peak memory 41 GB on a 48 GB card").
5Delivery
recommendations go to owners as tickets and pull requests against their manifests. The platform doesn't change workloads silently.

The code. A rightsizing recommender over a workload's usage profile (Python).

GPU_TYPES = {  # memory GB, price per GPU-hour (illustrative)    "H100-80GB": (80, 2.50), "L40S-48GB": (48, 1.10), "H100-MIG-3g.40gb": (40, 1.05)} def recommend(w: dict, headroom: float = 1.25) -> dict | None:    """w: kind, gpu_type, gpus, p99_mem_gb, p95_activity, hours_per_month, cpu_req, node_cpus, node_gpus."""    current = GPU_TYPES[w["gpu_type"]][1] * w["gpus"] * w["hours_per_month"]    need_mem = w["p99_mem_gb"] * headroom    fits = [(name, mem, price) for name, (mem, price) in GPU_TYPES.items() if mem >= need_mem]    if w["kind"] == "inference" and w["p95_activity"] < 0.3 and fits:        name, _, price = min(fits, key=lambda f: f[2])        new = price * w["gpus"] * w["hours_per_month"]        if new < 0.8 * current:            return {"action": f"move to {name}", "saving_usd_month": round(current - new), "evidence": f"p99 memory {w['p99_mem_gb']} GB, p95 activity {w['p95_activity']:.0%}"}    cpu_per_gpu = w["node_cpus"] / w["node_gpus"]    stranded = max(0, w["node_gpus"] - w["gpus"] - int((w["node_cpus"] - w["cpu_req"]) // cpu_per_gpu))    if stranded:                                                                     # GPUs nobody else can use        return {"action": f"lower CPU request to ≤ {int(cpu_per_gpu * w['gpus'])}", "stranded_gpus": stranded,                "saving_usd_month": round(stranded * GPU_TYPES[w["gpu_type"]][1] * w["hours_per_month"])}    return None print(recommend({"kind": "inference", "gpu_type": "H100-80GB", "gpus": 2, "p99_mem_gb": 18, "p95_activity": 0.09,                 "hours_per_month": 730, "cpu_req": 16, "node_cpus": 112, "node_gpus": 8}))
Going deeper2 points
  • Inference latency decides type changes: a smaller GPU may meet throughput but miss TTFT. Rightsizing serving goes through the benchmark gate (Design 22).
  • CPU requests are the silent GPU waste: stranded GPUs often cost more than oversized GPU requests. Admission policies can cap CPU and memory per GPU on GPU nodes.

Rightsizing the serving fleet

Scenario. Twenty-two fine-tuned 8B models each had a dedicated 2-replica deployment, most serving a few requests a minute. Together they held 44 H100s and averaged 4% activity.

What the picture shows. Fleet-level changes that reduce GPUs per unit of traffic.

1Consolidate fine-tunes
fine-tunes of the same base model served as LoRA adapters on shared base-model replicas, instead of one deployment each.
2Scale idle models to zero
low-traffic models with relaxed latency targets scale to zero and load on demand, with the cold-start time published.
3Quantize where the gate passes
FP8 or FP4 variants (Design 21) serve more traffic per GPU, after the accuracy gate.
4Right-size parallelism
smaller tensor parallelism and more replicas where it raises goodput.
5Retire unused models
deployments with no traffic for 30 days are flagged to owners and removed if unclaimed.

The code. Comparing dedicated deployments with shared adapter serving for a set of fine-tunes (Python).

import math def adapter_consolidation(models: list[dict], replica_capacity_rps: float, price_gpu_h: float,                          gpus_per_replica: int = 1, min_replicas: int = 2) -> dict:    """models: name, peak_rps, dedicated_replicas. Shared replicas serve all adapters of one base model."""    dedicated_gpus = sum(m["dedicated_replicas"] for m in models) * gpus_per_replica    peak_total = sum(m["peak_rps"] for m in models) * 1.3                       # adapter overhead + headroom    shared_replicas = max(min_replicas, math.ceil(peak_total / replica_capacity_rps))    shared_gpus = shared_replicas * gpus_per_replica    return {"dedicated_gpus": dedicated_gpus, "shared_gpus": shared_gpus,            "saving_usd_month": round((dedicated_gpus - shared_gpus) * price_gpu_h * 730)} fine_tunes = [{"name": f"ft-{i}", "peak_rps": 0.4 + (i % 5) * 0.3, "dedicated_replicas": 2} for i in range(22)]print(adapter_consolidation(fine_tunes, replica_capacity_rps=6.0, price_gpu_h=2.50))
Going deeper2 points
  • Adapters change the latency profile: many adapters on one replica share its batch. Benchmark with the real adapter mix and traffic before migrating.
  • Retirement needs an owner answer: a removal ticket that times out without a reply removes the deployment, and the model stays in the registry for redeployment.

Recovering idle capacity, commitments and orphans

Scenario. The hyperscaler commitment ran at 71% utilization, so 29% of committed hours were paid for and unused. At the same time, an evaluation backlog of 40,000 GPU-hours waited for "free capacity". Separately, an audit found $58,000 a month of resources with no owner: stopped instances with attached storage, detached volumes and a forgotten capacity reservation.

What the picture shows. Three recovery levers for capacity that's paid for and unused.

1Fill the base with preemptible work
a low-priority, preemptible queue (evaluations, data processing, hyperparameter sweeps) runs on idle committed and on-premises capacity, and is preempted when higher-priority work arrives (Design 17). This saves money only by displacing work that would otherwise have run on paid capacity, and the ledger counts it that way.
2Shrink what can shrink
if idle capacity persists after filling, the capacity plan (Design 25) reduces the next commitment or defers a purchase. That's where idle recovery becomes avoided cost.
3Orphan sweeps
weekly queries over billing and inventory find resources without an owner or a running workload. Owners get a notice, and unclaimed resources are deleted after a grace period, with snapshots where data is at stake.
4Commitment utilization as a metric
each commitment's used share is reported weekly, with an alert below a threshold.

The code. Finding billed resources with no owner and no recent use (warehouse SQL).

SELECT c.provider, c.resource_id, c.sku, SUM(c.effective_cost) AS usd_30d,       MAX(i.last_attached_at) AS last_used, MAX(i.owner_team) AS ownerFROM fact_cost_line cLEFT JOIN dim_cloud_inventory i ON i.resource_id = c.resource_idWHERE c.charge_period_start >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 30 DAY  AND c.charge_category = 'Usage'  AND (i.owner_team IS NULL OR i.last_attached_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 14 DAY)   -- no owner or idle 14 days  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fact_gpu_hour g                  WHERE g.node = i.node_name AND g.hour_ts >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 14 DAY AND g.allocated_frac > 0)GROUP BY 1, 2, 3HAVING SUM(c.effective_cost) > 100ORDER BY usd_30d DESC;
Going deeper2 points
  • Filling idle capacity isn't automatically a saving: if the evaluation backlog would otherwise never have run, filling it adds value but not savings. If it would have run on on-demand capacity, it's a cash saving. The ledger asks which.
  • Deletions are irreversible: orphan cleanup snapshots storage first, waits for the grace period, and logs every deletion with the evidence that the resource was orphaned.

Guardrails: savings that don't cost service

Scenario. A scale-down change on the coding assistant saved $40,000 in its first month. It also raised p95 TTFT above the SLO for two hours every weekday morning, while new replicas loaded. Users noticed before the dashboards did.

What the picture shows. The service levels each initiative must hold, and what happens when it doesn't.

1Guardrails per initiative
serving autoscaling holds TTFT and ITL SLOs. Queue-driven provisioning and dev scale-to-zero hold queue wait and start-time targets. Rightsizing holds the benchmark and accuracy gates.
2Measured continuously
the same dashboards and alerts as production (Design 24), labeled with the initiative that changed the configuration.
3Breach rules
a breach pauses the initiative's latest change (revert in Git). Savings from periods with breaches aren't booked.
4Trade-offs written down
where a guardrail is deliberately relaxed (a longer notebook start time), the new target is agreed with users and recorded with the initiative.

The code. Booking only savings from hours when the initiative's guardrails held (Python).

import pandas as pd def bookable_savings(hourly: pd.DataFrame, guardrails: dict[str, float]) -> dict:    """hourly: hour, saved_usd, and one column per guardrail metric (e.g. ttft_p95_s, queue_wait_p90_min)."""    ok = pd.Series(True, index=hourly.index)    for metric, limit in guardrails.items():        ok &= hourly[metric] <= limit    days_with_breach = hourly.loc[~ok, "hour"].dt.date.unique()    bookable = hourly[~hourly.hour.dt.date.isin(days_with_breach)]                  # breach voids the whole day    return {"claimed_usd": round(hourly.saved_usd.sum()), "bookable_usd": round(bookable.saved_usd.sum()),            "breach_days": len(days_with_breach)}
Going deeper2 points
  • Void the day, not the hour: voiding only breach hours would reward an initiative for being cheap in the hours around the breach that caused it.
  • Users are a guardrail too: a ticket volume or satisfaction signal catches problems that metrics miss, such as a slower notebook start.

Running the program and sustaining the results

Scenario. Six months after a previous push, half of its savings had disappeared. Minimum replica counts had been raised "temporarily" during an incident, dev pools had reappeared under new names, and nobody re-measured.

What the picture shows. The program as an ongoing operation with a cadence and owners.

1Weekly
backlog review ordered by expected dollars per engineering week, initiative status and guardrails.
2Monthly
the ledger, with projected, realized and sustained savings per initiative, reconciled with spend and reviewed with finance.
3Sustainment checks
each sustained saving is re-measured monthly against its counterfactual. A drop below half its peak marks it decayed and reopens it.
4Config drift detection
changes that undo an initiative (a raised minimum replica count, a new always-on pool) are flagged when their pull request is opened, with the cost impact.
5Incentives
team statements (Design 25) show each team's idle and oversized costs, and the savings attributed to them.

The code. The monthly savings report with decay detection (Python).

import pandas as pd def savings_report(ledger: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:    """ledger: one row per initiative per month with projected_usd, realized_usd (bookable), kind, state."""    peak = ledger.groupby("initiative").realized_usd.cummax()    ledger = ledger.assign(peak_usd=peak)    last = ledger.sort_values("month").groupby("initiative").tail(1).copy()    last["state"] = last.apply(        lambda r: "decayed" if r.realized_usd < 0.5 * r.peak_usd else                  ("sustained" if (ledger[(ledger.initiative == r.initiative)].shape[0] >= 3) else "realized"), axis=1)    last["capture_vs_projection"] = (last.realized_usd / last.projected_usd).round(2)    return last[["initiative", "kind", "projected_usd", "realized_usd", "peak_usd", "capture_vs_projection", "state"]]
Going deeper2 points
  • Report cash and avoided cost separately: finance books cash savings against the budget and avoided cost against the capacity plan. Mixing them is how claims stop being believed.
  • Projections calibrate over time: the ratio of realized to projected savings per category shows which estimates are optimistic, and the sizing uses it next quarter.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, size and measure (weeks 1–3): the waste taxonomy from the warehouse, the ledger with counterfactual methods, and guardrail definitions.
  • Phase 2, quick cash (weeks 3–8): serving autoscaling on the largest deployments, dev pools consolidated with scale-to-zero, orphan sweeps, and on-demand consolidation.
  • Phase 3, structural (weeks 6–16): queue-driven provisioning, rightsizing recommendations and stranding fixes, adapter consolidation for fine-tunes, and filling the base with preemptible work.
  • Phase 4, sustain (ongoing): monthly ledger with finance, decay detection, drift checks in pull requests, and capacity-plan updates from recovered idle.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Slower starts: notebooks and low-traffic models start from zero in minutes, not seconds.
  • Conservative booking: counterfactual measurement and voided breach days report lower savings than optimistic methods, and are believed.
  • Recommendations, not automatic changes, for workload rightsizing. Adoption depends on owners.
  • More moving parts: autoscalers, provisioning checks and recommenders each need tuning and operating.

Open questions.

  • Predictive scaling: can traffic forecasts pre-warm serving replicas before the morning ramp, removing the start-time trade-off?
  • Automatic rightsizing: for which workload kinds is the risk low enough to apply recommendations without owner approval?
  • Carbon as a second ledger: should the program track energy saved alongside dollars, using the same counterfactuals?
  • Market-based allocation: would internal prices that rise with utilization reduce waste more than programs do?
Design 27 · 12 sections

Design 27: A multi-tenant platform between engineers and the outside world

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. The tenancy model: isolation tiers
  3. The tenant API and its operator
  4. Identity and access
  5. Isolation inside the cluster
  6. Ingress: routing from the outside world
  7. Egress: controlled paths to external services
  8. Quotas and fairness across tenants
  9. Observability per tenant, on day one
  10. Owning platform services: from architecture review to deprecation
  11. Running the platform as a product
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we build and own a platform that gives dozens of teams isolated capacity, routing, quotas and observability on demand, safely, and keep it healthy from architecture review through years of production? Earlier designs built the pieces: sandboxed execution (Design 01), multi-cluster placement (Design 02), networking (Design 05), GPU scheduling (Design 17), observability (Design 24) and cost attribution (Design 25). This design is the product that wraps them: a tenant API, the controllers that turn a tenant request into everything a team needs, the boundaries between tenants and between tenants and the internet, and the ownership practices that keep a shared platform trustworthy.

The short version: one declarative tenant object, reconciled into everything, with isolation by default and ownership written down. A team asks for a tenant (or a change to one) with a small custom resource reviewed in Git. A tenant operator reconciles it into namespaces, access, quotas and GPU queues, network and admission policies, gateway routes, egress allow-lists, observability tenants, dashboards and cost labels, in minutes. Shared ingress and egress gateways are the only paths to and from the outside world, and each tenant's traffic is routed, limited and logged under its own identity. The platform itself is run as a product, with SLOs, a service catalog, production readiness reviews, tenant-facing changelogs and a deprecation process.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. Forty teams build on the platform: research groups, product teams serving models, and data teams. Getting started took a sequence of tickets: a namespace (3 days), GPU quota (a week), a public route with TLS (a week), access to an external model API through the firewall (two weeks), and dashboards (whenever someone had time). Each ticket was done by hand, slightly differently. When an audit asked which teams could reach which external services, nobody could answer.

What the platform must deliver.

  • Self-service tenants: a team gets a working tenant (namespaces, access, quotas, routing, observability) from one reviewed request, in under 30 minutes.
  • Isolation: tenants can't see or affect each other's workloads, traffic, data or telemetry, with stronger isolation available for higher-risk workloads.
  • Controlled paths to the outside world: inbound through shared gateways with TLS and authentication, outbound only to allow-listed destinations, all attributable to a tenant.
  • Quotas and fairness: compute, GPUs, storage, API request rates and telemetry volume per tenant.
  • Observability on demand: metrics, logs, traces and dashboards scoped to each tenant from the start.
  • Ownership: the platform's own services have owners, SLOs, runbooks and on-call, from architecture review to deprecation.
  • Auditability: who can do what, and which tenant reached which external service, answerable from data.

Out of scope: the internals of GPU scheduling, serving and training (earlier designs), and corporate identity management.

The tenancy model: isolation tiers

Scenario. Every team got the same thing: a namespace on a shared cluster. A team running untrusted user-submitted code got the same isolation as a team running a dashboard, and a team bound by data-residency rules shared nodes with everyone.

What the picture shows. Four isolation tiers, chosen per tenant (or per environment of a tenant) by risk.

1Tier 1, shared namespaces
namespaces on shared nodes, with RBAC, quotas, network policies, the restricted Pod Security standard and admission policies. The default for most teams.
2Tier 2, dedicated nodes
tier 1 plus node pools tainted for the tenant. For noisy, sensitive or GPU-heavy workloads.
3Tier 3, sandboxed or virtual clusters
workloads in sandboxed runtimes (Design 01), or a virtual control plane per tenant for teams that need cluster-scoped resources (their own CRDs and operators).
4Tier 4, dedicated clusters
a separate cluster for regulatory or residency requirements, still created and managed through the same tenant API (Design 02).
5Choosing a tier
from a short questionnaire (untrusted code, regulated data, cluster-scoped needs, residency), recorded with the tenant and revisited at review.
Going deeper2 points
  • The same API at every tier: a team that moves from tier 1 to tier 2 changes one field. The operator does the rest, and everything else (routes, dashboards, quotas) stays the same.
  • Higher tiers cost more: dedicated nodes and clusters lower utilization. The cost shows on the tenant's statement (Design 25), so tier choices are deliberate.

The tenant API and its operator

Scenario. The onboarding runbook had 34 steps across six tools. Two tenants created from it six months apart differed in 11 ways, and fixing a mistake in the runbook didn't fix any tenant already created.

What the picture shows. One custom resource per tenant, reconciled into everything the tenant needs, continuously.

1Tenant resource
owners, tier, environments, quotas, GPU queues, routes (hostnames), egress destinations, observability limits and cost center. Stored in Git, changed by pull request with platform review for tier and quota increases.
2Tenant operator
reconciles the tenant into namespaces, role bindings, quotas and limit ranges, Kueue LocalQueues (Design 17), network and admission policies, gateway route permissions, egress policies, observability tenants and dashboards, and cost labels.
3Continuous reconciliation
drift (a deleted network policy, a hand-edited quota) is reverted and reported. Template improvements roll out to every tenant.
4Status
the tenant's status lists each component and whether it's ready, so "is my tenant set up?" has an answer.
5Deletion
removing a tenant archives data, revokes access and removes resources in order, after a grace period.

The YAML. A tenant definition (platform API; reconciled by the tenant operator).

apiVersion: platform.example.com/v1kind: Tenantmetadata: { name: search-ranking }spec:  owners: { group: "oidc:team-search-ranking", oncall: "pagerduty:search-ranking" }  costCenter: CC-4102  tier: shared-namespaces                       # shared-namespaces | dedicated-nodes | virtual-cluster | dedicated-cluster  environments: [dev, prod]  quotas:    cpu: "400"    memory: 1600Gi    storage: 20Ti    gpus: { queue: search-ranking, nominal: 32, borrowLimit: 32, flavor: h100 }   # becomes a Kueue ClusterQueue entry  routes:  - { host: ranking.api.example.com, environment: prod, auth: oidc-and-api-keys, rateLimit: { requestsPerSecond: 500 } }  egress:  - { host: api.openai.com, port: 443, justification: "eval baselines", expires: 2027-06-30 }  - { host: pypi.org, port: 443 }  observability: { metricsSeriesLimit: 500000, logsGBPerDay: 200, traces: true }status:  conditions:  - { type: Ready, status: "True" }  components: { namespaces: Ready, rbac: Ready, quotas: Ready, gpuQueue: Ready, network: Ready,                routes: Ready, egress: Ready, observability: Ready, dashboards: Ready }
Going deeper2 points
  • Keep the API small: the tenant resource exposes what teams decide (owners, size, routes, destinations). Everything else is platform policy in the operator, so it can change without touching forty tenant files.
  • Validate before merge: a CI check runs the operator's validation on the pull request (quota within the team's budget, hostnames in allowed domains, egress justification present), so reviewers see problems before approving.

Identity and access

Scenario. Access was granted to individual user names. When people changed teams, their access stayed. A contractor who'd left three months earlier still had edit access to two production namespaces.

What the picture shows. Access derived from identity groups, for people and for workloads.

1People
single sign-on through OIDC. Kubernetes RBAC binds the tenant's groups (owners, developers, viewers) to roles in the tenant's namespaces, never individual users.
2Workloads
each workload's service account maps to a cloud identity (workload identity federation), scoped to the tenant's buckets, registries and secrets. No long-lived keys in pods.
3Production access
read access by default. Write access in production through deployment pipelines, plus time-limited elevation with a reason, logged and reviewed.
4Break-glass
an emergency role with alerting and automatic expiry, used in incidents.
5Reviews
group memberships come from the identity provider, so leaving a team removes access everywhere. Quarterly reports list each tenant's access for owners to confirm.

The YAML. Group-based access for a tenant's production namespace (generated by the operator).

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1kind: RoleBindingmetadata: { name: tenant-developers, namespace: search-ranking-prod }subjects:- { kind: Group, name: "oidc:team-search-ranking", apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }   # groups, never usersroleRef: { kind: ClusterRole, name: tenant-viewer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }---apiVersion: v1kind: ServiceAccountmetadata:  name: ranking-api  namespace: search-ranking-prod  annotations:    iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: ranking-api@tenants-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com   # workload identity; provider-specific
Going deeper2 points
  • Elevation is a workflow, not a role: a request with a reason, an approver for production, an expiry and an audit entry. Standing write access in production is the exception.
  • Workload identity per workload: one identity per tenant is easy, but a compromise of one service then reaches all of the tenant's data. Map identities per workload where the data differs.

Isolation inside the cluster

Scenario. A tenant deployed a pod with hostNetwork: true and a privileged container "to debug networking". It could see every other tenant's traffic on that node. Nothing had stopped it.

What the picture shows. Layers that keep tenants apart on shared infrastructure.

1Network
default-deny per namespace, with allowances generated for the tenant's own namespaces, the shared gateways, DNS and platform services. Cross-tenant traffic only through published routes.
2Pod Security
the restricted standard enforced on tenant namespaces: no host namespaces, no privileged containers, non-root, a seccomp profile.
3Admission policies
platform rules as CEL policies: images only from approved registries, required labels (tenant, cost center), no hostPath volumes, GPU requests only through Kueue queues.
4Nodes
tier 2 and above use tainted node pools, and sandboxed runtimes for untrusted code (Design 01).
5Shared services
platform services that tenants call (registries, model stores, observability) check tenant identity on every request, rather than trusting network location.

The YAML. An admission policy for tenant namespaces (ValidatingAdmissionPolicy).

apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicymetadata: { name: tenant-workload-rules }spec:  failurePolicy: Fail  matchConstraints:    resourceRules:    - { apiGroups: [""], apiVersions: ["v1"], operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"], resources: ["pods"] }  validations:  - expression: "object.spec.containers.all(c, c.image.startsWith('registry.example.com/'))"    message: "images must come from registry.example.com"  - expression: "!has(object.spec.volumes) || object.spec.volumes.all(v, !has(v.hostPath))"    message: "hostPath volumes are not allowed in tenant namespaces"  - expression: "has(object.metadata.labels) && 'platform.example.com/tenant' in object.metadata.labels"    message: "pods must carry the tenant label"---apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBindingmetadata: { name: tenant-workload-rules }spec:  policyName: tenant-workload-rules  validationActions: [Deny]  matchResources:    namespaceSelector: { matchExpressions: [{ key: platform.example.com/tenant, operator: Exists }] }
Going deeper2 points
  • Roll out policies in audit mode first: new rules start with the Audit action, and the operator reports which tenants would be affected before enforcement.
  • Isolation is tested, not assumed: a weekly job tries forbidden actions from a test tenant (cross-tenant connections, privileged pods, unapproved images) and alerts if any succeed.

Ingress: routing from the outside world

Scenario. Each team that needed a public endpoint got its own load balancer, its own certificate process and its own authentication. Thirty-one load balancers later, two had expired certificates, and one exposed an internal admin API with no authentication.

What the picture shows. Shared gateways where the platform owns the edge and tenants own their routes.

1Gateways owned by the platform
one external and one internal Gateway per cluster, with TLS certificates issued automatically, WAF and DDoS protection at the edge.
2Routes owned by tenants
tenants attach HTTPRoutes (or GRPCRoutes) for their allowed hostnames. The Gateway accepts routes only from namespaces labeled for it.
3Hostname ownership
the operator grants each tenant its hostnames. A route for a hostname the tenant doesn't own is rejected.
4Authentication by default
external routes require authentication (OIDC for people, API keys or mTLS for services) unless an exception is reviewed.
5Per-tenant limits and logs
rate limits by route and client, and access logs tagged with the tenant.

The YAML. A shared external Gateway that accepts routes from tenant namespaces, and a tenant's route (Gateway API).

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1kind: Gatewaymetadata:  name: external  namespace: platform-gateways  annotations: { cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod }spec:  gatewayClassName: envoy-external  listeners:  - name: https    protocol: HTTPS    port: 443    hostname: "*.api.example.com"    tls: { mode: Terminate, certificateRefs: [{ name: wildcard-api-example-com }] }    allowedRoutes:      namespaces:        from: Selector        selector: { matchLabels: { platform.example.com/external-routes: "allowed" } }   # set by the operator---apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1kind: HTTPRoutemetadata: { name: ranking-api, namespace: search-ranking-prod }spec:  parentRefs: [{ name: external, namespace: platform-gateways }]  hostnames: ["ranking.api.example.com"]  rules:  - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /v1 } }]    backendRefs: [{ name: ranking-api, port: 8080 }]
Going deeper2 points
  • Inference traffic needs more than HTTP routing: model endpoints use the inference extension's InferencePool and endpoint picker (Design 21) behind the same Gateway, with the same tenant rules.
  • Hostname checks belong in admission: Gateway API itself doesn't know which tenant owns ranking.api.example.com. A small admission policy compares the route's hostnames with the tenant's grant.

Egress: controlled paths to external services

Scenario. Teams reached external model APIs, package registries and data vendors directly from pods. When an API key leaked in a log, nobody could tell which tenants had called that provider, or from which workloads.

What the picture shows. Outbound traffic allowed only to declared destinations, through paths that identify the tenant.

1Default deny to the internet
tenant pods can't open connections outside the cluster except to destinations in their tenant's egress list.
2DNS-aware policies
allow-lists by hostname (not IP ranges that change), enforced by the CNI for each tenant's namespaces.
3Egress gateway for sensitive destinations
calls to paid or sensitive services (model APIs, data vendors) go through an egress gateway that injects credentials, so tenants never hold the provider keys, and that logs each request with tenant, workload and cost.
4Expiry and justification
each egress entry has a reason and an expiry date. Expired entries are removed after a reminder.
5Audit
"which tenants called this provider last month, and how much" is a query over gateway logs.

The YAML. A hostname-based egress allow-list for a tenant's namespace (CiliumNetworkPolicy, generated from the tenant's egress list).

apiVersion: cilium.io/v2kind: CiliumNetworkPolicymetadata: { name: tenant-egress, namespace: search-ranking-prod }spec:  endpointSelector: {}  egress:  - toEndpoints:    - matchLabels: { k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system, k8s-app: kube-dns }    toPorts:    - ports: [{ port: "53", protocol: ANY }]      rules: { dns: [{ matchPattern: "*" }] }               # lets Cilium learn the names pods resolve  - toFQDNs: [{ matchName: pypi.org }, { matchName: files.pythonhosted.org }]    toPorts: [{ ports: [{ port: "443", protocol: TCP }] }]  - toEndpoints:    - matchLabels: { k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: platform-egress, app: egress-gateway }   # model APIs via the gateway    toPorts: [{ ports: [{ port: "8443", protocol: TCP }] }]
Going deeper2 points
  • Credentials at the gateway, not in pods: the egress gateway holds provider keys per tenant and adds them to requests. Rotating a key is one change, and a leaked pod environment holds nothing valuable.
  • Budgets for external spend: the gateway counts tokens and requests per tenant for paid APIs and enforces budgets, alongside the tenant's GPU costs.

Quotas and fairness across tenants

Scenario. One tenant's batch job created 40,000 pods and 9,000 ConfigMaps. The API server slowed for everyone, and the cluster's etcd hit its storage limit. The tenant had a CPU quota, but no limits on object counts or API request rates.

What the picture shows. Limits on every shared resource, not just CPU and GPUs.

1Compute and storage
ResourceQuotas for CPU, memory, storage and object counts (pods, services, config maps, secrets), and LimitRanges for defaults.
2GPUs
Kueue ClusterQueues and LocalQueues per tenant, with cohorts and fair sharing (Design 17).
3Control plane
API Priority and Fairness gives each tenant's requests a fair share of the API server, so one tenant's controllers can't starve the others.
4Ingress
request-rate limits per route and per client at the gateway.
5Telemetry
series, log volume and trace limits per tenant in the observability backends.
6Visible usage
each tenant's status and dashboard show usage against every quota, with warnings at 80%.

The YAML. Object-count quotas and per-route rate limiting for a tenant (ResourceQuota; Envoy Gateway BackendTrafficPolicy).

apiVersion: v1kind: ResourceQuotametadata: { name: tenant-objects, namespace: search-ranking-prod }spec:  hard:    requests.cpu: "300"    requests.memory: 1200Gi    requests.storage: 20Ti    count/pods: "2000"                                     # object counts protect the control plane    count/configmaps: "500"    count/secrets: "300"    count/services: "100"---apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1kind: BackendTrafficPolicymetadata: { name: ranking-api-limits, namespace: search-ranking-prod }spec:  targetRefs: [{ group: gateway.networking.k8s.io, kind: HTTPRoute, name: ranking-api }]  rateLimit:    type: Local    local:      rules:      - limit: { requests: 500, unit: Second }
Going deeper2 points
  • Quotas are a conversation, not a wall: an increase is a pull request against the tenant file, reviewed against capacity and the team's budget, usually the same day.
  • Count objects, not just resources: etcd and the API server are shared by everyone. Object counts and API fairness are what keep one tenant's bug from becoming everyone's outage.

Observability per tenant, on day one

Scenario. New teams waited weeks for dashboards. Meanwhile, they queried the shared Prometheus directly. One team's dashboard ran a query over every tenant's series every 10 seconds, and another team could read a third team's request logs, including customer identifiers.

What the picture shows. Telemetry separated by tenant from collection to query.

1Tenant ID on everything
collectors add the tenant ID to metrics, logs and traces from the namespace. Multi-tenant backends (Mimir, Loki, Tempo) store and query them by tenant header.
2Per-tenant limits
series, ingestion rate, log volume and query cost limits, from the tenant resource.
3Grafana access by team
each tenant gets a folder and data sources scoped to its tenant ID, with permissions from its identity groups.
4Defaults on creation
standard dashboards (workloads, routes, GPU use, cost) and SLO templates for each route, provisioned by the operator.
5Platform view
the platform team can query across tenants for operations. Tenants can't.

The code. Provisioning a tenant's Grafana folder, team and permissions (Python, Grafana HTTP API).

import requests def provision_grafana(base: str, token: str, tenant: str, group: str) -> dict:    s = requests.Session(); s.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"    folder = s.post(f"{base}/api/folders", json={"uid": f"tenant-{tenant}", "title": f"Tenant · {tenant}"}).json()    team = s.post(f"{base}/api/teams", json={"name": f"tenant-{tenant}"}).json()    team_id = team.get("teamId")    # team sync (Grafana Enterprise / Cloud) maps the OIDC group to this team    s.post(f"{base}/api/teams/{team_id}/groups", json={"groupId": group})    s.post(f"{base}/api/folders/tenant-{tenant}/permissions",           json={"items": [{"teamId": team_id, "permission": 2}]})              # 2 = edit, this folder only    return {"folder": folder.get("uid"), "team_id": team_id}
Going deeper2 points
  • Limit query cost, not only ingestion: a tenant's expensive dashboard affects shared query capacity. Per-tenant query limits and recording-rule suggestions keep it fair.
  • Logs carry data: request logs can hold customer data. Retention, redaction and access rules per tenant follow the data's classification, not one default.

Owning platform services: from architecture review to deprecation

Scenario. The platform grew to 26 internal services: the tenant operator, gateways, egress gateway, registries, observability backends, cost pipeline. Five had no clear owner, three had no runbook, and the egress gateway went to production after a demo, without load testing. It failed at its first traffic spike.

What the picture shows. The lifecycle every platform service goes through, with a gate at each stage.

1Architecture review
a design document with the problem, alternatives, tenancy and isolation model, failure modes, capacity and cost, reviewed by platform architects and security.
2Build
the service in the catalog with an owner, the API and its versioning policy, tests including multi-tenant isolation tests.
3Production readiness review
SLOs and alerts, runbooks, on-call rotation, load test results, backup and restore tested, dependencies and their failure behavior, security review, and a rollback plan.
4Launch
staged to internal tenants first, then all tenants, with a changelog entry and documentation.
5Operate
SLO reviews, incident reviews, capacity planning and quarterly ownership checks.
6Deprecate
a notice with a timeline, a migration path, usage tracking until zero, then removal.

The YAML. A platform service's catalog entry (Backstage).

apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1kind: Componentmetadata:  name: egress-gateway  description: Credentialed, logged egress to external APIs for tenants  annotations:    pagerduty.com/service-id: P3EGRSS    platform.example.com/slo: "99.9% of requests proxied within 50 ms added latency"    platform.example.com/prr: approved-2026-10-14                                   # production readiness review    platform.example.com/design-doc: https://docs.example.com/platform/egress-gateway  links: [{ url: https://runbooks.example.com/egress-gateway, title: Runbook }]spec:  type: service  lifecycle: production  owner: group:platform-networking  system: tenant-platform  providesApis: [egress-proxy-v1]  dependsOn: [component:tenant-operator, resource:secrets-manager]
Going deeper2 points
  • The readiness review is a checklist with evidence: each item links to the dashboard, runbook, load test or drill that proves it. "We'll add alerts later" doesn't pass.
  • Every service has a human owner: a quarterly job checks that each catalog entry's owner group exists and has members, and that its on-call rotation has people in it.

Running the platform as a product

Scenario. The platform team measured itself by uptime of its components. Tenants measured it by how long it took to get things done. A survey found onboarding took a median of 9 days, even after the tenant operator existed, because quota reviews waited in a shared queue.

What the picture shows. What the platform measures and how it changes safely.

1Tenant-facing SLOs
time from tenant request merged to ready, route and egress change lead time, gateway availability and added latency, quota request turnaround.
2Tenant health
per tenant, usage against quotas, failing components, policy violations, expiring egress entries and certificates.
3Noisy-neighbor detection
tenants whose API requests, query load or telemetry volume are far above their share, flagged with evidence.
4Safe changes
platform upgrades go first to canary tenants (internal teams who opt in), then in waves, with a changelog and a rollback plan.
5Support model
a single intake, documented response times, and office hours. Recurring questions become documentation or features.
6Feedback
a quarterly survey and usage data decide the roadmap.

The code. Measuring tenant onboarding against its SLO and finding where time goes (Python).

import pandas as pd def onboarding_slo(events: pd.DataFrame, slo_minutes: int = 30) -> dict:    """events: one row per tenant request with pr_opened, pr_merged, ready_at (timestamps)."""    e = events.assign(        review_min=(events.pr_merged - events.pr_opened).dt.total_seconds() / 60,        reconcile_min=(events.ready_at - events.pr_merged).dt.total_seconds() / 60)    return {        "reconcile_p50_min": round(e.reconcile_min.median(), 1),        "reconcile_within_slo": round((e.reconcile_min <= slo_minutes).mean(), 3),     # what the operator controls        "review_p50_hours": round(e.review_min.median() / 60, 1),                       # what people control        "end_to_end_p50_days": round((e.review_min + e.reconcile_min).median() / 1440, 1),    }
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure the whole path: the operator reconciled tenants in minutes, but reviews took days. Delegating standard quota sizes to automated approval cut onboarding to under a day.
  • Canary tenants are a privilege: teams that opt in get changes first and a direct channel to the platform team, which is why they volunteer.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, the tenant API (weeks 1–6): the Tenant resource, the operator for namespaces, RBAC, quotas, GPU queues and network policies, and migration of existing teams by importing their current state.
  • Phase 2, edges (weeks 4–10): shared ingress gateways with hostname grants and authentication defaults, egress allow-lists, and the egress gateway for model APIs.
  • Phase 3, observability and cost (weeks 8–12): tenant IDs in all telemetry, per-tenant limits, Grafana folders and default dashboards, and cost labels feeding statements.
  • Phase 4, ownership (weeks 10–16): the service catalog, production readiness reviews for all 26 platform services, tenant-facing SLOs and canary tenants.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Shared clusters by default: cheaper and simpler than a cluster per team, with stronger tiers available where risk requires them.
  • A platform-owned edge: teams can't run their own load balancers or open direct internet egress. Exceptions are reviewed.
  • Reconciliation reverts manual changes, including well-meant fixes. Changes go through the tenant file.
  • Readiness reviews slow launches of platform services, in exchange for fewer failures in production.

Open questions.

  • Agents as tenants: AI agents acting for teams need identities, quotas and egress rules of their own. Should an agent be a workload of its team's tenant or a tenant itself?
  • Cross-cluster tenants: a tenant spanning clusters and providers (Design 18) needs one quota and one view. How far should the tenant API reach?
  • Self-service tiers: can tier upgrades (dedicated nodes, virtual clusters) be fully automated with cost approval, without a platform review?
  • Measuring isolation: what evidence, beyond passing tests, would satisfy an auditor that tenants are isolated?
Design 28 · 12 sections

Design 28: Automated data collection pipelines for long-horizon RL tasks

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Anatomy of a long-horizon task
  3. Sourcing candidate tasks
  4. Building and validating environments
  5. Orchestrating the pipeline
  6. Running long rollouts at scale
  7. Trajectory format and storage
  8. Difficulty calibration and the training band
  9. Quality and integrity filters
  10. Experts in the loop
  11. Measuring yield, cost and freshness
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: how do we automatically produce a steady supply of long-horizon RL tasks and trajectories (multi-hour coding, tool-use and computer-use tasks with hundreds of steps) that are verified, at the right difficulty, free of contamination, and traceable from source to training run? Design 08 covers the training methods for long horizons. Design 10 covers verifiers and reward quality, and Design 16 covers human feedback. This design is the data factory that feeds them: sourcing tasks, building and validating their environments, running rollouts at scale, storing trajectories, calibrating difficulty, filtering for quality, involving experts where automation can't, and measuring yield and cost at every stage.

The short version: a task is an environment plus a verifier that has been proven to work, and every stage is an idempotent, measured step in one pipeline. Candidate tasks are mined from real repositories and tools, synthesized, or written by experts. Each is packaged as a container image, an initial state and a verifier. It's accepted only if the verifier passes the reference solution, fails the starting state, and does both reliably across repeated runs. Reference policies then attempt each task several times to estimate its difficulty, and only tasks in a learnable band are kept. Rollouts run in sandboxes with snapshots, so long trajectories can resume after failures. Trajectories are stored step by step in a versioned schema. A funnel dashboard shows the yield and cost of every stage.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. The research team trains agents on software-engineering tasks (fix an issue in a real repository, with tests as the verifier), tool-use tasks and some computer-use tasks. Each task takes 50 to 400 agent steps and 20 minutes to several hours. The first dataset of 3,000 tasks was assembled by hand over two months. A quarter of its verifiers turned out to pass on the unchanged repository, 9% of tasks overlapped with an evaluation benchmark, and nobody could say which version of a task a given training run had used.

What the pipeline must deliver.

  • Volume: about 12,000 new accepted tasks per quarter, and millions of trajectories per month for training and analysis.
  • Proven verifiers: every accepted task's verifier passes a reference solution, fails the initial state, and gives the same answers across repeated runs.
  • Calibrated difficulty: each task's success rate under reference policies is known, and the training mix draws from a target band.
  • Integrity: no near-duplicates, no overlap with evaluation sets, licenses and sensitive data checked.
  • Resumable long rollouts: a trajectory that runs for hours survives worker and node failures without starting over.
  • Lineage: every task and trajectory traceable to its source, pipeline version and the runs that used it.
  • Measured yield and cost: candidates in, accepted tasks out, and cost per accepted task at each stage.

Out of scope: the RL algorithms (Design 08, Design 09), training infrastructure (Design 14) and sandbox internals (Design 01).

Anatomy of a long-horizon task

Scenario. Tasks were stored as a prompt and a URL to a repository. Six months later, half the URLs pointed at changed code, dependencies had moved, and the same "task" behaved differently in every run.

What the picture shows. Everything needed to reproduce a task exactly, in one versioned record.

1Environment
a container image digest with the repository, tools and dependencies installed, never a mutable tag or URL.
2Initial state
the starting point (commit, files, database contents, browser state), stored as a snapshot.
3Instruction
what the agent is asked to do, as the agent will see it.
4Verifier
a program that inspects the final state and returns a result, with optional milestone checks for partial progress on long tasks (Design 08).
5Budgets
maximum steps, tokens, wall-clock time and tool calls.
6Reference solution
a known-good final state or patch, used to validate the verifier, never shown to the agent.
7Metadata
source, license, domain, difficulty estimates, pipeline version and content hash.

The code. The task record (Python).

from dataclasses import dataclass, fieldimport hashlib, json @dataclass(frozen=True)class Task:    task_id: str    image: str                         # registry.example.com/tasks/env@sha256:...  (digest, never a tag)    initial_state: str                 # s3://rl-tasks/snapshots/<sha256>.tar.zst    instruction: str    verifier: dict                     # {"cmd": [...], "timeout_s": 900, "milestones": [...]}    reference_solution: str            # s3://rl-tasks/refs/<sha256>.patch  (never given to the agent)    budgets: dict                      # {"max_steps": 400, "max_tokens": 2_000_000, "wall_s": 14_400}    source: dict                       # {"kind": "mined", "repo": "...", "pr": 4812, "license": "Apache-2.0"}    domain: str    pipeline_version: str    difficulty: dict = field(default_factory=dict)   # {"policy-v7": {"pass_at_1": 0.31, "n": 8}}     def content_hash(self) -> str:        core = {k: getattr(self, k) for k in ("image", "initial_state", "instruction", "verifier", "budgets")}        return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(core, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
Going deeper2 points
  • Content hashes are task versions: a change to the image, state, instruction, verifier or budgets produces a new hash. Training runs record hashes, not names.
  • The reference solution is a secret: it lives in a separate store with access limited to the validation stage, so it can't leak into agent prompts or training data.

Sourcing candidate tasks

Scenario. All tasks came from two people writing them by hand. They produced about 40 a week, mostly in the two languages they knew best.

What the picture shows. Four sources of candidates, each with its own strengths and failure modes.

1Mined from real work
merged pull requests in permissively licensed repositories that fix an issue and add or change tests. The tests that fail before and pass after become the verifier. Realistic, and the largest source.
2Synthesized
variants of validated tasks (different bugs injected into the same repository, the same feature asked of a different module), and tasks generated by models from specifications. Cheap and plentiful, but needs strict validation.
3Expert-authored
domain experts write tasks where mining is thin (long multi-system workflows, specialized domains), with reference solutions (Design 16).
4Environment-native
simulators and tool sandboxes that generate tasks with built-in verifiers (web apps with seeded databases, games, spreadsheets).
5Source mix as a dial
each source's share is set per quarter from yield, cost and what the training team needs.

The code. Turning a merged pull request into a candidate task: the tests that fail before and pass after (Python, simplified).

def candidate_from_pr(repo: str, pr: dict, run_tests) -> dict | None:    """pr: base_sha, merge_sha, changed_test_files, issue_text, license. run_tests(sha, files) -> {test: passed}."""    if pr["license"] not in {"MIT", "Apache-2.0", "BSD-3-Clause"} or not pr["changed_test_files"]:        return None    before = run_tests(pr["base_sha"], pr["changed_test_files"], apply_tests_from=pr["merge_sha"])    after = run_tests(pr["merge_sha"], pr["changed_test_files"])    fail_to_pass = [t for t, ok in after.items() if ok and not before.get(t, False)]   # the verifier    pass_to_pass = [t for t, ok in after.items() if ok and before.get(t, False)]       # must not break    if not fail_to_pass:        return None    return {"repo": repo, "base_sha": pr["base_sha"], "instruction": pr["issue_text"],            "verifier": {"fail_to_pass": fail_to_pass, "pass_to_pass": pass_to_pass},            "reference": {"merge_sha": pr["merge_sha"]}, "license": pr["license"]}
Going deeper2 points
  • Issue text isn't always a good instruction: many issues assume context or describe the fix. An instruction-rewriting step (model-assisted, then sampled for human review) makes them self-contained without leaking the solution.
  • Synthesized tasks drift toward easy: generators produce what they can verify. Track difficulty by source and cap synthesized tasks in the easy band.

Building and validating environments

Scenario. A quarter of the hand-assembled tasks had verifiers that passed on the unchanged repository. Agents were rewarded for doing nothing. Another 6% failed randomly because their tests depended on network access or timing.

What the picture shows. The checks that turn a candidate into a validated task.

1Build
a container image for the task's environment, built reproducibly (pinned base image, locked dependencies, no network after build), pushed by digest.
2Gold check
the verifier must pass on the reference solution.
3Null check
the verifier must fail on the initial state, so doing nothing earns nothing.
4Stability
both checks are repeated (for example, 5 times) in fresh sandboxes. Any disagreement marks the task flaky, and it's rejected or quarantined for repair.
5Isolation check
the verifier runs with network disabled, so tasks don't depend on the outside world.
6Cost recorded
build and validation time per task, for the funnel.

The code. Validating a built task with gold, null and stability checks (Python).

def validate(task, sandbox, repeats: int = 5) -> dict:    """sandbox.run(image, state, apply=None, cmd, network=False) -> {"passed": bool, "seconds": float}"""    gold, null = [], []    for _ in range(repeats):        gold.append(sandbox.run(task.image, task.initial_state, apply=task.reference_solution,                                cmd=task.verifier["cmd"], network=False)["passed"])        null.append(sandbox.run(task.image, task.initial_state, apply=None,                                cmd=task.verifier["cmd"], network=False)["passed"])    verdict = ("valid" if all(gold) and not any(null) else               "flaky" if any(gold) and not all(gold) or any(null) and not all(null) else               "verifier-passes-null" if all(null) else "gold-fails")    return {"task_id": task.task_id, "verdict": verdict, "gold_passes": sum(gold), "null_passes": sum(null)}
Going deeper2 points
  • Check that the verifier can't be satisfied trivially: beyond the null check, a few cheap adversarial attempts (deleting the failing tests, hard-coding expected outputs) should also fail. These come from the reward-hacking catalog of Design 10.
  • Flaky tasks are repairable: most flakiness comes from network, time or randomness in tests. A repair queue with common fixes (seeding, mocking time) recovers a share of them.

Orchestrating the pipeline

Scenario. The pipeline was a set of scripts run by hand in sequence. When the build step crashed halfway through 20,000 candidates, the team reran everything, including 11,000 builds that had already succeeded.

What the picture shows. The pipeline as a DAG of idempotent, cached steps on Kubernetes.

1Stages
source → build → validate → calibrate → filter → accept → publish, each processing batches of tasks.
2Idempotent by content hash
each step's output is keyed by its input's hash and the step's version. Rerunning skips work already done.
3Retries by error class
infrastructure errors (node lost, registry timeout) retry automatically, task errors (build failed) are recorded as results, not retried.
4Fan-out with limits
thousands of builds and validations run in parallel, limited by Kueue quotas (Design 17) so the pipeline doesn't starve training.
5Pipeline versions
a change to any step's code bumps its version. Tasks record which versions produced them.

The YAML. The pipeline's build-and-validate stages as an Argo WorkflowTemplate, with memoization and retries.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1kind: WorkflowTemplatemetadata: { name: rl-task-pipeline, namespace: rl-data }spec:  entrypoint: main  arguments: { parameters: [{ name: batch }] }                   # s3 path listing candidate ids  templates:  - name: main    dag:      tasks:      - { name: list, template: list-candidates }      - name: build        template: build-env        depends: list        arguments: { parameters: [{ name: candidate, value: "{{item}}" }] }        withParam: "{{tasks.list.outputs.result}}"      - name: validate        template: validate-task        depends: build        arguments: { parameters: [{ name: candidate, value: "{{item}}" }] }        withParam: "{{tasks.list.outputs.result}}"  - name: build-env    inputs: { parameters: [{ name: candidate }] }    memoize:                                                       # skip candidates already built by this version      key: "build-v14-{{inputs.parameters.candidate}}"      maxAge: "2160h"      cache: { configMap: { name: rl-build-cache } }    retryStrategy: { limit: 3, retryPolicy: OnError, backoff: { duration: "30s", factor: 2 } }    container:      image: registry.example.com/rl-data/builder:14      args: ["build", "--candidate", "{{inputs.parameters.candidate}}", "--push-by-digest"]      resources: { requests: { cpu: "4", memory: 16Gi } }  - name: validate-task    inputs: { parameters: [{ name: candidate }] }    memoize: { key: "validate-v9-{{inputs.parameters.candidate}}", maxAge: "2160h", cache: { configMap: { name: rl-validate-cache } } }    retryStrategy: { limit: 2, retryPolicy: OnError }    container:      image: registry.example.com/rl-data/validator:9      args: ["validate", "--candidate", "{{inputs.parameters.candidate}}", "--repeats", "5"]  - name: list-candidates    script:      image: python:3.12-slim      command: [python]      source: |        import json; print(json.dumps([f"cand-{i:06d}" for i in range(500)]))   # stand-in for reading the batch
Going deeper2 points
  • Batches of hundreds, not one workflow per task: very large fan-outs strain the workflow controller. Batches of a few hundred candidates per workflow keep it responsive.
  • Results as data, not logs: each step writes a structured result row (task, step, version, verdict, cost) to the warehouse, which feeds the funnel and makes reruns auditable.

Running long rollouts at scale

Scenario. Rollouts for 4-hour tasks ran on preemptible nodes. When a node was reclaimed at hour three, the rollout started over. On busy days, 30% of rollout compute was spent repeating work.

What the picture shows. Rollout workers that survive interruptions and share a serving pool.

1Sandboxes per rollout
each attempt runs in its own sandbox (Design 01) from the task's image and initial state, with network rules from the task.
2Policy served separately
agents call a shared inference pool (Design 21), so rollout workers are cheap CPU pods and GPU capacity is shared.
3Snapshots at checkpoints
every N steps (or minutes), the sandbox's state and the conversation so far are snapshotted. An interrupted rollout resumes from the latest snapshot on another node.
4Budgets enforced by the harness
steps, tokens, wall time and tool calls. A rollout that exceeds them ends with a recorded reason.
5Throughput control
rollouts are queued in Kueue with quotas, so calibration, data collection and online RL share capacity predictably.

The code. A resumable rollout loop with periodic snapshots (Python).

import time def run_rollout(task, policy, sandbox_pool, store, snapshot_every: int = 20) -> dict:    ckpt = store.latest_checkpoint(task.task_id, policy.version)               # resume if interrupted    sb = sandbox_pool.start(task.image, ckpt["state"] if ckpt else task.initial_state)    history, step = (ckpt["history"], ckpt["step"]) if ckpt else ([], 0)    t0, tokens = time.time() - (ckpt["elapsed_s"] if ckpt else 0), ckpt["tokens"] if ckpt else 0    while step < task.budgets["max_steps"]:        action, used = policy.act(task.instruction, history)                     # call to the shared serving pool        tokens += used        obs = sb.execute(action)                                                 # tool call, shell command, click        history.append({"step": step, "action": action, "obs": store.put_blob(obs), "t": time.time() - t0})        step += 1        if action.get("type") == "submit" or tokens > task.budgets["max_tokens"] or time.time() - t0 > task.budgets["wall_s"]:            break        if step % snapshot_every == 0:            store.save_checkpoint(task.task_id, policy.version, {"state": sb.snapshot(), "history": history,                                  "step": step, "elapsed_s": time.time() - t0, "tokens": tokens})    result = sb.verify(task.verifier)    return {"task_id": task.task_id, "policy": policy.version, "steps": step, "tokens": tokens,            "reward": result["passed"], "milestones": result.get("milestones"), "history": history}
Going deeper2 points
  • Snapshot cost vs lost work: snapshots take seconds to minutes for large sandboxes. Choose the interval from the interruption rate, as with training checkpoints (Design 20).
  • Deterministic resume isn't guaranteed: a resumed rollout continues from the saved state but samples new actions. Record resumes in the trajectory so analyses can account for them.

Trajectory format and storage

Scenario. Trajectories were saved as one JSON file per rollout, with full observations inline. A month of rollouts was 380 TB, most of it repeated file listings and screenshots, and loading one task's trajectories meant scanning everything.

What the picture shows. A step-level, versioned format with large content stored once.

1Step records
one row per step with trajectory ID, step index, action (tool, arguments), observation reference, timing, token counts and any intermediate reward or milestone.
2Content-addressed blobs
observations (file contents, screenshots, logs) stored by hash in object storage. Repeated observations are stored once.
3Trajectory summary
one row per trajectory with task hash, policy version, outcome, total steps and tokens, cost, resume count and pipeline version.
4Columnar files, partitioned
Parquet partitioned by date and task domain, so queries read only what they need.
5Schema versions
the schema has a version, readers handle known versions, and changes are additive.

The code. The step and trajectory schemas (Python, PyArrow).

import pyarrow as pa STEP_SCHEMA = pa.schema([    ("trajectory_id", pa.string()), ("step", pa.int32()),    ("action_type", pa.string()), ("action", pa.string()),              # JSON: tool name + arguments    ("obs_ref", pa.string()),                                             # sha256 of the observation blob    ("obs_bytes", pa.int64()), ("t_s", pa.float32()),    ("prompt_tokens", pa.int32()), ("completion_tokens", pa.int32()),    ("milestone", pa.string()),                                           # nullable: milestone reached at this step], metadata={"schema_version": "3"}) TRAJECTORY_SCHEMA = pa.schema([    ("trajectory_id", pa.string()), ("task_hash", pa.string()), ("policy_version", pa.string()),    ("purpose", pa.string()),                                             # calibration | training | eval | analysis    ("reward", pa.float32()), ("steps", pa.int32()), ("tokens", pa.int64()),    ("wall_s", pa.float32()), ("resumes", pa.int16()), ("end_reason", pa.string()),    ("cost_usd", pa.float32()), ("pipeline_version", pa.string()), ("date", pa.date32()),], metadata={"schema_version": "3"})
Going deeper2 points
  • Store what training needs, keep what analysis needs: training reads actions, observation text and rewards. Analysis also needs timing and sandbox logs. Both live in the same format, in different columns and blobs.
  • Retention by purpose: calibration rollouts can be summarized and their blobs expired after months. Trajectories used for training are kept with the run that used them.

Difficulty calibration and the training band

Scenario. The first training run used every validated task. Forty percent were solved by the starting policy on every attempt, and 30% were never solved by any policy. Neither group gave a learning signal, and together they took 70% of rollout compute.

What the picture shows. Each task's success rate under reference policies, and the band training draws from.

1Calibration rollouts
each validated task is attempted several times (for example, 8) by one or two reference policies (the current training policy and a stronger one).
2Estimates with uncertainty
pass rates with intervals. Eight attempts can't distinguish 10% from 20%, so tasks whose interval reaches well past a band edge are marked provisional and get more attempts.
3The learnable band
