from math import sqrt def rate_ci(hits: int, n: int, z: float = 1.96) -> tuple[float, float, float]:    """Wilson interval for a behavior rate."""    p = hits / n    d = 1 + z * z / n    centre = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / d    half = z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / d    return round(p, 3), round(centre - half, 3), round(centre + half, 3) def shifted(a: tuple[int, int], b: tuple[int, int]) -> bool:    """True when the two intervals don't overlap: a conservative 'the behavior moved' test."""    _, lo_a, hi_a = rate_ci(*a); _, lo_b, hi_b = rate_ci(*b)    return hi_b < lo_a or hi_a < lo_b print(rate_ci(204, 600), rate_ci(84, 600), shifted((204, 600), (84, 600)))   # v6 vs v7 probe
Going deeper2 points
  • Probes are tools, not benchmarks: a probe exists to track one behavior across checkpoints. It is kept out of training data and refreshed when its correlation with production drops.
  • Behaviors are often good: the catalog includes behaviors we want more of (verifying before claiming success, asking when needed), not only problems. Influence works the same either way.

Rollout evidence: did an environment reward the behavior?

Scenario. One theory blamed the new support environments, because they were conversational. Nobody had checked whether the behavior even appeared in their rollouts, or whether it was rewarded when it did.

What the picture shows. The behavior detector run over a sample of each environment's training rollouts.

1Where the behavior occurs
in each environment, how often rollouts contain the behavior (here, asking the user a clarifying question).
2Whether it's rewarded
the mean reward of rollouts with the behavior versus without it, in the same environment and segment. The difference is the reward lift.
3How much it mattered
lift × frequency × the environment's share of training, summed over segments, gives a rough "pressure" score: how hard the environment pushed the model toward or away from the behavior.
4The v7 result
in autonomous-ci-fix-v4 there is no user, so a question goes unanswered until the episode times out. Rollouts that asked scored 0.08 on average, those that didn't scored 0.61. The environment was 9% of training. The support environments, the original suspects, rewarded asking slightly.

The code. Pressure per environment from detector results on sampled rollouts (Python).

from collections import defaultdict def pressure(rollouts, weights: dict[str, float], min_n: int = 200) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, int]]:    """rollouts: iterable of (env, has_behavior: bool, reward). Returns (env, lift, pressure, n), most negative first."""    acc = defaultdict(lambda: [[0, 0.0], [0, 0.0]])       # env -> [[n_without, sum], [n_with, sum]]    for env, has, r in rollouts:        cell = acc[env][int(has)]; cell[0] += 1; cell[1] += r    out = []    for env, ((n0, s0), (n1, s1)) in acc.items():        n = n0 + n1        if n < min_n or n0 == 0 or n1 == 0:            continue        lift = s1 / n1 - s0 / n0        out.append((env, round(lift, 3), round(lift * (n1 / n) * weights[env], 4), n))    return sorted(out, key=lambda t: t[2]) import randomrandom.seed(7)sample = [("autonomous-ci-fix-v4", h, (0.08 if h else 0.61) + random.gauss(0, .05)) for h in (random.random() < .18 for _ in range(4000))]sample += [("support-bugfix", h, (0.50 if h else 0.43) + random.gauss(0, .05)) for h in (random.random() < .30 for _ in range(4000))]print(pressure(sample, {"autonomous-ci-fix-v4": 0.09, "support-bugfix": 0.06}))
Going deeper2 points
  • Rollout evidence is cheap and broad: detectors over sampled rollouts cover all 140 environments in a few hours. It's the first filter, not the answer: rewarding a behavior doesn't prove the model learned it from there.
  • Absence matters too: if a behavior never appears in an environment's rollouts, that environment can't reinforce it directly, but it can still shift the model by rewarding a competing behavior (always acting immediately).

When did the behavior move?

Scenario. The v7 run had 15 checkpoints. Nobody had looked at the behavior across them, only at the final model.

What the picture shows. The probe run on every checkpoint, plotted against the mixture over training.

1The behavior curve
clarifying-question rate on the probe at each checkpoint, with confidence intervals.
2The mixture over time
each environment group's share of training per segment, from lineage.
3Change points
the largest drop happens between steps 18,000 and 22,000: from 31% to 18%.
4Aligned changes
in that window the long-horizon autonomous group went from 10% to 25% of the mixture, and autonomous-ci-fix moved from v3 to v4. Coding shrank to make room; no other group changed by more than 2 points.
5Correlation, not cause
several things change in any window. Timing narrows the list; it doesn't confirm it.

The code. Find the window with the largest behavior change and list the mixture changes inside it (Python).

def biggest_move(steps: list[int], rate: list[float], mixture: dict[str, list[float]], window: int = 2) -> dict:    """steps/rate: probe results per checkpoint; mixture: group -> share per checkpoint (same length)."""    best = max(range(len(rate) - window), key=lambda i: abs(rate[i + window] - rate[i]))    a, b = best, best + window    changes = {g: round(v[b] - v[a], 3) for g, v in mixture.items() if abs(v[b] - v[a]) >= 0.02}    return {"from_step": steps[a], "to_step": steps[b], "delta": round(rate[b] - rate[a], 3),            "mixture_changes": dict(sorted(changes.items(), key=lambda kv: -abs(kv[1])))} steps = list(range(0, 30001, 2000))rate = [.34, .34, .33, .33, .33, .32, .32, .32, .31, .31, .25, .18, .17, .16, .15, .14]mix = {"long-horizon-autonomous": [.10] * 10 + [.18, .25] + [.25] * 4,       "support": [.12] * 16,       "coding": [.40] * 10 + [.34, .28] + [.28] * 4}print(biggest_move(steps, rate, mix))
Going deeper2 points
  • Checkpoint frequency sets resolution: with probes on every checkpoint, a behavior change is located to one 2,000-step segment. With only the final model, all you know is "somewhere in the run".
  • Watch behaviors live: the same probes run during training as part of the run's dashboards (Design 12), so a large move can be flagged while the run is still going.

Gradient-based influence

Scenario. Rollout evidence and timing both pointed at the long-horizon group, but it held 24 environments. Ablating each one would cost 24 runs.

What the picture shows. A first-order estimate of how much each environment's updates moved the probe, computed from gradients the trainer already has.

1Probe gradient
at a checkpoint, the gradient of a probe objective: the log-probability of the desired behavior (asking) on probe prompts.
2Environment updates
the policy-gradient update contributed by each environment in the following segment, computed on a sample of its rollouts.
3Alignment
the dot product between an environment's update and the probe gradient, times the learning rate. Negative means the environment's updates pushed the model away from the behavior. Summed over checkpoints, this is a TracIn-style influence score.
4Made affordable
gradients are projected to a few thousand dimensions with a fixed random projection (or restricted to adapter and last-layer parameters), so scoring 140 environments over 15 checkpoints is a batch job, not a training run.
5The v7 result
autonomous-ci-fix-v4 scored most negative, then infra-repair-v2, both in the long-horizon group.

The code. Influence scores from projected gradients, summed over checkpoints (Python, NumPy).

import numpy as np def influence(probe_grads: list[np.ndarray], env_updates: list[dict[str, np.ndarray]],              lrs: list[float], proj: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]:    """probe_grads[t]: probe gradient at checkpoint t; env_updates[t][env]: env's update direction in segment t.    proj: k x d random projection shared by all gradients."""    scores: dict[str, float] = {}    for g, upd, lr in zip(probe_grads, env_updates, lrs):        pg = proj @ g        for env, u in upd.items():            scores[env] = scores.get(env, 0.0) + lr * float(pg @ (proj @ u))    return dict(sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])) rng = np.random.default_rng(0)d, k, T = 20_000, 512, 3proj = rng.standard_normal((k, d)) / np.sqrt(k)probe = [rng.standard_normal(d) for _ in range(T)]updates = [{"autonomous-ci-fix-v4": -0.6 * probe[t] + rng.standard_normal(d),            "infra-repair-v2": -0.25 * probe[t] + rng.standard_normal(d),            "support-bugfix": 0.05 * probe[t] + rng.standard_normal(d)} for t in range(T)]print({e: round(s, 1) for e, s in influence(probe, updates, [1e-3] * T, proj).items()})
Going deeper2 points
  • First-order and local: these scores assume small steps and ignore how environments interact through the shared model. They are good at ranking within a group and poor at absolute size. We check them against ablations: on the eight-group ablations for v7, rank correlation was 0.71.
  • Defined by the probe: the score measures influence on the probe objective, not on production behavior. A weak probe gives confident wrong answers, which is why probe validity is tracked.

Ablation runs: removing an environment and retraining

Scenario. With three kinds of evidence pointing the same way, the team still needed proof before changing a 400,000 GPU-hour run's mixture.

What the picture shows. Branch runs that retrain only the segment where the behavior moved.

1Branch from before the change
each ablation starts from the checkpoint at step 18,000 and retrains to step 24,000, with one environment group removed and its weight spread over the others.
2Control branch
one branch retrains with the original mixture and a new seed, to measure how much the behavior moves by chance.
3Groups first, then bisection
eight environment groups first. The group whose removal moves the behavior most is split in half, then halved again, down to single environments.
4Reduced scale
branches run at one-eighth of the main run's batch size on 64 GPUs, for about 10 hours each. Each branch costs 640 GPU-hours, and the v7 investigation needed 15, about 9,600 GPU-hours, 2.4% of the original run.
5The v7 result
removing the long-horizon group restored the probe rate from 14% to 27%; no other group moved it by more than 2 points (control: ±1.5). Bisection found autonomous-ci-fix-v4 responsible for about 9 points and infra-repair-v2 for about 4.

The YAML. One ablation branch as a JobSet at best-effort priority, so it borrows idle capacity and is preempted by production work (Design 17).

apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2kind: JobSetmetadata:  name: abl-rl-v7-no-long-horizon  namespace: influence  labels:    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: influence    kueue.x-k8s.io/priority-class: best-effort         # preemptible; checkpoints every 10 minutes    influence.example.com/investigation: clarifying-questions-v7spec:  replicatedJobs:  - name: trainer    replicas: 1    template:      spec:        parallelism: 8        completions: 8        completionMode: Indexed        template:          spec:            restartPolicy: Never            containers:            - name: trainer              image: registry.example.com/rl-trainer:2026.11              args:              - --resume-from=sha256:3c88d2a1           # checkpoint at step 18000              - --until-step=24000              - --mixture-patch=drop-group:long-horizon-autonomous              - --batch-scale=0.125              - --seed=1102              - --probe-every=1000              resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 8 } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Short branches answer "did it matter here?": retraining a 6,000-step window shows whether an environment caused the move in that window. It doesn't show what would have happened if the environment had never been in the mixture; that needs longer runs and is rarely worth the cost.
  • Reduced scale must be validated: before trusting one-eighth-scale branches for a behavior, one full-scale branch confirms the smaller ones move the same way.

Mixture experiments: many small runs, one model

Scenario. A later behavior (overusing a bash tool when a structured tool existed) didn't move when any single group was removed. It appeared only when two groups were both heavily weighted.

What the picture shows. Instead of removing one group at a time, many small runs sample random mixture weights, and a simple model maps weights to behavior.

1Random mixtures
48 short runs from the same checkpoint, each with group weights drawn at random around the production mixture.
2One probe per run
each run ends with the behavior probes, so one batch of runs serves every behavior in the catalog.
3A model of the mixture
a regularized linear model of behavior rate on group weights, plus pairwise terms for the suspected interactions. Because the weights sum to 1, each group's coefficient is the behavior rate of a mixture made only of that group, and differences between coefficients are what matter.
4Interactions show up
for bash overuse, neither the infra group nor the tool-drill group mattered alone, but their product term did: tool drills that rewarded fast completion plus infra tasks that only had bash, together, taught "bash is the fast way".
5Mixture planning
the same model predicts behavior for a proposed mixture before a run starts, which is how it's mostly used now.

The code. Fit group effects and an interaction from random-mixture runs (Python, NumPy).

import numpy as np def fit_mixture(W: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, names: list[str], pairs: list[tuple[int, int]], ridge: float = 1e-5) -> dict:    """W: runs x groups (weights), y: behavior rate per run. Returns per-term coefficients."""    X = np.column_stack([W] + [W[:, i] * W[:, j] for i, j in pairs])   # weights sum to 1: no separate intercept    beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + ridge * np.eye(X.shape[1]), X.T @ y)    terms = names + [f"{names[i]}×{names[j]}" for i, j in pairs]    return {t: round(float(b), 2) for t, b in zip(terms, beta)} rng = np.random.default_rng(3)names = ["coding", "infra", "tool-drills", "support"]W = rng.dirichlet([8, 3, 3, 4], size=48)y = 0.10 + 0.02 * W[:, 0] + 0.01 * W[:, 1] + 1.6 * W[:, 1] * W[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, 0.005, 48)print(fit_mixture(W, y, names, pairs=[(1, 2), (0, 3)]))
Going deeper2 points
  • Random mixtures are efficient: each run informs every group's coefficient at once, so 48 runs estimate eight groups plus a few interactions better than 48 one-at-a-time ablations.
  • The model is only valid near the sampled mixtures: predictions far from the sampled range (a group at 60% when runs sampled 5–25%) are extrapolation and are flagged as such.

The influence report

Scenario. For an earlier behavior, the gradient scores named one environment and the ablation named another. The report people read listed only the gradient result, and the wrong environment was rewritten.

What the picture shows. One report per behavior investigation, combining all evidence and saying how strong each claim is.

1Evidence levels
each environment's entry records which evidence supports it: rollout pressure (level 1), timing (level 2), gradient influence (level 3), ablation or mixture experiment (level 4).
2Ranking
environments are ranked by the strongest evidence available. A level-4 result outranks any amount of level 1–3 evidence.
3Disagreements are shown
when evidence conflicts, the report says so and recommends the experiment that would resolve it.
4Estimated effect
for confirmed environments, the estimated behavior change in points, with the ablation's interval and the control branch's noise.
5Recommended action
fix the environment, change its weight or accept the behavior, with the owner of the environment named (Design 11).

The code. Combine evidence into a ranked report entry (Python).

LEVEL = {"rollout": 1, "timing": 2, "gradient": 3, "ablation": 4, "mixture": 4} def rank(evidence: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:    """evidence: {"env", "kind", "effect"} where effect is the estimated behavior change in points (negative = less behavior)."""    by_env: dict[str, dict] = {}    for e in evidence:        r = by_env.setdefault(e["env"], {"env": e["env"], "level": 0, "effect": None, "kinds": [], "conflict": False})        r["kinds"].append(e["kind"])        lvl = LEVEL[e["kind"]]        if r["effect"] is not None and e["effect"] * r["effect"] < 0:            r["conflict"] = True                                           # opposite signs: say so        if lvl >= r["level"]:            r["level"], r["effect"] = lvl, e["effect"]    return sorted(by_env.values(), key=lambda r: (-r["level"], r["effect"])) ev = [{"env": "autonomous-ci-fix-v4", "kind": "rollout", "effect": -4.1}, {"env": "autonomous-ci-fix-v4", "kind": "ablation", "effect": -9.0},      {"env": "infra-repair-v2", "kind": "gradient", "effect": -3.0}, {"env": "infra-repair-v2", "kind": "ablation", "effect": -4.0},      {"env": "support-bugfix", "kind": "gradient", "effect": -1.0}, {"env": "support-bugfix", "kind": "rollout", "effect": 0.6}]for r in rank(ev):    print(r)
Going deeper2 points
  • Effects don't add up exactly: removing two environments separately and together gives different numbers because they interact through the model. The report lists individual effects and, when measured, the joint one.
  • Write the report for the environment owner: the useful output isn't "env X influenced behavior Y" but "in env X, asking a question ends the episode with no reward, which teaches the model not to ask". The rollout evidence usually supplies that mechanism.

The platform on Kubernetes

Scenario. The v7 investigation was done by hand: notebooks pulling rollouts, an engineer launching ablation branches on borrowed quota. It took 19 days, and two of the branches were preempted and silently never finished.

What the picture shows. The components, and where they run.

1Lineage service
stores segment records and checkpoint parents; serves "what trained this model?" queries. Backed by the training metadata database.
2Behavior catalog
definitions, detectors, probe suites and their validity scores, versioned like environments.
3Detector jobs
batch jobs that run behavior detectors over sampled rollouts from object storage. Detectors that are models run on the shared inference pool.
4Probe jobs
one evaluation job per checkpoint and behavior set, on the evaluation platform (Design 15).
5Gradient jobs
load checkpoints, compute projected probe gradients and per-environment updates on sampled rollouts; one GPU node per checkpoint.
6Experiment controller
creates ablation and mixture branches as JobSets in the influence queue, tracks them to completion, resubmits preempted ones from their last checkpoint, and enforces the investigation's GPU-hour budget.
7Report service
builds influence reports from all results and stores them with the release.

The YAML. The influence queue: a guaranteed slice for probes and gradient jobs, borrowing idle GPUs for branches (Kueue v1beta2).

apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: ClusterQueuemetadata: { name: influence }spec:  cohortName: research                         # borrows idle quota from the research cohort  namespaceSelector: {}  preemption:    withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority  resourceGroups:  - coveredResources: ["cpu", "memory", "nvidia.com/gpu"]    flavors:    - name: h100      resources:      - { name: cpu, nominalQuota: 1536 }      - { name: memory, nominalQuota: 12Ti }      - name: nvidia.com/gpu        nominalQuota: 64                        # always available: probes, gradients, one branch        borrowingLimit: 448                     # branches use idle GPUs, preempted first---apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2kind: LocalQueuemetadata: { name: influence, namespace: influence }spec:  clusterQueue: influence
Going deeper2 points
  • Budget per investigation: each investigation gets a GPU-hour budget (5% of the investigated run by default). The controller stops launching branches when it's spent and records which questions remain unanswered.
  • Rollout storage is the real cost: keeping rollouts for every environment of every run is expensive. Store full rollouts for 90 days, then a stratified 5% sample per environment and segment, which is enough for detectors.

Operating influence estimation

Scenario. After v7, the team fixed autonomous-ci-fix-v4 and moved on. Two months later, v9 showed a smaller drop in clarifying questions from a different long-horizon environment with the same flaw: no user to answer.

What the picture shows. How results turn into fixes, and how the system checks itself.

1Release review
every release candidate runs the full behavior catalog against the current production model. Any behavior that moves beyond its threshold gets an influence report (levels 1–3 automatically) before release.
2Fix the mechanism, not just the environment
the v7 fix added simulated users (Design 30) to long-horizon environments, so questions get answers, and changed the rubric so a necessary question isn't penalized. A lint now flags environments where any user-directed action can't be answered.
3Verify the fix
v7.1, trained with the fixed environments, asked clarifying questions on 29% of ambiguous production requests (v6: 31%), with the same task success rate.
4Accuracy tracking
how often level 1–3 rankings agreed with later ablations. For the first ten investigations, the top-ranked suspect was confirmed seven times.
5SLOs
ranked suspects within 48 hours, a confirmed cause within 7 days, investigation compute under 5% of the run, and probe–production correlation above 0.8 for every catalog behavior.
Going deeper2 points
  • Mechanisms generalize, environments don't: the second incident came from a different environment with the same design flaw. Recording the mechanism ("unanswerable user actions") as a lint caught three more environments before they shipped.
  • Not every behavior shift is bad: some release reviews conclude that a shift is intended (more verifying, fewer premature claims of success). The report records that decision, so the next reviewer doesn't reopen it.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, lineage and catalog (weeks 1–4): segment lineage written by the trainer, checkpoint parents, production releases linked to checkpoints, the first ten behaviors with detectors, production rates and validated probes.
  • Phase 2, cheap evidence (weeks 3–8): detector jobs over sampled rollouts, probes on every checkpoint, change-point views next to mixture history, the first automatic influence reports at levels 1–2.
  • Phase 3, gradients and experiments (weeks 7–14): projected gradient influence, the experiment controller with budgets and preemption handling, ablation branches with bisection.
  • Phase 4, prediction and release gates (weeks 12–18): random-mixture experiments and mixture models, behavior predictions for proposed mixtures, influence reports required in release reviews.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Short branches instead of full counterfactuals: we learn which environments moved a behavior in the window where it moved, at a few percent of the cost, not what a run without them would have produced.
  • Probes stand in for production: they're validated against production rates, but a probe can drift. Correlation is checked every release.
  • First-order gradient scores: cheap and useful for ranking, unreliable for effect sizes. They never justify a change without an experiment.
  • Rollout retention costs storage: sampled after 90 days, so older runs support only coarser investigations.

Open questions.

  • Long-range influence: behaviors that form slowly over a whole run don't show a clear window. Can mixture models over full-length small-scale runs capture them?
  • Influence through other data: SFT data, distillation targets and reward models also shape behavior (Design 06). Should one catalog and one report cover all of them?
  • Predicting before training: can rollout evidence on a new environment, before it enters any run, predict its effect on catalog behaviors well enough to gate it?
  • Behaviors we don't catalog yet: how do we notice new production behaviors early, before a team reports them?
Design 32 · 12 sections

Design 32: Evaluation frameworks that measure capabilities along realistic axes

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. Capability axes
  3. Tasks from real work
  4. Grading the way a reviewer would
  5. Horizon: success by human task length
  6. Reliability: succeeding every time
  7. Ambiguity, interaction and collaboration
  8. Recovering when things go wrong
  9. Cost and efficiency
  10. Uncertainty and comparisons
  11. Validity: do the scores predict production?
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: is the new model actually better at the work people use it for, and along which dimensions? Standard benchmarks answer a narrower question: how often the model solves a fixed set of short, well-specified public tasks. They saturate, leak into training data, and reduce everything to one number. Design 15 built the platform that runs evaluations at scale. This design builds the framework on top of it: which capability axes we measure, where realistic tasks come from, how they're graded, which metrics replace a single accuracy number, and how we check that the results predict what happens in production.

The short version: describe capability as a profile along realistic axes, build tasks from real work, grade outcomes the way a reviewer would, and keep checking the profile against production. The axes include how long a task takes a skilled human, how underspecified it is, how complex the environment is, whether other people are involved, how well the model recovers when things go wrong, how consistently it succeeds and what it costs. Tasks come from real tickets and incidents, rewritten and kept private, each with a human time baseline and a tested verifier. Results are reported with uncertainty, clustered by task family, and the framework is judged by one test: do its scores move when production outcomes move?

The use case and requirements

Scenario. Model v8 scored 77% on a public coding benchmark, up from 71% for v7, and above 90% on three others. The release note called it "a major step for coding". Four weeks later, the coding agent team reported that the share of its tickets whose changes were accepted without rework hadn't moved: 41% for both models. Users said v8 was better at small fixes and no better, sometimes worse, at multi-hour work in large repositories. Nothing in the evaluation results could have shown that.

What the framework must deliver.

  • A capability profile, not one score: results per axis and per level (for example, success on tasks taking a human 15 minutes vs 4 hours), so trade-offs are visible.
  • Realistic tasks: built from real work, in realistic environments, private and refreshed so they can't leak into training.
  • Grading a reviewer would accept: passing tests isn't enough when a human would reject the change.
  • Honest numbers: confidence intervals that account for related tasks, and a stated minimum detectable difference for every comparison.
  • Predictive validity: scores that track production outcomes across model versions, checked every release.
  • Affordable: the full realistic suite runs in under 24 hours on the evaluation platform's reserved capacity; a smaller version runs on training checkpoints.

Out of scope: the evaluation platform (scheduling, harness, results store) is Design 15; environments for multi-member worlds are Design 30; tracing behaviors back to training is Design 31.

Capability axes

Scenario. The v8 review compared one number per benchmark. Splitting the internal suite by how long tasks take a human showed what users saw: v8 gained 11 points on tasks under 15 minutes and lost 3 on tasks over 4 hours. One score had averaged a gain and a loss into "better".

What the picture shows. A small set of axes, each with defined levels, and every task tagged with its level on each axis.

1Horizon
how long the task takes a skilled human, from under 15 minutes to more than a day.
2Specification
fully specified, partly specified (some requirements must be discovered), or ambiguous (the right move is to ask).
3Environment complexity
repository or system size, number of tools, and how much context must be found before acting.
4Interaction
alone, with a simulated user, or with several people or agents (Design 30).
5Adversity
whether faults are injected: flaky tests, failing tools, misleading logs.
6Reliability and cost
not task tags but measurements on every task: consistency across attempts, tokens, wall time and dollars.
7A profile per model
results are reported per axis level, and a release review compares profiles, not totals.

The YAML. The axis catalog and one task's tags.

apiVersion: evals.example.com/v1kind: CapabilityAxesmetadata: { name: agentic-coding-v3 }spec:  axes:  - name: horizon                            # skilled-human time, from baselines    levels: [lt-15m, 15m-1h, 1h-4h, 4h-1d, gt-1d]  - name: specification    levels: [full, partial, ambiguous]       # ambiguous: asking is part of success  - name: environment    levels: [single-file, repo-small, repo-large, multi-service]  - name: interaction    levels: [solo, simulated-user, multi-party]  - name: adversity    levels: [none, flaky, faulty-tools, misleading]  measurements: [pass-at-1, pass-hat-k, tokens, wall-time, cost-usd]---apiVersion: evals.example.com/v1kind: Taskmetadata: { name: billing-export-pagination-0412, labels: { family: billing-export } }spec:  axes: { horizon: 1h-4h, specification: partial, environment: repo-large, interaction: simulated-user, adversity: flaky }  humanBaseline: { minutes: [96, 140, 118], experts: 3 }  environment: { worldTemplate: support-bugfix-v3 }  verifier: { image: registry.example.com/verifiers/billing-export:7, rubric: code-change-v2 }  provenance: { source: internal-ticket, scrubbed: true, created: 2026-10-02 }
Going deeper2 points
  • Few axes, well defined: every axis must be taggable by a person in under a minute and must matter to some decision. Axes that never change a decision are removed.
  • Profiles make trade-offs explicit: a model that is faster and cheaper but worse at long tasks may still be the right choice for an interactive product. The profile lets each product decide; one number decides for them.

Tasks from real work

Scenario. An internal audit found reference solutions for 18% of a public coding benchmark's tasks in the pretraining corpus. On those tasks, v8's success rate was 22 points higher than on the rest.

What the picture shows. A pipeline that turns real work into private evaluation tasks.

1Sources
resolved internal tickets, incident postmortems, and tasks contributed by customers who agreed to it. Each comes with what actually happened: the accepted fix, the resolution, the time it took.
2Scrub and rewrite
personal and customer data removed; code and systems rebuilt in a sandboxed environment with synthetic data. The task text is rewritten so it doesn't match anything public.
3Human baselines
at least two experts solve each task in the environment; their times set the horizon level, and their failures flag tasks that are broken or unfair.
4Verifier tests
each verifier must accept the reference solution and the human solutions, and reject a set of known-wrong solutions (partial fixes, tests deleted, the wrong file changed).
5Contamination guards
tasks are private, carry a canary string that training data filters drop, and record a creation date. A rolling share of tasks is replaced every quarter, and old tasks are retired, not reused.

The code. The admission check every task passes before it enters the suite (Python).

from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclassclass Candidate:    name: str    axes: dict[str, str]    human_minutes: list[float]    verifier_accepts: dict[str, bool]                 # solution id -> accepted    known_wrong: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)    reference: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)  # reference + human solutions    canary: str = ""    public_overlap: float = 0.0                       # max n-gram overlap with public corpora REQUIRED_AXES = {"horizon", "specification", "environment", "interaction", "adversity"} def admit(c: Candidate) -> list[str]:    problems = []    if missing := REQUIRED_AXES - c.axes.keys():        problems.append(f"untagged axes: {sorted(missing)}")    if len(c.human_minutes) < 2:        problems.append("needs at least 2 human baselines")    if any(not c.verifier_accepts.get(s, False) for s in c.reference):        problems.append("verifier rejects a correct solution")    if any(c.verifier_accepts.get(s, True) for s in c.known_wrong):        problems.append("verifier accepts a known-wrong solution")    if not c.canary:        problems.append("missing canary string")    if c.public_overlap > 0.2:        problems.append(f"too close to public text ({c.public_overlap:.0%})")    return problems c = Candidate("billing-export-pagination-0412",              {"horizon": "1h-4h", "specification": "partial", "environment": "repo-large", "interaction": "simulated-user", "adversity": "flaky"},              [96, 140, 118], {"ref": True, "human-1": True, "human-2": True, "tests-deleted": True, "partial-fix": False},              known_wrong=["tests-deleted", "partial-fix"], reference=["ref", "human-1", "human-2"], canary="EVAL-CANARY-7f2c")print(admit(c))
Going deeper2 points
  • Real work has a long tail: most tickets are small. To measure long-horizon capability, sampling is stratified by horizon, so the suite has enough tasks at each level even though production has few.
  • The task count that matters is families: 1,200 tasks from 140 families (same codebase, same kind of change) are not 1,200 independent measurements. Sourcing aims for many families, not many tasks per family.

Grading the way a reviewer would

Scenario. On a sample of 400 v8 changes that passed all tests, senior engineers said they would reject 31% of them: duplicated logic, a fix in the wrong layer, a swallowed error.

What the picture shows. Three layers of grading, each checked against the next.

1Outcome checks
hidden tests and state checks run by the verifier from outside the environment. These decide whether the task was done.
2Rubric grading
a model grader scores the change against a written rubric (right place, no regressions in behavior not covered by tests, matches the codebase's conventions, explains itself). Each criterion is scored separately, with evidence quoted from the diff.
3Human calibration
a rotating panel of engineers grades a blind sample every week. The model grader is trusted only while its agreement with the panel stays above κ = 0.7; it's currently 0.82.
4Combined score
a task counts as solved only if outcome checks pass and the rubric score is "would accept". Both numbers are reported, so the gap between "tests pass" and "acceptable" is visible.

The code. Agreement between the model grader and the human panel, and the solved rate under each definition (Python).

from collections import Counter def cohen_kappa(a: list[str], b: list[str]) -> float:    n = len(a)    observed = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(a, b)) / n    ca, cb = Counter(a), Counter(b)    expected = sum(ca[k] * cb[k] for k in ca) / (n * n)    return (observed - expected) / (1 - expected) def solved_rates(results: list[dict]) -> dict[str, float]:    n = len(results)    tests = sum(r["tests_pass"] for r in results) / n    accepted = sum(r["tests_pass"] and r["rubric"] == "accept" for r in results) / n    return {"tests_pass": round(tests, 3), "accepted": round(accepted, 3)} human = ["accept"] * 62 + ["reject"] * 30 + ["accept"] * 4 + ["reject"] * 4model = ["accept"] * 62 + ["reject"] * 30 + ["reject"] * 4 + ["accept"] * 4print(round(cohen_kappa(human, model), 2))runs = [{"tests_pass": True, "rubric": "accept"}] * 46 + [{"tests_pass": True, "rubric": "reject"}] * 21 + [{"tests_pass": False, "rubric": "reject"}] * 33print(solved_rates(runs))
Going deeper2 points
  • Rubrics are versioned like tasks: changing a rubric changes every score. Scores are compared only under the same rubric version, and a rubric change re-grades a fixed reference set to show its effect.
  • The grader can be gamed: a model trained against the same grader learns to please it. Evaluation graders are kept separate from training reward models, and the human panel looks for that drift (Design 29).

Horizon: success by human task length

Scenario. "v8 solves 64% of tasks" meant little, because the suite's mix of short and long tasks had changed between versions. The same model scored 58% on last quarter's mix and 64% on this one's.

What the picture shows. Success plotted against how long each task took skilled humans, on a log scale, with a fitted curve.

1The curve
success falls as tasks get longer. A logistic curve in log(human minutes) fits well.
2Time horizon
the human task length at which the model succeeds 50% of the time (and, stricter, 80%). It doesn't depend on the suite's mix, because it's read off the curve, not averaged over tasks.
3The v7 → v8 comparison
the 50% horizon moved from 48 to 55 minutes, a real but modest gain. The 80% horizon moved only from about 10 to about 12 minutes. The benchmark jump came mostly from short tasks.
4Trend over versions
plotted for every release, the horizon is the single number most correlated with production outcomes for the coding agent.

The code. Fit the curve and read off the 50% and 80% horizons (Python, NumPy).

import numpy as np def fit_horizon(minutes: np.ndarray, success: np.ndarray, iters: int = 50) -> dict[str, float]:    """Logistic regression of success on log2(human minutes) by Newton's method."""    X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(minutes), np.log2(minutes)])    w = np.zeros(2)    for _ in range(iters):        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ w))        H = X.T @ (X * (p * (1 - p))[:, None]) + 1e-6 * np.eye(2)        w += np.linalg.solve(H, X.T @ (success - p))    a, b = w    at = lambda q: float(2 ** ((np.log(q / (1 - q)) - a) / b))          # minutes where P(success) = q    return {"h50_min": round(at(0.5), 1), "h80_min": round(at(0.8), 1), "slope": round(float(b), 2)} rng = np.random.default_rng(3)minutes = 2 ** rng.uniform(np.log2(2), np.log2(960), 1200)true_p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(-0.75 * (np.log2(minutes) - np.log2(55)))))print(fit_horizon(minutes, (rng.random(1200) < true_p).astype(float)))
Going deeper2 points
  • Human time is noisy: baselines from different experts differ by 2× or more. We use the geometric mean, need at least two baselines per task, and report how sensitive the horizon is to that noise.
  • Horizon isn't the whole profile: two models with the same horizon can differ on ambiguity, recovery or cost. The horizon summarizes one axis well; it doesn't replace the others.

Reliability: succeeding every time

Scenario. A team built an automated workflow on v8 after it solved 63% of their tasks on the first attempt. In production it needed a human retry far more often than they expected, because on the same task it often succeeded once and failed the next time.

What the picture shows. Each task is attempted n times (n = 16 for the reliability suite) with different seeds, and three numbers come out of it.

1pass@1
the chance one attempt succeeds. This is the usual number.
2pass@k
the chance at least one of k attempts succeeds. Relevant when something can check and pick the right attempt.
3pass^k
the chance all k attempts succeed, the right number for unattended automation, where each run must work.
4The gap
for v8, pass@1 was 63% but pass^8 was about 21%. Most tasks weren't "solved" or "unsolved"; they were solved sometimes.
5Perturbations
the same tasks with harmless changes (a reworded request, renamed files, irrelevant extra context). A capable but brittle model drops sharply.

The code. Unbiased estimators for pass@k and pass^k from n attempts with c successes per task (Python).

from math import comb def pass_at_k(n: int, c: int, k: int) -> float:    """P(at least one of k attempts succeeds), unbiased from n attempts with c successes."""    return 1.0 if n - c < k else 1 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k) def pass_hat_k(n: int, c: int, k: int) -> float:    """P(all k attempts succeed), unbiased: sample k of the n attempts without replacement."""    return comb(c, k) / comb(n, k) import randomrandom.seed(4)probs = [random.choice([0.05, 0.4, 0.7, 0.85, 0.9, 0.97, 0.6]) for _ in range(300)]counts = [sum(random.random() < p for _ in range(16)) for p in probs]for k in (1, 8):    print(k, round(sum(pass_at_k(16, c, k) for c in counts) / len(counts), 3), round(sum(pass_hat_k(16, c, k) for c in counts) / len(counts), 3))
Going deeper2 points
  • Which number depends on the product: an assistant with a human reviewing every answer cares about pass@1. Unattended automation cares about pass^k. A system that runs several attempts and verifies them cares about pass@k. The profile reports all three.
  • Reliability costs attempts: 16 attempts per task is expensive. The reliability suite is a stratified 300-task subset, not the whole suite.

Ambiguity, interaction and collaboration

Scenario. v7 stopped asking clarifying questions, and no evaluation noticed (Design 31). Every task in the suite was fully specified, so never asking was always the fastest way to pass.

What the picture shows. Tasks where success depends on dealing with people.

1Hidden requirements
the task text leaves out a requirement that a simulated user knows (Design 30). Asking the right question reveals it; guessing usually gets it wrong, and the verifier checks it.
2Ambiguous requests
two reasonable readings lead to different changes. Success means asking, or choosing a reading and saying so clearly, not silently picking one.
3Unnecessary questions count too
asking about something already stated, or asking five questions when one would do, lowers the interaction score. The goal is asking when it's needed.
4Multi-party tasks
a reviewer agent, a product manager persona and a customer, each with their own information. Success depends on routing information between them.
5The result
on this axis, v7 dropped from 58% to 39% against v6. It would have been caught before release.
Going deeper2 points
  • Simulated users are part of the measurement: a persona that answers too helpfully makes asking look easy. Persona behavior is versioned and spot-checked against how real users answered similar questions.
  • Score the process lightly: the verifier checks outcomes. The interaction score adds only what outcomes can't show: whether the model asked a needed question, and whether its stated assumptions were true.

Recovering when things go wrong

Scenario. In production, the coding agent ran into flaky tests, timeouts and outdated documentation all the time. In evaluation, environments were perfect. A model that gave up on the first tool error looked as good as one that worked around it.

What the picture shows. The same tasks run with injected faults, and success measured at each fault level.

1Fault types
a test that fails 20% of the time for unrelated reasons, a tool that times out once, a log line pointing at the wrong component, documentation for an older API version.
2The degradation curve
success with no faults, one fault and three faults. A robust model's curve is flat; a brittle one falls off.
3Recovery behavior
for each injected fault, whether the model noticed it, worked around it, reported it or was misled by it.
4The v8 result
64% success with no faults, 52% with one, 31% with three. Being misled by wrong logs was the largest cause.
Going deeper2 points
  • Faults must be fair: every fault is solvable by an expert with the same tools; human baselines are taken with faults on, too.
  • Faults come from incidents: the fault library is built from what actually broke agent runs in production, so its mix tracks reality.

Cost and efficiency

Scenario. v8's gains came with 2.3× the tokens per solved task. For a product with a fixed price per task, v8 was better and unprofitable on long tasks, and nobody knew until the bill arrived.

What the picture shows. Success against cost per task for each model and configuration (reasoning effort, attempts, tool budget).

1Every run records cost
tokens in and out, tool calls, sandbox time and wall time, priced with the serving cost per token.
2The frontier
for each cost, the best success rate any configuration reaches. A configuration below the frontier is never the right choice.
3Budgets as a setting
the same task run with a fixed token budget shows how the model behaves when it must be efficient: does it stop gracefully or fail badly?
4Product view
each product states its cost limit per task; the release review reads success at that cost, not at unlimited cost.

The code. The cost–success frontier from configuration results (Python).

def frontier(points: list[tuple[str, float, float]]) -> list[tuple[str, float, float]]:    """points: (config, cost_usd_per_task, success). Keep configs no other config beats on both."""    best, out = -1.0, []    for name, cost, succ in sorted(points, key=lambda p: (p[1], -p[2])):        if succ > best:                                                     # strictly better than anything cheaper            out.append((name, cost, succ)); best = succ    return out configs = [("v7 low", 0.21, 0.44), ("v7 high", 0.62, 0.55), ("v8 low", 0.30, 0.52), ("v8 medium", 0.71, 0.61),           ("v8 high", 1.45, 0.64), ("v8 high x3 + verify", 4.10, 0.71), ("v7 high x3 + verify", 1.90, 0.60)]for p in frontier(configs):    print(p)
Going deeper2 points
  • Cost per solved task, not per attempt: a cheap configuration that fails often can cost more per solved task than an expensive one.
  • Wall time matters too: for interactive products, a configuration that takes 20 minutes is wrong even if it's cheap. The frontier can be drawn against wall time the same way.

Uncertainty and comparisons

Scenario. A release review celebrated a 3-point gain on the long-horizon slice. The slice had 90 tasks from 11 families; a rerun with new seeds showed a 1-point loss.

What the picture shows. How every reported difference gets an honest interval.

1Paired comparisons
both models run on the same tasks, so the per-task difference removes most of the variation between tasks.
2Clustered by family
tasks from the same family succeed and fail together. The bootstrap resamples whole families, which widens intervals to their true size.
3Minimum detectable difference
each slice has a stated MDD, the smallest difference it can reliably detect. The full suite's MDD is about 2 points; the 90-task long-horizon slice's is about 5. A difference smaller than the MDD is reported as "no detectable change".
4The example below
with no true difference, the 90-task slice can still show +3.6 points; its family-clustered interval runs from −0.2 to +7.3, so the honest report is "no detectable change".
5Seeds
at least 3 attempts per task in comparisons, so a single unlucky sample doesn't decide a task.

The code. A family-clustered, paired bootstrap interval for the difference between two models (Python, NumPy).

import numpy as np def paired_cluster_ci(families: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, n_boot: int = 4000, seed: int = 0) -> tuple[float, float, float]:    """a, b: per-task success rates (mean over attempts) for two models; families: family id per task."""    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)    ids = np.unique(families)    diffs = {f: (b[families == f] - a[families == f]) for f in ids}    est = float(np.mean(b - a))    boots = []    for _ in range(n_boot):        pick = rng.choice(ids, size=len(ids), replace=True)                  # resample whole families        d = np.concatenate([diffs[f] for f in pick])        boots.append(d.mean())    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])    return round(est, 3), round(float(lo), 3), round(float(hi), 3) rng = np.random.default_rng(4)fam = np.repeat(np.arange(11), 9)[:90]base = np.clip(rng.normal(0.3, 0.2, 11)[fam] + rng.normal(0, 0.1, 90), 0, 1)fam_effect = rng.normal(0.0, 0.08, 11)[fam]           # no true difference on averageprint(paired_cluster_ci(fam, base, np.clip(base + fam_effect + rng.normal(0, 0.08, 90), 0, 1)))
Going deeper2 points
  • Many slices, many false alarms: a profile with 20 slices will show one "significant" change by chance in most releases. Reviews treat single-slice changes as hypotheses to confirm with more tasks or seeds.
  • Spend tasks where decisions are: the slices that drive release decisions get more tasks, so their MDD is small enough to matter.

Validity: do the scores predict production?

Scenario. The framework existed for a reason: v8's benchmark gain didn't predict production. A new framework that also didn't predict production would be no better, only more expensive.

What the picture shows. Every release, the framework is checked against what happened in production.

1Production outcomes
for each product, outcomes agreed with the product team: accepted changes without rework, escalations, sessions abandoned, tasks completed by automation without a retry (Design 16).
2Correlation across versions
each axis score and the public benchmarks are compared with production outcomes across the last eight model versions. For the coding agent, the public benchmark correlated at r = 0.35 with accepted changes; the horizon-weighted realistic suite correlated at 0.86.
3Weights per product
each product gets a summary score that weights axis levels by how often they occur in its traffic. It's a weighted profile, not a new benchmark.
4Saturation and refresh
when a slice exceeds 85% for the best model, it stops discriminating. New, harder tasks are sourced for that level, and saturated tasks move to a regression suite.
5Contamination monitoring
canary strings are searched for in training data before every run; a hit retires the task family.
Going deeper2 points
  • Eight versions is a small sample: the correlations are evidence, not proof. They're reported with intervals and rechecked as versions accumulate.
  • Disagreement is the useful case: when the framework says a model improved and production says it didn't, either the tasks miss what users do or production metrics are confounded by product changes. Both have happened; both are worth finding.

Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

Rollout.

  • Phase 1, axes and first tasks (weeks 1–6): the axis catalog, the task admission pipeline, 300 tasks from internal tickets with human baselines and tested verifiers, run on the existing platform.
  • Phase 2, grading and reliability (weeks 5–10): rubric graders with the human panel, pass@k and pass^k, perturbation sets, clustered intervals and MDDs in every report.
  • Phase 3, realism (weeks 9–16): simulated users and multi-party tasks, fault injection, cost frontiers, the time horizon metric, 1,200 tasks from 140 families.
  • Phase 4, validity and governance (weeks 14–20): production outcome joins, per-product weights, refresh and retirement schedules, contamination checks before training runs, release reviews based on profiles.

Trade-offs we accepted.

  • Private tasks can't be compared with other labs: we keep reporting public benchmarks for that, but we don't use them for release decisions.
  • Human baselines are expensive: about two expert-hours per task-hour, which is why tasks are added gradually and retired slowly.
  • Model graders bring their own bias: kept in check by the human panel and agreement thresholds, not eliminated.
  • Realistic tasks are slow: the full suite takes most of a day. Training-time checks use a stratified 200-task subset.

Open questions.

  • Days-long tasks: a single attempt at a multi-day task can cost more than the rest of the suite combined. Can milestone grading on shorter segments stand in for full runs?
  • Capabilities without a product yet: realism comes from real work. How do we measure capabilities that no product uses yet?
  • Shared tasks across labs: could a private, rotating, jointly held task pool give realistic comparisons without leaking?
  • Measuring judgment: knowing when to stop, escalate or refuse is part of capability. Can it get its own axis without becoming a style preference?
Design 33 · 12 sections

Design 33: Continuous eval pipelines and fast regression detection

  1. The use case and requirements
  2. An event-driven pipeline
  3. Tiers: cheap signal first
  4. Running only what a change can affect
  5. Deciding early: sequential tests
  6. Baselines, noise and flaky items
  7. Slow drifts across checkpoints
  8. Triage: what changed, and which change did it
  9. Alerts people trust
  10. Running continuously on Kubernetes
  11. Testing the detector
  12. Rollout plan, trade-offs and open questions

This design answers one question: when something changes, a checkpoint, a serving image, a chat template, a grader, how quickly do we learn whether it made the model worse, and how much can we trust that signal? Design 15 built the evaluation platform and a nightly benchmark gate; Design 32 defined what to measure. Both assume someone runs the evaluations and reads the results. Here the evaluations run themselves: every change triggers the right evaluations in the right order, cheap ones first, and the system decides as early as the evidence allows, says what changed, and pages someone only when it's sure.

The short version: trigger on every change, run in tiers, stop as soon as the evidence is clear, and treat alert precision as a product requirement. Events from training, serving and the evaluation code start a pipeline that picks evaluations based on what changed and reuses stored outputs where it can. A 6-minute smoke tier catches breakages, a 40-minute fast tier catches material regressions with a sequential test that stops early, and the full realistic suite runs on the checkpoints that matter. Noise is measured, not assumed: repeated runs of the same model calibrate thresholds and expose flaky items. Slow drifts across checkpoints are caught by trend detection. Every alert carries the lineage diff and, when several things changed, an automatic bisection. The detector itself is tested every week with deliberately broken models.

The use case and requirements

Scenario. A serving image update changed the chat template for parallel tool calls. In 7% of multi-tool requests, the model's tool calls no longer parsed. The nightly full suite started at 20:00 and finished at 16:00 the next day; its one tool-use slice dropped by 2 points, which was inside its threshold. The problem was found three days later through customer tickets, after two training checkpoints had been evaluated with the broken template and a canary deployment had shipped on it. Meanwhile the evaluation channel received about 40 alerts a week. Six of them, on average, were real, and people had stopped reading them.

What the system must deliver.

  • Every change evaluated: about 72 checkpoints a day from six training runs, 15 serving changes, and a handful of grader, environment and prompt changes.
  • Time to signal: breakages (anything that drops a gated slice by 5 points or more) detected within 15 minutes of the change; regressions of 2–3 points on gated slices within 2 hours.
  • Trustworthy alerts: at most one false alert per team per week; at least 80% of alerts real.
  • Actionable alerts: every alert says what changed, shows failing examples, and names a likely owner.
  • Slow drifts caught: declines spread over many checkpoints, each too small to alarm on its own, are detected.
  • Bounded cost: a fixed GPU budget per day, with the cheapest evaluations always available.
  • A tested detector: known regressions injected regularly, and missed regressions ("escapes") reviewed like incidents.

Out of scope: what the suites contain (Design 32), the harness and results store (Design 15), and release decisions, which consume these signals (Design 11).

An event-driven pipeline

Scenario. Evaluations ran on a nightly schedule. A change made at 21:00 waited 23 hours to be evaluated, and four changes merged the same day landed in one run with no way to tell them apart.

What the picture shows. Changes become events, events become evaluation plans, plans become workflows.

1Sources
the trainer emits an event when a checkpoint is written (Design 31 lineage), CI emits one when a serving image or config is merged, and the evaluation repository emits one when a grader, environment or suite changes.
2One event schema
every event names the component that changed, its old and new digests, and the model it applies to.
3Planner
turns an event into a plan: which tiers, which slices, against which baseline, and whether stored outputs can be reused.
4Workflows
each plan runs as a workflow: smoke, then fast if smoke passes, then full if the change qualifies. A failing tier stops the rest and alerts immediately.
5Results and decisions
results go to the results store; the detector writes a decision (pass, regression, undecided) with its evidence, which gates promotion and drives alerts.

The YAML. The tiered workflow as an Argo Workflows template: later tiers run only when earlier ones pass.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1kind: WorkflowTemplatemetadata: { name: eval-tiers, namespace: evals }spec:  entrypoint: tiers  arguments:    parameters:    - { name: candidate }          # model + serving digests under test    - { name: baseline }    - { name: plan }               # from the planner: tiers, slices, reuse  templates:  - name: tiers    dag:      tasks:      - name: smoke        template: run-tier        arguments: { parameters: [{ name: tier, value: smoke }] }      - name: fast        template: run-tier        dependencies: [smoke]        when: "'{{tasks.smoke.outputs.parameters.decision}}' == 'pass'"        arguments: { parameters: [{ name: tier, value: fast }] }      - name: full        template: run-tier        dependencies: [fast]        when: "'{{tasks.fast.outputs.parameters.decision}}' == 'pass' && '{{workflow.parameters.plan}}' =~ 'full'"        arguments: { parameters: [{ name: tier, value: full }] }  - name: run-tier    inputs: { parameters: [{ name: tier }] }    outputs:      parameters:      - name: decision        valueFrom: { path: /out/decision }     # pass | regression | undecided    container:      image: registry.example.com/eval-runner:2026.11      args: ["--tier={{inputs.parameters.tier}}", "--candidate={{workflow.parameters.candidate}}",             "--baseline={{workflow.parameters.baseline}}", "--plan={{workflow.parameters.plan}}"]
Going deeper2 points
  • One change per evaluation: the planner evaluates each change against a baseline that differs only in that change, whenever it can. When it can't (two merges in quick succession), the alert says so and bisection takes over.
  • Events beat schedules for latency, schedules beat events for coverage: the nightly run stays, against fixed reference models, to catch what no event announces (an upstream API, a dataset mirror, the cluster itself).

Tiers: cheap signal first

Scenario. The tool-call breakage would have been visible in 300 requests. The only evaluation that included tool calls was a 20-hour suite.

What the picture shows. Three tiers with different jobs.

1Smoke (≈6 minutes, 300 items)
format and parsing (tool calls, JSON, chat template round-trips), refusals on clearly safe prompts, a few dozen short tasks per major capability. Runs on always-warm replicas. Catches breakages.
2Fast (≈40 minutes, 2,400 items)
a stratified sample of the gated slices from the realistic suite: enough items per slice to detect a 3-point regression with the sequential test. Catches material regressions.
3Full (≈18 hours)
the realistic suite with attempts per task (Design 32). Runs on release candidates, the latest checkpoint of each run every 12 hours, and anything the fast tier flags as undecided.
4Promotion gates read tiers
a serving change can reach the canary pool after smoke and fast; a model release needs full.

The code. Building the fast tier: a stratified sample with a minimum per gated slice, refreshed weekly (Python).

import random def fast_tier(items: list[dict], gated: dict[str, int], total: int, seed: int) -> list[dict]:    """items: {"id", "slice"}; gated: slice -> minimum items. Fills the rest proportionally."""    rng = random.Random(seed)    by_slice: dict[str, list[dict]] = {}    for it in items:        by_slice.setdefault(it["slice"], []).append(it)    chosen = []    for s, n in gated.items():        chosen += rng.sample(by_slice[s], min(n, len(by_slice[s])))    taken = {it["id"] for it in chosen}    rest = [it for it in items if it["id"] not in taken]    chosen += rng.sample(rest, max(0, total - len(chosen)))    return chosen items = [{"id": i, "slice": s} for i, s in enumerate(["tool-use"] * 900 + ["coding-short"] * 6000 + ["long-horizon"] * 400 + ["chat"] * 8000)]tier = fast_tier(items, {"tool-use": 600, "long-horizon": 300}, total=2400, seed=47)from collections import Counterprint(Counter(it["slice"] for it in tier))
Going deeper2 points
  • Smoke tests check plumbing, not only quality: the tool-call breakage was a parsing failure, not a capability drop. Smoke items include round-trip checks of every output format the product parses.
  • Rotate the fast sample: a fixed sample invites tuning to it. The sample is redrawn weekly with a recorded seed, so results stay reproducible.

Running only what a change can affect

Scenario. A one-line grader fix triggered a full rerun of every suite on four models: 9,000 GPU-hours, two days of queue, and no model had changed.

What the picture shows. The planner maps the kind of change to the work it requires.

1New checkpoint
inference on smoke and fast; full on schedule.
2Serving change
(image, template, sampling, quantization): smoke and fast on the production model, plus serving benchmarks (Design 22). The model is the same, so differences are the serving change.
3Grader or rubric change
no new inference. Stored outputs are re-graded with old and new graders, so the change's effect on scores is measured directly.
4Environment or task change
only the affected tasks rerun, on the current production model and the latest candidate.
5Output cache
model outputs are stored keyed by model digest, serving digest, item and sampling seed. Re-grading 2.1 million stored outputs takes about 50 minutes and no policy inference.

The code. The planner's mapping from change to plan (Python).

PLANS = {    "checkpoint":  {"inference": True,  "tiers": ["smoke", "fast"], "baseline": "parent-checkpoint"},    "serving":     {"inference": True,  "tiers": ["smoke", "fast", "serving-bench"], "baseline": "production-serving"},    "grader":      {"inference": False, "tiers": ["regrade-cached"], "baseline": "previous-grader"},    "environment": {"inference": True,  "tiers": ["affected-tasks"], "baseline": "previous-environment"},    "prompt":      {"inference": True,  "tiers": ["smoke", "fast"], "baseline": "previous-prompt"},} def plan(event: dict) -> dict:    p = dict(PLANS[event["component"]])    if event["component"] == "checkpoint" and event.get("release_candidate"):        p["tiers"] = p["tiers"] + ["full"]    if event["component"] == "environment":        p["tasks"] = event["affected_tasks"]    p["candidate"], p["changed"] = event["new"], event["component"]    return p print(plan({"component": "grader", "new": "grader@sha256:5d1e"}))print(plan({"component": "checkpoint", "new": "ckpt@sha256:9a07", "release_candidate": True}))
Going deeper2 points
  • Caching needs exact keys: a cached output is reused only if the model, serving stack, prompt, item and sampling settings all match. Anything less hides serving regressions behind old outputs.
  • Grader changes need their own baseline: after a grader change, every historical score is on the old scale. The re-grade produces a bridge (old vs new grader on the same outputs) so trends stay continuous.

Deciding early: sequential tests

Scenario. The fast tier ran all 2,400 items before deciding, even when the first 300 already showed a model that had collapsed. Severe regressions took as long to report as subtle ones.

What the picture shows. Items run in random order, and the decision is updated as results arrive.

1Paired items
candidate and baseline answer the same items. Items where both succeed or both fail carry no information about which is better; only disagreements do.
2The test
among disagreements, if the candidate is no worse, it wins about half; if it's materially worse, it wins fewer (here 40% or less, about a 2.4-point drop when 12% of items disagree). A sequential probability ratio test adds evidence after each disagreement and stops when either hypothesis is clearly favored.
3Error rates set in advance
at most 1% false alarms, at most 10% misses for a regression of the target size.
4The result
a severe break (the candidate wins 20% of disagreements) is decided after a median of about 370 items, roughly 6 minutes into the fast tier. A clean candidate is usually cleared after about 690 items. A borderline regression may need the full 2,400 or end undecided, which sends it to the full tier.

The code. A sequential test on disagreements, with a simulation of three cases (Python).

import math, randomfrom collections import Counter def sprt(pairs, delta: float = 0.10, alpha: float = 0.01, beta: float = 0.10) -> tuple[str, int]:    """pairs: (baseline_ok, candidate_ok) per item in random order.    H0: candidate wins half of the disagreements. H1: it wins 0.5 - delta."""    p0, p1 = 0.5, 0.5 - delta    upper, lower = math.log((1 - beta) / alpha), math.log(beta / (1 - alpha))    llr, n = 0.0, 0    for n, (b, c) in enumerate(pairs, 1):        if b == c:            continue        win = c and not b        llr += math.log((p1 if win else 1 - p1) / (p0 if win else 1 - p0))        if llr >= upper:            return "regression", n        if llr <= lower:            return "pass", n    return "undecided", n def simulate(win: float, disagree: float = 0.12, items: int = 2400, seed: int = 0):    rng = random.Random(seed)    for _ in range(items):        if rng.random() < disagree:            c = rng.random() < win            yield (not c, c)        else:            b = rng.random() < 0.7            yield (b, b) for win in (0.5, 0.4, 0.2):                       # no change, ~2.4-point drop, severe break    runs = [sprt(simulate(win, seed=s)) for s in range(500)]    print(win, dict(Counter(d for d, _ in runs)), "median items:", sorted(n for _, n in runs)[250])
Going deeper2 points
  • Peeking is allowed by design: checking a fixed-sample test after every batch inflates false alarms badly. The sequential test is built for continuous checking, which is why its error rates hold.
  • Undecided is an answer: a regression too small for the fast tier to settle goes to the full suite. The system reports "undecided, escalated", not "pass".

Baselines, noise and flaky items

Scenario. The tool-use slice's threshold was 3 points, chosen by hand. Ten identical runs of the production model on its 250 items spread over 3.2 points from noise alone, and almost all of that came from 27 items whose outcome flipped between identical runs.

What the picture shows. Noise measured from the system itself, every night.

1A/A runs
the production model is evaluated several times a night with the same configuration. The spread of its scores is the noise each slice really has.
2Flaky items
items whose outcome flips between identical runs, because of nondeterministic environments, timeouts, or a grader on the boundary. Items above a flip-rate threshold are quarantined and sent to their owners to fix.
3Thresholds from data
each slice's alert threshold and sequential-test settings come from its measured noise, recomputed weekly.
4Baselines by change type
a checkpoint is compared with its parent; a serving change with the production serving stack on the same model; a release candidate with the production model.

The code. Finding flaky items from repeated identical runs (Python, NumPy).

import numpy as np def flaky_items(runs: np.ndarray, max_flip: float = 0.15) -> tuple[np.ndarray, float]:    """runs: repeats x items (1 = pass) for the same model and config.    Returns flaky item indices and the run-to-run SD of the slice score in points."""    p = runs.mean(axis=0)    flip = 2 * p * (1 - p)                       # chance two identical runs disagree on the item    return np.where(flip > max_flip)[0], float(runs.mean(axis=1).std(ddof=1) * 100) rng = np.random.default_rng(0)n = 250                                          # one slice; ~8% of its items are flakyp = np.where(rng.random(n) < 0.08, rng.uniform(0.3, 0.7, n), np.where(rng.random(n) < 0.7, 0.998, 0.002))runs = (rng.random((10, n)) < p).astype(float)bad, sd = flaky_items(runs)keep = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), bad)scores = runs.mean(axis=1) * 100print("flaky:", len(bad), "sd:", round(sd, 2), "spread:", round(float(scores.max() - scores.min()), 1),      "sd without flaky:", round(float(runs[:, keep].mean(axis=1).std(ddof=1) * 100), 2))
Going deeper2 points
  • Quarantine, don't delete: a flaky item often points at a real problem (a race in an environment, a grader that can't decide). It leaves the gated set until fixed, and its owner gets a ticket.
  • Noise changes: a new environment version or grader can make a stable slice noisy overnight. Thresholds are recomputed from recent A/A runs, and a jump in noise alerts the slice owner.

Slow drifts across checkpoints

Scenario. A training run's coding score fell by 0.4 points per checkpoint for ten checkpoints. Each checkpoint was compared with its parent and was within noise. Four points were gone before anyone plotted the series.

What the picture shows. Each run's gated slices tracked as a series against a fixed reference model.

1Fixed reference
comparing each checkpoint only with its parent hides drift. Every checkpoint is also scored against the production model on the same items.
2CUSUM
a cumulative sum of how far each checkpoint falls below the reference, minus an allowance for noise. Small consistent declines add up; random ups and downs cancel.
3The example
with a decline of 0.4 points per checkpoint and noise of 0.8, CUSUM alarms at the third declining checkpoint. A fixed 3-point threshold waits until the seventh.
4Sent to the run's owner
drift alerts go to the training run's on-call with the mixture changes in the window (Design 31).

The code. CUSUM on the gap to the reference model (Python, NumPy).

import numpy as np def cusum_alarm(gap: np.ndarray, sd: float, k: float = 0.5, h: float = 4.0) -> int | None:    """gap: candidate minus reference, in points, per checkpoint. Returns the first alarming index."""    s = 0.0    for i, g in enumerate(gap):        s = max(0.0, s + (-g / sd) - k)        if s > h:            return i    return None rng = np.random.default_rng(3)gap = np.r_[rng.normal(0, 0.8, 6), -0.4 * np.arange(1, 15) + rng.normal(0, 0.8, 14)]   # drift starts at index 6fixed = next((i for i, g in enumerate(gap) if g < -3.0), None)print("cusum:", cusum_alarm(gap, 0.8), "fixed threshold:", fixed)
Going deeper2 points
  • Reset after action: once a drift alert is acknowledged and explained (an intended trade-off, or a fix), the sum resets so the same drift doesn't alert again.
  • Not every decline is a bug: a run that trades a little short-task accuracy for long-horizon capability will drift on some slices by design. The alert asks the owner to confirm it.

Triage: what changed, and which change did it

Scenario. When the tool-call regression was finally found, the serving image update had bundled four changes: a new vLLM version, the chat template, a sampling default and a tokenizer patch. It took a day to work out which one was responsible.

What the picture shows. Every alert arrives triaged.

1The lineage diff
model, serving image, template, tokenizer, sampling, grader and environment digests for candidate and baseline, with only the differences shown.
2Effect with uncertainty
the slice, the estimated drop and its interval, and the test that decided it.
3Failing examples
items that passed on the baseline and failed on the candidate, with both outputs side by side and the grader's reason.
4Automatic bisection
when the diff has several changes that can be applied separately, smoke runs on intermediate configurations find the first bad one. Four changes need two smoke runs in sequence, or three in parallel (one per intermediate configuration), which finish within one smoke interval.
5Owner
taken from the change that bisection points to, or from the slice owner when it can't be split.

The code. Binary search over an ordered list of changes using smoke runs (Python).

def bisect_changes(changes: list[str], is_bad) -> tuple[str, int]:    """changes: ordered, independently applicable changes from baseline to candidate.    is_bad(k): run smoke with the first k changes applied; True if it regresses."""    lo, hi, runs = 0, len(changes), 0          # invariant: first lo changes good, first hi bad    while hi - lo > 1:        mid = (lo + hi) // 2        runs += 1        if is_bad(mid):            hi = mid        else:            lo = mid    return changes[hi - 1], runs changes = ["vllm 0.11 → 0.12", "chat template: parallel tool calls", "sampling default top_p 0.95", "tokenizer patch"]culprit = 2                                     # applying change #2 breaks tool parsingprint(bisect_changes(changes, lambda k: k >= culprit))
Going deeper2 points
  • Bisect needs separable changes: a serving image built as one blob can't be split. Images are built from pinned, separately versioned components so the planner can apply them one at a time.
  • Show the outputs: engineers trust an alert that shows a broken tool call next to a working one far more than one that shows a number.

Alerts people trust

Scenario. Forty alerts a week, six real. The tool-call alert, when the smoke tier finally caught a similar issue later, sat unread for two hours in a channel everyone had muted.

What the picture shows. Alerts with severities, owners and a noise budget.

1Severities
page for decided breakages on gated slices (smoke or fast tier); ticket for decided regressions below breakage size and for drift; digest for undecided results and non-gated slices, summarized once a day.
2One alert per cause
results that share a lineage diff are grouped, so one bad template doesn't send 14 alerts for 14 slices.
3Pipeline health is alertable too
no smoke result for 30 minutes means the system is blind, which is as serious as a regression.
4Precision is tracked
each alert is marked real or false when closed. Teams have a noise budget (at most one false page a week); slices that exceed it get their thresholds reviewed.
5The result
about four alerts a week, 85% real.

The YAML. Alert rules over the detector's exported decisions (Prometheus Operator).

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1kind: PrometheusRulemetadata: { name: eval-regressions, namespace: evals }spec:  groups:  - name: eval-decisions    rules:    - alert: EvalBreakage      # 1 when the sequential test decided "regression" with effect >= 5 points on a gated slice      expr: max by (slice, candidate, change) (eval_decision_regression{tier=~"smoke|fast", gated="true", size="breakage"}) == 1      labels: { severity: page }      annotations:        summary: "{{ $labels.slice }} broke on {{ $labels.candidate }} (change: {{ $labels.change }})"    - alert: EvalRegression      expr: max by (slice, candidate, change) (eval_decision_regression{gated="true", size="material"}) == 1      for: 10m      labels: { severity: ticket }    - alert: EvalPipelineBlind      expr: time() - max by (pipeline) (eval_last_decision_timestamp_seconds{tier="smoke"}) > 1800      for: 5m      labels: { severity: page }    - alert: EvalCanaryMissed      # a deliberately broken model was injected in the last 2h and no breakage was decided for it      expr: |        max by (pipeline) (max_over_time(eval_canary_injected[2h])) == 1        unless on (pipeline) max by (pipeline) (max_over_time(eval_canary_detected[2h])) == 1      for: 15m      labels: { severity: ticket }
Going deeper2 points
  • Paging thresholds are about cost, not statistics: a 5-point drop on a gated slice is worth waking someone because it can reach users within hours. Smaller decided regressions are tickets for working hours.
  • Digests are where weak signals live: undecided results and non-gated slices go into a daily summary that slice owners read. They still matter; they just don't interrupt anyone.

Running continuously on Kubernetes

Scenario. The evaluation queue shared GPUs with research jobs. On busy days, smoke runs waited 90 minutes for capacity, which made them as slow as the fast tier.

What the picture shows. Capacity and scheduling built around time to signal.

1Warm replicas for smoke
a small, always-on serving pool per model family runs smoke within seconds of an event. New checkpoints load onto it with fast model loading (Design 20).
2Priorities
smoke above fast, fast above full, full above backfill, all through Kueue with a guaranteed share for smoke and fast (Design 17).
3Coalescing
when checkpoints arrive faster than the full tier can evaluate them, it runs on the newest and on every fourth one; smoke and fast still run on every checkpoint.
4Daily budget
about 2,400 GPU-hours a day, tracked per tier; backfill (re-grading, A/A runs, reference series) uses what's left.
5Results first, logs later
decisions are written as soon as a tier decides; full transcripts and traces upload in the background.

The code. Coalescing the queue of checkpoints waiting for the full tier (Python).

def coalesce(pending: list[dict], every: int = 4) -> tuple[list[dict], list[dict]]:    """pending: checkpoints waiting for the full tier, oldest first, each {"run", "step"}.    Keep the newest per run and every `every`-th step; skip the rest (smoke + fast already ran)."""    keep, skip = [], []    newest = {}    for c in pending:        newest[c["run"]] = max(newest.get(c["run"], -1), c["step"])    for c in pending:        if c["step"] == newest[c["run"]] or (c["step"] // 2000) % every == 0:            keep.append(c)        else:            skip.append(c)    return keep, skip pending = [{"run": "rl-v9", "step": s} for s in range(26000, 40001, 2000)] + [{"run": "rl-v9-long", "step": s} for s in (12000, 14000)]keep, skip = coalesce(pending)print([f'{c["run"]}@{c["step"]}' for c in keep], len(skip), "skipped")
Going deeper2 points
  • Warm capacity is the price of fast signal: the smoke pool sits partly idle most of the day. That's 64 GPUs reserved to turn a 90-minute wait into seconds, which is cheap next to three days of shipping a broken template.
  • Skipped is recorded: a checkpoint that skipped the full tier is marked as such. Release candidates never skip.

Testing the detector

Scenario. After the fixes, the team assumed regressions would be caught. Nobody had checked. When they did, by evaluating a checkpoint with a known 4-point drop on one slice, the fast tier's sampling for that slice turned out to have 60 items, far too few to detect it.

What the picture shows. The pipeline is tested the way it tests models.

1Canary regressions
every week, a deliberately degraded model is injected as if it were a new checkpoint: a known bug in the chat template, a slice-specific drop made by fine-tuning on wrong answers, a sampling bug. The pipeline must decide "regression" within its SLO.
2Escapes
